headline: Educated but unemployed: Inside India's broken jobs market and why the 'cockroaches' are fed up
full_text:
Educated but unemployed: Inside India's broken jobs market and why the 'cockroaches' are fed up
Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 02, 2026, 21:05 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India's un-employment crisis and helplessness of modern life. (Representative image)
Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis transformed an ordinary man into a giant insect to explore alienation, helplessness and the dehumanising pressures of modern life.More than a century later, India's self-styled Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has adopted a similarly unsettling symbol, not to tell a work of fiction, but to express the frustrations of a generation increasingly unsure whether years of education, expensive coaching and relentless competition will ever translate into a stable job.What began as a social media sensation with a strong and straightforward satirical structure, quickly evolved into one of the country's biggest youth-led movements in recent years.Calling itself the "voice of the lazy and unemployed," the movement grew from memes mocking joblessness, paper leaks, inflation and the political establishment into street protests.The protest may have become a trigger for a generation already grappling with shrinking employment opportunities, rising educational costs and growing uncertainty about the future.And at its heart lies a simple question. What happens when an economy produces millions of graduates every year but fails to create enough quality jobs?According to veteran economist Arun Kumar, a retired professor at JNU, "This unemployment crisis has created a huge gap between expectations and reality.""Young people earn degrees believing they will secure good jobs, but when those jobs do not materialise, they continue preparing for competitive examinations year after year. Many take these exams four, five or even six times because they still hope to secure an organised sector job.
Their parents also encourage them because they know such jobs offer stable salaries and social security," he said."But the increasing privatisation of education has intensified competition. Coaching institutes want to showcase high success rates because that is their biggest selling point. That creates incentives for unethical practices, including paper leaks. The greater the privatisation, the greater the pressure to resort to illegal methods to ensure students succeed. Fake degrees, cheating and question paper leaks are all symptoms of a much deeper problem. They are linked to unemployment and the shortage of quality jobs in the organised sector," he added.
India's employment challenge
India has spent decades expanding access to higher education. Universities have multiplied, enrollment has surged and millions of families have invested heavily in degrees, viewing education as the surest path to upward mobility.The numbers tell a remarkable story. According to the State of Working India 2026 report by Azim Premji University, the number of young graduates in India increased nearly 13-fold, rising from around 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023.But while the supply of graduates has grown rapidly, employment opportunities have not kept pace.The report estimates that graduate unemployment among people below the age of 25 is now close to 40%, while graduates accounted for nearly two-thirds of India's unemployed population in 2023.Even more striking is the rise in the number of unemployed graduates, which has increased from less than one million in 1983 to around 11 million in 2023, a 16-fold increase over four decades.The mismatch between education and employment has widened steadily since the mid-2000s as higher education expanded much faster than the creation of quality jobs. For millions of families, earning a college degree no longer guarantees stable employment or financial security.Recent government data suggest that the challenge is becoming even more severe.According to the government's flagship Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 rose to 16.2% in June, the highest level recorded since monthly estimates became available in April 2025. At that time, youth unemployment stood at 13.8%.The ministry of statistics and programme implementation (MoSPI) has cautioned that monthly figures may fluctuate because of seasonal factors, academic cycles and the increased frequency of surveys. Even so, the latest numbers are significant because they fit into a broader pattern rather than representing an isolated spike. Youth unemployment has increased across all six categories tracked by the survey, urban and rural areas, men and women alike, during the 15 months for which monthly data are available.At the same time, the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) among young people has declined from 42.7% to 40.3%. In simple terms, fewer young people are actively looking for work.Ordinarily, such a decline would be expected to reduce unemployment because fewer people are participating in the labour market. Instead, unemployment has continued to rise, suggesting that the economy is not generating enough opportunities even for the shrinking pool of job seekers.Annual PLFS data reinforce the same trend. Between 2022 and 2025, youth unemployment increased in 13 states and Union Territories, including Andhra Pradesh, Delhi, Telangana and West Bengal.The situation appears even more challenging for young women, with unemployment rising across 16 states and Union Territories during the same period.Taken together, the figures suggest that youth unemployment is becoming a structural challenge rather than a temporary fluctuation.
The problem isn't just unemployment, it's job quality
Headline unemployment figures often fail to capture the deeper challenges within India's labour market. Many graduates do find work, but not necessarily the kind of work they expected after spending years in higher education.Economist Arun Kumar said that the root of the problem is the sharp divide between India's organised and unorganised sectors."When unemployment rises, it inevitably leads to greater conflict because there are too few jobs for too many people. In India, this problem is even more pronounced because the unorganised sector employs around 94% of the workforce, while the organised sector employs only about 6%. The difference in wages and job security between these two sectors is enormous. A courier delivery worker may earn around Rs 10,000-12,000 a month, whereas a postman can earn around Rs 70,000. Naturally, nobody wants to lose an organised sector job, and everyone wants to secure one. That intense competition creates immense pressure," he added.
An analysis of India's Periodic Labour Force Survey illustrates this disconnect. Out of every 100 graduates aged between 15 and 29, only 50 are employed, 15 remain unemployed while actively searching for work, and the remaining 35 are outside the labour force altogether.Some continue their education. Others perform unpaid domestic work or have simply stopped looking for employment after repeated disappointments.Even among those who are employed, the quality of jobs remains a major concern. Only 26 out of every 100 graduates have regular salaried jobs. More strikingly, just four hold formal jobs that provide written contracts, paid leave and social security benefits.The remaining graduates are spread across self-employment, unpaid family work, casual labour and small household enterprises. Many earn irregular incomes and lack job security despite years spent pursuing higher education.The figures highlight a growing reality in India's labour market: employment alone is no longer an adequate measure of economic well-being. The challenge is increasingly about the availability of secure, productive and reasonably paid jobs.
Why educated youth feel left behind
The employment crisis begins long before students enter the labour market. Competition for limited seats in prestigious colleges has transformed education itself into an expensive investment.Government survey data show that Indian households now spend a significantly larger share of their education budgets on private coaching than they did seven years ago.The sharpest increase has been among higher secondary students preparing for engineering, medical and university entrance examinations.Families now spend nearly one-fourth of their higher secondary education budgets on coaching, compared with about 18% in 2018.Private coaching expenses have also increased steadily across primary, middle and secondary education, reflecting a growing belief that classroom teaching alone is no longer sufficient to compete in high-stakes entrance examinations.The pressure becomes particularly visible in engineering education. India had around 4.4 million undergraduate engineering students during the 2023-24 academic year. Yet the country's top 100 engineering institutions together offered only about 500,000 seats.
In effect, only one in nine engineering students can study at an institution widely regarded as offering strong placements and better career prospects.Students who fail to secure admission to elite institutions often graduate from colleges with weaker placement records, making it significantly harder to obtain well-paying jobs.The widening gap between educational aspirations and employment outcomes has created growing frustration among young people. The traditional promise that more education automatically leads to better employment is becoming increasingly uncertain.According to the State of Working India 2026 report, fewer than 7% of male graduates secure a permanent salaried job within one year of graduating. The figure is even lower, just 3.7%, when it comes to white-collar jobs.Using data from the PLFS and the earlier Employment-Unemployment Survey, the report estimates that 1.1 crore out of India's 6.3 crore graduates aged between 20 and 29 were unemployed in 2023.Graduate unemployment itself is not a new phenomenon. The report estimates that unemployment among graduates below the age of 25 increased from 35.02% in 1983 to 39.33% in 2023.What has changed, however, is the scale of the problem. India now produces far more graduates than ever before, while simultaneously entering the most important phase of its demographic transition.The country's median age currently stands at around 29 years and is expected to rise to 38 years by 2050.This is the period during which India's working-age population is expected to drive economic growth. If the economy fails to generate enough productive employment during this demographic window, the much-discussed demographic dividend could gradually turn into a demographic challenge.
India's employment paradox
India today is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. Even amid geopolitical tensions, volatile oil prices and slowing global trade, the country has continued to post robust GDP growth and position itself as a manufacturing and investment hub.The government has invested heavily in highways, airports, railways, ports and digital infrastructure. Global technology companies such as Apple have expanded manufacturing in India, electronics exports have surged and semiconductor investments are beginning to gather pace. Policymakers increasingly see manufacturing as the sector that can absorb millions of workers and turn India's demographic advantage into sustained economic growth.Yet for many young Indians entering the labour market, this optimism feels distant. The central contradiction facing the Indian economy is that rapid economic growth has not translated into an equivalent expansion in quality employment. Economists often describe this phenomenon as "jobless growth", an economy that continues to grow without creating enough secure and productive jobs.India's challenge is especially daunting because nearly eight million graduates enter the labour market every year. Generating employment for such a large number of educated young people has become one of the country's biggest economic challenges.This gap between economic growth and employment opportunities lies at the heart of the frustration that has fuelled recent youth protests.
Is India creating enough jobs?
Whether India is creating enough jobs depends largely on which dataset is examined. The Reserve Bank of India's KLEMS database estimated that the economy generated 4.7 crore jobs during 2023-24, the highest annual increase in more than four decades.However, labour economists caution against looking at headline employment numbers alone.Employment estimates differ across official surveys because they use different methodologies. More importantly, the definition of employment itself often masks the underlying quality of jobs being created.For instance, India's labour surveys classify a person as employed if they have worked even for a few days during the reference period. Likewise, unpaid family workers and subsistence self-employed individuals are counted as employed despite earning little or no regular income.As a result, headline employment figures may paint a healthier picture than what many young workers experience in reality. Increasingly, economists argue that the more important question is no longer how many jobs India is creating, but what kind of jobs they are.
The informal sector is slowing too
For decades, India's informal economy acted as a safety valve for the labour market. Workers unable to secure formal employment often found opportunities in small businesses, family enterprises, retail trade or self-employment.However, even this safety net appears to be weakening.According to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation's latest Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), the informal sector generated around 74.5 lakh jobs in 2025, significantly lower than the 1.1 crore jobs created during the previous survey period ending September 2024.Wage growth has also slowed sharply. Average wage growth in the sector declined to 3.9%, compared with 13% previously, suggesting that even workers who manage to find employment are seeing slower improvements in earnings.The figures reinforce concerns that employment opportunities are weakening across both formal and informal sectors, making it increasingly difficult for young people to find stable livelihoods.
India's employment quality lags behind peers
India's labour market also differs from many comparable economies because of the quality of employment available.International comparisons reveal another structural weakness: the quality of employment. Labour market studies show that around 93% of employed workers in Russia hold regular jobs. The share is about 68% in Brazil, 54% in China and 42% in Bangladesh, the PLFS 2022-23 & Jan-Mar 2024 data reported.In India, by contrast, only about 23% of workers are in regular salaried employment.This means that nearly three-fourths of Indian workers remain outside the formal sector, without written contracts, paid leave, provident fund benefits or social security.The shortage of secure employment also explains the extraordinary demand for government jobs. Whether it is railways, banking, the armed forces, civil services or state recruitment examinations, millions of candidates compete for relatively few vacancies because government employment still offers something much of the private sector cannot consistently provide stability.A government job often brings predictable salaries, pensions, housing allowances, healthcare benefits and long-term security.For many young Indians, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, these jobs represent far more than employment. They represent financial stability for entire families.According to Kumar, the desperation is visible in the jobs educated Indians are willing to apply for.
The real issue is the lack of decent employment opportunities. We saw this clearly in Uttar Pradesh in 2017, when more than two lakh people applied for peon posts. Many applicants held qualifications such as PhDs, MTech, BTech, MCom and BCom degrees. When highly educated people apply for peon jobs, it shows they are unable to find work that matches their qualifications.
Arun Kumar
AI adds a new challenge
Even as India grapples with creating quality jobs, technological change is reshaping the employment landscape. A government-backed research group estimates that artificial intelligence could displace around three million managerial and coding jobs by the end of this decade.Automation is expected to reduce demand for routine white-collar work at a time when India is producing record numbers of engineering and technology graduates.Overseas opportunities are also becoming more limited. Tighter immigration policies in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia have reduced opportunities for skilled Indian professionals.For decades, migration acted as a safety valve for India's educated workforce. That pathway is becoming increasingly uncertain."Many young Indians even leave the country in search of better opportunities. Some spend lakhs of rupees to migrate, while others take illegal routes because they see very few prospects at home. In many cases, they still end up doing low-paying or menial jobs abroad. That reflects the level of desperation created by the lack of opportunities in India,"Kumar noted on the brain-drain situation in India.
India's demographic dividend at a crossroads
India possesses one of the world's youngest populations, a demographic advantage that economists have long viewed as one of the country's greatest strengths.A growing working-age population has the potential to accelerate economic growth, boost productivity and expand domestic consumption.But demographic dividends are never automatic. They depend on whether an economy can generate enough productive employment for the millions entering the labour market every year.Research suggests that India's employment intensity of growth, the ability of economic expansion to generate jobs has steadily declined over the past four decades.
When NEET became the tipping point
Against this backdrop, the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak became much more than an examination controversy. Millions of students spend months and often years preparing for the country's most competitive entrance examinations.Families invest heavily in coaching classes, relocate to education hubs and, in many cases, students take gap years in pursuit of a medical seat.When allegations emerged that the examination paper had been leaked and sold before the test, the issue struck at the heart of a system that already demanded enormous financial and emotional investment.The government cancelled the examination, handed the investigation to the Central Bureau of Investigation and ordered a re-examination.For lakhs of aspirants, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, the cancellation meant far more than repeating a test. It meant another year of uncertainty after months of preparation and considerable financial sacrifice.Some students performed worse in the re-examination. Others worried they had lost their best chance of securing admission. Reports of severe psychological stress and alleged student suicides linked to the controversy further intensified public anger.What began as protests against examination irregularities gradually evolved into a wider movement about education, unemployment and shrinking opportunities.It was in this atmosphere that the Cockroach Janta Party found resonance among young Indians. Initially known for satirical social media posts, the movement soon expanded into organised protests questioning paper leaks, unemployment, inflation and what participants described as the growing disconnect between educational aspirations and employment opportunities.The group's unusual symbol, the cockroach, captured widespread attention.The insect represented resilience, survival and invisibility, mirroring how many young people felt overlooked despite years of education and preparation. Eventually, the protests became one of the biggest youth movements witnessed in recent years.The protests exposed far more than frustration over one examination. They revealed a widening disconnect between education, employment and economic expectations.Economist Arun Kumar says unemployment extends far beyond those who are officially counted as jobless. "Youth unemployment, particularly among those aged 15 to 29, is extremely high, and the situation is especially difficult for women. There are different forms of unemployment. First, there are those actively looking for work but unable to find it. Second, there are people who are technically employed but only in low-paid, part-time or menial jobs that do not provide a decent livelihood," he said."Third, there is disguised unemployment, where people appear to be working but contribute little to productive economic activity. Finally, there are those who have stopped looking for work altogether because they have lost hope. Women are disproportionately represented in this last category. Female labour force participation in India remains much lower than in many other major economies, which means many women are no longer even counted among active job seekers," he added.Over the past few decades, India has dramatically expanded access to higher education, produced record numbers of graduates and remained one of the world's fastest-growing major economies.But the growth in quality jobs has failed to keep pace with the growing pool of educated youth. For many young Indians, securing a degree no longer guarantees a stable career or upward social mobility.
That gap between aspirations and opportunities lies at the heart of the growing frustration. For millions of students, the question is no longer just whether examinations are conducted fairly. It is whether years of education, expensive coaching, repeated attempts at competitive exams and immense financial sacrifices will eventually lead to a secure, well-paying job. Without that, the frustrations exposed by such protests are likely to persist long after the headlines fade.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

headline: The Jharkhand Police have lodged an FIR against a man for "threatening to kill" Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, an officer said on Sunday (August 2, 2026).
full_text:

While reviewing the tender process, the TTD authorities found that the existing eligibility for procurement of medicines, injections, medical and surgical consumables, in terms of the minimum annual turnover for manufacturers, authorised distributors and importers has been on the higher side. The authorities also found the criterion to be restrictive, due to which the number of participants from eligible bidders remained “limited”, thus affecting competition and efficiency.
Revised cap
The committee was reconstituted to review the criteria met on July 3 under the Chairmanship of the BIRRD Director. The committee unanimously recommended revising the eligibility criteria for the minimum average annual turnover, currently capped at ₹100 crore, to ₹25 crore for the procurement of medicines and injections, and ₹15 crore for surgical and medical consumables for the laboratories and blood bank.
The panel recommended to the TTD trust board to continue the multi-vendor procurement system, which enables procurement from the willing L2 and L3 bidders at the rates quoted by and approved for the L1 bidder. This system provides relief to the TTD in case of a supply failure by the L1. The committee’s proposals were approved by the TTD’s trust board at its meeting held on July 14.

headline: Protests over paper leaks: SC to hear on Monday pleas relating to police action
full_text:
Protests over paper leaks: SC to hear on Monday pleas relating to police action
New Delhi, The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear on Monday a batch of pleas alleging police brutality during the recent protests against irregularities in exams and the NEET paper leaks.
A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana will be hearing the pleas in which the court had indicated that it might constitute an SIT headed by a former Supreme Court judge for a probe into the allegations made by protestors, pellet gun victims and to ascertain whether the attacks on policemen were carried out by students or some "miscreants".
On July 28, the top court had restrained states from taking any coercive action against protesters and directed them to release those under 18 on the condition that none should have any criminal antecedents.
The top court had observed that a fair and independent probe in the matter was required and whosoever committed excesses, took law into their hands should be taken to task.
It had directed, "All states are hereby instructed to release children under the age of 18, who have been reported to be arrested or detained in connection with the ongoing protests and who do not possess any criminal antecedents."
The top court had said if necessary, these children shall be released upon the execution of a simple bond by themselves or their family members, especially if such a requirement is insisted upon for surety.
It had taken note of allegations such as the use of pellet guns, lathis embedded with nails, rubber bullets and electric batons on protestors resulting in severe life threatening injuries to several students and young women.
The top court had directed that Delhi government and other states may proceed with the investigation of the FIRs registered but no coercive measures shall be taken against the protesting students.
"Such protection, nonetheless, shall not be extended to the persons with criminal antecedents," it had clarified.
Noting that the bench is mulling an independent, a transparent and thorough probe into all allegations by a task force, the bench had said a probe is also required to ascertain the attacks on policemen and whether they were by students or some "miscreants".
"Be that as it may, the allegations made by the petitioners, prima facie, establish a compelling case for an independent and impartial investigation into the incidents of violence. Such an investigation will adequately address the allegations presented by the family members of the police personnel, as well as the issues raised by the Solicitor General of India," it had said.
While posting the matter for further hearing, the top court had said in the interest of justice an opportunity was given to the Centre and the states concerned to place their versions on record before it considers constituting an independent committee or a Special Investigation Team .
The top court had issued notices to Maharashtra, Bihar, Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Kerala and asked their advocates general to appear online on the next date of hearing.
It had issued a slew of interim directions to states where protests were held to preserve CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-camera footage, wireless communication records, PCR logs and other digital evidence pertaining to the protests.
"Although it has already been stated at the bar by the Solicitor General of India, on instructions, we also, as an abundant precaution, direct that all CCTV footage, drone footage, body-worn camera recordings, videography, wireless communication records, and PCR lodge collections related to the students' protest be preserved," it had directed.
The top court had also ordered the police authorities to ensure that the personal information and digital data of the protestors, collected during the students' protests, are preserved and are not disclosed to the public domain for the time being.
It had emphasised that the authorities may not publish any public data/details of the protestors, especially students.
"The NCT of Delhi and other states may proceed with the investigation of the FIRs registered; however, no coercive measures shall be taken against the protesting students. Such protection, nonetheless, shall not be extended to the persons with criminal antecedents," it had ordered.
The Cockroach Janta Party -led march on July 20 in Delhi witnessed clashes between protesters and security personnel, who used lathis and teargas shells to disperse crowds attempting to move towards Parliament. The protests escalated and spread to several other states.
The protesters were demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak issue.
The agitation ended on Saturday with Pradhan's resignation and the government agreeing to the demand for compensation to the families of those who had ended their lives and no FIRs against the protesters.

headline: TN minister rejects demand for all-party meeting to discuss Cauvery water issue

TN minister rejects demand for all-party meeting to discuss Cauvery water issue
Chennai, Tamil Nadu Minister C T R Nirmal Kumar on Sunday rejected the demand for an all-party meeting made by various political parties in the state to discuss the ongoing Cauvery water row with Karnataka.
He said a detailed resolution was already passed unanimously in the Assembly with the support and participation of all political parties.
The DMK, AIADMK, PMK and VCK have demanded for an all-party meeting.
The minister also alleged that DMK President M K Stalin and Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar were working in tandem to undermine Tamil Nadu's interests in the ongoing Cauvery water dispute.
"In our Legislative Assembly, a resolution was passed unanimously with the support and participation of all political parties. They all nodded along and supported the resolution unanimously," he told reporters here.
"Everything regarding that resolution was debated right there. If there was opposition to be voiced, it could have been raised right then. They supported only after listening to everything, didn't they? Wasn't everyone given an equal opportunity to speak? Everyone spoke," he said.
"Then why, just four days ago, did they file a petition in the High Court challenging the very resolution they had supported? The moment they filed a case in the High Court, the DMK filed a petition in the Supreme Court two days later. Who ultimately suffers because of all this? It is the people of Tamil Nadu. Under the guise of creating trouble for the chief minister, they are acting against the interests of the public," he said.
"Under such circumstances, how can you expect us to invite these very people to an all-party meeting," he asked.
Kumar also said that the DMK's "hasty" petition in the Supreme Court has created undue confusion.
"Yesterday morning, after completing consultations with various stakeholders, the CM decided that we must file a case in the Supreme Court regarding this issue. By afternoon, our Supreme Court counsel, Umapathy, announced the decision, outlined the filing strategy after concluding all discussions, and initiated the process."
"While it was being processed, the DMK hastily filed their petition after 5 PM. It creates confusion when multiple petitions on the same issue are filed from the same state. What have they done over the last five years? Has the DMK filed even a single petition on this matter before this," he questioned.
"In Karnataka, everyone remains united on a single stance. They are adamant about not releasing water to us, and there are no two opinions on that among them. However, when it comes to our approach, how are we going to reclaim our rights? On one hand, there is the court, on the other, there are diplomatic channels. Yet, beyond all this, political parties here remain divided on the exact strategy to pursue," he said.
With regard to the reported release of 12,000 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu from the Kabini reservoir, the minister said it was not enough for the state. "We need to get 17 TMC water from Karnataka", he added.
The CWMA on Thursday rejected the Karnataka government's plea and upheld the CWRC recommendation ordering the release of 3,500 cusecs of Cauvery water daily to Tamil Nadu for the next 15 days.

"Regarding the case involving the purchase of our MLAs, most of the money was seized in Bengaluru, and the majority of the funds originated from there," he said.

Mr. Irfan went viral for reciting the Preamble to the Constitution during the recent Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar.

Mr. Irfan’s channel found a vocal supporter in veteran journalist Ajit Anjum, who posted several times on X in support of the page while it was active, and after it was taken down.
“A young man named Mohammad Irfan, who lives in a slum in Delhi, started his YouTube channel just yesterday with our support,” Mr. Anjum posted on X on Sunday (August 2, 2026). “From yesterday evening until this morning, his channel gained more than 70,000 subscribers.”

The operation targeted major opium trafficking routes linked to Manipur, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. More than 360 kg of opium has been recovered so far.
Rajasthan’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) has seized drugs worth more than Rs 700 crore over the past 10 months, marking what officials described as a record crackdown on narcotics trafficking in the state.
ANTF Inspector General Vikas Kumar said Rajasthan Police had seized narcotics worth around Rs 850 crore under the NDPS Act last year, while the total this year is expected to cross Rs 1,000 crore. The task force alone has accounted for seizures worth Rs 700 crore.
The operation targeted major opium trafficking routes linked to Manipur, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. More than 360 kg of opium has been recovered so far.
The ANTF also uncovered and dismantled 34 units allegedly manufacturing MD drugs across Rajasthan, seizing more than 185 kg of the synthetic narcotic. Officials said action was also taken against the illegal cultivation of opium and cannabis.
Working with agencies in five states and five central bodies, the task force arrested 84 alleged major drug traffickers. Several of them were wanted criminals who had been on the run for years, police said.
Officials claimed that sustained action across different supply routes had disrupted several trafficking networks and weakened the narcotics supply chain in the state.
Kumar appealed to the public to share information about drug trafficking and related crimes with the ANTF control room or through its WhatsApp helpline, assuring that the identities of informants would remain confidential.

headline: Researchers at the Central University of Kerala (CUK) have secured an Indian patent for a novel multifunctional catalyst preparation technology that could help convert biomass and petrochemical feedstocks into cleaner fuels and other value added chem...
full_text:
Researchers at the Central University of Kerala (CUK) have secured an Indian patent for a novel multifunctional catalyst preparation technology that could help convert biomass and petrochemical feedstocks into cleaner fuels and other value added chemicals more efficiently.
The patent was granted for ‘Method for the Preparation of ITQ-2 Metal Oxy-Hydroxide Composite Material Thereof’ (Indian Patent No. 596368). The innovation was developed by Prof. A. Sakthivel along with researchers Soumya B.N. and Nimisha N.P.
Prof. Sakthivel said the team had developed a multifunctional catalyst, a specially engineered synthetic material known as zeolite, that can speed up chemical reactions required to convert biomass and petroleum-based raw materials into useful products.
“The main innovation is the preparation of the material itself. It is a multifunctional catalyst that combines acidic and redox (reduction-oxidation) properties in a single material, making it more efficient than conventional catalysts,” he said.
According to the researchers, conventional catalysts generally perform only one function, limiting their efficiency. The newly developed catalyst integrates multiple functions enabling chemical reactions to proceed more effectively while improving access to active sites within the material.
The technology is expected to find future applications in the petroleum and petrochemical industries, particularly in the production of cleaner fuels, fuel additives, polymers and other value-added chemicals. Prof. Sakthivel said the research had so far focused on developing and patenting the catalyst material, and commercial fuel production using the technology was yet to begin.

The Bombay High Court, on Friday (July 31, 2026), refused to grant urgent bail to Ramesh Mhatre, the corporator accused of assaulting a doctor at a municipal hospital in Dombivli. Mhatre is a member of the Shiv Sena, led by Chief Minister Eknath Shinde.

Kamdar argued that Mhatre’s actions have created a sense of fear among doctors at the municipal hospital. He further alleged that the accused has a history of securing acquittals in multiple cases by pressuring witnesses. headline: Maharashtra’s anti-conversion law takes effect
full_text:
Maharashtra’s anti-conversion law takes effect
The gazette was published after the legislation was approved by President Droupadi Murmu on July 17, paving the way for its implementation in the state.
Maharashtra became the 13th Indian state to notify an anti-conversion law, with the controversial Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act taking effect after the state government published the legislation in its official gazette on July 30.
The gazette was published after the legislation was approved by President Droupadi Murmu on July 17, paving the way for its implementation in the state.
Also Read | Basic structure touchstone for anti-conversion laws
What is the law?
The law criminalises religious conversions carried out through force, allurement, fraud, inducement or marriage by making it a cognisable offence. This includes interfaith marriages where conversion is alleged to have taken place through such means, particularly if objections are raised by the families of either party.
The law makes unlawful religious conversion a cognisable and non-bailable offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years.
Among its most controversial provisions is the requirement that a person intending to convert must give 60 days’ notice to the designated authority.
The act also places the burden of proof that the religious conversion was voluntary on the person accused of carrying out the conversion, as well as on anyone alleged to have assisted or aided it.
The legislation has been widely opposed by civil rights groups as a violation of an individual’s right to freedom and personal privacy. It is seen as an attempt to curb interfaith marriages, particularly instances involving a Hindu woman marrying a non-Hindu man, where conversion to the latter’s faith may take place. Civil liberties groups believe the legislation could be misused in various ways, especially to harass interfaith couples.
Also Read | UP anti-conversion law doesn’t bar interfaith couples from live-in relationships: HC
When was the bill passed?
The Bill was passed by both houses of the Maharashtra legislature earlier this year, with governor Jishnu Dev Varma giving his assent on April 6. It was published in the state’s official gazette on July 30 after it received presidential assent.
“Legal action may now be initiated in cases involving unlawful religious conversions in the state, strictly in accordance with the provisions of the new act,” said a senior official from the state home department.
Provisions of law
The legislation is expected to make interfaith marriages difficult. Once an individual provides notice, the designated authority is required to make it public and invite objections within 30 days. They must then conduct a police inquiry into the intention, purpose and circumstances of the proposed conversion. If the inquiry concludes that the conversion is unlawful, criminal proceedings may be initiated.
Under the act, any religious conversion carried out through allurement, coercion, force, misrepresentation, fraud, deceit or other unlawful means is illegal. It also treats as unlawful any religious conversion carried out through the solemnization of a marriage or a relationship on the promise of marriage if such means are used.
The legislation further mandates that the individual or institution conducting the conversion must submit a declaration to the designated authority within 21 days of the ceremony. Failure to do so will render the conversion null and void.

headline: Climate change shifts malaria risk to southern, East Africa: Study
full_text:
Climate change shifts malaria risk to southern, East Africa: Study
The southern and East African regions expected to be hit the hardest in the future are also regions that aren’t accustomed to needing to fight the disease today
Climate change has increased childhood malaria and could continue to do so in southern and East Africa where communities are less experienced at tackling the disease, while reducing the risk in today’s hotspots as temperatures become too high for mosquitoes, according to a new study published in Nature.
The study— The past and future impact of climate change on childhood malaria in Africa— quantifies climate change’s historical and future impact in sub-Saharan Africa’s children, where most cases and deaths occur. It finds that climate change has slightly increased malaria overall.
Looking ahead, rising temperatures could increase the malaria risk in southern and East Africa while reducing it where it is most rampant today as it becomes so hot that even mosquitos struggle to survive.
“Climate change isn’t just making malaria worse or better—it’s moving it,” said co-author Tamma Carleton, faculty head of Research for the Climate Impact Lab and an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley, in a statement. “Whether a place sees elevated malaria risks or reduced burdens under climate change depends on how hot it is today. We see relief in the current hotspots and new risk nearly everywhere else.”
The study finds that climate change has slightly suppressed the spread of the disease in the warm, malaria hotbeds of today, and will continue to as it gets too hot for the disease to flourish—posing other human health threats. This is especially the case in many large West African nations (Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali), where climate change will reduce cases by 5 percent. In extremely hot Sahelian countries (Niger, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Somalia) the disease may actually be fully eliminated.
The opposite is true for cooler regions where malaria isn’t a significant problem today, such as southern Africa and high-elevation east Africa. In these areas, climate change is slowly making the temperature more suitable for mosquitoes to spread malaria, increasing cases by 5 percent in the Ethiopian highlands (Kenya, Burundi) and by similarly large increases in Angola, Zambia, and northeast South Africa. By 2100, the risk could increase by 20 percent in regions like the Rift Valley and coastal southern Africa, creating new malaria challenges.
But efforts to reduce emissions can change this trajectory. If the world is able to meet the 2°C warming threshold, this would avert 5 excess cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa and more in the east African highlands. It would also reduce the other widespread climate impacts that will be felt in central and western Africa as the planet continues to heat up. Further, while mitigation is crucial, so is adaptation. The southern and East African regions expected to be hit the hardest in the future are also regions that aren’t accustomed to needing to fight the disease today.
“Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to the evolving malaria threat,” said co-author Christopher Trisos, director of the Climate Risk Lab and Principal Research, Officer at the African Climate and Development Initiative at University of Cape Town. “That means getting ready now to implement more aggressive anti-malaria programs in cooler regions of sub-Saharan Africa where malaria risk is growing, and which can be less experienced at tackling it. Inclusive economic development, and global health financing of effective surveillance, disease control, and better healthcare will be crucial to help confront increased malaria rates caused by climate change in eastern and southern Africa.”
The authors make clear that both climate mitigation and adaptation actions, including malaria elimination strategies, will be needed.
“Malaria was one of the first health outcomes linked to climate change, but it’s taken a quarter century to be sure which direction things are headed,” said co-author Colin Carlson, assistant professor of Epidemiology at Yale University. “The big story here is the opportunity for action: so far, elimination efforts have counteracted climate change impacts by nearly 200-fold. Malaria elimination within a generation is not only possible, but one of the best ways to protect frontline populations from climate change impacts.”

headline: West Bengal to fine builders for dumping materials on roads from September 1
full_text:
West Bengal to fine builders for dumping materials on roads from September 1
Agnimitra Paul announced fines from September 1 for anyone storing construction materials on public roads. The warning broadens West Bengal's civic discipline drive to vacant plots, parking violations and footpath encroachment.
West Bengal Urban Development and Municipal Affairs Minister Agnimitra Paul said on Sunday that people who leave construction materials such as sand, bricks and stones on public roads while building houses will face penalties from September 1. She said roads cannot be used to store such materials and property owners must keep them within their premises.
Paul also said owners of vacant plots would be responsible for keeping their land clean, and warned of strict action against illegal parking. She urged hawkers not to occupy entire footpaths, but said no eviction drive against them would be carried out until the end of the Durga Puja festivities.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a programme at the Siliguri Municipal Corporation, Paul said, “People cannot leave stones, sand and bricks on the road while constructing houses. We will impose fines. Roads are not anyone's private property.”
She said landowners cannot leave vacant plots overgrown with bushes or clogged with drains and waterbodies for years, as such conditions could contribute to mosquito breeding and increase the risk of diseases such as dengue.
Maintaining vacant land, like maintaining one's house and its surroundings, is the responsibility of the owner, she said. Reiterating the government's recent measures to improve civic discipline, Paul said vehicles must be parked only in designated parking spaces and reminded people that the state government is introducing a dedicated parking app.
Those parking cars or motorcycles on footpaths would also face hefty fines, she added. Paul also urged hawkers occupying entire footpaths to move back and leave adequate space for pedestrians.
In summary, Paul announced fines from September 1 for keeping construction materials on public roads, said vacant plot owners would have to keep their land clean, warned of action against illegal parking and asked hawkers to leave space on footpaths, while saying no eviction drive against them would be carried out until the end of the Durga Puja festivities.

headline: Leading pharma company recalls eye drops in India after contamination scare | Full list of 10 products here
full_text:
Leading pharma company recalls eye drops in India after contamination scare | Full list of 10 products here
Sun Pharma says, “We have taken all necessary steps in the best interest of patients and in accordance with regulatory requirements."
Sun Pharma, one of the largest companies for medicines globally, has recalled 10 of its eye drop products in India amid concerns of contamination. A copy of the confidential letter by Sun Pharma Distributors Limited on July 17 asks distributors not to sell the existing batches of these products, news agency ANI has reported.
The “withdrawal of product” letter lists the following eye drops:
- Depopred2ML
- Brinolar (BKC Free)
- Brinzotim Eye Drops 5ML BKC Free
- Lotepred 5ML
- Lotepred 1% Eye Drops SML
- Lotepred LS 0.2%E/D5ML
- Lotepred T
- Nepalact OD Eye Drops 3ML
- Nepalact-Z
- Toba-F
- Nepalact E/D 5ML.
What Sun Pharma said
“In this regard, you are requested to immediately cease billing of the above-mentioned product and provide us details of any stock currently held by you. Further, you are requested to send back to us any stocks of the product available with you as well as those received from any sources on priority,” says the letter, as per ANI.
It calls the move “a precautionary measure”.
A Sun Pharma spokesperson also told ANI, “Patient safety remains our highest priority. We have taken all necessary steps in the best interest of patients and in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements. Our teams are working diligently to restore the availability of these products so that patients continue to have access to these treatment options.”
The news agency quoted an unnamed expert as saying that many of these eye drops are prescribed for patients recovering from eye surgery or managing chronic conditions such as glaucoma, eye infections, allergies, and ocular inflammation. “Interruption of treatment can have significant consequences,” the experts said.
“In a country like India, where millions rely on eye drops every day, maintaining sterility during manufacturing is non-negotiable. Even suspected contamination at a manufacturing facility can pose a serious risk to patient safety, making immediate product recalls essential. Patients should not continue using a recalled product or discontinue treatment on their own, but should contact their ophthalmologist promptly so that an appropriate alternative can be prescribed, ensuring continuity of care while safeguarding vision,” the expert added, as per ANI.

headline: Kerala rain fury leaves 8 dead; several missing as downpour triggers landslides, floods | Videos
full_text:
Kerala rain fury leaves 8 dead; several missing as downpour triggers landslides, floods | Videos
In an update shared on X, Kerala CM V D Satheesan on Sunday confirmed eight fatalities, while eight individuals remain missing and 13 others sustained injuries.
Heavy rain wreaked havoc across Kerala on Saturday, killing several people and destroying dozens of homes, as authorities remained on high alert.
In an update shared on X (formerly Twitter), Kerala chief minister V D Satheesan on Sunday confirmed eight fatalities, while eight individuals remain missing and 13 others sustained injuries.
Visuals emerge from Kerala rains
The rains in Kerala triggered landslides, flooding low-lying areas, and causing widespread destruction.
Visuals emerging from Kerala show rivers and dams swelling following torrential rainfall. In one clip, fast-flowing water can be seen rushing through a water body as a bridge was destroyed.
At the same time, five shutters of the Malankara Dam, a part of the Muvattupuzha Valley Irrigation Project, were opened after heavy downpours.
In Kozhikode, video footage captured inundated roads with vehicles navigating the flooded streets while pedestrians were seen wading through the water.
Meanwhile, life in Kozhikode was severely impacted as waterlogging reportedly disrupted traffic and flooded several local shops.
Separate visuals of street waterlogging showed a truck driving through deeply submerged roads in Kannur.
Further footage showed the Aluva Shiva Temple inundated by floodwaters.
Also Read | CPI(M) leaders criticise Kerala CM over attending events during rain disaster
Houses destroyed in Kerala rains
According to the statement of Kerala CM Satheesan, the severe weather destroyed 27 houses entirely and partially damaged 196 others.
The officials evacuated 5,792 residents to 209 relief camps set up across affected regions.
The chief minister also assured assistance to families who lost relatives, homes, or livelihoods.
The CM said that despite the reduction in rainfall since the previous day, people should be vigilant, especially in the hilly areas.
"Communications continue with the Revenue Minister, Ministers responsible for the districts, and district administrations regarding the rain disaster in the state," he said.
'Flood has badly affected people': Local shop owner
Speaking to news agency ANI, a local shop owner said that the flood had affected people in Ranni. He added that many traders were unable to open their shops, and several even suffered losses worth lakhs of rupees.
"Running this pharmacy medical store here. The flood has badly affected people in Ranni. The water level rose suddenly yesterday, and within one and a half hours, the river overflowed," he said.
"Most traders were unable to open their shops, and many have suffered losses worth lakhs of rupees. They say they did not receive any compensation during previous floods and are deeply disappointed as the situation continues to repeat every year," the local shop owner added.
Also Read | Revenue Minister says Kerala prepared, situation under control despite rain havoc
Parts of Kerala received over 300 mm rainfall
The data from the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) highlighted the severity of the rains.
According to news agency PTI, the KSDMA on Sunday noted that the state received up to 320 mm of rainfall in some parts on Saturday. The highest rainfall of 320 mm was at the Ayyankunnu area of Kannur district.

IMD alert for Kerala
The officials said that the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Saturday issued an 'orange alert' for 12 districts in Kerala, warning of very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms on Sunday, reported PTI.
The alert was issued for the following districts:
- Alappuzha
- Kozhikode
- Idukki
- Wayanad
- Kannur
- Kottayam
- Pathanamthitta
- Palakkad
- Malappuram

'Let Cauvery unite our people': Karnataka BJP chief calls on Tamil Nadu CM Vijay to bridge 'differences'

Karnataka BJP chief reaches out to CM Vijay over water-sharing dispute
NEW DELHI: Karnataka BJP president BY Vijayendra has written to Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay, urging him to adopt a cooperative approach to the long-running Cauvery water dispute and support the proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, saying the river should 'unite our people, rather than divide them.'The appeal comes amid renewed tensions between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu after the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water per day to Tamil Nadu for 15 days.
The direction has triggered protests in Karnataka, while the DMK has moved the Supreme Court seeking implementation of the water release order and clearance of the accumulated shortfall.In his letter, Vijayendra said differences between neighbouring states were natural but should be resolved through dialogue and statesmanship."As neighbouring states, differences are inevitable. What matters is how we resolve them," he wrote.
Referring to the earlier resolution of the dispute over the Thiruvalluvar statue in Bengaluru, Vijayendra said former Karnataka chief minister BS Yediyurappa and former Tamil Nadu chief minister M Karunanidhi had demonstrated that difficult issues could be settled when larger public interest prevailed."Their maturity demonstrated that even difficult issues can be resolved when the larger interests of our people prevail.
That is the spirit in which I appeal to you today," he wrote.The Karnataka BJP chief said the Cauvery was a lifeline for crores of people in Bengaluru and several towns across the Cauvery basin, including both Kannadigas and Tamilians living in Karnataka."At a time when inadequate and erratic monsoons have placed enormous stress on farmers and citizens alike, their concerns cannot be overlooked," he said.Vijayendra also urged Vijay to reconsider Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, saying it would help meet Bengaluru's drinking water needs without affecting Tamil Nadu's legitimate share of Cauvery waters."I also appeal to you to view the Mekedatu project in the spirit of cooperation. It can significantly address Bengaluru's drinking-water requirements without compromising the legitimate water needs of Tamil Nadu," he wrote."Your support for the project can become a powerful symbol of cooperation between our two states."He expressed hope that Vijay would take a 'statesmanlike position' that protected Karnataka's interests while respecting those of Tamil Nadu."I sincerely hope you will take a statesmanlike position that protects Karnataka's genuine interests while respecting those of Tamil Nadu, and help strengthen the historic bond between our two states. Let the Cauvery unite our people, rather than divide them," the letter said.
The Cauvery water dispute is one of India's longest-running inter-state river disputes involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. It centres on the sharing of the Cauvery river, which is a major source of drinking water and irrigation for millions of people.The Supreme Court's 2018 judgment largely upheld the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's water-sharing formula and led to the creation of the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) and the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) to oversee implementation.
However, disagreements frequently resurface during years of low rainfall, with Karnataka arguing it needs water for its own drinking and irrigation requirements, while Tamil Nadu insists on releases as mandated by the tribunal and the Supreme Court.The latest flashpoint is Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, which the state says is intended to improve Bengaluru's drinking water supply and generate hydroelectric power.Tamil Nadu has opposed the project, arguing that it could affect its allocated share of Cauvery waters and violate the existing water-sharing framework.

headline: Birbhum police raid aides of absconding stone quarry kingpin Tulu Mondal
full_text:
Birbhum police raid aides of absconding stone quarry kingpin Tulu Mondal
The operation against Mondal started on Wednesday when police seized 15kg of gold bars and ₹28.05 crore from his cousin’s home
The Birbhum district police in Bengal on Sunday raided the homes and offices of several people associated with Md Nazibuddin alias Tulu Mondal, the absconding kingpin of an illegal stone quarry and sand business.
Officials aware of the probe said the investigation focused on his modus operandi which deprived the state of revenue worth hundreds of crores during the Trinamool Congress (TMC) regime.
“Closure notices were sent to eight stone quarries because they were operating without a valid licence. Mondal’s nephew SK Wasim was arrested from Siliguri on Friday while trying to flee to Nepal. Police raided the homes and offices of more relatives and associates of Mondal on Saturday and Sunday,” a Birbhum district police officer said, requesting anonymity.
The operation against Mondal started on Wednesday when police seized 15kg of gold bars and ₹28.05 crore from his cousin’s home, whose husband, a retired state bus driver, was arrested.
After that, the police froze ₹93 crore found in Mondal’s bank accounts and seized 242 vehicles, including over 100 dumpers and some expensive Audi and BMW cars. At least 21 properties, including farm houses, were also sealed.
“Mondal started his career in around 2010-11 as a common labourer who carried stones from quarries to trucks. By 2015, he became the owner of several stone quarries because of his proximity to powerful politicians. By 2020, his company was collecting toll tax from around 2000 trucks that left Birbhum every day carrying stones and sand. He gave only a fraction of the collected tax to the government,” the police officer said.
On Sunday, police searched the home of Ijajul Sheikh, who worked as a manager in Mondal’s quarry business. “We are also on the lookout for Md Mohim, a man who rose fast under Mondal’s guidance,” a second police officer said.
“From the records we seized, it appears that besides his illegal quarry business, Mondal charged ₹2,500–3,000 from each truck loaded beyond the government-regulated limit. Around 1500-2000 trucks passed through the toll booths every day. Mondal used to give only around ₹22 lakh a day to the government,” the officer added.
Police suspect that Tulu Mondal invested in several properties in Dubai and may have fled there. On Thursday, the state told a Birbhum court that the seized gold bars were smuggled from Switzerland, Dubai and Malaysia.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari targeted his predecessor on Friday saying, “None of this would have been possible without the direct support of ex-chief minister Mamata Banerjee. Nobody can amass so much money and buy such properties and vehicles in one day.”
Adhikari told the state assembly on July 23 that revenue was stolen in Birbhum.
“The revenue from stone and sand in Birbhum used to be ₹65 crore a year. We collected ₹82 crore in the first month after coming to power. During the former regime the actual revenue was ₹1200 crore but only around ₹100 crore reached the state exchequer,” Adhikari said in his July 23 address before the assembly.
Since most of the TMC leaders from Birbhum, including former district unit president Anubrata Mondal have joined the rebel camp, the Mamata Banerjee faction said the police must take action against the politicians behind Tulu Mondal.
“If Tulu Mondal amassed such wealth then police must act against the politicians behind him,” TMC MLA Kunal Ghosh said.

We only want fair opportunities based on merit,â said Ankit Kumar from Giridih district.Sneha, a tribal student from Ranchi, said protesters wanted strict punishment for those involved in the alleged irregularities and cancellation of the 14th JPSC examination.âI have been preparing for competitive examinations since 2023. But if an equal and fair chance is not given, how can I get a job? I urge CM Soren to listen to our demands,â she said.
Archana Kumari from Palamu said the students would continue their agitation until the government addressed their demands and fixed accountability for the alleged irregularities.Despite days of protest, students said they were determined to continue their sit-in, with volunteers and supporters from different parts of the country helping sustain the demonstration.âThe state government is still in a sleeping mode. We are getting support from across the country. People from various cities are sending food items to the protest site. We are thankful to those helping us continue our protest,â said Shyam Bihari Gupta, a student from Balumath in Latehar district.

'Mekedatu project is permanent solution': Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar on Cauvery water dispute with Tamil Nadu

Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar (centre) and former CMs Siddaramaiah (left) and BS Yeddiyurappa
NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Sunday described the Mekedatu dam project, proposed by the state government on the Cauvery river, as a "permanent solution" to the long-standing dispute between Karnataka and neighbouring Tamil Nadu over the sharing of Cauvery river water."The Mekedatu project is the permanent solution. The Supreme Court has already delivered its judgment, and the central government has also given its response. Taking all that into consideration, we should move forward without wasting any more time," he said at a press conference after chairing an all-party meeting on the Cauvery water issue, which has flared up again in recent days.
The chief minister was referring to the Supreme Court's November 2025 dismissal of Tamil Nadu's objection to Karnataka's detailed project report on the Mekedatu project. In May this year, the top court also rejected Tamil Nadu's review petition challenging the earlier judgment.The Centre, meanwhile, informed Parliament in July that the Supreme Court's order does not state that Karnataka requires Tamil Nadu's consent for any new construction across the Cauvery river.Shivakumar further urged all stakeholders to move forward without wasting any more time, taking the developments into consideration.
"Taking all that into consideration, we should move forward without wasting any more time. This is not about Tamil Nadu getting more or Karnataka getting less. We should use this opportunity to bring both states to the table, hold discussions, and resolve the issue amicably. We expect everyoneâs cooperation in this effort," the Congress leader added.
The Cauvery water dispute revolves around how the river waters should be shared between the two states, particularly during years of low rainfall.The issue resurfaced amid developments concerning the Mekedatu balancing reservoir project, proposed by Karnataka. It has been a major point of friction between the two states, with Tamil Nadu traditionally opposing it on the grounds that it would affect the flow of water downstream.The latest tensions have emerged at a time when the Congress is part of the TVK-led new state government in Tamil Nadu. The party was also an ally of the DMK, the previous ruling party, but extended only external support to the government.

Heavy rainfall wrecks havoc in Kerala, Rahul Gandhi offers support
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday expressed deep sorrow over the devastation caused by heavy rains in Kerala, offering condolences to the families of eight people who lost their lives and urging party workers to assist in relief and recovery operations."Deeply saddened by the devastation caused by heavy rains across Kerala. My heartfelt condolences to the families of the eight people who have lost their lives. May those still missing be found safe, and the injured make a swift recovery," he said in a post on X.
The Congress leader also added that the state government was making every possible effort to support affected families and coordinate relief operations. "I urge all Congress workers and volunteers to assist these efforts in every possible way," he said, urging people to remain vigilant, especially in hilly regions, and follow authorities' guidance.
"Kerala stands united in this difficult hour. I stand firmly with every affected family," Rahul Gandhi added.Kerala chief minister V D Satheesan confirmed that eight people have died, an equal number are missing and 13 others injured in the heavy rains that triggered landslides, waterlogging and property damage across the state. In a statement, he said 27 houses were completely destroyed, 196 homes partially damaged and 5,792 people have been shifted to 209 relief camps.
Satheesan said that despite a reduction in rainfall, people should remain vigilant, especially in hilly areas. He said the government would ensure assistance to families of the deceased and those who lost homes and livelihoods.Revenue minister A P Anilkumar told reporters the situation was improving and was under control. He said damaged roads had been restored in many areas, though some restrictions on vehicular movement remained. Heavy rainfall was predicted on August 2, 3 and 6, with strong winds of up to 50 kmph.
The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services warned of huge waves of 2.7 to 3.5 meters along the northern Kerala coast and advised fishermen and coastal residents to be vigilant.On Sunday morning, while rains subsided, water had not receded from flooded areas, with people seen travelling using small boats. The water level in some power generation dams in Idukki, Pathanamthitta and Thrissur districts remained in red alert status, according to KSDMA.State tourism minister P C Vishnunadh said an additional NDRF team was deployed for rescue efforts in Pathanamthitta and Aranmula, with fire force units from Thiruvananthapuram, Palakkad and Ernakulam. Fishermen and fishing boats were also deployed for quick response.

headline: 4 held after 15-year-old girl found dead at Assam home; family claims rape: Cop
full_text:
4 held after 15-year-old girl found dead at Assam home; family claims rape: Cop
The victim’s sister alleged that the attackers used utensils and other objects to mutilate the body after the assault
Four people have been detained in connection with a rape and murder of a 15-year-old girl who was found dead at her home near National Highway-6 in Assam’s Hailakandi district on Saturday night, police said.
Senior superintendent of police (SSP), Hailakandi, Amitab Sinha, said Hailakandi police registered a case, however denied from sharing any details and detained four persons for interrogation. Sexual assault accusations are yet to be medically ascertained, police said.
“The family members are claiming it [rape], but we are waiting for the post-mortem report to draw any conclusions. We are investigating the matter thoroughly, and four persons are currently being questioned,” Sinha said.
The incident took place in the Aloichora area under Katlichera police station at 11pm on Saturday. The victim’s family said they were attending a feast at a nearby relative’s house at the time.
“It’s a neighbourhood where many members of the same extended family live together, and her family members were not far away when the incident happened,” SSP said.
“She was there at the feast too, but after an argument with a cousin, she left for home at 10.30pm. We thought we’d bring some food for her later, but when we reached home around an hour later, it was a horrible scene,” her mother said.
She said her body was found lying on the floor, almost unrecognisable.
“It was horrible; how can a human treat another human, a little girl, in such a brutal manner,” she said, while demanding capital punishment for the accused.
The victim’s sister alleged that the attackers used utensils and other objects to mutilate the body after the assault.
“Her face was smashed, her head was bludgeoned with a heavy object, and some rod-like object was inserted into her private parts,” she said. “They are not humans, even calling them animals would be wrong. They don’t deserve to live. I appeal to the police to shoot them, or they should be hanged,” she said.
Police said they received the information around 12.30am, and recovered the body on Sunday morning following protests by family members and neighbours. Locals in Aloichora blocked NH-6 on Sunday morning in protest against the alleged rape and murder, initially refusing to hand over the body to the police.
“If a 15-16-year-old girl is not safe in her own house, what kind of society have we become? There must be exemplary punishment so that nobody dares repeat such heinous acts,” one of the protesters said.
Local MLA Milon Das later intervened, helping police transport the body to SMCH for the post-mortem. Das met with the family members and assured them that the culprits would be arrested immediately.
“The body has been sent to Silchar Medical College and Hospital (SMCH) for a post-mortem, and we are investigating the matter further,” confirmed the additional superintendent of police (Crime), Hailakandi, Shamirdapar Baruah.

headline: 3 states, 3 bypolls: All eyes on PK, Ashutosh Tiwari as Bankipur, Datia, Manjalpur await verdict on Monday
full_text:
3 states, 3 bypolls: All eyes on PK, Ashutosh Tiwari as Bankipur, Datia, Manjalpur await verdict on Monday
Both Bankipur and Datia have become prestige battles for the Bharatiya Janata Party, with both being traditional strongholds of the saffron party.
The results of three assembly by-elections in three states will be declared on Monday, with the spotlight on Bihar's Bankipur and Madhya Pradesh's Datia.
The third seat is Gujarat's Manjalpur. Voting for all three bypolls was held on July 30.
Both Bankipur and Datia have emerged as prestige battles for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as both are considered traditional saffron party strongholds. Bankipur was previously represented by BJP national president Nitin Nabin, while Datia is the political bastion of former Madhya Pradesh home minister Narottam Mishra.
Datia assembly bypoll
Mishra did not get a ticket for the by-election for the seat he lost in the 2023 assembly polls to Congress candidate Rajendra Bharti.
The bypoll was necessitated after a Delhi court in April this year sentenced Bharti to three years' imprisonment in a cheating case, leading to the termination of his assembly membership.
Violence erupted in the aftermath of the ticket denial, with Mishra's supporters clashing with the police. The former minister later shed tears as he promised full support to the BJP candidate, Ashutosh Tiwari.
The outcome of the Datia assembly bypoll may not alter the stability of the BJP government in the state, but political observers believe it carries wider implications, coming against the backdrop of recent student protests and the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
According to analysts, the closely watched result, slated for Monday, could significantly shape the political standing of both the ruling BJP and the Opposition Congress in the state ahead of the 2028 assembly elections.
The main contest is widely seen as being between Tiwari and Congress nominee Ghanshyam Singh.
District Election Officer Swapnil Wankhede said counting would begin at 8 am on Monday with postal ballots, followed by votes polled through electronic voting machines (EVMs).
The Bankipur battle
The high-stakes assembly bye-election in Bihar's Bankipur-182 constituency concluded with a moderate turnout, recording approximately 34.16 per cent total voter participation on Thursday, according to the Election Commission.
The Bankipur seat fell vacant after BJP leader Nitin Nabin resigned as MLA following his election to the Rajya Sabha. The BJP has fielded Neeraj Kumar Sinha, while Jan Suraaj Party founder Prashant Kishor has thrown his hat in the contest.
What would have been a straightforward election for the BJP, which recently made Samrat Chaudhary its first-ever chief minister in the state, has been complicated by the entry and relentless campaigning of Prashant Kishor.
Kishor has claimed that he would defeat the BJP in the election, which, if it happens, would be a major embarrassment for the ruling party.
The BJP has fielded Neeraj Kumar Sinha from the seat, while RJD’s Rekha Kumari is also in the fray.
The Manjalpur election
The Manjalpur Assembly by-election in Gujarat was also held on July 30, recording a voter turnout of approximately 37.5 per cent. This high-stakes bypoll was triggered by the death of veteran Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MLA and former minister Yogesh Patel on June 2, 2026, who had held the consecutive legislative seat for decades.
The election is a direct face-off between BJP’s Satish Govindbhai Patel and Congress’s Bhikhabhai Rabari.
