headline: Solinas Integrity, an IIT Madras incubated climate deep tech and robotics company based at the IIT Madras Research Park, has secured $5.5 million in a Series A1 funding round led by Hero Enterprise Partner Ventures and co-led by Mela Ventures, with p...
full_text:
Solinas Integrity, an IIT Madras incubated climate deep tech and robotics company based at the IIT Madras Research Park, has secured $5.5 million in a Series A1 funding round led by Hero Enterprise Partner Ventures and co-led by Mela Ventures, with participation from the Luthra Group.
Existing investor SBI Ventures, through the SVL-SME Fund, doubled down on its position, alongside continued backing from Rainmatter and 8X Ventures Fund I. The round follows Solinas’s Series A, led by SBI Ventures through the SVL-SME Fund (Neev II) in May 2024. Kumbhat Advisors, led by Akash Sethia, served as Exclusive Financial Advisor to the transaction.
Solinas will use the fresh capital to scale aggressively and deepen its penetration in existing markets while expanding into new states and municipal corporations across India and building out its international footprint with a strategic focus on the Middle East and Southeast Asia.
Founded by Divanshu Kumar and Moinak Banerjee, Solinas builds robotics and AI systems that inspect, clean, and digitize underground water and wastewater infrastructure, solving problems of water leakages, contamination & elimination of manual scavenging. “We’re also planning to extend into sectors like Oil and Gas and Defence,” said Divanshu Kumar, Co-Founder and CEO of Solinas Integrity. Solinas is targeting ₹100 crore in revenue by Financial Year 2028.
“Their work directly addresses water security, worker safety, and the long-term resilience of our cities. This investment reflects our commitment to backing entrepreneurs who are building for India’s future with both scale and purpose,” said Sunil Kant Munjal, Chairman, Hero Enterprise.
“Current methods of maintaining India’s water infrastructure are manual, hazardous, time-consuming, and costly, with virtually no visibility into what lies beneath. Solinas is changing that through a vertically integrated robotics platform that maps underground infrastructure, diagnoses issues, and delivers end-to-end solutions,” said Krishnakumar Natarajan, Managing Partner, Mela Ventures.

headline: Several districts in the northern part of Andhra Pradesh, including Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Anakapalli and Parvathipuram-Manyam, received moderate rain on Thursday. But, it is barely enough to bridge the rainfall deficit recorded in these distri...
full_text:
Several districts in the northern part of Andhra Pradesh, including Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Anakapalli and Parvathipuram-Manyam, received moderate rain on Thursday. But, it is barely enough to bridge the rainfall deficit recorded in these districts, which ranges from 40% to 60%.
On Thursday, the day’s highest rain between 8.30 a.m. and 7 p.m. was recorded in Dattirajeru of Vizianagaram district at 82.7 mm.
Other places that received moderate rain on Thursday are: Salur of Parvathipuram Manyam (65.75 mm) , Butchiraju Palem of Visakhapatnam district (58 mm), Parvada of Anakapalli district (56.75 mm) , Kotapadu of Anakapalli (55.5 mm), Commonpoint area of Visakhapatnam district (53.75 mm) and Vijayarampuram in Srikakulam district (40.5 mm).
Other places in these districts received rain below 40 mm. However, it was not enough to bring down the deficit percentages, as Srikakulam recorded a deficit of 55.1%, followed by Parvathipuram-Manyam (49.3%), Anakapalli (41.8%) and Vizianagaram (42.4%).
As of August 6, the overall deficit in Andhra Pradesh stands at 49.1%, a slight fall from July 31 when it stood at 52.4%. So far, the State has received 146.1 mm of rain as against the normal of 286.9 mm between June 1 and August 6, according to the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES).
Annamayya district, with 71.7%, leads the State with the steepest rainfall deficit, followed by Chittoor (64.1%), Prakasam (60.6%) and Visakhapatnam by 60.3%.
According to the updated forecast issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Thursday, there may not be much rain in the State this week, until August 13.
According to the IMD’s rainfall outlook for August, a few stations in the State, especially coastal areas and those sharing a border with Telangana and Karnataka, may receive normal to above-normal rain. However, the State may see above-normal daytime temperatures and minimum temperatures this month.

headline: Kavya S., a housewife at BTM Layout in Bengaluru, bought a 26-kg bag of Sona Masoori rice in June for ₹1,560. “This month the cost for the same quantity in the same shop was ₹1,950,” she rued. Radha Shinde, a resident from Vijayanagar in the city, sa...
full_text:
Kavya S., a housewife at BTM Layout in Bengaluru, bought a 26-kg bag of Sona Masoori rice in June for ₹1,560. “This month the cost for the same quantity in the same shop was ₹1,950,” she rued. Radha Shinde, a resident from Vijayanagar in the city, said the second quality bullet rice that she bought last month was ₹1,600 for 26 kg, which is now ₹1,750. "I had to adjust by dropping some pulses from the grocery list,” she explained. Abdul Gafoor, a resident of J.C. Nagar, buys the exotic Jeera Fine variety of rice to cook only special dishes during weekends. “It now costs ₹285 per kg. A month ago, I bought it for ₹255,” he said.
The prices of all varieties of rice in Bengaluru’s retail market have gone up by anywhere between ₹10 and ₹15, even higher for the more exotic varieties. Traders in the city say that the upward trend is unlikely to change immediately, given the prevailing conditions on the agricultural fields and in the market.
Deficit rain in June and July because of El Nino, the impact of the West Asia war, and some local factors have all pushed the price of various rice varieties. Rice, a water-intensive crop and a staple across south India, has been impacted hard by poor monsoon in June-July and plummetting reservoir levels. Though rain has revived in some parts in August, too much time has been lost say farmers and experts. About 90% of the paddy is grown during the kharif season from June to October in Karnataka.
Technical snag adds to woes
About 500 km from Bengaluru, in the fields of Raichur and Koppal, key rice growing areas irrigated by the Tungabhadra Left Bank Main Canal, farmers are despondent for two reasons — delayed and deficit monsoon and technical snags that have cropped up just when the rains revived in August. The region remained dry in June and July, and when it is raining in August and reservoir levels are up, a breach near Mile 46 in Koppal district is causing delay in water release into the Tungabhadra Left Bank Main Canal, further delaying the kharif cycle.
The region is renowned for producing premium Sona Masoori rice, which is widely consumed not just across India but also exported to Sri Lanka, West Asia, several African nations, and other international destinations. This year, however, agricultural experts are advising cultivators to shift to less water-intensive crops such as jowar wherever possible.
Ideally, paddy transplantation should have been completed during July. Delayed transplantation not only reduces yield but also affects grain quality, thereby impacting the premium value of the rice produced in the region. According to Chamarasa Malipatil, honorary president of the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha and a farmer leader from Manvi in Raichur district, this year’s production loss is almost inevitable.
Less than 30% of sowing
According to data from the Karnataka State Department of Agriculture (KSDA), only 2.02 lakh hectares sowing has been completed as against the target of 10 lakh hectares during the kharif season. Sowing of seeds or transplantation of saplings for cultivation of paddy has not even completed 30% of the total target.
Last year, the target was more than 10.63 lakh hectares, of which sowing on 9.13 lakh hectares was achieved in the kharif season, 0.23 lakh hectares in the rabi season, and 2.34 lakh hectares during the summer season. Overall, a total of 11.07 lakh hectares was achieved at the end of financial year 2025-26. Around 56.23 lakh tonnes of paddy was produced and 4,904 kgs of paddy was cultivated per hectare.
The data from Karnataka State Natural Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) showed that the State recorded 357 mm of rainfall as against the normal 506 mm between June 1 and August 4, representing a departure of -28% and classified under the deficit category.
Most regions where paddy is cultivated in large quantities, including Raichur, Yadgiri, Ballari, Shivamogga, Mandya, and Mysuru, recorded large rainfall deficit. Agronomists and farmers across the State said that it is unlikely to achieve the target by the end of this month.
Malipatil said that nursery saplings that are available today are nearly two-and-a-half months old. Ideally, paddy should be transplanted using 30 to 35-day-old seedlings. “Aged seedlings cannot produce the same yield. Even if water reaches the fields now, the productivity will come down substantially,” he said. “Worse, most farmers did not even raise nursery beds this year because the government had announced that water from reservoirs would not be released for irrigation owing to poor storage. Only farmers who had access to borewells or other alternative water sources prepared nurseries. Those seedlings are not sufficient to cover the vast command area.”
Poor stocks in mills
While the future is not promising on the fields, in Bengaluru, Manjunath G., a rice trader on Millers Road, said that poor stock of paddy with the rice mills as well as farmers, and anticipation of poor arrivals owing to deficit rains this year, have pushed up prices in the past 15 to 20 days.
Manoj Jain, another rice trader in K.R. Market, said: “The price of rice will increase further in the coming days due to more demand and less stock. Hence, many are buying large quantities and stocking up.” Hoarding is only further pushing prices.
Shivakumar, general secretary, Karnataka State Rice Mills Association, said that they get paddy from Raichur, Ballari, Gangavati, Kampli, Siraguppa, and districts in Malnad region and Mandya. “Most of the available paddy stock was converted into rice in the mills in Karnataka and exported between January and April. Farmers sold off all their stock during this time assuming they can grow paddy this year.”
H.S. Basavarajappa, a farmer from Shivamogga, explained that small and marginal farmers across the State lack facilities like godown and sell off everything to the rice mills. Only a handful keep stock of paddy awaiting better prices. “Other farmers like me also buy 25-kg bags of rice from retail shops.”
Another reason for shortage in stocks of paddy was the damaged crest gates of the Tungabhadra dam that were replaced by Karnataka and Telangana in June 2026, he added. With gate number 19 washed away in 2024, the amount of water stored in the dams was low. As a result, many farmers could not cultivate paddy during the kharif season last year too. The Tungabhadra irrigation system supports nearly 12.1 lakh acres across Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, including about 8.7 lakh acres in Karnataka alone.
Ramesh Chandra Lahoti, member of Federation of Karnataka Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FKCCI), further explained that poor planning by government was another key reason for shortage. “There are two reasons behind the increase in the prices of rice in market — rain situation and the recent war. During the recent West Asia war crisis, rice was exported twice to Sri Lanka, West Asia, and other countries from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and other States. Usually, every year, it is exported only once. The Centre and the State should have planned the exports well keeping El Nino and its impact in mind. These countries majorly demand Sona steamed rice variety and Sona Masoori which is grown in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.”
Two methods of cultivation
G.R. Denesh, Professor of Agronomy and Scheme Head at All India Coordinated Research Projects (Rice) run by Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), explained that there are two methods followed by farmers in Karnataka for paddy cultivation. Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) method is a modern method where seeds are sown straight into the fields. It involves skipping the method of making nurseries and moving small plants and saves 30 to 50% water. “However, this method is followed by small percentage of farmers,” he said.
“Another method is transplantation which is popularly known as naati method. It involves transplanting saplings which actually requires a lot of water as the water has to remain stagnant in the fields. Usually during seasons like El Nino, agriculture scientists, institutions and even the state governments suggest farmers opt for DSR method. However, it is not easy to make the switch. Paddy being a water-intensive crop requires at least 4,500 to 5,000 litres of water for 1 kg of paddy cultivation,” he pointed out.
In Karnataka, another 25 to 30 days are left for sowing or transplanting, and the State government should take an immediate decision to release water from various dams for irrigation to salvage the situation, he suggested.
Concurring with the expert, Sudheer Kumar, a farmer in Mandya, explained, “So far, many farmers in Mandya district had not sown seeds or transplanted saplings. But after receiving rains recently, farmers have started the process with the water available from their borewells. However, borewell water is not sufficient. Now, we are waiting for the government to decide soon and release water from dams. Harangi and Kabini dams have sufficient water. The gods should bless farmers with rain for another 20 to 25 days.”
But for farmers like Basavarajappa, there is no hope even now. He said that no sowing or transplanting process had been done in the Malnad areas fed by water from the Bhadra reservoir. “Since the water levels are low in Bhadra, farmers are not likely to cultivate paddy for the kharif season.”
Mohan Gowda, a farmer from Mandya, emphasised the government’s role in making good the losses. “They must provide financial relief and increase the minimum support price.“ At present, it is only ₹2,441 per quintal which is not close to recovering the expenses. The cost of seeds, labour and pesticides have also increased recently. The basic price of seeds for 1 kg starts from ₹650 to ₹700,” he said.
No decision on water for irrigation
Speaking to the Hindu, Ramalinga Reddy, Minister for Major and Medium Irrigation for Karnataka, said, “The government is aware that the inflow of water in the Tungabhadra dam has increased. We will soon conduct Irrigation Consultative Committee meeting and decide on letting water for irrigation.“
However, in the Krishnaraja Sagar, the water level is still not even 50%, he said. “Hence for now, our priority is drinking water. Therefore, we are filling lakes and other sources with the inflow of water.”
On the other hand, water from the Almatti dam on the borders of Vijayapura and Bagalkot districts as well as water from the Narayanapur dam in Yadgir was let out for irrigation.
(With additional inputs by Kumar Buradikatti in Kalaburagi)

headline: Congress rebel leader Naresh Meena, accused of slapping a Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) during the Assembly by-election at Deoli-Uniara in November 2024, surrendered at Nagar Fort police station in Rajasthan’s Tonk district on Thursday following th...

Congress rebel leader Naresh Meena, accused of slapping a Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) during the Assembly by-election at Deoli-Uniara in November 2024, surrendered at Nagar Fort police station in Rajasthan’s Tonk district on Thursday following the cancellation of his bail. His bail was cancelled last month on the ground of violation of conditions.
The police produced Mr. Meena, 45, in the court of the Special Judge (SC/ST Atrocities) in Tonk, which remanded him to judicial custody. A large number of Mr. Meena’s supporters raised slogans outside the police station and the court, while the administration imposed prohibitory orders to prevent any untoward incident.
The Rajasthan High Court had granted conditional bail to Mr. Meena on July 11, 2025, after nearly nine months in jail. The Special SC/ST Court in Tonk cancelled the bail on July 13 this year, citing violation of conditions after his subsequent arrest during a protest in Jhalawar, and issued arrest warrants against him.
As the court directed the police to arrest Mr. Meena and produce him by Thursday, he himself surrendered at the police station, travelling from Jaipur in a procession of his supporters. The rebel leader’s supporters accused the Bharatiya Janata Party government of trying to curb his growing popularity by keeping him behind bars ahead of the upcoming Panchayati Raj elections.
Contesting as an independent candidate in the bypoll, Mr. Meena had allegedly slapped SDM Amit Chaudhary at a polling station in Samrawata village on November 13, 2024, while claiming irregularities in voting. Mr. Meena accused the SDM of forcing the villagers to cast their votes despite their boycott call and taking at least three fake voters inside the polling booth.
During the violence and arson which erupted after the incident, two dozen two-wheelers and 18 four-wheelers, including police vehicles, were torched. Senior police officers from Tonk, who arrived in full gear, arrested Mr. Meena from a dharna site in Samrawata the next day, while his supporters created a ruckus and blocked several roads in Tonk district.
The villagers at Samrawata had announced boycott of polling in support of their demand to shift their village from Nagar Fort to Uniara tehsil in the revenue records because of the distance issue. BJP’s Rajendra Gurjar defeated Mr. Meena by a margin of 41,121 votes in the by-election.
Mr. Meena, since suspended by the Opposition Congress, also unsuccessfully contested the Assembly by-election at Anta in Baran district in November 2025, where he made the fight triangular. Congress candidate Pramod Jain won the Assembly seat, while Mr. Meena stood a close third with just 159 votes less than the BJP candidate, Morpal Suman.

headline: Karnataka recorded highest number of challans followed by Rajasthan, Andhra, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand
full_text:
Karnataka recorded highest number of challans followed by Rajasthan, Andhra, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand
NEW DELHI: More than 5.7 lakh people were fined for smoking in public across India in 2025-26, with authorities collecting over Rs 5.1 crore in penalties under the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), according to data tabled in the Rajya Sabha. The figures, however, revealed wide variations in enforcement, with several states reporting no violations or fines during the year.Health ministry said enforcement of the ban on smoking in public places was primarily the responsibility of state governments, while the Centre issued advisories and implementation guidelines, including a dedicated handbook for law enforcers issued in 2024. Smoking in public places is prohibited under Section 4 of COTPA, and violations attract a fine of up to Rs 200 under Section 21 of the Act.
Karnataka recorded the highest number of challans at 1,59,041, followed by Rajasthan (99,789), Andhra (55,850), Tamil Nadu (47,941) and Uttarakhand (40,545). Karnataka collected the highest amount in fines, at over Rs 1.4 crore.In contrast, Assam, Chandigarh, Manipur, Puducherry and Telangana reported zero challans and no fines, pointing to differences in enforcement across states. Delhi reported 574 challans, with fines amounting to Rs 2.5 lakh.

headline: 'What's all this about Hinduja brothers, CBI?': SC draws curtain on Bofors case, rejects plea against 2005 acquittal
full_text:
'What's all this about Hinduja brothers, CBI?': SC draws curtain on Bofors case, rejects plea against 2005 acquittal
With Thursday’s dismissal, the last judicial challenge to the 2005 acquittal has come to an end, bringing the Bofors prosecution to its final legal closure.
The Supreme Court on Thursday effectively brought the curtain down on the politically-sensitive Bofors pay-off case by dismissing the only surviving appeal against the 2005 Delhi High Court judgment that quashed all criminal proceedings against the three Hinduja brothers and Swedish arms manufacturer AB Bofors.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran declined to grant any further time to advocate and BJP leader Ajay K Agrawal, who had challenged the high court verdict, observing that it was not inclined to adjourn a matter that had remained pending since 2018 only on the question how a private individual’s appeal could survive after the investigating agency’s own challenge had already been dismissed.
Also Read | SC to examine plea for CBI probe into alleged breach of 1.5 lakh medical records
Scandal that rocked Rajiv Gandhi government
The order effectively seals the fate of one of India’s longest-running corruption cases, nearly four decades after allegations surfaced that kickbacks were paid in the ₹1,437-crore Bofors gun deal.
The scandal rocked the Rajiv Gandhi government, severely dented his clean image, dominated the 1989 general election campaign and is widely regarded as one of the factors that contributed to the Congress losing power that year.
Also Read | SC agrees to examine Madras HC order on Karthigai Deepam near dargah
What happened in court
At the outset of Thursday’s hearing, Agrawal, appearing virtually in person, sought four weeks’ time to delete the names of two deceased respondents, Srichand P Hinduja and Gopichand P Hinduja, from the array of parties. The other respondents in the case included Prakash P Hinduja, who is currently the chairman of Hinduja Group in Europe.
The bench, however, appeared unconvinced about continuing with the proceedings. “What is all this about the Hinduja brothers and CBI?” it asked.
When informed that the Delhi High Court had exonerated the accused by quashing the proceedings, the top court bench remarked: “All proceedings were quashed. What is this? How many years have passed?”
As Agrawal pointed out that the defence deal dated back to 1986 and attempted to explain that CBI’s separate appeal had earlier been dismissed because it was already a respondent in his petition and that the agency were asked to appear in his matter, the bench cut him short.
“No, no...dismissed,” said the bench.
When Agrawal sought to make further submissions, the bench refused to adjourn the matter, observing, “No question of adjournment. It is a 2018 matter,” before dismissing the appeal.
2005 judgment
The dismissal marks the end of the litigation arising out of the high court’s May 31, 2005 judgment, in which Justice RS Sodhi quashed all charges against Srichand, Gopichand and Prakash Hinduja as well as the Bofors company, while strongly criticising the Central Bureau of Investigation’s handling of the prosecution and observing that the investigation had cost the exchequer nearly ₹250 crore.
The Supreme Court had, in November 2018, refused to entertain CBI’s own appeal against the same high court judgment after finding no satisfactory explanation for the agency’s delay of 4,522 days in approaching the court.
It had then held that the court was “not convinced” with the reasons furnished to condone the extraordinary delay, though it had observed that CBI could advance its contentions in Agrawal’s pending appeal.
The top court had first questioned Agrawal’s locus in January 2018, asking how a private individual could maintain an appeal in a criminal prosecution when the investigating agency itself had not challenged the acquittal.
Also Read | SC upholds life term for serial killer Chandrakant Jha
What is the controversy about?
The controversy traces its origins to the ₹1,437-crore agreement signed on March 24, 1986, between the Government of India and Swedish arms manufacturer AB Bofors for the supply of 400 155 mm howitzer guns for the Indian Army.
The scandal erupted after Swedish Radio reported in April 1987, that illegal commissions had been paid to influential Indian politicians and defence officials to secure the contract.
CBI registered an FIR in January 1990 alleging offences including criminal conspiracy, cheating, forgery and corruption against former Bofors president Martin Ardbo, alleged middleman Win Chadha and the Hinduja brothers.
The central agency later filed charge sheets against several accused, including Italian businessman Ottavio Quattrocchi, before adding the Hinduja brothers through a supplementary charge sheet in October 2000.
Over the years, however, the prosecution steadily unravelled. Before Justice Sodhi’s 2005 judgment, another judge of the Delhi High Court, Justice JD Kapoor, had in February 2004 cleared former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi of any criminal culpability in the case while directing that a forgery charge be framed against the Bofors company.
Subsequently, Quattrocchi was discharged by a Delhi trial court in 2011 after repeated efforts to extradite him failed. He died in 2013, while several other accused, including Win Chadha, Martin Ardbo and former defence secretary SK Bhatnagar, also passed away during the prolonged proceedings.
With Thursday’s dismissal of Agrawal’s appeal, the last judicial challenge to the 2005 acquittal has come to an end, bringing the Bofors prosecution to its final legal closure after nearly 40 years.

headline: Tamil Nadu to table Assembly resolution seeking fairer share of central taxes
full_text:
Tamil Nadu to table Assembly resolution seeking fairer share of central taxes
Tamil Nadu is set to move an Assembly resolution seeking a fairer share of central taxes. The move renews the debate over devolution rules and the state's fiscal autonomy.
The Tamil Nadu government is likely to table a resolution in the Legislative Assembly today seeking a fair and equitable share of central taxes for the state. The resolution is expected to reiterate Tamil Nadu's demand for a larger share under the fiscal devolution mechanism, through which the Union government distributes a portion of its tax revenues among states.
According to government sources, the resolution will urge the Union government to ensure a more equitable distribution of tax revenues to Tamil Nadu and reiterate the state's longstanding demand for a larger share in fiscal devolution. It will also emphasise that the state's financial interests "will not be allowed to be compromised."
The move comes amid the continuing debate over the formula used to distribute central taxes among states, with Tamil Nadu maintaining that progressive states with stronger economic performance and better population control should not be penalised in the devolution process. Successive state governments have argued that the existing formula disproportionately disadvantages southern states despite their significant contribution to the national economy.
The issue has gained prominence in recent years as several southern states have raised concerns over the Centre's tax devolution formula, arguing that states which have performed well on economic and demographic indicators should not receive a smaller share of central resources.
The resolution is likely to trigger a fresh political debate over Centre-state financial relations, with the Tamil Nadu government expected to reiterate that ensuring a fair share of central taxes is essential to sustaining the state's development and welfare programmes while safeguarding its fiscal autonomy.

headline: The road that branches off the Thiruvalla-Kozhencherry State Highway towards Kumbanad in Pathanamthitta district in Kerala wears an air of permanent stillness.
full_text:
The road that branches off the Thiruvalla-Kozhencherry State Highway towards Kumbanad in Pathanamthitta district in Kerala wears an air of permanent stillness.
The heavy flow of vehicles and chatter of the highway quickly give way to an uncanny stillness. Behind ornate gates stand sprawling houses shaded by towering trees, their balconies empty, windows closed, and courtyards overrun by weeds.
On gates, compound walls and electricity poles, weather beaten flex boards announcing deaths ripple in the wind. Elsewhere in central Travancore, they merely announce deaths. But in Kumbanad, they seem to chronicle something far larger. Together, they tell the story of a village slowly outliving the generation that built it.
“You won’t believe this, but among all these houses in this entire neighbourhood, there is only one child, a three-year-old one. Now and then, the young boy comes out onto the terrace and calls out, ‘Appacha’, to me. That is one of the greatest joys of my life these days,“ says Brigadier (retired) Varghese Jacob, an octogenarian.
Like the countless parents in Kumbanad, Varghese too returned home after retirement while his children built their lives elsewhere. His two sons are living away from their hometown.
A few kilometres away, Joseph Mathew Kulathungal has watched the same story unfold over half a century. “The population of this village has more than halved over the decades. Who knows, one day it might even disappear from the map altogether,” he fears.
“It is almost like a clock ticking away. Either our village becomes a ghost, or we will become ghosts,” he laments.
Joseph, who left India in 1969 for Uganda, returned to the area in 2000. “Every time I came back, fewer people were living here,” he recalls.
His life traces the arc of a migration story shared by generations of Syrian Christian families across the lush plains between the Pampa and the Manimala rivers. Grand houses built with money earned overseas have fallen silent as succeeding generations chose to remain abroad, where they built their careers and lives.
Creepers have climbed compound walls, tiled roofs have disappeared beneath thick vegetation, and provision stores that once bustled with customers have slowly surrendered to the wilderness. One of Kerala’s most prosperous regions has thus become a settlement of ageing parents waiting for children who seldom return.
Dwindling numbers
The consequences are impossible to miss.
The anganwadi in Ward 12 of Koipuram panchayat, where Kumbanad falls, has just 11 children.
Enrolment at Koipuram Government Higher Secondary School, once among the largest schools in the region, has plunged from nearly 2,500 students two decades ago to around 80, according to Sharanya Vijayan, a civic representative from the region.
Private schools are battling the same decline.
For nearly a century, villages such as Kumbanad stood at the heart of one of Kerala’s most remarkable migration stories. Generation after generation left first for other parts of the country, then to the Gulf countries, and eventually to the United States, Canada, Europe or Australia. Their earnings transformed an agrarian landscape, funding schools, hospitals, and churches while filling the countryside with sprawling houses that became enduring symbols of prosperity.
Unlike northern Kerala, where migration was to the Gulf region and remained largely Gulf-oriented, Pathanamthitta witnessed successive waves of migration that eventually produced one of the State’s largest Western diaspora. Today, however, that cycle has broken.
The migrants remained overseas while their children built lives there. Increasingly, even the wealth that migration once poured into districts such as Pathanamthitta is beginning to flow back.
Peelipose Thomas, a veteran politician, recalls that a study conducted by the Reserve Bank of India a few decades ago had identified Kumbanad, Chavakkad and Varkala as the three regions receiving the highest foreign remittances. “However, Kumbanad stood apart with 80% of the deposits never withdrawn as families which earned it had already settled overseas.”
English education pays
Schools established by the Christian Missionary Society and the rapid expansion of higher education after Independence produced generations of English-educated youth ready to seize opportunities abroad. Migration rewarded those aspirations, fuelling a construction boom through the 1980s and 1990s and palatial houses in the region became monuments to this success.
“Migration from Pathanamthitta district began during the inter-World War period, when people first moved within Kerala in search of land and work. Later they migrated to Indian cities and, after Independence, increasingly overseas,” points out Varughese George, a veteran politician and a former member of the Kerala State Planning Board.
“Earlier, some cooperative banks even offered loans to obtain Gulf visas. Many who first migrated to the Gulf later moved directly to the United States or Canada instead of returning home,” he notes.
According to Varughese, the arrival of missionary institutions such as the Brethren Mission in Kumbanad helped reshape local aspirations by expanding access to education and exposing communities to Western ideas and culture. As families prospered overseas, remittances financed the rapid expansion of Pentecostal denominations such as the Indian Pentecostal Church and the Brethren Church, which reshaped the region’s social geography.
Several institutions, jokingly called Kumbanad University, had sprung up in the region offering diploma programmes in several trades, which helped thousands secure jobs abroad.
Ginu Zacharia Oommen, social scientist, notes the “liberalisation of United States immigration laws in 1965 unlocked unprecedented opportunities for skilled migrants from Central Travancore, mostly comprising Kottayam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha and Idukki districts which brought back wealth and reshaped the life and culture of the region.”
“The children raised abroad gradually lost the emotional bond their parents had with their homeland and don’t want to maintain these houses. They come here for family functions, stay for a couple of weeks and leave.”
Ageing population
The consequences are etched all across Pathanamthitta district. Official estimates suggest that more than 61,000 houses in the district remain unoccupied for most of the year, averaging nearly 1,000 locked houses in every local body. Eraviperoor panchayat alone has 2,632 such houses.
A 2025 report by the Department of Health paints the picture of a district growing old at remarkable speed. Nearly 19% of Pathanamthitta’s population is above 60 years of age, while only 6.8% is below six. The district’s Total Fertility Rate has fallen to 1.3, the lowest in Kerala and far below replacement level.
“The most obvious impact is the steady population decline, which could eventually affect the number of Assembly constituencies in the district. Church leaders have already expressed concern over this,” notes Ginu.
Economic impact
Social scientists feel that the story is not just about migration, but about economic and demographic decline too.
S. Irudaya Rajan, Chairman of the International Institute of Migration and Development and a migration studies expert, observes that the locked houses are merely the most visible markers of a much deeper shift. “The abandoned houses are the most visible manifestation of a demographic shift that has been unfolding quietly for decades. Every young person who leaves in search of higher education or better opportunities abroad also takes away the district’s future. What is left behind is an ageing population, empty classrooms, and villages slowly losing the critical mass needed to sustain their economy, institutions and community life,” he notes.
The Kerala Migration Survey 2023 captures that transformation in numbers. The number of emigrants from the district has fallen from around 1.41 lakh a decade ago to 1.01 lakh, while return migrants have declined from 54,537 in 1998 to 40,921 in 2023. Although remittances per household have increased, the district’s share of Kerala’s inward remittances has dropped from 7.2% to 4.3%.
For the first time, the survey also estimated Kerala’s outward remittances at ₹43,378 crore, nearly one-fifth of inward remittances. The finding signals a profound shift. Money, like people, has begun to flow out.
Irudaya Rajan notes that at least 5% of Pathanamthitta district’s elderly now lives alone, while another 10-15% lives only with their spouses as their children are settled overseas.
The changing priorities of expatriates are becoming all the more evident in their financial decisions as well.
“When the Kerala State Financial Enterprises launched Pravasi Chitty in 2008 for the expats, we received an overwhelming response from the Gulf countries, but it received very little participation from those settled in the West. They no longer want to invest their savings in a land to where they do not intend to return,” feels Peelipose Thomas.
Varghese Alexander, a senior chartered accountant based in Thiruvalla, observes that there is a definite decline in inward remittances, while outward flows are increasing, impacting the local economy, particularly the real estate market.
As the district enters this new demographic phase, it is confronted with a question no previous generation had to grapple with: what remains after the migration wave has finally run its course?
For Irudaya Rajan, that question defines the future of the central Travancore region. “Kerala is no longer losing its human capital alone but its assets accumulated through generations as well. Expatriate families from districts such as Pathanamthitta are now influencing housing markets abroad with investments financed by the sale of ancestral properties here.”
“First the people left. Now their assets are leaving too. That may well be the dead end of a century-long migration story,” he notes.
As the sun sets, sitting on the portico of his house, Varghese Jacob waits for his favourite young neighbour to appear, to call him Appacha, once again. A call that connects him to his life and land, which is fast disappearing.

headline: Under the revised norms, candidates won't be denied admission merely because their UDID card or disability certificate is temporary.
full_text:
Under the revised norms, candidates won't be denied admission merely because their UDID card or disability certificate is temporary.
NEW DELHI: Candidates cannot be denied admission to MBBS courses under the PwBD quota solely because they hold a temporary disability certificate or Unique Disability Identity (UDID) card, National Medical Commission (NMC) said. However, it made it clear that their disability status will continue to be verified by medical assessment boards (MABs) before they are declared eligible for counselling.In an addendum to "Guidelines on Assessment of Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) for Admission to the MBBS Course, 2026", NMC Wednesday said the change has been made to ensure that the guidelines are interpreted in line with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, 2024 Rules and a 2025 office memorandum issued by the department of empowerment of persons with disabilities.Under the revised norms, candidates whose disabilities are categorised as progressive, non-progressive or not likely to improve will not be denied admission merely because their UDID card or disability certificate is temporary. Their disability status, however, will continue to be verified by designated MABs before an eligibility certificate is issued. Candidates holding temporary UDID cards whose disability has been recorded as "likely to improve" will undergo reassessment before their eligibility is decided.
MABs will also assess each candidate's functional competency."This year's revised guidelines unnecessarily created a new hurdle by introducing a distinction between temporary and permanent disabilities. I received multiple representations from students who were being harassed at assessment centres in Agartala, Mumbai and Delhi. That prompted us to submit a representation to NMC and raise this issue in the ongoing SC hearing as well," disability rights activist Prof Satendra Singh said.NMC said the addendum has been issued to ensure uniform implementation of admission guidelines and should be read as an integral part of the July 27 notification.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

headline: Renukaswamy murder case: Fresh setback for Darshan as aides seek approver status
full_text:
Renukaswamy murder case: Fresh setback for Darshan as aides seek approver status
The move by three accused to seek approver status marks a significant twist in the high-profile murder case. If one or more of them are ultimately granted pardon and testify before the trial court, their evidence could play a key role in the prosecution's case against Darshan and the other accused.
In a significant development in the Renukaswamy murder case involving actor Darshan and others, three accused have approached the Sessions Court seeking approver status, a move that could potentially strengthen the prosecution's case.
Accused No. 14, Pradosh, was the first to move the court, seeking pardon under the law in return for making a full and truthful disclosure of the circumstances surrounding the murder. Soon after, accused Nos. 8 and 10 — Ravi Shankar and Vinay — also filed applications seeking approver status.
Special Public Prosecutor (SPP) Prasanna Kumar has given his consent to Pradosh's request by submitting a memo before the 59th Sessions Court. The prosecution said Pradosh would be granted approver status subject to certain conditions, including making a full and truthful disclosure of the role of every accused in the case.
During the hearing, senior advocate Divakar, appearing for Pradosh, argued that his client's application should be considered independently and not be clubbed with those filed later by Ravi Shankar and Vinay. He contended that the prosecution alone has the authority to decide who should be made an approver.
Appearing for Vinay, advocate Ranganath Reddy argued that merely because an accused files an application seeking pardon, the prosecution should not automatically accept it. He said the decision on selecting an approver rests solely with the prosecution after examining the circumstances.
Darshan's counsel, Hashmath Pasha, strongly opposed the prosecution's move to grant approver status to Pradosh. He argued that the defence had not been informed about the filing of the application during the previous hearing and sought a copy of the plea. He further contended that pardon cannot be granted immediately upon an accused seeking it and insisted that the accused's statement must first be recorded before the prosecution extends its consent. The defence argued that an approver should aid the cause of justice rather than merely strengthen the prosecution's case.
Countering these submissions, Special Public Prosecutor (SPP) Prasanna Kumar argued that the remaining accused have no legal right to object to an application seeking approver status. He submitted that while the remaining accused may challenge the procedure adopted by the prosecution and the court, they cannot object to the prosecution's decision to consider an accused for approver status. The SPP also informed the court that the prosecution's consent had been given after considering Pradosh's statement.
During his arguments, the prosecutor relied on a High Court order relating to Basavaraj Muttagi, who turned approver in the Yogesh Gowda murder case. He argued that courts must evaluate whether the accused seeking pardon is the principal offender or someone with a comparatively lesser role before deciding on the application.
Pradosh has also filed a separate plea requesting prison authorities to keep him away from Darshan and the other accused during judicial custody. He told the court that he feared pressure and possible intimidation if housed in the same prison barrack and sought to be lodged in a separate cell. He also requested to be produced before the court separately during future hearings.
According to the prosecution's chargesheet, Pradosh allegedly received Rs 30 lakh from Darshan and played a key role in arranging for other accused to surrender. Investigators alleged that he was present at the Pattanagere shed where the victim was allegedly confined, informed Darshan about Renukaswamy's death, brought actor Pavithra Gowda (an accused) to the shed, actively participated in the alleged conspiracy, and now faces charges of murder, destruction of evidence and joint criminal liability.
Investigators have also alleged that Pradosh was present at the crime scene and had asked Darshan to stop the assault on Renukaswamy. If accepted as an approver, his testimony could prove crucial, as he is considered both an eyewitness and an insider to the alleged conspiracy.
The 59th Sessions Court heard detailed arguments from all sides on Pradosh's application and reserved its order until August 10. The court will also decide on the objections raised by the other accused regarding the prosecution's decision. The matter has been posted for further hearing on Monday.
The move by three accused to seek approver status marks a significant twist in the high-profile murder case. If one or more of them are ultimately granted pardon and testify before the trial court, their evidence could play a key role in the prosecution's case against Darshan and the other accused. However, the final decision on granting approver status rests with the Sessions Court after considering the prosecution's recommendation and the legal requirements under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

headline: How Tata, Vembu's Zoho saved India's first MRI machine maker from MNC shark
full_text:
How Tata, Vembu's Zoho saved India's first MRI machine maker from MNC shark
Bengaluru startup Voxelgrids is making India's first MRI machine, which will reduce scan cost by up to 70%. However, a global giant sought to buy it out. It was funding from Tata Trusts and Sridhar Vembu's Zoho that helped stave off any buyout bids, reveals Arjun Arunachalam, founder and CEO of Voxelgrids.
The world's Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) industry is dominated by a handful of global giants. Some of those giants are sharks as well. They are always on the hunt to gobble up smaller manufacturers that bring innovative technologies and retain their dominance. That's what India's first MRI maker, the Bengaluru-based Voxelgrids faced. However, funding support from Tata Trusts and Sridhar Vembu's Zoho helped Arjun Arunachalam continue on the path of his dream to build an affordable MRI machine and provide it to every corner of India.
For decades, countries like the US, Germany, Japan, China, Italy and the Netherlands have built MRI machines that hospitals across the world use, and India is one of their biggest customers.
Voxelgrids founder and CEO, Arjun Arunachalam, was running out of money while building one of the world's most complex medical devices, and competing against corporations worth billions of dollars. So when a multinational giant approached Voxelgrids with an offer during the Covid-19 pandemic, Arunachalam could have taken the easy way out.
Instead, Arunachalam walked away. He viewed that partnering with a multinational would come at the cost of the very innovation he was trying to build. It is common knowledge that most MNC giants offer to be partners and then gobble up their partners.
What made the 47-year-old electronic engineer Arunachalam's resolve stronger was a financial lifeline from Tata Trusts, then led by Ratan Tata, and later Vembu. The funding allowed the startup to survive long enough to develop what could become India's first indigenous MRI scanner — a machine that Arunachalam says could eventually reduce the cost of an MRI scan by around 70% and make advanced diagnostics accessible in every corner of the country.
"We thought partnering with the company would risk our innovation," Arunachalam told India Today Digital.
What Voxelgrids has manufactured is almost a miracle in the field of medical devices. Its MRI machines will be 40% cheaper and 50% lighter, which will further reduce the installation costs. This will be a mini-revolution in a country that imports Rs 3,500 crore worth of MRI-related products annually.
HOW ARUNACHALAM DECIDED TO BUILD INDIA'S FIRST MRI MACHINE
Arunachalam, speaking to India Today Digital, said that building an MRI scanner is often compared to building a jet engine or a rocket.
MRI machines are among the most expensive and technologically demanding medical devices ever created, requiring years of research, enormous capital and expertise across physics, electronics, software and precision engineering.
Arunachalam knew exactly what he was taking on.
An electrical engineer specialising in MRI physics, he studied at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the US before spending nearly three years at GE HealthCare's research centre in America around 2008-09.
"I was very fortunate enough to work at GE's research centre. That experience is coming of help in the building of MRI machines in India," he said.
After his stint at GE, Arunachalam moved to Singapore, and having briefly taught at IIT Bombay, he realised what was frustrating him.
"I wanted to do research on MRIs and build something innovative, but we had to beg to use somebody else's machine. Companies that built MRIs had no interest in working with Indian institutes because they didn't consider us a serious country," Arunachalam told India Today Digital while remembering his days at IIT Bombay as a professor.
That frustration gradually evolved into a mission.
"I also wanted to do something meaningful in India and stay here," Arunachalam said, adding, "My father was an Indian Air Force officer."
Patriotism must have been an everyday lesson for Arunachalam at home.
WHY DIDN'T INDIA BUILD AN MRI MACHINE? NO, IT'S NOT ABOUT THE COST
For Arunachalam, the problem extends beyond imports. "The harsh truth of us as a country is that we don't build anything," he said.
India imports every MRI scanner installed in its hospitals. "Last year alone, MRI imports were valued at roughly Rs 3,500 crore," Arunachalam told India Today Digital.
Those imports eventually translate into higher costs for patients.
An average MRI scan in India costs nearly Rs 10,000, making it unaffordable for many families in the country.
"The demand is huge. Anybody who buys a CT scanner wants an MRI," Arunachalam said.
Yet MRI adoption continues to lag behind CT scanners.
According to him, India has nearly three times more CT scanners than MRI machines, largely because imported MRI systems remain expensive to purchase, install and maintain.
"There is a global product-fit issue with MRI machines," Arunachalam said.
HOW A SMALL BENGALURU-BASED PLAYER BUILT MRI MACHINES
Instead of trying to imitate established manufacturers, Arunachalam's Voxelgrids started with a blank sheet of paper.
"The bigger giants have restrictions. They can't innovate and pivot quickly because of regulatory structures. That's an advantage for smaller players like us," he said.
According to Arunachalam, initially, his company wanted to develop only MRI imaging software and intellectual property.
But existing manufacturers would not allow outsiders to innovate in their systems.
"They would attach monetary value to our IP," he said.
That forced a far bigger decision, and Arunchalam decided to build his own MRI machine.
Everything, from software to electronics, was designed in-house by a team that has grown from just four engineers to 33 now.
"Our image quality is equal to any MRI. Our design is different," Arunachalam told India Today Digital.
HOW MACHINE BUILT BY VOXELGIRDS WILL CUT MRI COSTS
The biggest promise of Voxelgrids' MRI isn't simply that it is made in India. It is that it has been designed differently from the ground up.
Its internal magnet architecture is different. It uses around one-third the number of cables found in conventional MRI systems, according to Arunachalam.
The electronic packaging consumes significantly less power. The MRI machine is lighter.
Most importantly, it has an option of using nitrogen instead of helium, one of the world's most expensive non-renewable gases that India imports for MRI systems.
"Every software is in-house, and that is the most expensive thing anyone can achieve," Arunachalam said.
All these changes dramatically reduce manufacturing and operating costs.
The savings, he says, will eventually reach patients. "MRI scanning will become affordable," he said.
Arunachalam estimates that scan prices could fall by around 70%, with costs eventually dropping to nearly 40% of current prices as indigenous manufacturing scales up.
"Our goal is simple. The Indian-made MRI should reach every corner of the country," he told India Today Digital.
RATAN TATA'S SUPPORT FOR MADE-IN-INDIA MRI MACHINE
The vision of Arunachalam nearly ended before it began. Funding remained the biggest challenge.
"Tata Trusts was the first organisation that believed in us," Arunachalam recalled while speaking to India Today Digital.
He first approached the Trust in 2015, when Ratan Tata was still actively involved.
The then Managing Trustee, R Venkataramanan, invited Arunachalam to Mumbai after seeing potential in the technology he was building.
"The Tatas showed genuine interest," Arunachalam said, revealing that he met Ratan Tata, then Chairman of Tata Trusts, twice.
"Ratan Tata wanted to see technologies that helped the country grow," he added.
The relationship became even more critical during Covid-19, when Voxelgrids was struggling to survive.
Arunachalam revealed that he continuously wrote to Tata Trusts updating them about the progress of the machine.
Eventually, Ratan Tata's then personal secretary, Delnaz Gilder, helped arrange another meeting.
Tata Trusts agreed to financially support the company by placing what Arunachalam describes as an "order for the machine".
"We didn't have a product, and Ratan Tata had provided us with orders. That's how great and humble he was. I'm so grateful," Arunachalam said.
WHEN SRIDHAR VEMBU'S ZOHO BACKED INDIA'S MRI MACHINE
Even after Tata's support, the journey remained uncertain. Following Ratan Tata's passing, Arunachalam says the startup's relationship with Tata Trusts naturally evolved, and new sources of support became crucial.
Government funding through the National Biopharma Mission helped keep development alive.
But another breakthrough came through an introduction to Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu. One of Arunachalam's acquaintances connected him to Vembu in 2021.
Being an electrical engineer himself, Vembu immediately understood both the technological challenge and the long-term national importance of the project.
"He said, I know this is a big challenge. I'll still give the money. Let us see if you develop a good product," Arunachalam told India Today Digital.
That investment allowed Voxelgrids to continue independently instead of compromising its technology through a partnership with a multinational.
WHY ARUNACHALAM REJECTED OFFER FROM MNC MRI GIANT
According to Arunachalam, multinational manufacturers understand just how difficult it is for startups to survive in MRI manufacturing.
"They know small firms cannot survive because building an MRI machine needs a lot of money," he told India Today Digital.
Many expect startups to eventually run out of cash. That's precisely why Voxelgrids refused to surrender control.
"We had no interest in partnering with a bigger firm," he said.
Instead, the startup chose the harder route of building patiently, spending cautiously and making fewer expensive mistakes than global corporations could afford.
"People ask why it is taking longer," Arunachalam said. "That is exactly how we are building a cheaper machine," he added.
For a company competing against some of the biggest names in medical technology, survival itself has been a victory. If Voxelgrids succeeds in bringing its indigenous MRI to hospitals across India, Arunachalam believes the impact will go far beyond one machine.
It could mean that a technology once reserved for major cities and expensive hospitals finally becomes affordable enough to reach distant hospitals, smaller diagnostic centres and millions of patients who currently cannot afford it.

headline: The Supreme Court on Thursday allowed interim bail to a cyber-security researcher accused by the Chennai Police of unauthorisedly accessing computer networks and extracting insurance-related data.
full_text:
The Supreme Court on Thursday allowed interim bail to a cyber-security researcher accused by the Chennai Police of unauthorisedly accessing computer networks and extracting insurance-related data.
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant issued notice to the State of Tamil Nadu, returnable on September 18.
The petitioner-cyber researcher, Himanshu Pathak, had moved the Supreme Court after the Madras High Court, on July 3, rejected his plea to quash the chargesheet filed against him by the CCB Cyber Crime Police Station for offences under Sections 66 (punishment for accessing computer systems or networks without permission) read with 43(b) (extraction of data from a computer) under the Information Technology Act.
The special leave petition filed by Mr. Pathak, besides the State of Tamil Nadu, has arraigned Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd as respondents. Mr. Pathak was represented by advocates Prashant Bhushan and Cheryl Dsouza. Advocate B. Karunakaran accepted notice on behalf of the State. Advocate Shloka Narayanan, who appeared on caveat on behalf of the respondent insurance company, accepted notice on behalf of her client.
The court asked the State to also “furnish details of similar cases/criminal antecedents, if any, pending/registered against the petitioner”.
The Bench directed the petitioner to appear before the Saidapet Magistrate court concerned to furnish bail bonds to be admitted to interim bail. The apex court also allowed the petitioner to apply for exemption from personal appearance.
The petition argued that the case raised “important questions concerning the threshold at which criminal prosecution under Sections 43(b) and 66 may be legitimately be permitted to proceed and the duty of the High Court to interdiction prosecutions, which, even if accepted at their highest, fail to disclose the essential ingredients of the alleged offence”.
The petitioner’s case was that he, while accessing the insurance records of his father’s policy issued by the insurance company in 2022, “discovered that its digital infrastructure exposed complete policyholder records through an unsecured legacy API which responded to unauthenticated requests merely upon alteration of the policy number”.
The petitioner blamed “pre-existing vulnerability” in the company’s own legacy application. He said he had also communicated with CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team).
The petition also recorded the prosecution version which said the petitioner “deliberately accessed Respondent 2’s (company) computer resources without authorisation, extracted approximately 8000 policyholder records, demanded annual consultancy charges of USD 65000 together with monthly maintenance charges of USD 3000 and threatened leaking of confidential customer information…”

headline: 'Shaking' well in Gujarat's Morbi sparks curiousity among villagers
full_text:
'Shaking' well in Gujarat's Morbi sparks curiousity among villagers
A farm well in Morbi has shown continuous waves and overflow for five days. Officials suspect groundwater recharge and trapped air, not seismic activity, behind the disturbance.
An 18-foot-deep well in Gujarat's Morbi district has become the centre of curiousity after its water began showing continuous waves and ripples for the past five days, attracting hundreds of villagers and passersby eager to witness the unusual phenomenon.
The well, located on the farm of Pranjivan Sadariya in Virparda village of Morbi taluka, has sparked widespread speculation, with many initially fearing the movement could be linked to seismic activity.
However, district officials have ruled out any connection with earthquakes, saying preliminary findings point to a natural geological process.
WATER HAS BEEN SHAKING FOR FIVE DAYS
According to the well's owner, Pranjivan Sadariya, he first noticed the unusual activity on August 2.
"When I arrived at my farm on Sunday, water from the well was spilling over the edge, and the same thing has continued ever since," he said.
Sadariya said the well was constructed around three months ago.
Local residents said the water was first seen shaking on Sunday and Monday. The movement briefly stopped on Tuesday before resuming on Wednesday and Thursday, fuelling further curiosity.
As news of the mysterious well spread, people from Virparda and neighbouring villages began gathering at the site. Travellers passing along the nearby highway have also been stopping to watch the continuously rippling water.
The unusual sight has become a major talking point across the region, with many waiting for experts to determine the exact cause.
EXPERTS RULE OUT EARTHQUAKE
District Geologist J S Vadher said there was no evidence of seismic activity behind the phenomenon.
"This is not seismic activity. Prima facie, it appears that following heavy upstream rainfall, groundwater is recharging and air trapped in the pore spaces of rocks is being released, causing the disturbance in the well," Vadher said.
Officials also consulted the Institute of Seismological Research (ISR) in Gandhinagar, which reportedly confirmed that there is no active fault line in the area.
Morbi District Collector Swapnil Khare said the state government had been informed and a team from Gandhinagar would visit the site for a detailed scientific investigation. "We have informed the Gujarat government about it, and a team from Gandhinagar will visit the site for further investigation," Khare said.
GROUNDWATER RECHARGE SEEN AS LIKELY CAUSE
According to the preliminary assessment by the district administration, the well's behaviour is most likely linked to recent heavy rainfall.
Officials believe the rains have rapidly recharged underground aquifers, forcing trapped air through pores and fractures in the rocks beneath the well. The escaping air is believed to be creating continuous turbulence, resulting in the persistent ripples seen on the water's surface.
While the initial findings point to a natural hydrogeological process, officials said the exact cause would be confirmed only after the expert team from Gandhinagar completes its investigation.

FIR against PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti, daughter Iltija for ‘assaulting’ cops

headline: The Centre maintained that altering reservation policies requires empirical research and legislative action.
full_text:
The Centre maintained that altering reservation policies requires empirical research and legislative action.
NEW DELHI: Opposing the application of the 'creamy layer' criterion for exclusion of affluent members of scheduled caste and scheduled tribe communities from benefits of reservation in jobs and admissions to educational institutions, the government has told the Supreme Court that discrimination against SCs/STs and OBC/SEBC communities do not happen only due to economic considerations."Keeping the broader concept of equality in view, discrimination against SC, ST and OBC/SEBC communities do not happen only based on economic conditions. The system of reservation aims to provide fair opportunities, reduce economic disparities, and foster diversity in governance and academia by addressing historical marginalisation," it said.On Aug 1, 2024, a seven-judge top court verdict permitted states to sub-categorise castes within SC communities based on socio-economic backwardness and the degree of under-representation in government jobs to ensure that the larger pie of 15% quota goes to the most backward. The court had asked governments to devise suitable criteria to bar the 'creamy layer' among the Supreme Court from availing reservation.Filing the affidavit nearly a year after Supreme Court sought response to a PIL by two people - one belonging to SC community and the other to OBC category - on Aug 11 last year, the government said, "Modification of reservation policy, particularly to introduce income-based preferences within reserved categories, should be preceded by a holistic review and thorough empirical study, including socio-economic data of reserved category beneficiaries" and could be done only by Parliament.
Parliament alone can modify the list of SC and ST communities entitled to quota, it further stressed.Elaborating upon, it said caste, tribe or part of or group within any caste/tribe can be included or excluded from the list of SCs or STs issued under Articles 341(1) and 342 only by Parliament by law and it is not open to state governments or courts or tribunals or any other authority to modify, amend or alter the list of SCs or STs specified in the notification issued under Clause (1) of Article 341 or 342.
Now similar provisions have been made for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBC) through the Constitution (One Hundred and Second Amendment) Act, 2018, it said.The government said, "In the majority of schemes of welfare and development of SC, ST, and SEBC, excepting reservation in educational institutions and reservation in services under the state, there is a means test which ensures that benefits of schemes percolate to those who actually deserve them."
