headline: From NTA's Delhi building to Pune: How NEET questions made it out
full_text:
From NTA's Delhi building to Pune: How NEET questions made it out
At the centre of the 20,000-page chargesheet are three Pune-based experts appointed by the NTA who allegedly originated the leak.
NTA reused the same three subject experts across multiple stages of preparing NEET-UG 2026’s question paper — one of them across all four stages, from item writing to back-translation — and allowed them to see all four of the exam’s master question sets during the final stage, according to the Central Bureau of Investigation’s charge sheet in the paper leak case. Both design choices, the charge sheet sets out, violated NTA’s own protocols. Together, they gave a small group of experts continuous access to most sensitive material for weeks.
“Many experts have been involved in multiple stages,” the charge sheet states. “From the moderation step onwards, the experts concerned have full access to the final sets of questions. This is particularly so in the translation/back-translation stage as a single expert can see all four of the final master sets.”
Also read: 'Hands off our Jantar Mantar': CJP reacts sharply to HC's remarks on protest site
A special court in Delhi is listed to take cognisance of the charge sheet, roughly 20,000 pages, on Monday. At its centre are three Pune-based experts appointed by the National Testing Agency — Manisha Gurunath Mandhare for Botany and Zoology, Prahlad Vithalrao Kulkarni for Chemistry, and Manisha Sanjay Havaldar for Physics. The charge sheet names 13 accused in all; the three experts, who allegedly originated the leak, have been charged under sections covering criminal breach of trust and misconduct by public servants. The CBI has said it found no evidence implicating any government official, including any NTA office-bearer.
Where the access came from
The charge sheet places the theft at NTA’s NSIC Building in Okhla, where all four stages of paper preparation were conducted in what the agency itself calls a “sanitised environment.” Mandhare, per the charge sheet’s timeline, was engaged there across every stage: item writing between February 20 and 24, vetting from March 5 to 7, translation from March 9 to 14, and back-translation from March 31 to April 2. Kulkarni’s services were used for item writing (February 22 to 26) and back-translation (March 31 to April 2). Havaldar’s engagement was shorter — translation on March 14, then back-translation from March 31 to April 2.
Also read: WhatsApp groups, photographs, Telegram: The digital trail that led to NEET UG paper leak
In that three-day window, all three could see all four master sets at once — internally identified as Kailash, Shivalik, Set 2 and Set 3. NTA had not built firewalls between the sets.
Kulkarni allegedly took plain rough-work paper supplied inside the confidential hall and transcribed 135 Chemistry questions with their answer options onto small chits, which he then walked out of the building with. Mandhare and Havaldar, the CBI alleges, memorised the framing and exact parameters, returned to their Delhi hotel rooms, cross-referenced them against textbooks, and transcribed them into personal notebooks.
The charge sheet’s findings sit awkwardly against what the Centre told the Supreme Court just days ago. In an affidavit on the NEET-UG 2026 matter on August 4, the government said question-paper preparation happens in complete isolation, with no electronic devices allowed and every entrant frisked, and that the premises are “under CCTV surveillance and are guarded round the clock by the Central Armed Police Forces.” CBI’s charge sheet alleges that no frisking or metal-detector checks were conducted when experts entered or exited the confidential section, that CCTV feeds were not monitored live, and that only 20-25 days of footage were available when investigators sought the recordings — work in the confidential section had ended on April 7, and the case was only lodged on May 12, so none of the retained backup covered the relevant period.
The government’s affidavit also said no single individual has visibility of the complete paper at any stage, and that multiple question sets are developed independently by separate teams before moving in parallel through translation, printing and storage. By CBI’s account, from the moderation stage onwards, experts handling the papers had access to the complete final sets, with translation and back-translation providing visibility of all four master papers simultaneously.
The ‘leak’
Back in Pune, each of the three ran a different operation with what they had taken.
Mandhare ran her Biology classes at her residence in Ganga Osian Park, Pune, for eight students. Class coordination went through a WhatsApp group she had created in November last year and named “Fifa world cup 2026.” Her method, as the charge sheet describes it, centred on the students’ own textbooks — they bought fresh NCERT Class XI and XII copies, on which she marked exact paragraphs containing the leaked questions and dictated the question formulations into the margins. Students transcribed these into a “fair notebook,” which Mandhare corrected herself. Manisha Sanjay Waghmare, a Pune facilitator the CBI describes as running the operation out of her husband’s dental clinic, later collected the physical registers from students, including two named in the charge sheet— Diya Shinde and Snehanjali Deshmukh — to have them digitised.
Also read: How a 'Fifa world cup 2026' WhatsApp group exposed NEET leak
Kulkarni’s Chemistry classes ran at his house in Nanded City, Pune, from April 25-27, for nine students arranged by Waghmare. Investigators corroborated the timing independently: MyGate, the access-control app used by his housing society, had logged the entry, exit and biometrics of visiting students and parents through April, which the CBI cross-checked against call records and phone-location data. CBI also recovered nine images of Chemistry questions and answer slips from Kulkarni’s phone that matched the actual paper, alongside WhatsApp chats in which a parent asked for his address to hand him a watch in exchange for questions.
Havaldar did not run classes of her own. CBI’s account places her at the centre of a series of one-off transactions instead. On April 14, at her home, she dictated 68 Physics questions to Tejas Harshadkumar Shah, COO at Dr Abhang Prabhu Medical Academy in Pune, in exchange for ₹25,000 in cash and a box of mangoes. Shah transcribed them onto 16 pages. On April 25, he sent high-resolution WhatsApp images of the transcript to Havaldar’s husband, Sanjay Sudhakar Havaldar, who forwarded them to Mandhare. On April 27, Mandhare brought one Dr Usha Adhav to Havaldar’s office. Havaldar transferred the images to her office computer by USB, printed hard copies for Adhav for another ₹25,000, and — the charge sheet notes — the CCTV captured the exchange.
Kulkarni’s chits also travelled outside Pune. Kulkarni dictated the leaked questions to the son of Shivraj Motegaonkar, who runs the Renukai Career Centre in Latur, as part of the special classes. Motegaonkar circulated handwritten Chemistry questions to his own students through a coaching-centre WhatsApp group and later posted a video on social media claiming he had “predicted the entire Chemistry paper for NEET UG 2026.” Most questions in his April mock test appeared in the actual exam, CBI has said.
Also read: 47 NTA officials sacked amid nationwide student protests, more cleanup to follow
An expert panel constituted by Delhi University later matched the recovered leaked material against the four master sets at CBI’s request. Of the 68 Physics questions Havaldar had dictated to Shah, the panel found that only two did not appear in any of the four master sets; the other 66 did. Across the wider body of material recovered from aspirants and intermediaries, the match ran as high as 85% on sets the three experts had access to.
How it came apart
A Kerala MBBS student forwarded the leaked PDFs to his father’s landlord in Sikar. The landlord took them to a local Chemistry teacher, Shashikant Suthar. Suthar reported the leak directly to the director general of NTA on May 7. NTA cancelled the exam five days later and handed the case to CBI.
Arrests began within days. Waghmare was picked up on May 14, Kulkarni on May 15, Mandhare on May 16, and Havaldar on May 22. Nine others named in the charge sheet — including Shah, the Pune intermediary Dhananjay Nivrutti Lokhande, and Nashik-based Shubham Madhukar Khairnar, who allegedly paid Lokhande ₹25 lakh for the digitised material — were arrested through the same period. As the digital chain widened, intermediaries used disguised usernames to blur the trail — Yash Yadav operated on Telegram as “hunter23i” and communicated with Mangilal Biwal under “@Hindustan8360”; PDFs were printed at cyber cafes with instructions to delete the files afterwards.
Efforts to destroy the record began around the same time, per the charge sheet. Havaldar burned her master Physics notebook in her kitchen. Shah destroyed his 16-page handwritten notebook. Lokhande, who had typists digitise Waghmare’s collected registers at her husband’s dental clinic, threw his iPhone 14 Pro Max onto a highway. Khairnar said he had dropped his primary phone from a moving motorcycle. Shopkeepers along the chain were forced to Delete for Everyone on their messaging apps.

headline: August keeps the needle moving forward for monsoon | Number Theory
full_text:
August keeps the needle moving forward for monsoon | Number Theory
El Niño may hurt India’s monsoon, making August crucial. IMD data shows rainfall is reducing deficits in many states, but the rain is not ideal everywhere
An El Nino that is currently underway is expected to crimp India’s June-September monsoon, which accounts for 75% of the country’s annual rain. This makes rainfall trends very important in August, which is the second rainiest month of the year after July and accounts for 30% of monsoon rain. HT’s analysis of the gridded rainfall data of the India Meteorological Department (IMD) shows that August rain has not disappointed in filling up country-level rain deficit and decreasing seeing deficit rain in many states. However, not all of the rainfall has been ideal. Here is why.
- This is an average first week of August, but it has decreased monsoon deficit to its lowest level since June 5According to IMD’s gridded data, India has received 63.1 mm rain in the first week of August. This is 61st highest or 66th lowest rain since 1901, the first year for which IMD has published gridded data, making this an average August so far. As expected, rain’s departure from the 1971-2020 average, which IMD currently considers as the Long Period Average (LPA) for tracking rain’s performance, is also modest so far: 1.6%. To be sure, any surplus is welcome this monsoon season, which was reeling with a 31% deficit compared to the LPA at the end of June. The August surplus, for example, has now brought the cumulative deficit down to 9%, the lowest it has been since June 5, when the season had just started.
- The surplus this week also came without a big surplus in intense rainAccording to IMD’s gridded data, India has received 63.1 mm rain in the first week of August. This is 61st highest or 66th lowest rain since 1901, the first year for which IMD has published gridded data, making this an average August so far. As expected, rain’s departure from the 1971-2020 average, which IMD currently considers as the Long Period Average (LPA) for tracking rain’s performance, is also modest so far: 1.6%. To be sure, any surplus is welcome this monsoon season, which was reeling with a 31% deficit compared to the LPA at the end of June. The August surplus, for example, has now brought the cumulative deficit down to 9%, the lowest it has been since June 5, when the season had just started.
- The geographical distribution of rain was not always idealTo be sure, India’s heavy rain total can look usual irrespective of whether it falls in Goa (a place used to such rain) or Gurugram (a place not used to such rain). Some of the heavy rain this month has indeed fallen over Gurugram. This is also reflected in the skew in the geographical distribution of rain. IMD describes a surplus of 60% or more as “large excess” and that between 20% and 60% as “excess”. Deficits of similar levels are described as “large deficient” and “deficient”, with rain within 20% of LPA called “normal”. 49% of the country is either deficient or large deficient in rain this month and 32% has got either excess or large excess of rain. Clearly, the average-looking surplus this month has been distributed unevenly geographically.
- But the places with surplus were often places running deficit before AugustSome states might welcome the geographical skew in August rain somewhat. Of the 33 states and UTs for which this calculation is possible using the gridded data, 19 saw the area under deficient and large deficient categories decrease this week compared to the cumulative status on July 31 and another four saw no change, with only 10 seeing a growth in such area. Even among these 10, only six have seen the area under the two categories grow to more than one third of the state’s area. Rajasthan, Haryana, and Madhya Pradesh are the only big states among these six states. This means that big surplus in August often happened in places that needed it. That helped with rain accumulation, but has also led to disasters.
- ABOUT THE AUTHORAbhishek JhaAbhishek Jha is Assistant Editor-Data at Hindustan Times. He uses statistical programming to generate newsworthy insights from large datasets. He is part of the team that produces Number Theory, a daily data story feature of the paper’s print edition. Since March 2024, he has been writing Weather Bee, a weekly column for the Hindustan Times website. headline: The measure — known officially as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026 — sets a headline ceiling but leaves the actual rate to be set by the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), and carries a presidential waiver requirin...
full_text:
The measure — known officially as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026 — sets a headline ceiling but leaves the actual rate to be set by the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), and carries a presidential waiver requiring certification to Congress with reassessment every 180 days. The bill permits — but does not necessarily compel — the executive to act against the five named purchasers — China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan — with sponsors saying the rate should be pitched high enough to deter Chinese and Indian buying.
India has in the past, when it was slapped with a 25% additional levy that has since been removed after trade negotiations, called such moves unfair since Russian exports are soaked up by a number of other countries. India has also stated that its energy purchases are guided by its energy security needs.
The bill now moves to the House of Representatives, where Republicans control the floor calendar and where its passage in identical form is the last hurdle before it reaches President Donald Trump for signature. Trump, whose officials helped shape the softened text now before Congress, has signalled support for House passage.
“Today, President Zelenskyy is watching from Ukraine — and Putin is watching from Moscow,” Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who worked with Graham on the package, said on the Senate floor. “I would like to think Lindsey Graham is watching, too. Today we say to the people of Ukraine: You are not alone. And today we say to Vladimir Putin: You will not conquer Ukraine.”
For India, the vote comes as it and the US are attempting to hammer out a trade deal. It potentially offers Washington another lever over New Delhi even as the first — the Section 301 forced-labour tariff imposed last month, and the excess-capacity investigation still open — reshapes the arithmetic on which those talks proceed.
To be sure, Washington itself has tolerated purchases of Russian crude when it waived sanctions to ease an energy crisis its own actions in West Asia had created following the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz. That waiver has since expired.
The bill’s mechanism gives both governments room. The USTR rate-setting discretion is the first pressure point: an executive branch that was involved in drafting the softening can, if it chooses, set the rate below the 100% ceiling, or invoke the presidential waiver on certified national interest grounds. Reassessment every 180 days keeps the instrument reversible.
Indian negotiators have pressed their American counterparts to offer New Delhi a competitive advantage to its trade rivals, such as Bangladesh and Indonesia.

headline: With Nitish Kumar stepping down as CM on April 15, the council of ministers was dissolved; Samrat Choudhary's council, constituted on May 7, included Prakash
full_text:
With Nitish Kumar stepping down as CM on April 15, the council of ministers was dissolved; Samrat Choudhary's council, constituted on May 7, included Prakash
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday sought records from the Bihar government relating to the appointment of Deepak Prakash, who was not a member of the assembly, as a minister in Nov last year, his re-induction into the cabinet in May and his recent hurried nomination as an MLC allegedly to skirt around the six-month deadline within which such a minister must get elected to the House.A PIL has challenged his continuance as minister after the expiry of the six-month deadline within which a person, who is not a member of the assembly or legislative council, must get elected as a member of either house.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, for the Bihar government, told a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justices Joymalya Bagchi, and V Mohana that the minister has since been nominated as an MLC by the governor; hence, his continuance was not unconstitutional.However, the petitioner, relying on the SC's 2001 judgment in the SR Chaudhari case, which had categorically stated that the six-month deadline was non-negotiable, said the six-month deadline expired on May 20. With Nitish Kumar stepping down as CM on April 15, the council of ministers was dissolved. The new council of ministers was constituted under Samrat Choudhary on May 7, which included Prakash. The bench asked the Bihar government to place on record all documents relating to the appointment of Prakash in the first instance, his re-induction and subsequent nomination as MLC.
In its 2001 judgment by a three-judge bench, SC had ruled, "Permitting a non-legislator minister to be re-appointed, without getting elected within the period prescribed by Article 164(4) (six months), would amount to ignoring the electorate in having its say as to who should represent it - a position which is wholly unacceptable."The seductive temptations to cling to office regardless of constitutional restraint must be totally eschewed. Will of the people cannot be permitted to be subordinated to political expediency of the prime minister or the chief minister as the case may be, to have in his cabinet a non-legislator as a minister for an indefinite period by repeated re-appointments without the individual seeking popular mandate of the electorate."The SC added, "Chief ministers or governors must... not sacrifice either political responsibility or parliamentary conventions at the altar of political expediency."

headline: Russia, India's biggest supplier during the quarter, supplied crude at an average cost of $2,408 per tonne, while UAE crude cost $2,213 per tonne
full_text:
Russia, India's biggest supplier during the quarter, supplied crude at an average cost of $2,408 per tonne, while UAE crude cost $2,213 per tonne
NEW DELHI: India's crude import bill rose 26% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026-27, despite volumes falling 18%, as the West Asia conflict disrupted supplies and pushed up oil prices.Commerce department data showed India imported 59.7 million tonnes (MT) of crude between April and June this year, down from 73 MT in the corresponding period last fiscal. Import bill, however, rose to $49 billion from $39 billion in April-June 2025.India is the world's third-largest crude importer, with imports meeting 88% of annual consumption. Global oil prices, which were below $70 per barrel before the US-Iran conflict broke out in Feb, surged after shipments through the Strait of Hormuz - which handles a fifth of global oil transit - were disrupted. Around 40% of India's crude imports came through the strait from West Asian suppliers. Brent crude touched nearly $120 per barrel at the conflict's peak. The weakening rupee also added to the import bill.Since India imports 1.8-2 billion barrels of crude a year, every $1-per-barrel increase in oil prices can add up to $2 billion to its oil import bill.
Average cost of crude sourced from different countries varied, partly because of differences in freight, insurance and war-risk premiums.
Russia, India's biggest supplier during the quarter, supplied crude at an average cost of $2,408 per tonne, while UAE crude cost $2,213 per tonne."Our priority at that time was to secure supplies from wherever possible to ensure energy security for 1.4 billion people," said an executive of a state-run refining company, adding that discounts available before the conflict had disappeared and refiners were forced to pay hefty war-risk premiums.Russia remained India's top crude supplier in the first quarter of FY27, accounting for more than 40% of imports. UAE (14.6%), Saudi Arabia (9.9%), Venezuela (5.2%) and Oman (4.5%) were the other major suppliers.

headline: India growing old faster than it grows rich, study warns
full_text:
India growing old faster than it grows rich, study warns
A Transform Rural India white paper says India could have 347 million people above 60 by 2050, with most living in rural areas. The study says shrinking families, chronic illness and unpaid care burdens are straining the rural care system.
India could have 347 million people over the age of 60 by 2050—equivalent to one in every five citizens—with nearly 70 per cent of them living in rural areas, according to a new study that warns the country is ageing rapidly while still far from the income levels many developed nations had reached before undergoing similar demographic transitions.
The findings were released by Transform Rural India (TRI) in a white paper titled “Demographic Transition, Evolving Families and the Future of the Care Ecosystem in Rural India”, launched during the organisation’s India Rural Colloquy (IRC).
The study projects that nearly seven out of every 10 elderly Indians will be living in rural areas by 2050, placing enormous pressure on families and local care systems.
“By 2050, one in five Indians — around 347 million people — will be over the age of 60, with nearly seven in 10 older adults living in rural India. Unlike many developed nations that became wealthy before their populations aged, India is undergoing this demographic transition at much lower income levels,” the report said.
The paper highlights a shrinking support base for the elderly. The number of working-age adults available to support each older person is expected to fall sharply from 8.4 in 2001 to 5.2 by 2026.
Drawing on data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS), the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, Census projections, Time Use Surveys and other national datasets, the report says India’s traditional family-based care model is coming under increasing strain as families become smaller, younger members migrate for work and life expectancy rises.
“Yet nearly 94 per cent of care for older people is still provided within households, leaving fewer family members to meet growing and increasingly complex care needs,” the study noted.
The burden of caregiving continues to fall disproportionately on women. According to the report, women spend about 305 minutes a day on unpaid care work, compared to just 56 minutes by men, limiting women’s participation in the workforce.
The study also points to climate change as an emerging challenge, saying that extreme weather events such as heatwaves and floods are adding significantly to women’s unpaid workload.
At the same time, India’s disease profile is changing rapidly. The report notes that nearly two-thirds of all deaths in the country are now caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and cancer. It also observes that an increasing share of the health burden stems from people living longer with disabilities and chronic illnesses rather than dying prematurely.
The authors argue that India’s healthcare system was largely designed for episodic interventions such as childbirth, immunisation drives and treatment of acute illnesses, making it ill-equipped for the challenges of an ageing population.
“The next phase of healthcare is about supporting people living with chronic illnesses, disabilities and the challenges of ageing — something hospitals alone cannot do,” the white paper said.
To address the challenge, TRI has proposed a “neighbourhood of care” model that would connect existing rural institutions—including Gram Panchayats, self-help groups, ASHA workers, Anganwadi centres and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs—into a unified community-based care network.
The model aims to ensure integrated care services are available within walking distance of every household. According to the report, rural India does not need entirely new infrastructure but better coordination among institutions that already exist.
The white paper also frames caregiving as a major economic opportunity. It estimates that investing 2 per cent of India’s GDP in the care economy could create around 11 million jobs, most of them for women in rural areas.
“India has made remarkable progress in helping people survive. The next challenge is ensuring they can live well for longer. Our demographic transition requires us to redesign care delivery itself — beyond facility-based care, it will require to facilitate as shared community function and improving sustainable living conditions,” said Shyamal Santra, Practice Director, Transform Rural India.
“The institutions needed to make this possible already exist across rural India. By connecting them through a common care mandate, an eco-system needs to be built that supports families, caregivers, strengthens local governance and prepares villages for the decades ahead,” he added.

headline: Accused Kulkarni chose to share questions with students who paid to attend 'special classes' he conducted in his apartment just before the exam
full_text:
Accused Kulkarni chose to share questions with students who paid to attend 'special classes' he conducted in his apartment just before the exam
NEW DELHI: A seemingly innocuous WhatsApp message from a parent asking chemistry professor PV Kulkarni for his address to gift him a watch rang the first alarm-bells for CBI sleuths probing the NEET-UG paper leak. What followed was a scan of an access control app used in residential societies (Mygate) and analysis of a WhatsApp group named 'Fifa world cup', which helped the agency trace the students who bought papers and ultimately the question setters who leaked them.The chargesheet filed by CBI revealed that Mygate app logs confirmed the presence of students in the apartment of the arrested accused Kulkarni. The logs matched mobile logs, corroborating their location.Kulkarni was engaged as a subject expert (chemistry) by NTA for NEET-UG 2026 - the medical entrance exam being cancelled on May 3 due to a paper leak. The test was reconducted on June 21.Though sworn to secrecy, Kulkarni chose to share questions with students who paid to attend "special classes" he conducted in his apartment just before the exam, the agency said in the chargesheet.His greed put paid to measures that NTA had taken to plug vulnerabilities in the logistics chain that were exploited by an organised gang.
The testing agency had not factored in the possibility of subversion by a subject expert."Kulkarni and other accused paper setters would memorise or mark in a book the questions that were being set at NTA's office, later note down those questions at a hotel, and then pass these on to other accused," CBI said.The handwritten notes matched the leaked question papers. Kulkarni's seized phone contained pre-exam leaked papers in circulation and contacts with candidates, parents and co-accused. The phone contained nine images of the chemistry question paper and answer slips matching NEET-UG papers.Kulkarni, CBI said, also created a Whatsapp group called "special class" on April 25. The money, in lieu of questions, was directly collected from parents of candidates by Kulkarni or sent through co-accused Manisha Waghmare, a beautician.Nine students attended Kulkarni's classes between April 25 and 27, officials privy to investigations said. Besides, three candidates attended special classes in Latur. Eight students, who joined the WhatsApp group created by Kulkarni, and his scouts have confirmed to CBI that the leaked paper was shared with them.Kulkarni even made an attempt to get the physics paper for students, but it was leaked by another paper setter, Manisha Havaldar. She was on NTA's panel to set the physics paper and also to translate the question paper from English to Marathi and vice versa. Despite an oath of confidentiality, she allegedly leaked physics questions to the mother of a candidate for Rs 25,000 at the insistence of another accused.
Trail Led CBI To Students And Question Setters
Eight days before the exam, Havaldar had handwritten notes of the leaked paper on her phone. She dictated the leaked paper to accused Tejas Shah for further circulation. On April 14, Shah, a member of physics faculty and chief operating officer of Abhang Prabhu Medical Academy, noted down the leaked questions dictated by Havaldar.The leaked papers also reached Rajasthan. Four days ahead of the test, 11 sets of leaked question papers were transported in a black Hyundai Verna to Jhunjhunu. The chargesheet details revealed that Mangilal Biwal and Dinesh Biwal - Sikar-based family at the core of the leak - were carrying printed material spanning the complete exam syllabus, across physics, chemistry and biology.
One of the receivers, Amit, kept Class X and XII marksheets of candidates as security, and they were assured they would only need to pay if more than 150 questions matched the actual paper, CBI said.Another accused, Shivraj Motegaonkar, managing partner of RCC coaching centre, circulated leaked question papers to students, claiming these would be the "most expected" paper appearing in the exam. The night before the NEET-UG exam, a PDF file containing the question paper was leaked to 40-50 hostel students of RCC coaching students, sleuths said.On May 3, after the exam, students appeared in a video where they claimed questions predicted by Motegaonkar actually appeared in the test. The "RCC MOCK test question paper" was the leaked question paper, CBI has found.
Raj Shekhar Jha is a journalist for the Times of India with over a decade of experience in reporting on national security, terrorism, crime and prisons.

headline: How US bill proposing 100% tariffs over Russian oil purchase could hurt India

How US bill proposing 100% tariffs over Russian oil purchase could hurt India
India, China, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan will face tariffs as the bill aims to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.
India is likely to feel the heat of sanctions over its purchase of Russian oil as the US Senate on Friday approved by 86 votes to 11 a bill that would authorise tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian fuel and other exports.
India is among five target economies by the bill’s sponsors even as US allies in Europe are spared for similar purchases. This sweeping sanctions legislation has been authored by late Senator Lindsey Graham and was moved in the Senate late last month.
The bill now moves to the House of Representatives, where Republicans control the floor calendar and where its passage in identical form is the last hurdle before it reaches President Donald Trump for signature. Trump, whose officials helped shape the softened text now before Congress, has signalled support for House passage.
Also read: ‘America shooting itself in the foot’: US Senators Wyden, Paul oppose 100% tariffs on India, China
The countries that will face steep tariffs are India, China, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan as the bill aims to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.
India is the second largest buyer of Russian crude oil after China.
Introduced in April 2025, Graham earlier this year announced that the bill had been greenlit by President Donald Trump amid trade tensions between US and India.
How the bill impacts India
Since the war in the West Asia broke out in February this year, India's dependence on Russian energy has increased as the shipping route via the crucial Strait of Hormuz passage remained disrupted. The Iran-US war has choked off Gulf crude supplies that previously accounted for roughly 40% of India’s oil imports, forcing refiners to turn to Russian crude as an alternative source.
Senator Richard Blumenthal had earlier stated that the bill would make an exception for countries purchasing Russian gas if their purchase is less than 15 per cent of Russia's total gas imports.
Also read: 21 land areas, four passes, a lake: List of Arunachal locations India named to counter China
Exactly a year earlier, the US penalised India over its energy trade with Russia when President Donald Trump announced an additional 25 per cent tariff against India for "fueling Putin's war".
The revised tarrifs pushed the total against India to 50 per cent, the highest along with China and Brazil. The new tariff also set off tensions between the two allies as the trade negotiations also came to a halt.
Months later, when the Iran-US war caused major disruption of energy supplies, the US announced a waiver on Russian oil, which allowed India to resume its purchase.
As per the US, these purchases would not bring any profits for Russia.
Amid the waiver, Indian imports of Russian crude oil rose 34% in June 2026 to record levels. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, these imports were valued at €4.5 billion, accounting for roughly 36% of Russia’s crude oil export revenues.

The student-led agitation against alleged corruption in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) intensified on Tuesday as protest leader Devendra Nath Mahto vowed to continue his indefinite hunger strike despite deteriorating health.

Local administrative officials, including the SDM and the police station in-charge, have repeatedly urged him to seek treatment.
However, Mahto remains defiant.
In an interaction with Aaj Tak, he said he would not leave the protest site until meaningful talks with the government are held and students' concerns are addressed.
“The white sheet I am wrapped in may well become my shroud, but I will not end my fast until the talks are successful,” Mahto said.
He also revealed the personal toll the agitation has taken on him. Mahto said he avoids speaking to his family because he fears becoming emotionally vulnerable and losing focus on the movement.
“I do not talk to my family. They would become emotional, and I might become weak toward the movement,” he said.
The protest site also witnessed emotional scenes as another hunger striker, Mahendra Prasad from Hazaribagh, broke down in tears while speaking about his struggles. Prasad has been fasting for four consecutive days in support of the movement.
Recalling years of hardship, he said he earned an engineering degree in 2014 but never secured a job. The prolonged unemployment led family members to view him as a failure, forcing him to leave home and continue his struggle on his own.
Prasad alleged that repeated paper leaks in JPSC and JSSC examinations shattered the hopes of countless aspirants.
“I did not have the money to buy a seat. Exams kept getting affected by paper leaks,” he said.
Fighting back tears as he remembered his two young daughters, Prasad said his struggle was not just for himself but for future generations.
“I am crying and fighting so that the next generation does not have to cry,” he said.
The ongoing protest has become a rallying point for job aspirants demanding transparency and accountability in recruitment examinations, with protesters insisting they will continue their agitation until concrete action is taken against alleged irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment processes.

headline: Leaders of several political parties in Tamil Nadu on Friday urged the State government to convene an all-party meeting on the proposed Mekedatu dam project in Karnataka, saying a united political and legal response was essential to protect the State...
full_text:
Leaders of several political parties in Tamil Nadu on Friday urged the State government to convene an all-party meeting on the proposed Mekedatu dam project in Karnataka, saying a united political and legal response was essential to protect the State’s share of Cauvery water.
Speaking at a demonstration organised by Puthiya Tamilagam in Chennai, the leaders accused successive governments in Karnataka of failing to release Tamil Nadu’s due share of Cauvery water in accordance with tribunal and Supreme Court orders.
They contended that the State had often received only surplus water released during periods of heavy rainfall rather than its allocated share.
Naam Tamilar Katchi chief co-ordinator Seeman alleged that Karnataka had repeatedly failed to comply with Cauvery water-sharing orders. He said the State should insist on receiving its legally allocated 177.25 tmcft of water. He alleged that successive governments at the Centre had failed to safeguard Tamil Nadu’s interests and urged the State government to pursue all available political and legal measures to secure the State’s rightful share of Cauvery water.
Puthiya Tamilagam founder K. Krishnasamy said the proposed Mekedatu dam would further reduce flows to Tamil Nadu if constructed. He claimed Karnataka had failed to release the quantity of water due to Tamil Nadu, affecting kuruvai cultivation this season in the Delta districts.
Mr. Krishnasamy also criticised the State government for not initiating stronger legal action to secure the release of water.
Tamilaga Vaazhvurimai Katchi president T. Velmurugan called on political parties in Tamil Nadu to unite on the Mekedatu issue, including during the upcoming byelection.
Representatives of the Pattali Makkal Katchi, Indiya Jananayaga Katchi, and other parties, also participated.

headline: On Friday, Delhi HC issued the consequential transfer and posting orders for judges Sunena Sharma and Dheeraj Mor
full_text:
On Friday, Delhi HC issued the consequential transfer and posting orders for judges Sunena Sharma and Dheeraj Mor
NEW DELHI: Barely six months after appointing a sessions judge to exclusively hear coal scam cases in Delhi, Supreme Court has replaced her, acting on an unusual request from the Delhi high court, which said she and another special CBI judge were âbetter suited for certain other responsibilitiesâ.A bench of Chief Justice Suryakant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana, in an order, recorded that Delhi high court had sought the transfer of special judges Sunena Sharma and Dheeraj Mor so they could be assigned other responsibilities.Sharma had assumed charge in January after SC approved Delhi HCâs request to relieve then incumbent Sanjay Bansal, who had presided over the special coal scam court for nearly four-and-a-half years. Mor was appointed special judge in April 2025. The latest request came with Sharma barely six months into her tenure and Mor having completed just over a year in the post.SC noted that it had received a letter from the registrar general of Delhi HC stating that Sharma and Mor were âbetter suited for certain other responsibilitiesâ. The HC also described both judicial officers as âof outstanding meritâ and said it wished to utilise their services elsewhere.
Accepting the request, the top court permitted Delhi high court to transfer Sharma and Mor from the posts of special judges hearing CBI coal scam cases. It also approved the appointment of Virender Kumar Kharta, earlier special judge of the NDPS court at Saket, and Ajay Garg, previously an additional sessions judge at a fast-track court in Tis Hazari, as their replacements. Kharta will succeed Sharma, while Garg will take over from Mor.
On Friday, Delhi HC issued the consequential transfer and posting orders. Interestingly, neither Sharma nor Mor has been assigned a fresh judicial posting. According to the notification, both have been attached to the office of the principal district and sessions judge (CBI).The high court directed both officers to notify all matters in which judgments or orders had been reserved before relinquishing charge and pronounce them on the scheduled date or, at the latest, within two to three weeks despite the transfer. The dates fixed for pronouncement must also be reflected in the cause lists of both the previous and new courts, as well as on the courtâs website.Last year, 29 CBI corruption cases were pending before two special coal scam courts, while more than 27 had already been disposed of.
As legal editor for Delhi, Abhinav Garg handles coverage of courts and connected legal challenges shaping the capital. From breaking down complex law related jargon to simplifying how a particular verdict or development in courts may impact the readers, Abhinav brings with him over two decades of experience in the field.

headline: Explained: Bhopal Declaration adopted at BRICS culture ministers' meeting
full_text:
Explained: Bhopal Declaration adopted at BRICS culture ministers' meeting
BRICS culture ministers adopted the Bhopal Declaration at their meeting in Bhopal. The pact broadens cooperation on heritage, creative industries and AI-linked cultural governance.
The 11th BRICS Culture Ministers' Meeting on Saturday adopted the Bhopal Declaration, aimed at strengthening the institutional framework for cultural cooperation among BRICS nations, Union Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said in Bhopal.
He said the declaration provides a shared roadmap across a broad range of contemporary and traditional areas linked to culture and heritage.
Shekhawat said the declaration identifies ‘provenance research’ relating to cultural property and its restitution as an area for greater cooperation, including exploring the use of AI-based tracing tools. He said another major focus is cooperation in cultural and creative industries and the creative economy, including exchange of methodologies, experiences and best practices, support for creators, networking, and wider market access through digital tools.
Calling the adoption of the declaration ‘a key outcome’, Shekhawat told reporters: ‘It aims to strengthen the institutional framework for BRICS cultural cooperation and provide a shared roadmap covering a wide range of contemporary and traditional areas of culture and heritage.’
He said the declaration also includes provisions to enhance cooperation on UNESCO’s multinational nomination processes to strengthen a collaborative approach towards the recognition and preservation of shared and interconnected cultural heritage.
The preservation of traditional knowledge systems and traditional cultural expressions is another significant area covered in the declaration, he said. It also seeks to promote cooperation among museums, libraries and archives, which Shekhawat said would open up wide possibilities for institutional exchange and sharing expertise in preserving cultural and documentary resources.
Shekhawat said the rights of creators also form part of the areas of cooperation. He added that the declaration addresses transparency and fair and equitable remuneration in the use of copyright-protected works in artificial intelligence systems.
Under India’s presidency, he said, a structured process of consultation and deliberation was followed through three meetings of the BRICS Culture Working Group before the ministerial-level discussions in Bhopal.
WHEN AND WHERE THE MEETINGS HAPPENED?
The deliberations were guided by India’s BRICS theme, ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability’.
The first Culture Working Group meeting was held virtually on April 29-30, 2026, the second in Varanasi on June 4-5, and the third in Bhopal on August 5-6. Shekhawat said these discussions culminated in the 11th BRICS Culture Ministers’ Meeting held on Saturday.
A total of 55 delegates from 14 countries took part in the ministerial-level meeting. The BRICS member nations in the culture track were Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. Egypt participated online.
The four participating partner countries were Belarus, Cuba, Kazakhstan and Thailand. Shekhawat said the participation of culture ministers from Indonesia, South Africa and the UAE reflected the high-level commitment of the participating nations to the BRICS culture track.
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, Chief Secretary Ashok Barnwal, Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal and state culture secretary Sheo Shekhar Shukla were present on the occasion.
Yadav said the BRICS meeting in Bhopal, the city of Raja Bhoj, was a matter of pride for the people of the state. Overall, the meeting ended with the adoption of the Bhopal Declaration, setting out areas of cooperation ranging from heritage and traditional knowledge to creative industries, institutional exchange and the use of AI in culture-related work.

headline: Long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code
full_text:
Long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code
NEW DELHI: The long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code. In a sign of India's growing digital health footprint, patients have now completed 25 crore outpatient (OPD) registrations through the ABHA-based 'Scan and Register' service under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), with nearly four lakh people using the facility every day.Introduced in October 2022, the service allows patients to register for an OPD consultation by simply scanning a QR code displayed at participating hospitals through an ABDM-enabled health app. Once they give consent, their ABHA-linked details are shared with the hospital, eliminating paperwork and reducing waiting time at registration counters.The service is now available in 30,800 hospitals and healthcare facilities across 36 states and Union Territories and 756 districts, making it one of the country's fastest-growing digital public health services. More than 24,000 government facilities and 6,400 private hospitals have adopted the system.The biggest users of the platform are in Bihar, which has recorded over 7.3 crore digital OPD registrations, followed by Uttar Pradesh (4.09 crore), Andhra Pradesh (3.38 crore) and Jammu & Kashmir (1.39 crore).Among hospitals, AIIMS New Delhi has emerged as the country's busiest digital registration centre, recording over 54.29 lakh Scan and Register transactions.
It is followed by AIIMS Bhopal (29.1 lakh), AIIMS Bhubaneswar (23.93 lakh), AIIMS Patna (19.62 lakh) and AIIMS Raipur (18.63 lakh).Officials said the service has particularly eased hospital visits for senior citizens, pregnant women and patients requiring frequent follow-ups by cutting time spent at registration counters and doing away with repeated form filling.
"This milestone reflects the growing trust that citizens and healthcare providers have placed in India's digital health ecosystem. By simplifying one of the most common touchpoints in healthcare, OPD registration, the service has enhanced patient convenience while improving efficiency for hospitals," National Health Authority CEO Dr Sunil Kumar Barnwal said.The National Health Authority said the service is now operational across AIIMS, central and state government hospitals, medical colleges, district hospitals, ESIC and railway hospitals, as well as private healthcare facilities, and is expected to expand further as more hospitals adopt ABHA-enabled digital services.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

headline: A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprise of women.
full_text:
A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprise of women.
Indiaâs instant domestic help economy is expanding faster. App-based platforms promise cleaners, cooks and household workers within minutes. However, the real contest here is no longer just about speed, convenience or pricing. It is increasingly about trust.A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprises women.For years, domestic work in India has operated through informal neighbourhood networks, word-of-mouth referrals and personal recommendations. The new generation of platforms is attempting to formalise that ecosystem by adding identity verification, digital payments, ratings, training, insurance and customer support.But unlike food delivery or ride-hailing, these services involve something far more intimate: a stranger entering a private home.That has forced platforms to solve an unusually difficult problem. They must simultaneously protect women who enter unfamiliar homes for work and women who may be home alone when they invite those workers inside.The result is a rapidly evolving safety architecture built around background checks, restricted service hours, real-time monitoring, SOS systems, human escalation teams and, increasingly, AI-assisted risk detection.
Formalising trust in an informal workforce
Indiaâs domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base.But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.A spokesperson for Pronto shared the measures it takes to ensure transparency, saying that every worker completes criminal court record verification and police verification before joining the platform. Customers, too, verify their name, phone number and address through OTP authentication and must agree to a code of conduct before placing a booking.Pronto's workers, for example, receive training before taking their first assignment, and that low customer ratings are investigated by trainers rather than triggering automatic deactivation.âEvery hub we operate doubles as a training centre, and a professional takes her first booking only after she is trained, background-verified and dispatch-ready, a process that takes about four days,â the spokesperson said.Similarly, Snabbit, whose workforce consists entirely of women professionals, said it has built a multi-layered safety framework supported by a dedicated Trust & Safety team.A spokesperson said the system includes âmandatory KYC and background checks for all experts on the platform, verified customers, address-level traceability and controlled job allocation.â
Safety vs surveillance divide
The sharpest divide between platforms and customers is emerging around body-worn cameras.Pronto has begun experimenting with optional recorded bookings designed to protect workers from false allegations in cases of disputes with customers.For many users, however, the presence of a camera inside a private home changes the nature of the interaction. âI know some platforms are starting to equip their workers with chest-mounted bodycams for transparency, and while I understand it protects the worker from false claims, it completely freaks me out as a customer,â a Delhi resident said.âMy home is my private sanctuary. The idea of a stranger walking through my living room with an active lens, recording the exact layout of my home, my entrances, my exits, my personal belongings, and where my work setup or valuables are, feels like an extreme invasion of privacy.âHer concerns extend beyond the recording itself. âWhere is that video footage stored? Who at the tech company has access to it? Could that footage leak or be hacked?â she said. âI would honestly think twice before booking a service that mandates live video recording inside my private space. There has to be a boundary between physical safety and digital surveillance.âPronto, however, ensured that the sole mechanism of this process is to ensure safety and privacy.It said that additional video data is collected only on opt-in verified bookings. According to its spokesperson, customers choose the feature during booking and confirm it again when the worker arrives. The camera is tilted downward to capture only the work area, records no audio, blurs faces and personal information on the device itself, deletes raw footage immediately, and retains only an anonymised encrypted version for a limited review period and AI training.
Safety by design
One of the most striking trends across the sector is that many safety measures are designed not around responding to incidents, but around preventing high-risk situations from arising in the first place.Several platforms have restricted service hours, particularly avoiding late-evening and night bookings when women workers may be required to enter unfamiliar homes after dark.Snabbit said its safety system monitors active jobs in real time and can identify anomalies that may require intervention. According to its spokesperson, âActive jobs are monitored in real time, with the dedicated Trust & Safety team supporting rapid escalation and incident response.â
What women check before opening the door
For many women, however, trust begins long before a worker arrives.A 24-year-old student in Jaipur said she has developed a consistent checklist before booking any on-demand domestic service. She checks whether the app displays a verified profile with a photograph, ID verification, ratings and reviews, and prefers platforms that offer real-time tracking and OTP-based service verification.âThe first thing I check is whether the app shows a verified profile with a photo, ID verification, ratings, and reviews from other women,â she said. âReal-time tracking and an OTP-based start and end of the service also make me feel more comfortable.âBefore the worker arrives, she follows a set of precautions that have become almost automatic. She keeps her phone fully charged, informs at least one friend that someone is coming over, avoids leaving valuables or personal documents in plain sight, and stays in a part of the house where she can easily monitor what is happening.âI usually make sure my phone is fully charged and I let at least one friend know that someone is coming over,â she said. âIf itâs a longer service, I stay in a part of the house where I can easily see whatâs happening.âShe is also careful about digital privacy. âI prefer apps that mask phone numbers, and I never share extra details unless theyâre necessary for the service,â she said. âI avoid mentioning that I live alone or discussing my schedule. Once the job is done, Iâm careful not to continue communication outside the platform.âFor her, safety is not just about preventing a crime; it is about minimising information that could make her vulnerable later.
The rituals of being home alone
Minal, a 26-year-old professional in Delhi described a different set of habits that have emerged through repeated use of instant service platforms. While the agent is at home, she stays in the hall rather than a closed bedroom, keeps her phone in her hand, and deliberately leaves a pair of her partnerâs or male flatmateâs shoes near the entrance.âI never sit in my bedroom with the door shut. I stay in the main living area, usually at the dining table with my laptop,â she said. âI also leave a pair of my male flatmateâs or partnerâs shoes near the entryway. Itâs a small mental trick, but it makes me feel less exposed.âShe and two close friends have an informal safety protocol built around messaging apps.âI have a private WhatsApp group with two close friends. We have a tacit rule: whenever an instant maid or repair person is assigned, I drop the tracking link, their name, and a quick âExpected time: 45 mins,ââ she said. âI donât overthink it, but it gives me a safety net.âWhen asked what app features actually make her feel secure, she was sceptical of marketing labels.âHonestly, badges and âpolice verifiedâ tags on an app screen donât mean much to me anymore. Anyone can upload a document,â she said. âWhat actually makes me feel safe is seeing a real-time, live selfie of the person taken right when they accept the job, matching the photo on their profile. Plus, knowing thereâs a strict OTP entry system where they canât start billing until I give them a code at the door.âHer distinction is important: she is less interested in historical verification and more interested in real-time authentication.
The older customerâs definition of trust
For older users, digital verification often feels less persuasive than physical verification.Sarita, a 52-year-old homemaker in Delhi-NCR, said she places greater trust in tangible indicators such as uniforms, identity cards and residential security systems.âA professional now gets to share her version of events and any relevant information before a decision is taken, and we work to keep investigations balanced and transparent,â Pronto spokesperson said.That shift, from treating workers merely as service providers to treating them as rights-bearing participants in the platform ecosystem, may prove as important as any technological innovation.
As instant domestic help services expand beyond metropolitan cities into smaller urban centres, safety may become the industryâs primary competitive differentiator.Speed is easy to advertise. Trust is harder to build.Women are asking for features that combine digital verification with human accountability: live identity confirmation, female-worker filters, trusted-contact notifications, residential gate integration, discreet exit mechanisms, neighbourhood-level reputation and transparent data governance.Platforms, meanwhile, are investing in training hubs, background verification, restricted service hours, SOS networks, counselling, insurance and AI-assisted monitoring.

headline: Rahul Gandhi, left, with Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during the Monsoon session of Parliament
full_text:
Rahul Gandhi, left, with Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during the Monsoon session of Parliament
Rahul Gandhi's interaction with Kalavati went viral in 2008, back when "viral" meant something very different. The widow of a farmer who died by suicide, she was raising nine children in Vidarbha when Rahul met her, and he later invoked her life in Parliament during the Indo-US nuclear deal debate.Eighteen years later, the Leader of Opposition stood beside Rhiya Ahir, the 27-year-old Mumbai woman who became a social-media sensation during the student protests after standing in front of a police van carrying detained protesters.Between those two moments, an entire generation grew up and largely walked away from the Grand Old Party in search of achhe din. Broadly speaking, Congress lost the millennials in large parts of the country, barring the South. Now, as anti-incumbency gradually catches up with the ruling regime, Congress is looking at a fresh crop of voters who could form a decisive electoral bloc by 2029.Rahul's communication strategy over the past month has laid out the approach clearly. From an unparliamentary expression inside Parliament that was later expunged, to telling protesting students they did not need to apologise to the prime minister, to an Instagram outreach mixing serious student questions with playful jibes at âAmarinder Uncleâ, the attempt to speak Gen Z's language is unmistakable.
Former Congress leader Sanjay Jha, speaking to TOI, said he believes Rahul's natural lingo is more attuned to Gen Z than Modi's. He says the prime minister's recent Instagram outreach came across as condescending to sections of young users, while Rahul seems more natural. Jha is categorical, according to him, Rahul represents the future and Modi the past.Despite successive Assembly victories after its underwhelming 2024 Lok Sabha performance, the BJP suddenly appears to be on a slightly sticky wicket. The NEET agitation has claimed a high-profile political scalp, a rarity in this government. For Rahul, it is a no-brainer to cash in on that advantage.
The generation that got away
The generation that was in its 20s and early 30s during the 2014 election firmly reposed its faith in the BJP or, more specifically, in Narendra Modi. His appeal as an outsider breaking through Delhi's entrenched power elite resonated with aspirational young voters. The pitch around development, technology, entrepreneurship and muscular nationalism continued to reap dividends election after election.An analysis of Lokniti-CSDS National Election Study data shows BJP support among voters aged 18-25 rising from 34% in 2014 to 41% in 2019. Congress remained stuck at 19%. The personal gap was even wider, with 51% of young respondents preferring Modi as prime minister in 2019, against 23% for Rahul.The BJP did more than defeat Congress among the young; it captured their imagination about what the future could look like. By 2024, however, a subsequent Lokniti-CSDS analysis found that no party had succeeded in carving out a distinct youth constituency. That churn is precisely what makes 2029 interesting.The beauty of democracy is that there is always a fresh test after five years. The next general election can be a very different proposition, or at least that is what Congress would hope.
The 36-crore election
By 2029, Gen Z will be far from a niche constituency.Using the common definition of Gen Z as those born between 1997 and 2012, its voting-age members in 2029 will be roughly 18 to 32 years old. An interpolation of the National Commission on Population's 2026 and 2031 age-group projections suggests India could have around 36.4 crore people in the voting-age Gen Z cohort by then. These are projected people of voting age, not registered electors, and actual turnout will obviously be lower.The arithmetic is still striking. Uttar Pradesh could have around 6.65 crore Gen Z adults in 2029, Bihar 3.73 crore, Maharashtra 3.18 crore, West Bengal 2.40 crore, Madhya Pradesh 2.34 crore and Rajasthan 2.25 crore. Gujarat could have 1.86 crore, Tamil Nadu 1.67 crore, Karnataka 1.63 crore, Andhra Pradesh 1.22 crore, Odisha 1.15 crore and Telangana around 92 lakh.
Supporters of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate after Dharmendra Pradhan resigned
Together, these 12 states could contain nearly 29 crore voting-age Gen Z Indians. On the current electoral map, they account for 420 Lok Sabha seats, though delimitation could change that arithmetic before 2029.Awkwardly for Congress, it remains organisationally weak in several states where the Gen Z pool will be largest. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar alone could contain more than 10 crore Gen Z adults. Instagram can reach these voters, but holding on to them requires organisation.Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy has taken the outreach a step further, proposing that the minimum age to contest Lok Sabha and Assembly elections be lowered from 25 to 21, and that for the Rajya Sabha and legislative councils from 30 to 25.But the question comes back at Congress. Even if the legal age is lowered, will it actually give tickets to 21-year-olds?
The break Congress could not manufacture
The party has been trying, with limited success, to get into the youth mind space for years. Rahul's campus visits, student conversations, attacks on unemployment and repeated interventions on paper leaks all predate the present protest cycle.The Bharat Jodo Yatra tried to remake Rahul as a leader who would walk and listen rather than merely speak. The Bharat Jodo Nyay Yatra before the 2024 election sharpened that pitch. That eventually became the five-part Yuva Nyay offer. Yet it did not acquire a life beyond the election cycle. There was no large youth groundswell speaking the language of Yuva Nyay. Like many Congress programmes, it was launched, discussed and eventually sank without a trace.The Cockroach Janta Party began as a satirical, digital-first intervention with what old political parties lacked: irreverence, little legacy baggage and a vocabulary born on social media. It gave accumulated frustration a conduit. Online anger over examination leaks spilled onto the street and widened into a protest over education costs, employment and institutional accountability. For Congress, this was the break it had spent years trying to manufacture but failed to produce.Jha offers perhaps the sharpest explanation for why CJP succeeded where conventional opposition parties struggled. The Modi government, he argues, can use agencies and the coercive power of the state to pressure political adversaries. It can also resort to what he calls âconvenient whatabouteryâ about 60 years of Congress rule. Students have fewer institutional or political stakes that can be turned against them, and familiar political labels do not work on them, according to Jha.
The challenge in front of Congress
The opposition, he says, failed to galvanise frustration that has now âerupted like a volcanoâ. A party serious about youth politics, he asks, must also explain why the NSUI and Youth Congress were not present at Jantar Mantar in much larger numbers.Political expert Subhamoy Maitra sees the emergence of figures like Abhijeet Dipke as evidence of a wider leadership crisis in mainstream political parties. Ashutosh Chatterjee, general secretary of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress and a former student leader, rejects that charge. Leaders are not âpropped upâ, he argues; those who consistently echo public sentiment eventually get recognition. He cites Kanhaiya Kumar, Manish Sharma and Vinod Jakhar among Congress's next generation and credits Rahul's Chhatra Ki Goonj with helping catalyse the student movement. He is categorical that there is no dearth of talent in Congress.Rahul has meanwhile walked a tightrope with CJP, amplifying the issues, raising them in Parliament and meeting protesters while keeping a measured distance from Dipke and the core leadership. Congress wants to latch on to the momentum without getting directly associated with it, believes Maitra. Since the leaders of CJP are relatively unknown, he argues, it makes more sense for Rahul Gandhi to share a stage with the likes of AISA's Neha Bora. With Sonam Wangchuk revealing that Rahul Gandhi even declined to break his fast, it is clear that the Congress leader is trying to keep the protesters at arm's length.Political scientist and former Calcutta University registrar Dr Rajagopal Dhar Chakraborti believes the NEET agitation was unusual because it organically brought sections of Gen Z together around a wider sense of institutional failure and caught the government off guard. Students, he agrees with Jha, have little to lose and are harder to intimidate.But Dr Chakraborti doubts Congress can simply inherit the dividend. CJP, he suggests, could eventually test the electoral waters itself rather than hand its constituency to any established party. He echoes the sentiments of Prashant Kishore that Bankipur result too is an indication of the mood inside the Gen Z constituents.
Jobs may be the bigger trigger
The World Bank estimates that around 11 million young Indians will enter the labour market every year over the next two decades. Increasingly, the crisis is about the quality of employment, not just its availability. The gig economy cannot be a panacea for an increasingly educated and aspirational society. For decades, the implicit social contract was simple: a higher-education degree would culminate in a well-paying job. That notion is now under stress.AI, automation and other macroeconomic pressures could sharpen the mismatch. If India produces ever larger cohorts of graduates but a disproportionate share of new work remains temporary, informal or low-productivity, education itself could become a source of discontent. Congress leader Chatterjee believes that the combination of unemployment, recurring paper leaks, shrinking space for public education and growing commercialisation of education will eventually push younger voters towards Congress. He says Congress can offer Gen Z âtotal transparencyâ.
Can Congress states offer an alternative?
States do not control the entire macroeconomy, but they still have a large role to play in shaping the future of Indians, especially in areas like education, which is on the Constitution's Concurrent List. Jha believes Congress needs an alternative model of governance where performance can speak for itself. He earmarks states like Karnataka and Kerala that could effectively be projected as models of governance.But the inferno of student unrest has the potential to spill into opposition-ruled states, as Jharkhand is showing.Congress is a partner in the JMM-led government, where students and government-job aspirants have protested alleged irregularities involving JPSC and JSSC recruitment examinations. Rahul Gandhi, to his credit, has addressed the issue head-on, describing the education system as having âcollapsedâ and become expensive and oppressive.More importantly, he refused to exempt governments involving his own party, saying every government, including the one in Jharkhand, should listen to students and act.
From Rajiv's computers to Rahul's paper leaks
Congress has travelled this road before.NSUI channelled students into party politics, and Youth Congress provided the next rung. Rahul himself has spent almost two decades trying to build a younger political layer, with limited gains. Across large parts of India, the party remains top-heavy.Dr Chakraborti turns almost wistful recalling how Rajiv enthused younger Indians before getting bogged down by a coterie of older Congress hands. Rajiv Gandhi once captured the young imagination far more successfully. In a pre-liberalisation India, computers and telecommunications became symbols of a future arriving early. His government also lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.The recent NEET debate in Parliament showed how Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi are operating. Rahul sought to legitimise student anger without claiming ownership of it. He told Parliament that Indians should be proud of the protesters, described students as people willing to question and keep their minds open, and called an expensive and commercialised education system an âextortion systemâ.Priyanka spoke about injured students, asked whether protesters were âterroristsâ, and delivered a sharp line: if the prime minister wanted to win them back, he needed to change the âangle of his heartâ, not the camera angle.
Rahul Gandhi protesting in front of PM Modi's residence
Gen Z doesn't owe its vote to anyone
Political pundit Subhamoy Maitra offers the necessary caution.It is far from clear, he says, how protest politics translates into electoral democracy. Barring movements such as Anna Hazare's anti-corruption agitation and the RG Kar protests, relatively few civil-society uprisings have produced durable electoral consequences in the last decade and a half. He also believes Rahul still needs to shed the perception of being a âpart-time politicianâ. Chatterjee rejects that description, asking when a Leader of Opposition had previously had to shed blood while standing with protesters, as Rahul did during the NEET agitation.
For all the marketing jargon, Gen Z is not one homogeneous political community. Caste, religion, region, class and gender will not disappear merely because everyone uses Instagram. Students can welcome Rahul as an amplifier and still refuse to accept him as their leader. CJP has already shown that young Indians can organise outside both the ruling party and the established opposition. The party has already announced its next campaign " Kya Bolti Public". Dr Chakraborti believes that this may well be a precursor to CJP testing waters in next year's Uttar Pradesh elections.Gen Z content creators often harp on one word, which is consistency. That, they say, is what eventually produces organic reach. Rahul Gandhi might want to borrow the lesson, believes Sanjay Jha. Between Kalavati and Rhiya Ahir, Rahul Gandhi has toiled hard, often without much to show for it. Maybe that is because the party is yet to fundamentally establish how a Congress-ruled India would be different. That targeted messaging and, more importantly, tangible execution will be crucial.Nearly 36 crore young Indians could be up for grabs in 2029. Sooner or later, they will ask what actually changed after they were heard.

headline: Zero compromise on Cauvery, Mekedatu dam halt: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay affirms stance
full_text:
Zero compromise on Cauvery, Mekedatu dam halt: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay affirms stance
C Joseph Vijay, Tamil Nadu chief minister, said that his government is firm on dealing with the Cauvery issue legally and that there is no change about it.
Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Friday said there would be no compromise on the Cauvery issue or on fighting against the construction of the Mekedatu dam in Karnataka, adding that the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) had no intention of playing politics over the dam issue.
“On the Cauvery issue, some members have asked for details. Cauvery is our lifeline; it is an emotional issue for us,” Vijay said in his first comments on the issue during the state assembly session on Friday.
Also Read | ‘Ready to face insults’: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay amid face-off with Udhayanidhi over Cauvery dispute
Tamil Nadu assembly's unanimous resolution
Recalling that the Tamil Nadu assembly passed an unanimous resolution in June and sent it to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Vijay said: “On learning that the Union Minister of State for Jal Shakti did not mention full details regarding the dam, we immediately wrote another letter to the Prime Minister the very next day quoting the rules and clauses of the Cauvery Tribunal’s final verdict and the Supreme Court’s final verdict, stating that no legal or administrative approval should be granted for the construction of the dam at Mekedatu.”
He underscored that whether on sharing Cauvery river water with Karnataka or stopping the construction of the dam at Mekedatu, his government would not yield even a fraction of Tamil Nadu’s rights. “That is our clear stand,” Vijay said.
Also Read | A duel whose name was writ on Cauvery waters
Vijay vs Udhyanidhi Stalin on Cauvery issue
Responding to the leader of the opposition from DMK, Udhyanidhi Stalin, who raised the Cauvery issue and targeted the ruling party in a special calling attention motion, Vijay traced how Tamil Nadu had handled the issue since 1969 -- from considering dialogue to sticking to legal recourse.
Vijay said that his government is firm on dealing with the Cauvery issue legally and that there is no change about it.
Opposition leader Stalin pointed out that political parties in Karnataka stand united despite political differences on the issue and that is why he has been demanding the ruling TVK government convene an all-party meeting.
