headline: Gen Z our children, some people misled them during NEET protests: Dharmendra Pradhan
full_text:
Gen Z our children, some people misled them during NEET protests: Dharmendra Pradhan
Former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan alleged that some people misled Gen Z during the NEET protest row and defended his resignation, saying he offered to step down from his post.
Former Education Minister and senior BJP leader Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday said some people had tried to “mislead” Gen Z during the protests over the NEET paper leak issue, which led to his resignation. Breaking his silence on the matter, Pradhan said the ministerial post had never been important to him, and he had himself approached Prime Minister Narendra Modi with an offer to resign from the Union Council of Ministers.
Pradhan made the remarks while addressing students and teachers at GM University in Bhubaneswar, exactly two weeks after stepping down amid the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests at Delhi's iconic Jantar Mantar over the NEET paper leak row. He resigned from the ministry on July 25.
“Gen Z is our children. Some people attempted to mislead them. I had no personal issues then. At least two crore children are born in India every year. During the last 10 years, 20 crore children were born. They have aspirations, and they will make India a ‘Vishwa Guru’. The post was not important to me,” Pradhan said.
At another meeting in Rairakhol, Pradhan also hit out at former Odisha Chief Minister and BJD president Naveen Patnaik, saying he was not disturbed by protests by BJD workers and slogans asking him to “go back”.
Referring to a protest by BJD youth and student wing activists near the airport, where slogans such as “Dharmendra Pradhan Go Back” were raised, he said, “I am a farmer’s son. Even if you tell me to go back, I will come back.”
“Naveen Babu also calls me a disgrace to the people of Odisha and a bad person,” Pradhan said, accusing the BJD president of engaging youths in protests against him. “Have I ever done anything that will shame the people of Odisha?” he asked, drawing a loud response of “No” from the gathering.
“I may not be bringing laurels for the state, but I have never disgraced the people by my work. I will never do any work which will tarnish the state’s reputation,” he said.
Pradhan said he became a Union Minister 12 years ago with the blessings of Lord Jagannath and Goddess Samaleswari, the presiding deity of Sambalpur. His remarks against Patnaik were made from a dais also attended by BJD MLA and deputy leader in the Odisha Assembly Prasanna Acharya.
“Keeping in view the BJD’s protests, I had consulted Prasanna Bhai about whether I should go. Prasanna Babu told me to come and assured me that I would be welcomed. I came here after taking his permission,” Pradhan said.
BJD HITS BACK
BJD’s Sambalpur district president and former minister Rohit Pujari hit back, saying Pradhan had been criticised over the handling of the student protests.
“Nobody had defamed Pradhan. His party and government have defamed him by police resorting to lathi-charge, tear gas and atrocities during the peaceful student agitation at Jantar Mantar. Pradhan was facing criticism because of such incidents. I do not understand why he blames Patnaik for the police excesses on agitating students,” Pujari said.
“Why would Patnaik want to defame him? The whole country knows that 21 children died by suicide because of him. Of the 22 lakh students who appeared for the examination, around 21 lakh students must be under depression. Nobody needs to defame him; he has defamed himself,” the BJD leader claimed. Pujari said it was the BJP government’s “wrong policy” that had brought a bad name to Pradhan.
Meanwhile, sources said Sambalpur police detained around 30 BJD workers as a precautionary measure, anticipating protests by the party’s youth and student wings.

headline: The spokesman said the surge in tourist arrivals during June and July has also been supported by a calendar of cultural, spiritual and experiential events organised across Ladakh
full_text:
The spokesman said the surge in tourist arrivals during June and July has also been supported by a calendar of cultural, spiritual and experiential events organised across Ladakh
SRINAGAR: Ladakh continues to witness a surge in tourist arrivals, with the union territory recording 330,332 tourists from Jan to July this year, already reaching 98.35% of the 335,872 tourists recorded last year, a govt spokesman said.Air travel remained the most popular mode of reaching Ladakh, accounting for 47.64% of the total arrivals. Among tourists arriving by road, the Kashmir route continued to be more popular than the Manali route, with 35.27% entering Ladakh through Kashmir compared with 17.09% through Manali, according to the latest figures released by the Ladakh govt.âThe surge in tourism numbers has been particularly noticeable in June and July, when more than 2.12 lakh tourists visited Ladakh, accounting for nearly 65% of the total 3.30 lakh tourist arrivals recorded so far this year,â the spokesman said.He said the growth in tourism coincides with a major and rapid transformation in Ladakhâs connectivity infrastructure since the formation of the UT. âThe total road network has increased from 1,799 km in 2019 to over 4,200 km in 2026, while the number of bridges has increased from 19 to 72,â he added.He said the period of seasonal disruption on key routes has also reduced substantially. Zoji La, the gateway to Ladakh from Kashmir, which earlier remained closed for around 127 days annually, now remains closed for only 16 days.
âSimilarly, the annual closure of the Kargil-Zanskar Road has declined from 154 days to 11 days, significantly improving near-year-round connectivity for tourists,â he said, adding that the number of homestays has increased from 128 in 2019 to 2,275 in 2026, creating new livelihood opportunities for local households.
The spokesman said the surge in tourist arrivals during June and July has also been supported by a calendar of cultural, spiritual and experiential events organised across Ladakh.Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, in a statement, attributed the growing tourist footfall, particularly domestic tourism, to the sustained infrastructure development in Ladakh and the appeal of PM Narendra Modi to citizens to visit tourist places in India and promote domestic tourism.âThe fact that Ladakh has crossed the 1 lakh mark in tourist arrivals for two successive months and has already achieved more than 98% of the entire 2025 footfall by the end of July is a very encouraging milestone,â Saxena said.

headline: At IIT-Delhi, PM Modi asks students to measure career by nation's needs, not salaries: 'Basis of every decision'
full_text:
At IIT-Delhi, PM Modi asks students to measure career by nation's needs, not salaries: 'Basis of every decision'
Addressing the 57th convocation ceremony, PM Modi told the graduating class that an IIT degree was “a mandate to contribute to the nation.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged graduating engineers at IIT-Delhi on Saturday to measure their careers against the country’s needs rather than salary slips or startup valuations, telling students that “the basis of every decision of yours should be what the benefit to the country will be.”
Addressing the 57th convocation ceremony, Modi told the graduating class that an IIT degree was “a mandate to contribute to the nation,” and framed the years ahead as a test distinct from anything the students had faced in the classroom. “Unlike your university exams, life’s most critical challenges are entirely out of syllabus,” he said, urging students to identify “the questions the world has stopped asking” rather than simply answering the ones already set for them.
Also Read | You will influence journey of 'Viksit Bharat': PM Modi's message to Gen Z at IIT-Delhi convocation
Rapidly shifting global landscape
Modi set that challenge against a rapidly shifting global landscape, telling students that the pace of technological change made it impossible to predict with confidence what industries or professions would look like in 20 or 30 years. “The strategic equations of the world are changing rapidly. The global balance of power is shifting every moment. And the biggest force driving these changes is the speed of technology,” he said. “No one can say with certainty what the world will look like 20 or 30 years from now... but remember what I am saying: the one who keeps learning will win.” He drew a distinction between generations, saying the cohort that fought for independence had a single, clearly defined national goal, while today’s graduates would shape India’s development over the next three decades.
Appeal to young India
Much of the address doubled as an appeal to young India more broadly, days after Modi released a video on Instagram offering to “forgive” students who had hurled abuse at him during weeks of protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party over the NEET-UG paper leak — remarks the opposition said should have been an apology, not an offer of clemency. Modi did not refer to the protests, the leak or examination reform at IIT Delhi. He instead cast the country’s youth as the driving force behind its economic rise, pointing to India’s startup ecosystem, its growing semiconductor base and a new generation of engineers “designing and launching their own rockets” — themes closely echoing his remarks in Mysuru on August 1, when he credited young Indians with “giving impetus to the development of the world.”
He singled out the pressures of comparison as a threat to student wellbeing, telling the students, “life is absolutely not a leader-board; your real race is not with anyone else, it is with yourself,” and urged them to stay off the scoreboard of salaries and placements that circulates on social media.
Education minister Prahlad Joshi accompanies PM Modi
Modi, who spoke for 34 minutes, was accompanied at the ceremony by education minister Prahlad Joshi, attending his first major public event at an educational institution since he took charge of the ministry on July 26, succeeding Dharmendra Pradhan. Joshi called the appearance a personal milestone. “After taking additional charge as the education minister, this is my first-ever public programme in any education institution alongside the PM,” he said. “I have complete faith in the potential of India’s youth and regard them as the foremost architects of Viksit Bharat 2047. I urge them to innovate with purpose and lead with integrity, recognising that excellence must go hand in hand with strong ethics and moral values.”
Also Read | US Vice President JD Vance dials PM Modi, discusses deepening India-US strategic ties
AI-powered supercomputing facility
Modi inaugurated an AI-powered supercomputing facility, Param Pragya, at IIT Delhi’s Sonipat campus via video conferencing during the ceremony, and pointed to continuing state support for research: the Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation, which carries a funding target of up to ₹1 lakh crore, and the One Nation One Subscription scheme, which extends access to international research journals to institutions beyond the major cities.
He returned to the theme of youth-led growth across sectors including space, semiconductors, startups, digital payments and fintech, and pointed to drones transforming agriculture, medical deliveries and national defence. “Today, that same space sector has beautifully become a sky of new opportunities for thousands of our youth,” he said, adding that “all these revolutions have given millions of youths of the country an incredible opportunity to do something completely new for the first time.” He listed artificial intelligence, data centres, critical minerals, deep-sea exploration, quantum computing and energy security as emerging fields that would depend on the graduating cohort’s research and innovation.

More than 3,000 students received degrees at the convocation, including 587 PhD scholars.

headline: As loud as chainsaw at close range? Kanwar Yatra boomboxes deafen Delhi above permitted limits, law on mute
full_text:
As loud as chainsaw at close range? Kanwar Yatra boomboxes deafen Delhi above permitted limits, law on mute
Delhi Traffic Police has designated 8 Kanwar corridors along the city’s busiest arterials, including Ring Road, Mathura Road, Wazirabad Road. Grand Trunk Road.
An HT sound meter registered peaks of 110 decibels at two Kanwar Yatra rest camps in east Delhi as loudspeaker-mounted convoy trucks rolled past. That is roughly as loud as a chainsaw at close range, and more than 30 decibels above every legal ceiling that applies to noise in a residential area.
Even between the passing trucks, ambient noise at both camps — HT took the measurements at multiple occasions on Friday and Saturday — held between 80 and 88 decibels — 25 to 33 decibels above the 55-decibel daytime residential limit set by the Central Pollution Control Board. Because the decibel scale is logarithmic, the 85-decibel readings HT recorded carry roughly a thousand times the sound intensity of that ceiling.
Also read: Shahi paneer, pizza, momo without onion, garlic. The menu at Kanwar camps
The trucks have been grinding into the capital for over a week, and Saturday’s surge — the first of the yatra’s three peak days, which will send thousands more through the city until Tuesday — swelled the flow further.
What HT investigation found
HT ran the meter at two of those camps in east Delhi: one beside the Dilshaad Garden metro station on Grand Trunk Road, through which kanwariyas enter the capital from Uttar Pradesh, and one on Delhi-Haridwar Road near the Mandawali-West Vinod Nagar metro. Both fronted onto residential blocks. At Dilshaad Garden on Friday evening, six to seven convoy trucks rolled past within the half-hour between 5.30 pm and 6 pm, each pushing the meter into the 90-to-107 decibel range, with the evening’s peak of 109.3 decibels registering at 5.51 pm as one boombox truck ground past.
The second camp saw one such truck during HT’s Friday visit; it took the meter to 109.4 decibels.
Similar readings were recorded late on Saturday, well after the nationwide 10pm curfew for loud speakers, when peaks hit 89.5db at 11.35pm near Kalkaji, while the average persisted around 75db.
The routes crisscross Delhi. Delhi Traffic Police has designated eight Kanwar corridors along the city’s busiest arterials, including Ring Road, Mathura Road, Wazirabad Road, Grand Trunk Road, Rohtak Road and Najafgarh Road, with 308 rest camps set up along them. Eastern Delhi carries the heaviest concentration at 120 camps. From Sunday morning, the GT Road stretch between Apsara Border and Yamuna Bridge will be closed to general traffic until Tuesday evening. Residential blocks along every route face the same convoys.
CPCB limits on loudspeakers
Three legal ceilings apply. CPCB rules cap ambient noise in residential areas at 55 decibels between 6 am and 10 pm, and at 45 decibels through the night. Loudspeakers face a further, hard limit of 75 decibels at the boundary of the public place where they are used. In 2005, the Supreme Court affirmed those CPCB thresholds, prohibited the use of loudspeakers and sound amplifiers between 10 pm and 6 am except in public emergencies, and locked the 75-decibel loudspeaker ceiling in place.
The underlying Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 permit state governments to push the night cut-off to midnight on up to 15 religious or cultural days a year, but even that carve-out is bound by the 75-decibel maximum, and does not authorise 109-decibel peaks.
The Motor Vehicles Act separately prohibits both the boomboxes themselves and the vehicle modifications that mount them.
Delhi Police officers on yatra duty say that framework unravelled at the state borders. “Despite discussions, thousands of such vehicles playing loud music entered Shahdara through the borders, which means that the states’ police made no efforts in controlling them,” a senior officer involved in the security arrangement said.
Verbal agreements with counterparts in Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand — worked out to keep the modified convoys out of the capital — had not held. Once the trucks were inside Delhi, the officer said, the police could do little beyond asking drivers to lower the volume or physically cutting the cables, and even that had to be handled cautiously to avoid confrontation with pilgrims who could turn aggressive.
No FIRs have been filed by the police. Police spokespersons did not respond to requests for a comment.
Immeasurable effects
The readings themselves understate what residents actually endure. Standard sound meters use A-weighting, or dB(A), which is calibrated to the frequencies the human ear finds most sensitive — the mid-range where speech lives — and discounts the low-frequency energy that dominates the boombox trucks. Most of what the speaker walls produce sits below 200 hertz, in the sub-bass range that A-weighting suppresses.
HT’s dB(A) reading of 109 is a conservative floor; the same sound measured on a flatter, C-weighted scale would run substantially higher. Low-frequency waves carry long wavelengths and high energy, pass through walls, and shake structures at their resonant frequencies — which is why residents describe walls vibrating and window panes rattling in their frames.
The World Health Organization’s Guidelines for Community Noise flag this specifically, warning that A-weighting is inadequate for the non-auditory effects of low-frequency noise and that such noise disturbs rest and sleep well below the levels standard meters register.
Residents along the yatra routes will be exposed to that noise, in the busiest stretches, for three consecutive days. Rajesh Bhardwaj, consultant ENT specialist at MedFirst ENT Centre, said prolonged exposure at the intensities HT recorded could produce auditory fatigue, tinnitus and, if sustained, permanent damage to the sensory cells of the inner ear. “Chronic exposure to excessive environmental noise has been associated with broader cardiovascular and psychological health effects,” he said.
Children were particularly vulnerable, he added, because sustained noise interfered with sleep, concentration and learning, and the elderly with existing hearing loss faced compounded difficulty communicating. “Religious celebrations should absolutely be respected, but they should not come at the cost of public health,” Bhardwaj said.
At the Dilshaad Garden camp, police were on site, but were directing pilgrim movement — not stopping the boombox trucks that rolled past unchallenged. headline: Hilsa spotted in Ganga near Ghazipur in UP, decades after barrage cut off migration route
full_text:
Hilsa spotted in Ganga near Ghazipur in UP, decades after barrage cut off migration route
Scientists spotted two hilsa in the Ganga along Ghazipur town in Uttar Pradesh earlier this week
New Delhi : Scientists spotted two hilsa in the Ganga along Ghazipur town in Uttar Pradesh earlier this week, decades after they were believed to have disappeared from the upper and middle stretches of the river, a sighting that scientists said may be an indication that the waters were once again conducive for the species.
A senior Namami Gange official in Ghazipur confirmed the sighting.
“Some more hilsas were reportedly spotted by the locals in two more riverine villages on Saturday. However, their details have not yet come to the district headquarters,” said the official, who asked not to be named.
The sighting was also confirmed by officials at the Central Inland Fisheries Research Institute (CIFRI).
The two together weighed 740g, said officials.
Officials said the finding was significant not because two fish alone can establish a population, but because Ghazipur lies well upstream of the Farakka Barrage in West Bengal that has disrupted the hilsas’ travel and migration patterns since the 1970s.
The species was once known to travel towards the Ganga’s upper reaches, with historical records showing its presence as far upstream as Prayagraj and parts of the Ganga-Yamuna system.
Hilsas spend much of their adult life in the sea and along coastal waters before entering rivers to breed. This adaptability has helped the fish survive and fend off the adverse impacts of shifting aquatic conditions.
But that cycle was shattered after the Farakka Barrage opened in 1975. Changes in river flow, obstruction of migration, pollution, habitat degradation and increasing human pressure together contributed to the disappearance of hilsa from large portions of the upper and middle Ganga.
Barrage that stonewalled their journey
Farakka was built primarily to divert water towards the Hooghly river in West Bengal to improve navigation and maintain the river’s navigability near Kolkata. At the same time, it reshaped the ecology of its waters.
For hilsa, the problem was particularly acute. Unlike fish that can complete their life cycle within a limited stretch of water, hilsa requires open channels between the marine environment and freshwater spawning grounds.
Scientists have regarded the species as an important indicator of river health because its presence depends on several ecological dovetailing – adequate flow, suitable dissolved oxygen, appropriate temperature and accessible breeding habitats.
The Ghazipur finding also comes in the backdrop of attempts to rebuild the lost hilsa population. In January, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) issued directions to Delhi and other states along the Yamuna to restore native fish populations and control exotic species in the river as a priority.
The January 29 order asked Delhi, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh to all implement and consider recommendations submitted in an earlier report by the ICAR-CIFRI, which listed measures which could be adopted to stem the count of exotic species in the river.
HT on August 6 also reported the Upper Yamuna River Board (UYRB) asked Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh to develop “fish ladders” at the Wazirabad, Okhla and Hathnikund barrages respectively to allow native fish species in the river to migrate. A fish ladder is a stepped water structure that helps fish bypass obstacles – such as dams and barrages – during their migration upstream.
Ranching gives the Ganga another chance
CIFRI and NMCG have been working on hilsa conservation through a combination of fish ranching, tagging, monitoring and habitat-related interventions. Ranching is the practice of breeding fish in controlled environments before releasing them into open waters.
Earlier experiments have provided encouraging evidence, said experts involved in the project. Tagged hilsa released near Farakka have been detected hundreds of kilometres away, including in Uttar Pradesh. But scientists urged caution and underlined that last week’s sighting was not a reliable barometer of success.
Himanshu Thakkar, Coordinator at South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People (SANDRP) said a more positive indicator would be if the fish were to breed and “complete a life cycle or two”.
“At present, other evidence -- including water quality parameters through government data related to the river shows the water’s increasingly deteriorating situation,” he said.
Neeta Sehgal, senior professor (fish biology) at the zoology department at Delhi University, said the discovery was only a start.
“Hilsa are migratory fish, which migrate upstream to breed.The barrage altered water flows in the river and the pollution and habitat degradation have disrupted hilsa migration into the upper Ganga. Hilsa can travel hundreds of kilometres upstream. But breeding in freshwater is the most important.
“Two fish do not prove population recovery. True restoration would require evidence of natural migration, spawning, survival and successful reproduction,” she said, calling for sustained monitoring. “Evidence of natural breeding will eventually determine whether hilsa is genuinely reclaiming its historic migration route,” she added.

headline: 'Been a victim of Gen Z': Dharmendra Pradhan breaks silence on his resignation says youth were 'misled'
full_text:
'Been a victim of Gen Z': Dharmendra Pradhan breaks silence on his resignation says youth were 'misled'
Speaking at a ceremony, Dharmendra Pradhan said he had met PM Modi and sought his permission to acknowledge the aspirations of the younger generation.
Former Union education minister and Sambalpur MP Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday broke his silence on his resignation and said Gen Z was misled during the protests over the NEET paper leak controversy that eventually led to his resignation. He added that he had urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to acknowledge and address the concerns of the protesters.
Speaking at a felicitation ceremony for Padma awardees in Sambalpur, Pradhan said he had met PM Modi and sought his permission to acknowledge the aspirations of the younger generation rather than allow their grievances to be exploited for political ends. “Modi agreed and later addressed the issue himself,” he said.
“I have been a victim of Gen Z. For some time, the way this whole episode unfolded, I felt some people tried to mislead the children of the new generation,” Pradhan said.
“I met the Prime Minister and requested him to agree to the desire of Gen Z. I told him to allow me to acknowledge this in front of the children. I never staked my personal honour in the matter,” he said.
“The Prime Minister accepted this, and later he himself spoke about it in front of the children.”
Also Read | Dharmendra Pradhan resigns as education minister amid massive paper leak protests
Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation
Pradhan resigned on July 25 amid weeks of student protests over the NEET paper leak controversy.
In his resignation note, he had said the move was aimed at ensuring that “anti-national forces” did not exploit the agitation, that the unity of the country remained intact and that the future of students did not get “entangled in legal complexities”. “It is not a matter of individual prestige for me,” he had said in the note.
Pradhan had also said the government had acted immediately after irregularities were reported in the May 3 NEET-UG examination. The probe was handed to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), the test was cancelled and a re-examination was conducted on June 21, with results declared on July 16.
He said he had taken responsibility from the beginning and would not allow the prospects of meritorious students to be affected by the examination system. “From the very first day, I took responsibility for this, and I never turned away from this situation,” he said.
Also Read | ‘Not a matter of personal prestige’: Dharmendra Pradhan quits over paper leaks
'20 crore children of the new generation…': Pradhan
On Saturday, Pradhan said India’s young population would be crucial to the country’s ambition of becoming a global power.
“Every year, around two crore children are born in India. If we look at those between the ages of 15 and 25, within a period of 10 years, there will be 20 crore children of the new generation on whose shoulders India will become a global leader,” Pradhan said.
Efforts to engage with Gen Z
His remarks come as PM Modi and Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat have stepped up efforts to engage with Gen Z, which has emerged as a major political force following the protests.
Also Read | 'Pradhan never ran education ministry, RSS did': Rahul Gandhi's dig over resignation
BJD's reaction hits back at Pradhan
BJD’s Sambalpur district president and former minister Rohit Pujari hit back at Pradhan, saying the BJP leader had been criticised over the handling of the student protests.
“Nobody had defamed Pradhan. His party and government have defamed him by police resorting to lathi-charge, tear gas and atrocities during the peaceful student agitation at Jantar Mantar. Pradhan was facing criticism because of such incidents and ultimately he resigned,” Pujari said, alleging that more than 20 students had died by suicide over the controversy.
Pujari said it was the BJP government’s “wrong policy” that had brought a bad name to Pradhan.

headline: Havildar Shere Thapa of the 2nd Battalion, Jammu & Kashmir Rifles, was credited with saving the Subansiri Valley during the 1962 Chinese aggression
full_text:
Havildar Shere Thapa of the 2nd Battalion, Jammu & Kashmir Rifles, was credited with saving the Subansiri Valley during the 1962 Chinese aggression
NEW DELHI: Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, set up in memory of 1962 China war hero Havildar Shere Thapa, is one of the 27 places in Arunachal that the Union government on Friday formally named by their standard names on the official Indian map.Havildar Shere Thapa of the 2nd Battalion, Jammu & Kashmir Rifles, was credited with saving the Subansiri Valley during the 1962 Chinese aggression. He was part of a team to delay the advance of the enemy. On Nov 18, 1962, undaunted by the advance of the Chinese troops, he continued to engage the enemy from his position despite his buddy succumbing to enemy action. The Chinese suffered heavy losses, and their advance was delayed by 72 hours. The Indian Army installed a memorial in his name.Another name, Jaswant Garh, which houses the memorial of Indian martyr Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat on Tawang Road, also figured in the list. Located at 10,000 feet on the highway to Tawang, it marks the site where he single-handedly fought Chinese forces for 72 hours during the 1962 war. The memorial has been built in honour of his extraordinary bravery at the Battle of Nuranang.
Jairampur, an important logistics hub in Changlang district which is known as the gateway to the eastern border region supporting movements of security forces towards eastern Arunachal and the Myanmar frontier, also figures in the list.
One of the most strategically important high-altitude passes, Thag La, where one of the opening battles between Indian and Chinese forces took place in 1962, has also been formally identified. The list also includes Bisa village and strategically important high-altitude mountain passes in the region: Dzo La, Riza La and Pukur La.By formally naming some of the places, famous for the memorials of the Army war heroes, the government is paying homage to bravehearts who laid down their lives fighting for India in the northeastern state.

Badal's announcement conveyed the governmentâs efforts to realign the numbers in its favour this time round, after a similar exercise was defeated in the last session by a joint opposition, which has since been considerably weakened
NEW DELHI: A day after his meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Akali Dal president Sukhbir Singh Badal on Saturday reversed his party's earlier opposition to the rollout of the women's reservation law from 2029 with an increase in the Lok Sabha's strength by 50% and supported any fresh move to implement the two together, signalling the possibility of the govt reviving the Constitution amendment bill soon.Akali Dal had walked out of the BJP-led NDA government in September 2020, ending a 23-year-old alliance, due to the Centre's passage of the three farm bills. DMK, another opponent being eyed by the government as a potential supporter of its renewed bid, snubbed governing TVK's all-party meeting on delimitation. NDA is also banking on NCP(SP) to support the measure.
Government likely to bring back delimitation bill, but timing not clear yet
While Sukhbir Singh Badalâs party has only one MP â his wife Harsimrat is a Lok Sabha member â his announcement conveyed the governmentâs efforts to realign the numbers in its favour this time round, after a similar exercise was defeated in the last session by a joint opposition, which has since been considerably weakened.While DMK called it a diversionary tactic and wondered why CM Vijay did not summon the meeting on a pressing issue like the Mekedatu dam row, the party clearly did not want to be part of an exercise to frame delimitation as damaging to the interests of the state, with TVK ally Congress up in arms against it.Developments in governing BJP-led NDA and opposition camps are a clear indication that the government is bringing back the bill, which will need two-thirds support in Parliament.
Its timing, however, remains uncertain, with a section of lawmakers being of the view that Parliament can be summoned after Independence Day to debate it.The ongoing monsoon session is scheduled to end on Aug 13, leaving the government with not much time to pursue its ambitious agenda that seeks to raise Lok Sabhaâs maximum strength from the existing 550 to 850.
Sukhbir demanded implementation of one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha and state assemblies. He said, âSAD also demanded a fair and equitable delimitation.â Incidentally, his wife had made a fiery speech against a similar bill last time, flaying the government for linking reservation for women to delimitation.The changed political environment and the fact that the government may write into the new bill all the assurances it has made verbally may have persuaded his party and DMK to consider a rethink.NCP MP Supriya Sule had earlier suggested that if the bill proposes a rise in Lok Sabha seats of every state by an equal proportion, it would not create any problem, though she had added that they will be part of opposition consultations before making a final decision.

headline: New Delhi: The Centre's meetings with Meta have brought into sharp focus whether the social media giant’s recommendation systems and paid content promotion are consistent with its status as an intermediary under the Information Technology Act, govern...
full_text: New Delhi: The Centre's meetings with Meta have brought into sharp focus whether the social media giant’s recommendation systems and paid content promotion are consistent with its status as an intermediary under the Information Technology Act, government sources said..The key issue is whether a platform that actively decides “what content is shown to whom” continues to qualify as an intermediary or crosses into the role of a publisher. Section 79 of the IT Act grants intermediaries “safe harbour” protection from liability for third-party content, provided they comply with the law and due diligence requirements under the IT Rules, 2021..Govt examines if Meta recommendation system deciding what-to-show-to-whom fits intermediary status.Sources in the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology said if Meta’s algorithms determine visibility and promote content for payment, such functions raise questions about consistency with the legal definition of an intermediary. Determining what users see could amount to publishing, making platforms responsible for their actions..Intermediaries are obligated to observe due diligence to avail exemption from liability. Failure to do so may result in loss of protection under Section 79 and consequential action under the IT Act or Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The government will review the outcomes of the engagements before deciding whether to seek legal opinion and will also examine other platforms on the same issue, an officer told DH..This week, officials questioned Meta’s global team, led by global affairs head Joel Kaplan, on deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, unlabelled synthetic content and recommendation systems. The discussions followed the temporary restriction of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook post. After intensive questioning on Wednesday and Thursday with IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and IT Secretary S Krishnan, talks shifted to technical details on Friday, during which Meta outlined plans to address the concerns..Officials flagged the continued circulation of AI-generated harmful content even after it was flagged and sought greater human oversight in moderation with better understanding of Indian languages and local nuances. Meta admitted there were “serious issues” and assured continuous action..Sources said the objective is not censorship but ensuring compliance with Indian laws. Officials will follow up regularly, and another meeting is expected next week.

headline: The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
full_text:
The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
NEW DELHI: India remains just above Unesco's minimum GDP benchmark for education, but the sector's share in government spending has slipped below the prescribed threshold. Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure, down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco's 2026 SDG 4 scorecard has shown.The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion. Its latest lower secondary (Classes VI-VIII) completion rate is 86% as against its 99% national benchmark for 2025, while upper secondary (Classes IX-XII) completion rate is 51% as against 84%. Unesco classifies progress at both levels as slow.Under the Education 2030 framework, countries committed to spending 4-6% of GDP and/or 15-20% of public expenditure on education. The scorecard uses the lower thresholds as minimum benchmarks. India meets one. Its spending on education has remained at 4.1% of GDP since 2015, but its share of public expenditure has declined 1.5 percentage points to 14.2%.Among major emerging economies, China too meets one benchmark, at 4% of GDP (11.9% of public spending), while figures for Brazil are 5.6% and 12.9%. South Africa meets both, at 6% and 19.1%, while Indonesia, Bangladesh and Pakistan meet neither.
The pattern is common among developed economies too: the US, UK, Germany and France meet the GDP threshold but not the public expenditure benchmark, while Sweden and Switzerland meet both.Unesco noted that richer countries tend to meet the GDP benchmark but not the public expenditure threshold because they raise more revenue, while education often accounts for a larger share of budgets in poorer countries.Latest data show 39 of 205 countries, or 19%, meeting both benchmarks, while 72, or 35%, meet neither. Another 64 countries, including India, spend above 4% of GDP but below 15% of public expenditure. Among high-income countries, 11% meet both benchmarks and 50% follow India's pattern.India, however, has larger unmet schooling needs. Lower secondary completion has risen from 81% in 2015 to 86% but remains 13 percentage points below its 99% benchmark. Even Unesco's "feasible" 2025 benchmark of 90% is four points above the latest rate.
This is despite programmes operating at scale. Unesco's India profile says Samagra Shiksha supports about 15.6 crore learners, while PM-Poshan covers around 11.8 crore children in 11.2 lakh government and aided schools. The trend is part of a broader global concern. The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportageâboth reflective and news-drivenâadds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

headline: In Maharashtra’s drought-prone regions, widow remarriage is gradually shifting from a social taboo to wider acceptance. The shift is partly shaped by the growing number of unmarried farmers struggling to find women willing to marry them. Faced with l...
full_text:
In Maharashtra’s drought-prone regions, widow remarriage is gradually shifting from a social taboo to wider acceptance. The shift is partly shaped by the growing number of unmarried farmers struggling to find women willing to marry them. Faced with low incomes, agrarian uncertainty and the social challenges of farming, many such men are now turning to widows. But Radheshyam Jadhav finds that many women are declining these proposals, choosing financial independence and personal autonomy over the complexities that often accompany remarriage
Severe cramps gripped her abdomen. Neelima Renge ached to scream her heart out in anguish and anger. She was eight months pregnant when her husband Moreshwar died by suicide. Crushed under the burden of debt, he decided to end his life. In that haze of grief, anger and pain, she decided never to remarry. More than a decade later, she has not wavered from that decision.
“That decision was correct,” she asserts, standing in the corner of her dingy two-room mud house in Zadgaon, a remote village in Yavatmal district of Vidarbha region, the epicentre of Maharashtra’s farmer suicide crisis.
Inside, a broken charpai (cot), farming tools and stacked soybean sacks leave barely enough room for two people to sit. “This is what I have built on my own — my house and my life,” she says.
Married in 2011, Neelima was unable to complete her secondary school education. Her husband, who cultivated the family’s land, struggled with alcoholism. She says she made every effort to persuade him to stop drinking, but failed. Barely three years into their marriage, he died by suicide, leaving her widowed at the age of 26. A month after his death, she gave birth to a son.
In the years that followed, marriage proposals came through her parents and relatives, while several suitors expressed interest in marrying her, both directly and indirectly.
According to Kishor Tiwari, leader of the farmers’ advocacy and social action group Vidarbha Jan Andolan Samiti, western Vidarbha recorded 30,969 farmer suicides between 2001 and 2024 across Akola, Amravati, Buldhana, Washim and Yavatmal districts. Agrarian distress remains acute, with Yavatmal alone recording 102 farmer suicides between January and May 2026, according to Kishor.
When young women are widowed, their parents often urge them to remarry for financial security and social acceptance.
At times, social activists act as matchmakers, helping widows and prospective grooms connect. In Buldhana, a young farm widow and an unmarried farmer fell in love but, unable to openly announce their intention to marry, sought the help of a local non-profit organisation.
Yet, for widows such as Neelima, whether a man has been married before matters far less than whether he treats her as an equal partner. She did not believe she would find such a relationship and has therefore remained single.
Alongside women widowed by farmer suicides, rural Maharashtra is also home to many never-married farmers who struggle to find wives because of unstable incomes. A network of matchmakers assists these farmers, often searching for prospective brides in the relatively underdeveloped regions of Vidarbha and Marathwada. While prospective grooms initially hesitate to consider widows, many eventually do after repeated rejections from previously unmarried women and their families.
Many widows also turn down proposals from farmers, most of them over the age of 40. They are unwilling to give up their autonomy or risk reliving the trauma of an earlier marriage.
Over the past seven to eight years, the problem has grown into a social crisis. It gained political visibility during the 2024 Lok Sabha election, with both farmers and political parties calling for government intervention.
Also Read | Maharashtra, Karnataka report most number of farmer suicides
Navigating life
Neelima’s in-laws declared that she was no longer part of the family and had no claim to its land. They were also resentful that the government compensation released after her husband’s death had been deposited directly into her account rather than theirs.
Neelima took shelter at her parents’ home in Hinganghat, about 55 km from her marital village. She began working as a tailor. Her parents urged her to remarry, arguing that it would be difficult for a young woman to raise a child alone without a man’s support. But even as marriage proposals came her way, Neelima remained convinced that she did not want to step into that “trap” again.
“At the same time, I was terrified about how I would navigate my life and what the future held for my son. I didn’t want to become a burden on my parents and brother. It took me three years to gather the courage to return, knock on my in-laws’ door and demand my share of the land. It was the only source of livelihood for me and my son,” she says.
When her in-laws once again refused to accept her and her son, she insisted on claiming her husband’s share of the land and demanded a meeting of village elders to “do justice”.
Eventually, her in-laws agreed to let her cultivate a three-acre plot. However, they made it clear that its legal ownership would pass only to her son once he attained adulthood. Her in-laws and fellow villagers feared that if Neelima remarried, the land would eventually go to her new husband.
“I was not bothered about what they thought. My priority was to secure a foothold on the land and begin cultivation,” she says, adding that she has successfully experimented with different crops even though her land is entirely rain-fed, with no irrigation facilities. Even now, her relatives and neighbours remain unconvinced that a single woman can survive independently without a man’s support.
Also Read | Pre-poll promises, post-poll precarity
Breaking the taboo
Just 22 km from Zadgaon, Chhabutai Waghade, Kusum Aaglane and other women farmers gather at Vanita Shende’s home in Tirzada village. All of them lost their husbands to suicide and have walked a path similar to Neelima’s. They are waiting for the remaining members of their self-help group to arrive. Together, they plan to discuss loan schemes that could support them.
“Life must revolve around men; otherwise, it has no value. That’s what I was taught, and I experience it every day,” says Chhabutai.
Her husband died by suicide after repeated crop failures and mounting debt. Her two daughters are now married. Her brother-in-law seized her land, arguing that a woman without a son “had no need for it”. Living with her widowed mother and having no brothers, Chhabutai says she has spent the past 15 years being reminded that she needs a man’s support. “Yet I have managed well and fought back in my own way,” she says. The other women in the group agree that remarriage often brings more complications than relief.
“Women like us have suffered in marriage, carrying heavy emotional and financial burdens. The thought of remarriage raises one overriding fear: what if the second husband is like the first? That is simply moving from one trauma to another,” says Vanita. Many young widows, she says, were married as children and denied even a basic education. Becoming mothers at a young age and then widows, Vanita adds bitterly, “There was no room for dreams. Here, girls are raised only to marry and bear children.” Kusum and Chhabutai silently affirm her words with a nod.
Women are expected to bear sons, and those who do not are often pressured into repeated pregnancies until they do. Tears well up in Vanita’s eyes and her voice trembles with suppressed anger. Within moments, she regains her composure and says she wants to show what she has achieved on the farmland she wrested from her brother-in-law after a long legal and social struggle.
Walking through her fields, she explains that she adopted farming practices her husband would never have permitted. She has introduced a multi-cropping system and grows vegetables organically. “Men chase only cash crops. If that crop fails, everything is lost,” she says. Stopping at one corner of the field, Vanita points proudly. “This is a turmeric plant.”
Her smile comes after years of struggle. A few years ago, Vanita and a group of farm widows began cultivating turmeric, sending shockwaves through the community. “The turmeric plant is accorded an upper-caste status, and menstruating women are forbidden from cultivating or even approaching it,” she says wryly.
A long-held superstition maintained that the touch, or even the shadow, of a menstruating woman would pollute the crop. Widows were already excluded from haldi-kumkum ceremonies, in which married women exchange turmeric and vermilion as symbols of marital bliss, making it unthinkable for a menstruating widow to handle the plant. Caste and gender taboos intersect closely in local agricultural practices. Yet as families sought alternative sources of livelihood during the COVID-19 pandemic, Vanita broke the taboo. Along with other widows, she planted turmeric in backyards, kitchen gardens, pots and grow bags, tending to the plants through every season and every menstrual cycle.
Today, many women in the region cultivate turmeric in their fields. The belief that men are farmers while women are merely helpers is another stereotype that has been sustained for generations, says Vanita. She adds that she and other farm widows have shown that women can farm successfully without men’s support.
Vanita had, in any case, been fending for herself even while her husband was alive. He had thrown her out after she developed leukoderma, a non-contagious skin condition that causes white patches on the skin. By the time he died by suicide, she had already learned to live independently. Remarriage was never an option. “Even when a man is willing to marry a widow with children, he still expects her to be physically ‘whole’,” she says.
The men and markets
In Buldhana district, social activist D.S. Lahane runs the Manas Foundation, which supports widows and single women seeking remarriage. Working in a region marked by severe agrarian distress, he has observed that many women who approach the foundation eventually decide against remarriage.
Among those open to a second marriage, almost none are willing to marry a farmer, even if it would be the man’s first marriage. Lahane says this reflects a deepening crisis across agrarian Maharashtra. “Despite owning land and earning a modest income, farmers are no longer considered desirable marriage prospects because of the declining social status of farming and the uncertainty of agricultural incomes,” he says.
Many young farmers, he adds, have registered with the foundation in search of brides. Most initially seek previously unmarried women but, after repeated rejections, become willing to marry widows with children.
However, such marriages often bring their own complexities. Women in the region say those who remarry frequently face intense social and familial pressure to have children in their second marriage, even when they do not wish to. Although a previously unmarried man may marry a widow with children, many still want biological children of their own.
In Chikhali, about 40 km from Buldhana, a farm widow with two children received a marriage proposal from a young man from her village whom she already knew. After they married, he insisted on having a child of his own.
“When I gave birth to a son, both my older children began to experience neglect. My elder son, who was old enough to understand what was happening, eventually left to live with my parents. It is deeply painful for me,” she says, requesting anonymity. “Life has become immensely complicated as I try to navigate the demands of being a wife again. Sometimes I think I should have remained unmarried, but I lacked the courage to live entirely on my own in a society that is always ready to exploit a single woman.”
Neelima says choosing to remain single comes at a price. “You can live alone only if you have courage. It requires tremendous resilience and a strong support system of family and friends. Otherwise, women should remarry,” she says.
By choosing to remain single, Neelima, Vanita, Kusum, Chhabutai and many others have challenged deeply entrenched social norms. They continue to wear kumkum and the mangalsutra, traditional symbols of a married Hindu woman. Relatives and fellow villagers routinely criticise them for doing so, objecting to what they see as a violation of local custom.
“We don’t wear them out of attachment. We wear them as protection against predatory behaviour when we travel outside the village. Men often assume that a single or widowed woman is vulnerable and therefore available. To avoid unwanted attention, we wear the mangalsutra and kumkum, even if reluctantly. People in our villages know our circumstances, but this helps protect us when we travel to nearby markets or government offices,” Neelima explains.
When Neelima and Vanita took their soybean and cotton harvest to the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) at Ralegaon for the first time, they found little encouragement from traders.
“They asked why I had come to the market myself instead of sending the produce through a middleman. I told them I wanted to know the market price of my soybean directly and decide for myself whether to sell it,” Neelima says.
She adds that the sight of women—whether married, widowed or single—selling their produce directly at APMC markets remains unfamiliar and, for many traders and market officials, uncomfortable.
Standing with courage
Yavatmal-based activist Madhuri Khadse, who works with Prerna Gram Vikas Sanstha to help farm widows rebuild their lives, says many widows approach her seeking help to find a husband.
“I ask them why they want to remarry, and the primary reason they give is protection from persistent harassment and unwanted advances,” she says. Young widows, she adds, remain highly vulnerable to exploitation wherever they go, and remarriage is often seen as a means of protection. Simply being perceived as a married woman shields them from much of the abuse they would otherwise face.
Madhuri says that while widow remarriage was traditionally discouraged among some upper-caste farming communities, attitudes have gradually begun to change and marriage proposals are becoming more common.
In a region where thousands of widows are struggling to rebuild their lives, many also face sexual abuse within their own families, a reality documented in several studies, including a 2018 report by the Maharashtra State Commission for Women and Mahila Kisan Adhikar Manch, a nationwide alliance of women farmers. While such abuse is often concealed in villages, everyday actions—such as riding pillion with a man, working alongside male labourers or even speaking to male relatives—are enough to trigger gossip.
Markets, village panchayats, government offices and police stations are rarely welcoming spaces for women. Widows who have built resilient and independent lives must summon additional strength simply to navigate everyday life.
“Even mata (mother) lived this way,” says one woman.
The mata they refer to is Sita. Unlike in many other parts of the country, where idols of Ram, Sita, Laxman and Hanuman are worshipped together, the ancient Sita Mata temple at Raveri in Yavatmal district houses only an idol of Sita. She stands alone in the temple and is especially revered by women. Local belief holds that after being abandoned by Ram, Sita found refuge at Sage Valmiki’s ashram in this region. Stripped of her royal status and forced to endure hardship, she rebuilt her life on her own terms and is believed to have spent the rest of her life here.
Sita’s story later became a powerful symbol of the women’s farmers’ movement in Vidarbha. When the late Sharad Joshi, founder of the Shetkari Sanghatana, helped rebuild the temple, he placed Sita’s legacy at the centre of the 2001 women farmers’ convention held at Raveri. He also developed the concept of “Sita Sheti” (Sita farming), which placed women farmers at the forefront of agricultural decision-making, crop experimentation and household food security.
While much of the country celebrates Ram Navami, many women in this region reserve their celebrations for Sita Navami.

headline: Arjun Ayanki, a key accused in several criminal cases, was arrested by the police in Kannur after more than two days of intensive search. He was reportedly taken into custody on Sunday (August 9, 2026) from an apartment in Kannur city, where he had b...
full_text:
Arjun Ayanki, a key accused in several criminal cases, was arrested by the police in Kannur after more than two days of intensive search. He was reportedly taken into custody on Sunday (August 9, 2026) from an apartment in Kannur city, where he had been staying in hiding.
The arrest was made by a police team led by the Northern Range Deputy Inspector General. Ayanki allegedly attempted to flee when the police reached the apartment and was apprehended at around 2.30 a.m. Another person believed to be his friend was also present at the apartment. He was arrested based on a tip off from an auto driver.
The police had intensified the search after Ayanki allegedly threatened police officers through social media following his release on bail. The Kerala High Court had rejected his anticipatory bail in the case.
Ayanki and his associates had earlier been taken into custody on suspicion of assembling near Kothamangalam for criminal activities. After securing bail, Ayanki allegedly posted threatening and abusive messages targeting the Kothamangalam inspector who led the raid and the Oonnukal Station House Officer through social media platforms.
Despite the rejection of his anticipatory bail plea, Ayanki allegedly continued to remain in hiding while challenging and threatening police officers through social media, prompting the police to intensify efforts to locate him.
After his arrest, he was brought to Kannur District Hospital for medical examination and taken back to Kannur Town station. He is likely to be shifted to Ernakulam after formally registering his arrest in Kannur. Further action is expected to be taken on the direction of the Additional Director General of Police in charge of law and order.
Ayanki, a native of Kappakkadavu in Azhikode, began his political activities as a DYFI unit secretary and later became prominent on social media as a CPI(M) cyber activist. He gained a substantial following by aggressively targeting political opponents online.
His name, however, later became associated with organised criminal activities. He gained notoriety in connection with the Karipur gold smuggling case and was allegedly involved in gangs that intercepted and robbed smuggled gold being transported from airports.
He is also a key accused in the Ramnattukara gold smuggling-related incident in which five people were killed.
Cases relating to an alleged attempt to run over members of a gold smuggling gang with a vehicle, besides cases registered by the Customs Department in connection with gold smuggling, are also pending against him.
Following the emergence of his alleged criminal links, the DYFI expelled Ayanki from the organisation. CPI(M) leadership has repeatedly maintained that the party has no association with cyber or quotation gangs.
