headline: Assam flood: Homemaker returns home after 20 days, finds memories destroyed
full_text:
Assam flood: Homemaker returns home after 20 days, finds memories destroyed
A Sivasagar homemaker returned after 20 days to find her flood-hit home and belongings destroyed. Her plea now is not just for rebuilding, but for assurance that heavy rain will not bring the same devastation again.
A homemaker in Assam's Sivasagar town returned to her flooded home on Sunday, 20 days after fleeing with her two minor daughters, to find wedding photographs ruined, her late mother's dinner set scattered, and her daughters' study tables toppled with their books and supplies destroyed.
With ankle-deep water still inside the house, Nasiman Zaman said her biggest worry was not just rebuilding her home, but whether there would be any assurance that such devastation would not happen again when it next rains heavily.
Zaman and her daughters have been staying at her husband's sister's house in another part of the town since escaping on July 21. She said around 15 people, including her brother-in-law's family and a sister-in-law's family, are now living there together. While she said they were fortunate to have relatives to stay with, she added that both she and her daughters were afraid of returning to their own home.
"Our house is on the ancestral land of my husband's family. My brother-in-law's house is next to ours, and besides his is the house of their cousin. All our houses have been inundated, with some facing worse situation than us even," Zaman told PTI.
She said the water was four feet high and had entered the ground floor of her two-storeyed house over the lower sill of the window when she left at around 6 pm on July 21. During the day, she had engaged four workers to move some household goods to the upper floor, which is still under construction. "My husband, who is a government employee, was away on official work in Guwahati. Water started entering the house around noon, and within six hours, it was nearly at my chest level. It was getting dark, power had been cut off, and we somehow managed to come out," she recalled.
Zaman said she was able to save a few electronic gadgets, some clothes, ornaments and important documents, but most other things in the house, from the sofa set to beds, almirahs and utensils, were damaged. "My husband and I went to see the house today, and found ankle-level water still. The study tables of our girls have been toppled and all their supplies destroyed. The album with our wedding memories has been destroyed. Every small thing that made the house our 'home' has been damaged," she said.
Describing their present situation, she said, "We are about 15 people now living under one roof. We are among the luckier ones as we have our own family to stay with. But we have to go back to our own place. My daughters are scared to return, and so am I. What will happen when it rains again?"
Zaman said water from the Nazira side, one of the worst-affected areas in the flood, entered their locality behind the Circuit House before flowing into the Dorika river, which was already in spate, and then submerged nearby areas. "I am no expert, but as a resident of the area, I can understand that there is a problem of drainage. Natural culverts and outlets have narrowed due to road and bridge constructions. Water is being pumped out, but it is not adequate," she said.
She said starting again would be difficult, but added that cleaning and setting up the house was not her main concern. "That we are safe is our biggest blessing. Our daughters will also come to terms with the loss, and we can rebuild our home and memories again. But we need the assurance that such havoc won't be unleashed again. Even after 20 days, water is stagnant in our area, a locality which has never seen floods. We can't abandon our homes nor can we live there safely," she said.
For Zaman and others in the area, the immediate loss is being counted in damaged homes and belongings, but the larger concern remains the same: when they return, they want reassurance from the authorities that they will be protected from a repeat of the flooding.

headline: The women who paint Jharkhand: Sohrai-Khovar's journey from ritual to global gallery
full_text:
The women who paint Jharkhand: Sohrai-Khovar's journey from ritual to global gallery
Prisha Patnaik / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 09, 2026, 18:57 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Sohrai-Khovar, an ancient women-led art tradition from Jharkhand (Image: TWAC)
A local artisan crouches by her doorstep, her hands stained with mud and colour drawn straight from the earth around her. The warmth of rust red, the hush of chalky white, the depth of a black gone nearly charcoal. With nothing more than a broken comb and a steady hand, she draws a peacock on a wall still damp from its coating of clay. In a few hours, this wall, like thousands of others across Hazaribagh, will carry the story of the land of Jharkhand, a mural to its beauty.Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. In 1991, celebrated and renowned environmentalist Bulu Imam documented rock shelters in the Isco hills of Hazaribagh district and noticed that the motifs on the ancient cave walls closely resembled the paintings still being made on village homes nearbyImam was able to sketch out a connection between the 21st century walls of a home to the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic caves of 10,000 to 5,000 BCE. Other researchers, citing the Archaeological Survey of India, place the rock art closer to 7,000-4,000 BCE, in the Paleolithic period.The dates might be contested but what remains true is that Sohrai and Khovar painting represent one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent, a line running from cave wall to mud wall across several thousand years.
What is Sohrai-Khovar?
Ganju Sohrai painted house (Source: TWAC)
Sohrai was originally a season specific craft style painted around the harvest festival of the same name, celebrated after Diwali in the month of Kartik, when households give thanks to their cattle and to the land.
Inside of a Khovar room (Source: TWAC)
Khovar, the word draws from "kho," meaning cave, and "var," meaning groom, is painted for weddings, decorating the room where a newly married couple will spend their first nights together.Both styles of art are made almost exclusively by women. Even its heritage tracing follows matrilineal succession, passed down from mothers to daughters. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.
From mud walls to airport terminals
Sanjeev Kumar (IFS), principal chief conservator of forests and head of forest force for Jharkhand, has spent much of his career working alongside these villages. He offers a structural explanation for why this art form became a livelihood tool in the first place, rather than staying purely ceremonial.Jharkhand's rural economy runs largely on two crop cycles a year, he points out, which leaves long stretches when women in farming households have little steady work. Between the sowing and the harvest, there is a kind of enforced pause â and in that pause, an entire category of household income simply goes quiet.Painting, once confined strictly to festival and wedding seasons, has increasingly moved to fill exactly that gap, giving women a way to keep earning in the months the land itself has nothing to offer.It isn't only about income, in Kumar's telling. Starting in 2007, as Divisional Forest Officer in Dhanbad, he began organising folk art camps to give Sohrai a wider audience, drawing participants from across India and as far as Australia and Bangladesh. The camps followed him through later postings â Jamshedpur, Hazaribagh, and beyond â running until the pandemic forced them online, then resuming after. The same women who might once have sat out the off-season are now, through this ecosystem, training relatives, negotiating with buyers, and travelling to exhibitions. Kumar also frames the work as central to the state's eco-tourism ambitions.
Sohrai-Khovar finally received Geographical Indication status in May 2020, reportedly approved in under nine months, unusually fast for a process that typically takes two to three years. The tag, granted by the Geographical Indication Registry in Chennai, formally recognises the art as unique to the Hazaribagh region, and gave it a marketing foothold it hadn't had before.The state took the recognition further. Hazaribagh became the first district in Jharkhand to commit to painting all its government buildings with Sohrai motifs â the chief minister's residence, the state secretariat, Ranchi's Birsa Munda Airport, railway stations across Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro, and Tata Nagar all now carry the same red-black-white language once found only on village walls. The art has travelled further still: Prime Minister Modi is reported to have gifted a Sohrai painting to President Putin, a livelihood project turned, however briefly, into an instrument of diplomacy.
Painting gifted to Russian President Putin by PM Modi
That visibility has translated into real, traceable livelihoods, in at least some cases. Local organisers connecting artists to buyers report dozens of women directly employed through their networks, hundreds more earning supplemental income in season. Cooperatives built specifically to give village women an alternative to farm labour have carried this work to dozens of international exhibitions across Europe and the US, and increasingly Canada, South Africa, and Japan. Trusts have gone further still â training programmes, small museums, free pigment, and the paperwork that eventually secured the GI tag itself.
Tensions surrounding the craft
Not everyone close to this history agrees the shift toward livelihood has been a clean win. Gustav Imam draws a distinction between his father's original vision and the state's current one. Bulu Imam treated Sohrai as fine art from the start â building an exhibition circuit that ran shows in Australia and Europe. The government's livelihood framing, Gustav argues, risks something narrower: pay an artist per piece for a product and you've quietly converted her into daily-wage labour rather than treating her as an artist. He isn't against commercialisation itself; he simply thinks dignity has to come first, and that dignity requires recognition at the very top of the field, not just income at the bottom. Traditions like Madhubani, Warli, and Gond painting have each produced nationally awarded artists, Padma Shri recipients among them; Sohrai-Khovar has not, despite women keeping the tradition alive through real struggle and real limitation. Until a handful of individual artists receive that kind of recognition, he argues, younger painters have no one concrete to aspire to become.
Gangwa's Lotus - archival art (Source: TWAC)
He also offers a blunt estimate on the schemes meant to help: of the artisans meant to benefit from government portals and initiatives like Mudra loans, perhaps 5 to 10 percent actually do, largely because many are semi-literate and simply can't navigate the registration process. The rest, in his account, remain outside the system entirely, not excluded by design, but by a bureaucracy that was never built with them in mind.Coal mining is often folded into this story as a single, simple threat, but the picture splits in two once you look closely. The Isco rock art site itself, the discovery that started everything, has not been destroyed. Dust from nearby mines has crept close and settled on it, but the site was declared a national monument around 2023. Other rock art caves in the region, more than a dozen now identified, remain safe largely because, in his words, no one knows about them, obscurity standing in for conservation.
Pashupati by Kunti Devi (Source: TWAC)
The villages are a different story. The North Karanpura coalfield sits beneath a large number of tribal villages across Hazaribagh, Ramgarh, and Chatra, and coal projects in the area have displaced multiple villages over the years, acquiring significant stretches of agricultural land in the process. Residents who've lost land describe rebuilding elsewhere, often some distance from where their families had always lived; local activists warn that further mining could displace still more. Bulu Imam's decades of opposition â intellectual rather than confrontational, built on letters to officials rather than protest, work that earned him the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2012 â was never really about the rock art surviving. It was about whether the people who kept painting around it would get to stay.There is another complication that has nothing to do with mining. Since 2018â19, a central housing scheme, the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Awas Yojana, has replaced mud-and-thatch homes across rural India with brick and cement â a genuine welfare improvement. But Sohrai and Khovar are painted on mud, and the same pigments don't take to cement the same way. One arm of government is quietly removing the canvas that another arm is simultaneously celebrating, not through malice, but through two policies that were never built with each other in mind.
A seat at the table for indigenous art
The most important complication was hinted at earlier. The market for Sohrai-Khovar remains thin, prices stay low relative to the labour involved, and no fixed floor price exists to stop buyers from talking artists down. Imam suggests that the district administration consider setting a standard pricing for the art to battle some aspects of the issue.The proposed fix, in Gustav's telling, isn't more schemes. It's status. He points to what happens when a piece lands somewhere with real institutional weight â a Sohrai painting, sold to the American ambassador during a visit to Kolkata, now hangs in a prominent hall at the US consulate.Contemporary Indian art by named painters routinely sells for crores; indigenous art too deserves a seat at that table. A tradition this old survives not just on income, but on being taken seriously by the people who could otherwise walk past it without a second look.
Exhibition in Rome, 2008 (TWAC)
The artisan finishes her peacock as the light starts to fade. Somewhere else in Hazaribagh, another woman is doing the same. Her red may no longer come from soil gathered by hand, but from a tube of paint bought at the market. The image on the wall is still recognisably Sohrai.
For thousands of years, the art has adapted to changing walls, changing materials and changing lives. But preserving it may require more than putting its motifs on government buildings or selling its paintings to new markets. It may mean preserving the women who make it, the homes they paint and the communities that taught them how.The paintings began on cave walls, moved to mud homes and have now travelled to airports, exhibitions and diplomatic gifts. What happens next will depend on whether Sohrai-Khovar is treated simply as a product to be sold â or as a living tradition whose value lies in the people who keep painting it.

headline: Congress sees FCRA Bill as 'anti-Christian', readies for Parliament showdown
full_text:
Congress sees FCRA Bill as 'anti-Christian', readies for Parliament showdown
Congress is preparing to oppose the proposed Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill in Parliament. The party says the changes could hit Christian-run schools, hospitals and welfare bodies and widen the political fight.
The Congress is preparing for a fresh showdown with the government over the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, fearing that proposed changes could affect Christian-run educational, healthcare and welfare organisations across the country.
Amid speculation that the government could introduce the Bill during the ongoing Monsoon Session, the Congress has decided to mount strong opposition, with party leaders describing the proposed legislation as an “anti-Christian” move.
The party has already issued a whip to its Lok Sabha MPs for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, signalling that it expects several “very important issues” to come up for discussion during the three days.
CONGRESS FEARS IMPACT ON CHRISTIAN NGOs
A section of Congress leaders believes changes to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) could particularly affect Christian-run schools, hospitals and other organisations working in rural, tribal and difficult-to-reach parts of the country.
Congress General Secretary KC Venugopal indicated that the party would oppose any attempt to bring the Bill during the current session.
“If the Central Government thinks they can cook up and introduce the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill within these two or three days, they should keep that wish to themselves,” Venugopal told reporters in Alappuzha, Kerala.
Congress MP Hibi Eden, speaking to India Today, alleged that several Christian NGOs and organisations provide healthcare and education in some of the country’s most challenging and remote areas.
He accused the NDA government of trying to “suppress” their activities.
“The Bill says DM, SDM can take over assets if they find violations, that too retrospectively. Similarly, there are other loopholes and so in totality, it's an attempt to suppress microscopic minority (Christians). We have already seen attacks on Churches, Nuns and Missionaries by BJP-RSS people,” Eden told India Today.
CONGRESS SEES WIDER POLITICAL BATTLE
According to sources, the Congress is looking at the FCRA issue as more than another confrontation between the Opposition and the government. The party sees it as an issue that could bring other Opposition parties together while also helping it reach out to minority voters.
A senior Opposition leader told India Today that while Christians are concentrated largely in Kerala and the Northeastern region, there are also sections of “crypto-Christians” in states including Andhra Pradesh and Punjab.
The Opposition believes the issue could help consolidate these voters against the BJP-led NDA, similar to what it claims happened during the recent Kerala Assembly elections, which coincided with Parliament’s Budget Session.
FCRA ISSUE HAD SURFACED DURING KERALA POLLS
The Congress had raised concerns over a possible FCRA amendment during the Budget Session as well and mounted a campaign against the proposed legislation.
The party not only opposed the Bill but also deployed senior Minority leaders in Kerala to campaign among the community. Congress leaders alleged that the proposed changes could adversely affect minority-run institutions and organisations.
The issue led to protests by Opposition parties in Parliament.
With the Kerala Assembly elections approaching, the government sought to counter the Congress campaign. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju told the Lok Sabha on April 1 that the government did not intend to introduce a Bill to amend the FCRA during the Budget Session.
Rijiju had accused the Opposition of misleading people in Kerala and across the country ahead of the Assembly elections.
However, the Congress believes the FCRA controversy had already reached minority voters before polling. The party subsequently returned to power in Kerala, where Christians account for roughly one-fifth of the population.
With the possibility of the Bill being brought during the Monsoon Session, the Congress is now preparing to revive its opposition to the proposed FCRA changes in Parliament.

headline: More DGCA officials under scanner over Drone Federation's alleged forged document
full_text:
More DGCA officials under scanner over Drone Federation's alleged forged document
A fresh complaint before the CVC alleges officials ignored findings in the DFI forgery case. It seeks a vigilance inquiry into alleged inaction, regulatory lapses and collusion.
A fresh complaint has been filed before the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) alleging corruption, regulatory lapses and collusion involving additional officials of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) in connection with the alleged Drone Federation of India (DFI) forgery case.
The complaint, filed by RTI activist Tejpratap Singh, alleges that officials failed to act despite an official inspection reportedly finding that the Drone Federation of India had used forged government documents while seeking to change its corporate name.
On August 3, the CVC forwarded the complaint to the Chief Vigilance Officer of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for further investigation.
The latest complaint comes even as the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is already probing the matter.
Earlier this year, the agency arrested DGCA Deputy Director General Mudavath Devula and Bharat Mathur, an executive associated with Asteria Aerospace Ltd., a member company of the DFI, in a separate alleged bribery case linked to drone import approvals.
According to the CBI FIR, Devula allegedly demanded Rs 5 lakh per application to clear pending files. During searches, the agency reportedly recovered Rs 37 lakh in cash, along with gold, silver coins and electronic devices.
FORGERY ALLEGATIONS DATE BACK TO 2023
The forgery allegations relate to a 2023 application filed by the DFI seeking to change its registered name from "Drone Federation India" to "Drone Federation of India".
Under the Companies Act, prior approval from the Central Government is required for such a name change.
According to the complaint, after the Registrar of Companies raised objections, the DFI submitted a No-Objection Certificate (NOC) purportedly issued by the DGCA and bearing the signature of then Director General Arun Kumar.
INSPECTION FOUND NO NOC ISSUED
However, an inspection conducted by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs under Section 206 of the Companies Act reportedly concluded that the document was forged.
The inspection found that the DGCA's Drone Directorate had never issued such an NOC, the file number mentioned in the document did not exist, and Arun Kumar had already been transferred before the date shown on the document.
Singh has alleged that despite these findings, officials failed to initiate appropriate action.
He has also questioned why the prosecution complaint filed before a Mumbai Sessions Court allegedly did not include charges related to forgery, cheating or the use of false evidence, despite the inspection report's findings.
The complaint seeks a vigilance inquiry into the role of the officials concerned, alleging deliberate inaction, regulatory failure and misuse of administrative procedures. Further investigation into the matter is underway.

headline: SC to hear plea seeking time-bound NDPS probes, confiscation of traffickers' properties on Monday
full_text:
SC to hear plea seeking time-bound NDPS probes, confiscation of traffickers' properties on Monday
New Delhi, The Supreme Court is slated to hear on Monday a plea seeking a slew of directions to strengthen the fight against drug trafficking, including time-bound investigation and trial of narcotics cases, confiscation of properties of traffickers and creation of a uniform investigation protocol across the country.
A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana is likely to hear the matter.
The PIL, filed by advocate Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay, has sought directions to the Centre and states to prescribe mandatory timelines for submission of forensic reports in cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act and frame standard operating procedures for search, seizure and sampling of narcotic substances.
"Keeping in view the menace of drug mafia network operating in India, the court may be pleased to issue a writ, order or direction to, a) direct the Centre and state governments to prescribe a mandatory timeline for submission of FSL reports in all NDPS cases; b) direct the Centre and states to formulate a SOP for search, seizure and sampling in small and intermediate quantity cases," read the plea filed through advocate Ashwani Kumar Dubey.
The petition also sought constitution of special courts for speedy trial of NDPS cases and implementation of mandatory digital recording and videography of search, seizure and sampling proceedings.
Claiming that drug abuse and trafficking had assumed alarming proportions, the plea said there was a 53 per cent rise in drug cases in 2025 and 1,240 tonnes of narcotic substances were seized during the year, indicating the growing scale of the problem.
It referred to incidents from Punjab and other states to argue that drug addiction was destroying families and affecting public health and law and order.
The plea said the existing framework lacked uniform investigation standards, time-bound forensic examination and effective coordination among enforcement agencies, leading to delays in prosecution and avoidable acquittals.
Seeking stricter action against organised drug syndicates, the petition urged the court to direct authorities to carry out time-bound assessment and confiscation of properties of traffickers, financiers and their family members under the NDPS Act, Prevention of Money Laundering Act, Benami Property Act and Black Money Act.
"Direct the Centre to constitute an Expert Committee for identification and timely scheduling of New Psychoactive Substances and constitute Special Courts under Sections 36 and 36A, and frame SOP for time-bound investigation and speedy trial," it said.
The plea further sought directions for the creation of an expert committee to identify and regulate new psychoactive substances, establishment of rehabilitation and wellness centres for addicts and formulation of a graded sentencing policy that distinguishes traffickers and financiers from addicts and personal-use offenders.
The petitioner has also sought a direction to the Law Commission to prepare a comprehensive report on the issue and a declaration that sentences in NDPS cases should run consecutively.

headline: Right-wing commentator Mohandas taken into custody over remarks on NEET protest
full_text:
Right-wing commentator Mohandas taken into custody over remarks on NEET protest
A team from Thiruvananthapuram Cyber Police Station, which is probing the case, reached Mohandas' residence at Koovappadam near Mattancherry on Sunday evening
Right-wing political commentator T G Mohandas was taken into custody from his residence in Mattancherry here on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made in a YouTube video about a student protest in New Delhi over the NEET paper leak, police said.
A team from the Thiruvananthapuram Cyber Police Station, which is probing the case, reached Mohandas' residence at Koovappadam near Mattancherry on Sunday evening along with officials from the local police station.
Police said Mohandas was present when the team arrived.
The police team collected information about his YouTube account and digital devices allegedly used to create and upload the video, officials said.
Police sources said Mohandas would be questioned in detail as part of the investigation.
By around 7.45 pm, Mohandas was brought out of his residence and taken to a hospital for a medical examination.
As Mohandas came out of the house, his supporters raised slogans in his support.
After undergoing a medical examination at a government hospital, Mohandas was taken to Thiruvananthapuram.
The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos uploaded on Mohandas' YouTube channel, 'Pathrika', were intended to disturb public peace and create fear and unrest among the public.
In the video, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi students' protest "could lead to incidents of gang rape" and claimed that there would be no complaints because "those attending the protest like rape and there are girls who enjoy being raped".
He also allegedly said that, if he were in charge, he would impose a curfew and order the protesters to disperse and, if they refused, "open fire".
He further claimed that although some people would be killed or permanently injured, the situation would be brought under control within hours and the bodies shifted to hospitals.
Police alleged that the videos were uploaded and circulated on July 24 and 25 with the intention of disturbing public tranquillity and creating unrest by spreading fear among those who participated in the protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.
The LDF had initially raised questions over the delay in registering a case against Mohandas.
After the case was registered last month, questions were also raised over the delay in arresting him.
Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala had maintained that the police would decide whether to arrest Mohandas after conducting the probe.
Earlier in the day, when reporters asked AICC general secretary K C Venugopal about the delay, he said registration of an FIR should be followed by an investigation and appropriate action.
"Filing an FIR means an investigation has to take place. These RSS people think that they rule this entire country and the whole world, and that they can say anything," he said.
Venugopal said he believed the Kerala Police was capable of taking action against those responsible.
"I firmly believe that the Kerala Police is capable of controlling such people now," he said.

headline: From a legacy handloom brand to a Gen Z wardrobe contender, Co-optex, a household name for generations in Tamil Nadu, is giving itself a makeover.
full_text:
From a legacy handloom brand to a Gen Z wardrobe contender, Co-optex, a household name for generations in Tamil Nadu, is giving itself a makeover.
The 90-year-old cooperative is revamping its designs to appeal to younger consumers, introducing newer products, and foraying into the men’s segment, which it believes is a growth market.
“There is a perception that Co-optex is primarily for women. We are now looking to change that by introducing a wider range of products for men, including silk ties, designer dhothis, linen shirts, and kurtas,” said T.N. Venkatesh, Principal Secretary, Department of Handlooms, Handicrafts, Textiles, and Khadi.
“We are coming out with products for the young crowd. We also want to weave elements that are deeply associated with Tamil Nadu into our fabrics such as the iconic Thanjavur Thalayatti Bommai and the Kurinji flower to the intricate motifs of Karuppur Kalamkari,” he added.
“In 1935, this was the largest federation and the leading handloom society in South India. It is a brand with a rich legacy, and we have continued to uphold that legacy. Unlike in the past, people today want clothes for different occasions, which is why we are now moving towards fast fashion. We have to evolve with the changing times, and that is why we introduced ‘Vetri Thari’,” said J. Innocent Divya, Managing Director of Co-optex.
Co-optex’s ‘Vetri Thari’ is a new retail concept aimed at younger consumers. The outlet was recently launched by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay. The department plans to open six stores a year over the next five years. “Home textiles are another segment that Co-optex is betting on. We currently export these products, but we now want to bring them to the Indian market as well,” Ms. Divya said.
Co-optex is widening its digital footprint. While it already has its presence on Amazon and Flipkart, the cooperative is now exploring platforms such as Instamart and Blinkit, with plans to use consumer demand and sales trends to decide which products to take forward.

headline: All 3 JPSC members quit amid CID summons; Jharkhand Governor accepts resignations
full_text:
All 3 JPSC members quit amid CID summons; Jharkhand Governor accepts resignations
The resignations of Ajita Bhattacharya, Anima Hansda, and Jamal Ahmed were accepted by Jharkhand Governor Santosh Gangwar.
All three members of the Jharkhand Public Service (JPSC) Commission resigned on Sunday, after over two weeks of protests over the alleged irregularities in the JPSC and JSSC recruitment examinations.
The resignations of Ajita Bhattacharya, Anima Hansda, and Jamal Ahmed were accepted by Jharkhand Governor Santosh Gangwar, the Lok Bhavan said in a statement.
This comes even as the government agreed to the cancellation of the 14th JPSC preliminary exam, the JPSC Backlog 2023, and the JPSC Backlog 2025. The state government said it would take a “two-pronged” approach to address the irregularities, and announced measures including the setting up of fast-track courts and constituting a committee to determine necessary reforms in the examinations.
What measures has the Jharkhand govt announced?
The state government, after the sixth round of talks with the student delegation on Sunday, said a CID probe would be pursued against the criminal aspects of the cases related to irregularities in the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and 2023-25 backlog recruitments. Jharkhand education minister Sudivya Kumar said that for suspected financial irregularities, Enforcement Directorate would be asked to step in.
Kumar announced the setting up of fast-track courts in the cases and the filing of chargesheet within 90 days. He said a committee comprising experts from IIT-ISM, IIM and XLRI would be formed to recommend necessary reforms. Kumar added that a committee headed by a retired judge was suggested to monitor the investigations, but the proposal was rejected by the protesters. The minister said the state government could not accept the demand to cancel the CGL examination because it was being conducted under the directives and oversight of the high court an Supreme Court.
The protesters demand included cancellation of all JSSC CGL, JSSC JE, and PGT exams after 2019 and a CBI investigation into the irregularities. The students have said that they will continue with their protest march to the Jharkhand Assembly on Monday, unless a CID probe is announced. The protesters had also called for strict action against those accused in the cases, and the disclosure of category-wise cut-offs (UR, EWS, BC-I, BC-II, SC, ST), OMR copies, and response sheets for transparency.
Jharkhand CM Soren promises ‘justice’, Governor Gangwar urges dialogue to resolve issues
Jharkhand chief minister Hemant Soren earlier on Sunday said the state government would ensure “justice” in the cases related to alleged irregularities in recruitment exams.
“The youth will receive justice, and those responsible for the irregularities will face the severest possible punishment,” ANI news agency cited Soren as saying. He said the solution to every issue lay in dialogue, “not in the use of batons or bullets.”
Jharkhand Governor Gangwar also appealed to the protesting aspirants to resolve the issue through dialogue, saying the chief minister was “very concerned” about the students' problems.

headline: Rekha Gupta govt plans 'Child Beggar-Free Delhi' drive to protect children begging
full_text:
Rekha Gupta govt plans 'Child Beggar-Free Delhi' drive to protect children begging
Delhi will launch a citywide campaign to help children found begging and counsel their families. The plan pairs rehabilitation with legal action against organised gangs exploiting vulnerable children.
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the city government will soon launch a 'Child Beggar-Free Delhi' campaign to protect children found begging at public places and major road intersections across the capital. In a video posted on X, she said the campaign would cover all 13 districts and aim to secure a better future for children forced into beggary.
Gupta said children would not be removed by force. Instead, the government, along with the Delhi Commission for Protection of Child Rights (DCPCR) and NGOs, would counsel their families, address their difficulties and provide better alternatives. She also said the campaign would seek to identify and expose organised gangs that force children into begging.
"The campaign will also identify and expose organised gangs forcing children into begging," Gupta said, while asking people to send their comments and suggestions on the campaign. DCPCR Chairman O P Vyas said that after public feedback is considered, the campaign is expected to be launched around Independence Day.
Vyas said the issue of child begging has two aspects. "First, we will focus on parents and ensure their counselling so that children are weaned away from begging. The other is the involvement of organised gangs who force small, homeless and poor children into begging, which will require strict legal action," he said. He added that apart from NGOs, child welfare committees would also play an active role in the campaign.
Under the Juvenile Justice Act, child welfare committees are empowered to take decisions on children in need of care and protection, Vyas said. He added that children freed from beggary would need care and protection, and would be supported through education and skill training. According to him, the DCPCR will ensure that younger children are given formal education, while older children are empowered through skill training.
According to estimates by social organisations, Delhi has around 70,000 street children, with thousands engaged in begging at public places, including religious sites, bus and Metro stations, marketplaces and major road intersections. The proposed campaign aims to address both family distress and organised exploitation while providing support to children rescued from beggary.

headline: NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule on Saturday said whether the Sunetra Pawar-led Nationalist Congress Party wanted to work with political strategist Prashant Kishor was an "internal matter" of the rival faction.Sule said Kishor had b...
full_text:
NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule on Saturday said whether the Sunetra Pawar-led Nationalist Congress Party wanted to work with political strategist Prashant Kishor was an "internal matter" of the rival faction.Sule said Kishor had been her friend for several years and praised his recent electoral performance in Bihar. "Prashant Kishor has been a good personal friend of mine for several years. I have closely followed his work and I have never hidden our friendship," the Baramati MP told reporters.She said Kishor worked independently in his professional capacity and that it was his decision to choose whom he wanted to work with.
"Whether the Sunetra Pawar-led NCP wants to work with Prashant Kishor or not is their internal matter," Sule said.Her remarks came days after Kishor met Nationalist Congress Party chief and Maharashtra deputy chief minister Sunetra Pawar and her son, MP Parth Pawar.Sule also praised Kishor for his political work in Bihar, saying he had won a "very big battle" in Bankipur despite facing the BJP's formidable political machinery. She pointed to data showing that the BJP had performed poorly even at "the booth of its national president" where Nitin Nabin is registered as a voter.
"Given this situation, we should appreciate Prashant Kishor. He is hardworking and has worked with several political parties over the years," she said.Sule also drew a comparison with her own political base in Baramati, saying, "If we had been in power from the local level to Delhi, and if there had been a negative result in our own booth in Katewadi in Baramati, I would have felt that something was seriously wrong with me," she said.

headline: ‘Apologise or meet in court’: Sirsa warns AAP leaders over rice scam allegation, gives 24-hour ultimatum
full_text:
‘Apologise or meet in court’: Sirsa warns AAP leaders over rice scam allegation, gives 24-hour ultimatum
Majinder Singh Sirsa said he would initiate legal proceedings if Saurabh Bharadwaj and Sanjeev Jha failed to withdraw their claims.
Delhi minister and BJP leader Manjinder Singh Sirsa on Sunday threatened legal action against AAP leaders Saurabh Bharadwaj and Sanjeev Jha over allegations of a purported ₹22,000 crore rice scam, giving them 24 hours to withdraw their claims and issue a public apology.
Sirsa hit back after Bharadwaj alleged a ₹22,000-crore scam involving the diversion of subsidised rice meant for Delhi’s poor, accusing a BJP-run Delhi government department, a corporation based in BJP-ruled Assam and an unnamed private firm in Haryana, also governed by the BJP, of being linked to the alleged diversion.
Sirsa gives AAP leaders 24 hours
In a post on X, Sirsa accused Bharadwaj and Jha of making false and malicious allegations against him and said he would initiate legal proceedings if they failed to withdraw their claims.
“I give both Saurabh Bharadwaj and Sanjeev Jha 24 hours to withdraw these false allegations and issue a public apology, failing which I shall be constrained to initiate appropriate legal proceedings against both of them and hold them accountable for these malicious acts.”
“Apology or will meet in court,” Sirsa said, adding that the claims are “clearly intended to defame and malign” him.
“Such a malicious campaign appears to be their modus operandi. But enough is enough,” he wrote.
AAP alleges ₹143 crore weekly scam
Earlier, Bharadwaj, at a press conference, alleged that the Rekha Gupta government and an Assam-based corporation had formally approached the FCI for subsidised rice meant to be distributed among poor and needy people in Delhi.
According to Bharadwaj, around 31,000 metric tonnes of rice per week were sought under the arrangement.

He alleged that instead of reaching beneficiaries, the rice was subsequently sold to a private company in Haryana.
"The rice, obtained at around ₹23.20 per kg, was allegedly being sold in the open market for ₹46 per kg, resulting in a commission of ₹23 per kg, amounting to around ₹143 crore scam every week," Bharadwaj alleged.
He further claimed that the arrangement was planned to continue for three years, with the total value of the transactions estimated at around ₹22,000 crore.
Bharadwaj and Jha have said documents relating to the alleged arrangement would be made public. They also sought an explanation from the Delhi government over the procurement and distribution of the subsidised rice.

headline: Andhra CM directs officials to make Jaladhara-Jalaharathi continuous programme
full_text:
Andhra CM directs officials to make Jaladhara-Jalaharathi continuous programme
Amaravati, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has directed officials to make the Jaladhara-Jalaharathi programme a continuous initiative and plan to ensure there is no drinking water shortage, amid projections of rainfall being 39 per cent below normal due to the El Niño phenomenon.
The chief minister reviewed the programme through a video conference and directed officials to focus on water conservation, drinking water supply and protection of standing crops, as the El Niño impact could be more severe than anticipated.
"We should make the Jaladhara-Jalaharathi programme a continuous initiative and plan to ensure there is no drinking water shortage, particularly in view of the forecast of 39 per cent lower rainfall than what is normal," Naidu was quoted as saying in a release issued on Sunday.
Officials informed the chief minister that 82,865 works have been identified under Jaladhara-Jalaharathi, of which 79,826 have been completed.
Works worth ₹3,409.3 crore consisting renovation of tanks and feeder channels, farm ponds and excavation of trenches, have been accorded sanction,
Normal rainfall meant 867 mm rainfall during June to December, but current estimates indicated that only 525 mm could be realised during the period this year, officials said, adding that rainfall could be 56 per cent deficient in August and that the impact of El Niño was already visible in reservoir storage.
Water availability in various basins across the state stood at 563.05 TMC, compared with 825.6 TMC during the same period last year. Officials also warned that groundwater levels were likely to decline further from August.
In view of the expected severe El Niño impact, Naidu directed officials to prepare firm plans for drinking water storage and supply.
He suggested storing water in reservoirs including Velugodu, Gorakallu, Owk, Jeedipalli and Cherlopalli for drinking water needs and making arrangements for water allocations through the Nagarjuna Sagar canals to meet drinking water requirements in various districts.

In the video, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi students’ protest “could lead to incidents of gang rape." He also allegedly claimed that there would be no complaints because “those attending the protest like rape and there are girls who enjoy being raped."

A team from the Thiruvananthapuram Cyber Police Station, which is probing the case, reached Mohandas’ residence at Koovappadam near Mattancherry on Sunday evening along with officials from the local police station. Police said Mohandas was present when the investigation team arrived.
The police team collected information about his YouTube account and digital equipment allegedly used to create and upload the video. Police sources said they would question Mohandas in detail as part of the investigation.
Police registered the case following a complaint alleging that videos uploaded on Mohandas’ YouTube channel, ‘Pathrika’, were intended to disturb public peace and create fear and unrest among the public.
In the video, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi students’ protest “could lead to incidents of gang rape." He also allegedly claimed that there would be no complaints because “those attending the protest like rape and there are girls who enjoy being raped."
Mohandas also allegedly said that, if he were in charge, he would impose a curfew and order the protesters to disperse. He allegedly said that if they refused, he would “open fire."
He further claimed that although some people would be killed or permanently injured, the situation would be brought under control within hours and the bodies would be shifted to hospitals.
A case had earlier been registered against Mohandas for allegedly calling for the shooting of student protesters in Delhi. There was strong public reaction over the delay in initiating action against him despite the registration of the case.

headline: Inside Indiaâs complex journey from transplant registration to surgery
full_text:
Inside Indiaâs complex journey from transplant registration to surgery
For a patient facing end-stage organ failure, being told that a transplant may be required is only the beginning. The journey from a hospital referral to an actual transplant involves medical evaluation, registration, documentation, waitlist management, organ matching, allocation and, eventually, surgery and long-term follow-up.In India, the process is coordinated through a network involving the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), regional and state-level bodies, registered transplant hospitals and transplant coordinators.The scale of that system has changed sharply. In a February 2026 release, the Press Information Bureau said India recorded nearly 20,000 organ transplants in 2025, compared with fewer than 5,000 in 2013. More than 1,200 families donated the organs of loved ones after death in 2025, the release said.Yet the numbers tell only part of the story. Behind every transplant is a sequence that begins long before the surgeon enters the operating theatre â and, for the recipient, often long before an organ is ever offered. Nottoâs says patients are evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, registered through a transplant centre, verified by the relevant allocation body and, once cleared, placed on the appropriate waiting list.
The process starts at the transplant centre
A patient with advanced organ failure is first referred to a licensed transplant centre. Doctors assess the underlying disease, the extent of organ damage and whether transplantation is medically appropriate.Not every patient with end-stage organ failure will necessarily be fit for transplantation.Talking about the initial evaluation before transplantation, Dr Manoj Gupta, senior director and HOD, liver transplant, Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, said, âIt typically includes a review of the patientâs medical history, physical examination, blood and tissue tests, imaging, assessment of organ function, infection screening and evaluation of any underlying conditions. Eligibility is determined by several factors, including the patientâs overall health, the extent of organ failure, surgical suitability, the likelihood of benefiting from transplantation and the ability to adhere to the post-transplant treatment regimen.âHowever, other factors can also determine eligibility. Dr Goutham Kumar, consultant, HPB & liver transplant services, SPARSH Hospital, added that eligibility also depends on the âabsence of absolute contraindications, including active systemic infections, untreated malignancies, severe substance abuse or irreversible co-morbidities.âThe hospital and transplant coordinator then compile the information required for registration.Once the application is accepted, the patient's details enter the relevant transplant registry and waiting list. The waiting period can range from the same day to several years.
What being on the waiting list actually means
Being on a transplant waiting list is not simply being in a queue. Notto says patients are listed according to medical criteria, with regular and urgent categories, while priority varies by organ. For kidney transplants, time on regular dialysis is among the factors considered; other organs follow different criteria.Dr Kumar explains how these organ-specific criteria work in practice, âLiver allocation often uses the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score, while heart allocations prioritize patients on mechanical support. Pediatric patients and high-urgency acute cases frequently receive priority.âNottoâs manual also provides for urgent or âPriority Oneâ categories for patients meeting organ-specific requirements. Such cases may be reviewed by an expert committee before priority is granted, with hospitals required to provide regular clinical updates.Registration does not freeze a patientâs status. Their medical condition continues to be monitored and records updated. Depending on their health, a patient may remain active, be made inactive or become medically unfit for transplantation.
Live Kidneys lead Indiaâs transplant numbers
When a donor organ becomes available
The next turn in the journey comes when an organ becomes available. It may come from a living donor, commonly a kidney or part of a liver, or from a deceased donor after certified brain-stem death. At that point, Organ India says, âthe transplant coordinator of the hospital will counsel the family and give them the option of donating organs and tissues.âThe next of kin must consent before retrieval. That makes a donor pledge only at the beginning of the conversation. Organ India puts it plainly: âIn India it's more important to talk to your family about your decision than it is to pledge your organs and get a donor card.âOnce a donor organ is identified, a rapid, highly coordinated race against time begins. Blood group compatibility and cross-matching are verified between the donor and potential recipient, while the organ is assessed for suitability.Dr Kumar explains, âA surgical retrieval team harvests the organ and preservation solution is administered. Transport logisticsâoften utilising dedicated âgreen corridorsâ or air transportâare activated to move the organ immediately.âThe recipient is called to the hospital, re-evaluated and prepared for surgery, with the surgical team ready to proceed as soon as the donor organ arrives.
From brain-stem death to retrieval
A deceased donor is medically maintained while permissions and retrieval arrangements are completed, helping preserve viable organs until they can be recovered. Once retrieved, however, the clock begins to run: each organ has a limited preservation window.
4â6 hours for heart and lungs, 6â10 hours for intestine, 12â15 hours for liver, 12â24 hours for pancreas and 24â48 hours for kidneys
Cost remains another major barrier to transplantation in India. Dr Kumar said the âinitial surgical costs range from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 35 lakh depending on the organ (kidney vs. liver/heart) and hospital sector (public vs. private).â But the financial burden does not end with the operation. Lifelong immunosuppressants, anti-rejection treatment and âregular diagnostic monitoring add Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 monthly.âThat narrow window makes allocation a tightly coordinated process. Organs are assessed, potential recipients identified and transport arranged.
India's transplant numbers are rising
The national system has expanded significantly over the past decade.The ministry said more than 1,200 families came forward to donate the organs of loved ones after death in 2025."More than 4.8 lakh citizens have registered to donate organs and tissues after death through a Aadhaar based verification system, since 17th September 2023," the PIB release said.The release also said India had developed expertise in complex heart, lung and pancreas transplants and claimed the country "leads the world in hands transplants and performs a greater number of hand transplants than any other country."The government said the increase reflected improvements in deceased donation, transplant coordination and national organ sharing.
The gap between demand and supply remains
Even after surgery, the process continues. Recipients need lifelong follow-up and immunosuppressive medication, which can also carry long-term risks.Dr Jagriti Yadav, medical director â lab operations, Cryoviva Life Sciences, said, âThe major long-term risks include acute or chronic graft rejection, opportunistic infections, cardiovascular complications, kidney toxicity, and metabolic side effects related to immunosuppressive medicines.âThe increase in transplant numbers has not eliminated the shortage of organs.
How Indiaâs transplant numbers have surged
A 2024 article published in the National Library of Medicine's PubMed Central noted that India was performing around 17,000-18,000 solid organ transplants a year, making it the world's third-largest transplant country by volume after the United States and China, while transplant rates per million population remained lower than in several high-income countries.Organ India's data and awareness material has similarly highlighted the disparity between the number of patients requiring organs and the number of deceased donors available. The organisation has estimated that India has a large pool of potential brain-stem-death donors but a much smaller number of actual deceased donors.For a patient on a waiting list, that gap translates into uncertainty: being medically eligible and registered does not guarantee that a suitable organ will become available in time.Delhi remains one of the country's major transplant centres.The Delhi government's organ-donation portal provides information on registered hospitals and transplant services and operates under the Health & Family Welfare Department and the State Appropriate Authority. The department's published information lists registered facilities for kidney, liver, heart, lung and pancreas transplantation, as well as eye and cornea services.
Foreign recipients are also part of the system
Indiaâs transplant system also treats foreign nationals, subject to additional safeguards. Government guidance says an Indian living donor may donate to a foreign recipient only if they are near relatives; donors must be at least 18, with medical-visa and registration requirements applicable to both parties.
Data shows organ transplants for foreign recipients in India
In 2023, India recorded 18,378 transplants and 18,336 individual recipients, including 1,851 foreign nationals, according to Notto data reported in 2024. Delhi recorded the highest number involving foreign recipients at 1,445, followed by Rajasthan at 116 and West Bengal at 88. Only nine involved unrelated deceased-donor organs.For a transplant recipient, perhaps the least visible part of the process is the period between registration and an organ offer.During this period, the patient's condition can change. Tests may have to be repeated, treatment may need adjustment and the transplant centre may update the patient's status on the registry.The patient therefore remains under the care of the transplant team while the allocation system searches for a medically suitable organ.Notto says special requests do not guarantee an immediate organ or override the established rules for matching and allocation.
The next stage is a more connected transplant system
Indiaâs transplant system is becoming more digitally connected, with national coordination and data-sharing expanding alongside transplant numbers. Aadhaar-verified donation registrations crossed 4.8 lakh, while nearly 20,000 transplants were recorded in 2025.The next challenge is ensuring potential donors are identified, families counselled and organs retrieved, transported and allocated efficiently. For recipients, that means staying medically fit, updating the transplant centre and following clinical advice.

headline: AAP's Saurabh Bharadwaj alleges ‘ ₹22,000 crore rice scam plan’ by Delhi govt

AAP's Saurabh Bharadwaj alleges ‘ ₹22,000 crore rice scam plan’ by Delhi govt
Saurabh Bharadwaj alleged that Delhi government sought highly subsidised rice to distribute among poor people but it never reached the public.
Aam Aadmi Party leader and former Delhi minister Saurabh Bharadwaj alleged that the current Bharatiya Janata Party government in the national capital planned a scam of subsidised rice of “ ₹22,000 crore” to be played out over three years.
He alleged, through a post on X (formerly Twitter), that a corporation based in Assam and the Delhi government sent a “formal request” to the Food Corporation of India to get “heavily subsidised rice” to be distributed among the poor people of the national capital.
However, he alleged, that no such rice ever reached the poor public and was rather sold to a private company in Haryana to make profits.
Also read: NDMC takes over maintenance of Central Vista roads
“A corporation based in Assam and the Delhi government sent a formal request to FCI to get heavily subsidised rice from FCI (Food Corporation of India). A huge quantity of 31,000 metric tons of rice per week was demanded to be distributed among the poor of Delhi,” Bharadwaj wrote in a post on X.
“This subsidised rice never reached even a single poor person. All the rice was sold to a private company in Haryana at heavy profits,” he added.
‘Scam of ₹143 crore a week’
The AAP leader added that that this meant the Delhi government planned “a scam of ₹143 crore per week was planned for 3 years”.
Also read: Delhi records 98% of August’s rainfall in just five days
“This was a planned scam of ₹22000 crore in 3 years,” he wrote.
He also shared a video of himself describing the scam.
“The way the Delhi government and the Assam corporation were looting the people of Delhi, it was going to go on for three years,” Bharadwaj is heard saying in the video.
Manjinder Singh Sirsa is Delhi's minister of food, supplies and consumer affairs.
Bharadwaj claimed that Sirsa's department wrote to the FCI demanding 31,000 metric tons of rice every week to be sent to the corporation based in Assam. However, he said, that instead of distributing this rice amongst the poor people, the Assam based corporation was selling that rice to a private firm in Haryana for profit.
“It can be said that the Assam-based corporation was earning a commission of ₹70 crore every week, and if this would have continued for three years, this loot would have been of around ₹11,000 crore,” he said in the video.
Bharadwaj also claimed that it was the Central government's vigilance department which identified the scam.

full_text:
Tiranga Yatra: Patriotic marches held across UP, Haryana ahead of Independence Day
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 09, 2026, 10:50 IST

School students and local residents hold national flags during a 'Tiranga Yatra' rally taken out ahead of Independence Day, in Ranchi, Jharkhand. (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: Tiranga Yatras were held across several parts of the country on Sunday as political leaders and citizens joined marches carrying the Tricolour ahead of India's 80th Independence Day on August 15. The events were organised as part of the broader 'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign, with participants paying tribute to freedom fighters and promoting the message of national unity and patriotism.From Lucknow and Kharagpur to Narnaul, the marches brought together political leaders, students, young people and citizens. Participants carried the national flag and raised patriotic slogans as part of events planned in the run-up to Independence Day.The celebrations are also being linked to the commemoration of 150 years of 'Vande Mataram', with activities planned across states during the campaign period.
In Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh chief Minister Yogi Adityanath participated in a Tiranga Yatra organised by the Bharatiya Janata Party. The march began from the chief minister's residence at 5, Kalidas Marg and proceeded towards the Vidhan Bhavan.Thousands of young people participated in the procession, carrying the Tricolour and raising slogans including "Bharat Mata Ki Jai" and "Vande Mataram".Adityanath said the yatra was an expression of gratitude towards freedom fighters and martyrs and urged participants to maintain discipline during the march.
"This Tiranga Yatra is an expression of gratitude towards all those martyrs and a resolve to carry forward Prime Minister Narendra Modi's mantra of 'nation first'," he said.He also urged people to participate in the 'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign and hoist the national flag at their homes with due respect.In Kharagpur, West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh participated in another Tiranga Yatra and said similar programmes would be organised across the state."The Tiranga Yatra is being held across Bengal, with the 'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign taking the national flag to every household... The programme has started today and will be held in other districts as well. A major event will take place in Kolkata on the 10th, with thousands of people expected to participate," Ghosh said.The West Bengal government has announced plans to distribute 70 lakh national flags across the state as part of the campaign. A major Tiranga rally is also scheduled in Kolkata on August 10.
Haryana combines Tiranga campaign with fitness drive
In Haryana's Narnaul, chief minister Nayab Singh Saini flagged off a state-level half marathon organised under the 'Haryana Uday Abhiyan' with the theme "Har Ghar Tiranga".The event combined the Independence Day campaign with a message on fitness and the need to tackle drug abuse among young people."Carrying this vision forward, we have taken the message of a drug-free Haryana to the masses through the 'Haryana Uday' initiative. Whether through marathons, cyclothons, Raahgiri events, or various public awareness programs, we are actively engaging lakhs of young people and citizens in this mass movement," Saini said.He also spoke about action against drug trafficking in the state, saying illegal assets worth approximately Rs 53 crore had been seized and 111 properties acquired through illicit means had been demolished.
What is Har Ghar Tiranga?
The 'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign was launched in 2022 as part of the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav celebrations. The initiative encourages citizens to hoist the national flag at their homes and develop a personal connection with the Tricolour.The campaign also seeks to honour the sacrifices of freedom fighters and strengthen the spirit of patriotism among citizens.
This year's campaign includes Tiranga rallies and processions, exhibitions, concerts, bike and cycle rallies, tricolour lighting of important locations, decorations and Rangoli programmes.Special activities are also being organised under the theme "Tiranga Salute to the Spirit of Vande Mataram", along with the "Selfie with Tiranga" initiative.The National Flag will also be hoisted at households and government offices during the campaign period.With Independence Day approaching, more Tiranga Yatras and public programmes are expected to be held across states as part of the nationwide celebrations.

headline: Adhikari orders probe into cremation of RG Kar rape-murder victim; names 3 TMC leaders
full_text:
Adhikari orders probe into cremation of RG Kar rape-murder victim; names 3 TMC leaders
The memorial event was also addressed by Ratna Debnath, the victim’s mother, who won the Panihati assembly seat in May
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday ordered an inquiry into the alleged hasty cremation of the victim’s body in the 2024 RG Kar Hospital rape and murder case. He also named three Trinamool Congress (TMC) leaders accused by the victim’s family, as the government observed a two-minute silence across all hospitals to mark the second anniversary of the incident.
“The CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) is probing the main crime and also the alleged corruption at RG Kar Hospital under orders from the Calcutta high court. I cannot do anything there. But I have found one aspect that the police can probe. It is the cremation at the obscure Nataghat crematorium in the Ghola police station area,” Adhikari said at an event in Panihati, North 24 Parganas district, held in memory of the junior doctor whose body was found at the hospital, where she was a student, on the morning of August 9, 2024.
The post-mortem examination was completed within hours and the body was cremated by evening.
“I am asking the Barrackpore police commissioner to start an inquiry. In the cremation schedule, it was the third body on the list that day but the number was changed from three to one. According to rules, relatives of a deceased person must pay a cremation fee and sign documents but the victim’s family did neither,” Adhikari said.
“Nirmal Ghosh (TMC’s ex-Panihati MLA), Somnath Dey (TMC’s Panihati municipality councillor), and Sanjib Mukherjee (local TMC leader) did all this. They must be punished,” Adhikari added.
“I have not forgotten Abhaya (the name people gave to the victim). I am committed,” he added.
The memorial event was also addressed by Ratna Debnath, the victim’s mother, who won the Panihati assembly seat in May after contesting on a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ticket against Nirmal Ghosh’s son.
“We will not rest till our daughter gets justice,” she said.
In May this year, the Calcutta high court division bench of Justices Shampa Sarkar and Tirthankar Ghosh ordered the formation of a three-member CBI special investigation team (SIT) headed by a joint director for a second investigation.
The victim’s parents, however, have expressed disappointment several times because the first CBI probe ordered days after the crime, reached the same conclusion as the Kolkata police, resulting in the life sentence of just one suspect, former Kolkata police civic volunteer Sanjay Roy.
“I know that the family is not happy with the CBI investigation. But the court has ordered it. We have to wait and see. I have been unable to find out even to this day why the Supreme Court took up the case suo motu in 2024 when the Calcutta high court was already hearing it. Nobody knows why Supreme Court intervened in the RG Kar case. It is a court monitored case. Hence as chief minister I cannot say anything more,” Adhikari said.
Nirmal Ghosh, who is wanted in a criminal case, Somnath Dey and Sanjib Mukherjee could not be contacted on Sunday evening despite several efforts. All three, however, denied the allegation over the past two years, saying they merely tried to help the young doctor’s grief-stricken parents.
The RG Kar crime was one of the key issues in the assembly polls that the BJP swept.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah both campaigned for the victim’s mother who alleged after the crime that senior TMC leaders and government officials hatched a conspiracy to kill her daughter to hide something.
On May 15, six days after being sworn in as the CM, Adhikari suspended former Kolkata police commissioner Vineet Goyal and two other Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, Indira Mukherjee and Abhisek Gupta, on charges of mishandling the case and offering money to the victim’s parents. Adhikari ordered a probe against them.

headline: Avoid making statements to appease BJP: Congress's veiled dig at Shashi Tharoor
full_text:
Avoid making statements to appease BJP: Congress's veiled dig at Shashi Tharoor
Shashi Tharoor had said at an event in Maharashtra on Friday that Rahul Gandhi's 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' campaign was raising many of the same issues as the Cockroach Janata Party protests.
AICC general secretary KC Venugopal on Sunday cautioned Congress leaders against making public remarks that could give the BJP political ammunition, as he responded to Shashi Tharoor’s comments on Rahul Gandhi’s outreach to Gen Z.
Venugopal was reacting to Tharoor’s reported observation that Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ programme had not resonated with young people as strongly as the Cockroach Janata Party protests.
“I have only seen his statement reported through some media channels. I haven’t been able to hear exactly what he said,” Venugopal told reporters.
He said Tharoor should clarify his remarks himself, but added that Congress leaders needed to exercise caution.
“Even if Congress members do not always strictly abide by party frameworks or discipline, we must be careful to avoid making statements that merely appease the BJP,” he said.
“The BJP will be delighted if someone finds fault with Rahul Gandhi or says two negative things about him. That would make them the happiest,” Venugopal added.
He, however, said he did not believe Tharoor had made the remarks deliberately.
“All of us should take care, knowingly or unknowingly. I don’t believe he said it knowingly, nor is he likely to say it intentionally,” he said.
VENUGOPAL DEFENDS RAHUL’S GEN Z OUTREACH
Venugopal strongly defended Rahul Gandhi’s student outreach, saying the programme in Allahabad had drawn young people beyond the Congress’s traditional organisational base.
“What was the scene witnessed there yesterday in Allahabad? Those were not typical Congress workers, Youth Congress or NSUI members. That was India’s real Gen Z,” he said.
He claimed similar participation had been seen at programmes in Kota and Dehradun.
Venugopal also accused the Uttar Pradesh government of trying to disrupt the Allahabad event, alleging that pressure had initially been exerted to deny the venue and that unsanitary conditions were later created along the route.
He further said Rahul had consistently raised issues concerning students who faced police action during protests, including those injured by pellet guns and women protesters allegedly assaulted by male police personnel.
Venugopal also referred to the Congress march towards the Prime Minister’s residence in solidarity with protesting students, calling it one of the biggest recent demonstrations in support of Gen Z.
WHAT THAROOR SAID ABOUT CONGRESS CAMPAIGN
Tharoor had said at an event in Maharashtra on Friday that Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ campaign was raising many of the same issues as the Cockroach Janata Party protests.

headline: Shinde Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre moves to Goa after bail in doctor assault case

Shinde Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre moves to Goa after bail in doctor assault case
Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre left jail and shifted to Goa after getting bail in the doctor assault case. The Bombay High Court tied his release to staying outside Maharashtra and ordered a fast-tracked trial.
Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre, accused of assaulting doctors at a civic hospital in Thane district, was released from jail on Saturday and moved to neighbouring Goa in line with a Bombay High Court bail condition requiring him to stay outside Maharashtra.
Mhatre walked out of Adharwadi jail in the Kalyan area a day after the High Court granted him bail. The court also ordered that the trial be fast-tracked and completed in a time-bound manner.
Speaking to reporters before leaving, Mhatre said he would stay in Anjuna in Goa along with three of his supporters, who are co-accused in the case. "The matter is currently sub-judice. I have complete faith in the court and will fully accept whatever verdict the judiciary delivers," he said before being escorted into a vehicle.
While granting bail to Mhatre, a bench of Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge and Justice Gautam Ankhad imposed strict conditions on him and the other accused. The High Court said they must stay outside Maharashtra until the chargesheet in the case is filed.
"The accused will be allowed to return to Maharashtra only when the trial court frames charges in the case. Even then, they shall not contact the witnesses in the case or tamper with any evidence," the High Court said.
A court in Thane district had earlier granted bail to Mhatre, a corporator of the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation, on July 15. However, taking suo motu cognisance, the High Court on July 18 stayed that bail and asked him to surrender before the police. The High Court stayed the Kalyan court's order, calling it "perverse", and said the magistrate had taken the issue very lightly and had not considered Mhatre's criminal antecedents.
The case relates to an incident on July 6, when Mhatre and the other accused allegedly gathered at Shastri Nagar Hospital and assaulted doctors. The incident took place after family members of a pregnant woman accused the hospital staff of delaying treatment. With his release from jail, Mhatre has now shifted to Goa as required under the High Court's bail conditions while the case moves ahead.

headline: Opposition gears up to resist Centre's FCRA amendment; why foreign funding bill is under fire
full_text:
Opposition gears up to resist Centre's FCRA amendment; why foreign funding bill is under fire
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 seeks to make amendments to the existing foreign funding law.
The Opposition is gearing up to resist the Centre's Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, which is expected in Parliament this week. The amendment would reportedly strengthen the government's control over foreign-funded assets in case organisations lose their registration.
Congress MP Mallikarjun Kharge said the Opposition intends to block the government's FCRA move and a decision in this regard will be taken on Monday. "We will make a decision tomorrow after convening an all-party meeting, specifically of floor leaders."
ALSO READ: 'Our internal matter': India rebuffs US lawmakers’ criticism of FCRA bill
Speaking against the FCRA Bill, NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule said one cannot always view foreign funding with suspicion. Sule opposed the current form of the bill and called for its withdrawal. "If the government is not ready to withdraw the bill, then it should send it to a JPC," she further said.
Cong issues whip in Parliament
The party, anticipating the tabling of "very important" matters, issued a whip to its MPs in the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha to ensure their presence in Parliament on August 10, 11 and 12. Congress asked all INDIA bloc allies to ensure that their MPs remain present on the three days, news agency PTI reported.
However, the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs has not mentioned the FCRA amendment bill in the tentative government business for next week.
What is FCRA Bill 2026?
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 seeks to make amendments to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, which regulate foreign donations received by individuals, associations and organisations. According to official records, as seen on July 15 this year, there were 14,449 FCRA active registrations while 22,498 stood cancelled and 15,212 had expired, news agency ANI reported.
The FCRA Bill proposes to set up a 'designated authority' which will take control of the foreign contributions in case an entity's FCRA registration stands cancelled, surrendered or lapsed.
The assets created out of such foreign funds will initially come under the control of the 'designated authority' and may subsequently be transferred entirely if the entity fails to reacquire its registration within a specified period. The authority will also hold the power to manage assets and monitor the activities of such entities if required.
Points of contention in FCRA bill
There has been contention over three sections of the FCRA Bill - Section 14B, Section 16A and Section 16B, the .
Section 14B, which talks about "cessation" of an FCRA certificate, specifies that a certificate will be considered to have ceased if an entity does not apply for renewal, is refused renewal or it expires without being renewed.
Section 16A proposes that the foreign funds received by the organisation, whose certification has ceased, and its assets will be vested in a Designated Authority.
The third issue of contention is Section 16B, which would allow the new framework to be applied on assets already vested under the earlier law. This raises fears of adverse impact on organisations whose FCRA registrations lapsed years ago, but are now functioning on domestic funds.
Why Oppn is against FCRA bill?
Congress general secretary K C Venugopal called the FCRA bill 'completely unconstitutional' and expressed fears that the new legislation could hurt NGOs and community groups, particularly those run by minorities. He called it a deliberate attempt to intimidate and control organisations, particularly Christian groups in Kerala. The bill, he said, would tighten the noose over voluntary and social service organisations.
Trinamool Congress MP Derek O'Brien termed the bill 'draconian' and wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi against it. He said the proposed law could lead to "excessive executive control" of NGOs and other organisations working in education and healthcare sectors.
Mizoram Congress held protest in Aizawl on July 21 with its senior vice-president Lalnunmawia Chuaungo alleging that the FCRA bill would make it more difficult to obtain FCRA certification or seek legal remedies in case applications were rejected.
Mizoram chief minister Lalduhoma on Thursday met Union home minister Amit Shah to present recommendations and register regional concerns regarding the FCTA. Shah also met members and representatives of the Christian community, who have raised objections to provisions of the bill.
DMK president MK Stalin urged the Centre to withdraw the FCRA Amendment Bill and repeal Section 15 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010.
In Kerala, the Catholic Church has also voiced concerns over the proposed amendments to the existing FCRA law.
