headline: PK, Vijay and Annamalai: Has the start-up moment arrived in Indian politics?
full_text:
PK, Vijay and Annamalai: Has the start-up moment arrived in Indian politics?
Indian politics has long been a market dominated by established players, built on caste, religion, dynasties and decades-old political machinery. But Prashant Kishor, C Joseph Vijay and K Annamalai are trying to disrupt like start-ups do. They are challenging the old business model in politics, with Vijay emerging as the first political unicorn.
For decades, Indian politics has followed a pattern. It has been all about building a caste coalition, consolidating a religious voter bloc, cultivating a family legacy, and then fighting elections through an organisation that may have existed for quite some time. But a new political template or start-up-like mode is beginning to take shape in the political spectrum of the world's largest democracy. The early signs of it are being seen in three different figures. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, political strategist-turned-politician Prashant Kishor and former BJP Tamil Nadu chief K Annamalai.
These three are not ideological triplets, nor do they have the same political resources. Yet each is attempting, in his own way, to build politics from scratch rather than operate within an established political juggernaut. The hint of this pivot has come with Prashant Kishor, or PK as he is popularly known, winning Bihar's Bankipur Assembly seat by-election on August 3.
PK was a political consultant before he dived into politics with the idea of transforming his home state of Bihar. He is a leader whose party had drawn a blank in its first Assembly election and returned to defeat the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in one of the strongholds it had dominated for 30 long years.
It is PK's victory that has pushed everyone to think about whether Indian politics is entering another generational transition? Will the next generation of political leaders look more like startup founders than traditional politicians?
Indian politics has never remained static. Every generation has brought a new organising principle. The Congress's one-party dominance system was challenged by the rise of regional parties in 1967. Mandal in 1990 transformed the political importance of caste. The Ram Janmabhoomi movement's peak year, 1992, reshaped the role of religion in electoral politics. Economic liberalisation changed aspirations, television changed political communication, and social media's dominance since 2014 allowed politicians to speak directly to voters without depending entirely on traditional media or party structures.
The emerging model might be different again. It is politics built around a leader's personal brand, direct citizen engagement, youth networks, data, technology, issue-based mobilisation and a promise to disrupt an existing political order.
Tamil Nadu's CM Vijay has already demonstrated how quickly such a political startup can scale. PK appears to have found electoral validation after a difficult beginning. Annamalai, meanwhile, has walked away from an established political organisation to build a new one almost from the ground up with a different working structure.
One is the unicorn. One is the startup trying to find its market. One is still building the company. But together, they offer a glimpse of what Indian politics could look like in the next generation.
PRASHANT KISHOR: FROM SELLING STRATEGIES TO BECOMING THE PRODUCT
Prashant Kishor's transition into politics was perhaps the most unusual of the three. For years, PK operated from behind the political scenes, as the strategist who helped leaders understand voters, shape messages and build winning campaigns. He worked with some of the country's most powerful political outfits and its leaders, across India's political landscape from north to south and east to west, before deciding that he would no longer merely design political victories for others.
In 2022, he began the Jan Suraaj campaign in Bihar with a roughly 3,000-km padyatra (foot march). It was a strikingly old-fashioned method for a politician whose reputation was built on data, technology and modern campaign management. PK travelled through villages and towns, meeting people and attempting to understand the problems of Bihar at the grassroots level.
Jan Suraaj eventually transformed from a movement into the Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) in 2024. The pitch was equally unconventional. Instead of placing caste arithmetic at the centre, Kishor spoke about education, employment, migration, healthcare, pensions, agriculture, women's economic empowerment and governance. He argued that Bihar's political stagnation was partly the consequence of a political system that had spent decades fighting over power without adequately addressing why young people were forced to leave the state in search of work.
PK's party was built differently. He gave tickets to academicians, intellectuals, retired bureaucrats and legal experts to contest the Assembly election, while also ensuring proportional representation for backward classes, women, transgender and the youth.
But the first electoral test of PK and his JSP was brutal. The party contested 238 of the 243 Assembly seats in the 2025 Bihar election and failed to win even one. The party secured only around 3% of the vote. PK himself had chosen not to contest. For a conventional politician, such a result could have been the end of the project.
But PK continued to insist that Jan Suraaj was not designed around a single election. He had attempted to build a political organisation, not merely a campaign.
Then came Bankipur's bypoll. Kishor's victory there does not automatically transform JSP into a major political force in Bihar. A bypoll is not an Assembly poll, and one constituency cannot erase the structural advantages enjoyed by established parties. But politically, the symbolism is difficult to ignore. The strategist who spent years helping others win elections has now demonstrated that his own political vehicle can win one.
What makes Bankipur more than a constituency story is that it suggests a new political organisation can survive its first major failure, rebuild and return with electoral credibility. And that is precisely how startups work.
Start-ups go to the market with their business model, fail, return to the drawing board, and pivot quickly for a comeback.
THALAPATHY VIJAY: THE UNICORN OF THE START-UP POLITICS OF INDIA
If PK represents a political startup searching for scale, Vijay represents the unicorn, which is an exceptionally rare political enterprise that achieved extraordinary growth in a short period.
C Joseph Vijay entered politics in 2024 by launching his party, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK). The actor-turned-politician already possessed a massive public following that most political leaders spend years trying to acquire. But converting film popularity into political power is not as easy as converting fans into voters.
Tamil Nadu has one of India's most sophisticated political ecosystems. The two Dravidian giants, Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), have spent decades developing dominance in the state. The land of the Tamils has rarely been kind to outsiders attempting to break that duopoly of the DMK and the AIADMK.
Vijay nevertheless tried to create a new political brand. His politics did not completely revolve around caste nor Periyar. When the TVK chief spoke about social justice, it was largely framed through equality and welfare rather than caste mobilisation. He positioned TVK against communal politics and attempted to attract young voters.
Vijay's manifesto focused heavily on everyday concerns like women's welfare, employment, education, healthcare, farmers, pensions, free electricity, drinking water and social security.
But the real achievement of TVK was the speed. Traditional parties take years to establish themselves, whereas Vijay's party not only built itself from scratch but also formed the government within two years of its birth.
In the 2026 Tamil Nadu Assembly election, TVK emerged as the single largest party with 108 seats in the 234-member Assembly. With support from Congress and other regional partners, Vijay was sworn in as Tamil Nadu CM, ending the 60-year dominance of the Dravidian heavyweights.
That is why the startup analogy fits him better than almost any recent political entrant. Vijay created a new brand, entered a market dominated by established players, converted an existing community into a political base and then captured power. But the unicorn story comes with its own warning.
A political startup can scale rapidly because of the founder's brand. Governing, however, requires institutions. A fan base can fill a rally, but it cannot by itself run a government. The real test for Vijay will therefore be whether TVK can transform the extraordinary popularity of its founder into a durable political institution. If it can, the Vijay experiment could become one of the most consequential examples of political entrepreneurship in contemporary India.
ANNAMALAI: THE FOUNDER WHO LEFT THE ESTABLISHED COMPANY
K Annamalai represents a different kind of political entrepreneur when compared to PK and Vijay. He did not spend years crafting elections from outside the political system like PK, nor did he enter politics with a film star's fan base like Vijay. The IPS officer-turned-politician entered conventional politics in 2020.
Annamalai spent around six years with the BJP and was the party's Tamil Nadu president. He experienced the machinery of a national political organisation from the inside. He attempted to bring his own style to the party, but reached the point where he believed the existing structure could not accommodate the kind of politics he wanted to pursue.
So he quit the established party like some start-up founders who quit established companies to work on their passion. Annamalai is very much like Tony Fadell and Martha Stewart, who left their safe harbours to pursue their dreams.
On June 5, 2026, Annamalai launched We The Leaders, a political movement that he says will become a political party slowly. Unlike a conventional politician launching a new party before an election, Annamalai has chosen to build the organisation first and contest later, with the 2031 Tamil Nadu Assembly election as the larger objective.
That makes his experiment perhaps the most literal political startup of the three. There is no immediate election to fight, and Annamalai's movement is emphasising rather on membership, civic engagement, leadership training and building an organisational structure.
We The Leaders has spoken about term limits, age limits and rotation of leadership for elected representatives. Annamalai has described himself as the movement's "Chief Servant", rather than building the organisation around the conventional idea of a supreme leader. His movement also seeks to position itself against caste and religion-based politics, asking citizens to approach political participation as citizens first.
In this sense, Annamalai is not merely trying to create another party. He is trying to redesign the organisational structure of one. But unlike Vijay and PK, Annamalai does not yet have an electoral victory to demonstrate that the model works. That is precisely what makes his experiment interesting and uncertain at the same time.
THREE FOUNDERS FOR THE POLITICS OF NEXT GEN?
PK, Vijay and Annamalai have different traits as politicians. PK has experience designing political strategy. Vijay has an enormous fan base. Annamalai has administrative and political experience.
Their political environments are different too. PK's fray is Bihar's deeply involved caste and alliance structures. Vijay's battlefield is Tamil Nadu's established Dravidian political order. And Annamalai's is to create political space outside the structures he once operated within.
But there is a common thread running through all three. They are attempting to manufacture a political constituency rather than inherit one. That is a significant departure from the conventional Indian political model. That is startup politics of India.
But this does not mean caste and religion are suddenly irrelevant in the country's politics. They remain powerful forces in Indian elections. Nor does it mean traditional parties are disappearing. Established parties have local leaders, grassroots workers, resources and social relationships built for decades, which is something startups cannot manufacture overnight.
Yet the startup analogy captures a genuine shift in political behaviour. The recent student agitations and emerging political developments across the country offer a hint of a broader change.
Indian politics has evolved with every generation that found a new way to organise voters. On the ground sense is that the next generation might see politics beyond caste, religion and division. The political market is looking like it is changing. The question is no longer whether politics can be built differently. Bankipur, Vijay and Annamalai suggest that it could. The question now is whether this new model can scale.

headline: Tamuli Gaon, a village in eastern Assam’s Jorhat district, is about 40 kilometres west of neighbouring Sivasagar district’s Bihubar, the epicentre of destruction by one of Assam’s worst localised floods since the 1950s. The gushing waters that submer...
full_text:
Tamuli Gaon, a village in eastern Assam’s Jorhat district, is about 40 kilometres west of neighbouring Sivasagar district’s Bihubar, the epicentre of destruction by one of Assam’s worst localised floods since the 1950s. The gushing waters that submerged much of Sivasagar and adjoining Charaideo districts on July 19–20 lost momentum by the time they reached the periphery of Tamuli Gaon, but inundated the surrounding, low-lying paddy fields, to turn this village of 110 families into an island.
The village’s Biju Kumar Sarmah, a teacher nicknamed Gospuli for his obsession with plantation drives to “reclaim what’s lost”, explains why Tamuli Gaon was spared. “The water did not have enough force to cut through the embankments in our area, unlike those a few kilometres to the east, toward Sivasagar district,” he says. He is not sure whether the distance from Bihubar would provide Tamuli Gaon with insurance against a bigger disaster, with at least two more months of rain to go this year. “The floodwaters have less than half the distance to travel from Bihubar to Tamuli Gaon than from Mon to Bihubar,” he says.
Mon, the headquarters of Nagaland’s district of the same name, bore the brunt of extremely heavy rainfall that drenched parts of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, and Nagaland from July 18 to 22. The rainfall triggered landslides, killing 11 people in Mon town, and large volumes of water from five major rivers and numerous streams originating in Mon district gushed downstream, carrying earth and debris, to swamp more than 80% of Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.
“The water trickled in gently around noon on July 19. It suddenly became a mahapralay (total destruction), and before we could understand what was happening, we were being thrashed about in neck-deep water,” says Shivraj Sharma of Bihubar Nepalikhuti, a village near the Assam-Nagaland border that was home to some 200 families of mostly dairy farmers.
Nepalikhuti is close to the Dikhow River and along the axis of the road connecting Mon to Naginimora, a border town in Nagaland that thrives on coal mining and trade. Several stretches of this road were almost erased by the overflowing Dikhow.
Sharma and other members of his family clambered atop their tin-roofed house to save themselves, watching helplessly as a few villagers were swept past, flailing their arms to grab anything to anchor them. As the water level kept rising, the Sharma family — drenched from the incessant rainfall and without food for two days — feared meeting a watery grave like their cattle. “Our tethered cows could have survived if we had the time to cut the ropes,” he says.
When the floodwaters receded, Bihubar Nepalikhuti was under at least 4 feet of silt with branches of trees, upturned furniture, household appliances, clothes, books, bags, footwear, utensils, mattresses, and bloated carcasses of livestock sticking out from the surface.
Silt-smeared refrigerators, television sets, two-wheelers, sofa sets, packaged foods, and other items continue to flank a 19-km road from Bihubar to Simaluguri, where floodwaters caused extensive damage to an arterial railway track, snapping train services between eastern Assam and the rest of the State for almost a fortnight.
The road was largely cleared a fortnight later, but most houses and structures on either side continued to be enveloped in debris. Septuagenarian Habibur Rahman recalls a “terrifying sound” as the floodwaters approached their house at Santak Bihubar village, snapping trees and slicing through anything in the way. “I don’t know when we can go back to our house. I no longer have the money and the energy to clear the head-high debris from our house,” he says.
The ordeal has been similar or worse for Moromi Bora Bordoloi of Bihubar Siloni Majgaon, Ranjit Gogoi of Charing Gogoi Ali, Pithuram Konwar of Dighalijan, and Jatin Saikia of Bhitoruwal Gaon. “We were just not prepared, maybe because we are not used to such water fury,” Bordoloi, a weaver-homemaker, says.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Assam floods: is development or climate change to blame? | Above the Fold | Aug 5 2026
Caught unaware
The Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat district authorities, too, were caught unawares by the deluge. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, after touring the flood-hit districts, admitted that the administration in each could not mobilise rescue and relief operations for seven days since the disaster struck. He said this was understandable, as these districts do not have a history of major floods and the authorities were not as disaster-ready as other districts that experience floods regularly.
These three districts accounted for 71 of the 99 people who died in the floods across 16 districts from April to August 8, 2026, and more than 94% of some 7.21 lakh flood-affected people. The scale of the disaster across much of the 4,426 sq. km covered by the three districts is perhaps comparable to the 11-day flooding of southern Assam’s Silchar town in June 2022, with water levels rising to 12 feet in some areas. There’s a difference though: Silchar is prone to flooding or water-logging, often fleetingly, unlike Charaideo or Sivasagar.
Disaster management experts explained why the government machinery was underprepared in the three districts. “There’s a flaw in the government’s approach to disaster management, which is to identify risks and concentrate on high-risk areas. The planning needs to change. If low or zero-risk areas become high-risk overnight, there’s very little people can do, as was the case with the three districts,” says Partha Jyoti Das, a climate, water, and disaster specialist with Assam-based biodiversity conservation group Aaranyak. He adds that getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management is crucial. “Ditto with factoring in fluctuating climate change scenarios in everything to minimise disasters.”
According to the 2018 Climate Vulnerability Assessment prepared by the Indian Institute of Technology-Guwahati and IIT-Mandi in collaboration with Bengaluru’s Indian Institute of Science, Assam was the most vulnerable State in the Indian Himalayan region.
The 2021 index of the same assessment ranked Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Bihar as the States most vulnerable to extreme climate events and hydro-meteorological disasters. The index analysed 640 districts in India and found that 463 of these were vulnerable to extreme floods, droughts, and cyclones, and that more than 80% of the country’s population resides in districts highly exposed to climate risks.
Rainfall-induced floods, landslides, and erosion indicate that people in all 35 districts in Assam are highly exposed to climate risks. Often, 25-32 districts experience floods in a year, more severe in districts perched below 88 metres, the average elevation of Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.
This is not unusual. A combination of geography, medium-to-heavy monsoon rainfall for almost six months, and a network of silt-laden rivers has made floods an annual phenomenon in Assam.
Experts say the pattern of flooding changed after the Assam-Tibet earthquake in 1950 triggered massive landslides across the eastern Himalayas, sending large volumes of sediment into the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries and permanently altering the river system.
Deforestation (Assam lost about 3,600 sq. km of tree cover from 2001–2025, accelerating soil erosion and making the rivers shallower with silt), infrastructure push in the geologically young and fragile hills, ageing breach-prone river embankments, and climate change amplified the recurring disaster, often suddenly in specific areas instead of the “laahe-laahe (slow) flooding” of yore.
Hydrologists and disaster specialists are baffled by the ever-changing rainfall pattern, drenching some areas heavily and barely wetting others. For instance, while Sivasagar and Charaideo districts drowned, their western neighbours, the perennially flood-prone Morigaon and Nagaon districts, faced drought-like situations. This, perhaps, explains the monsoon paradox.
According to the India Meteorological Department, Assam recorded a 28% rainfall deficit in June and July, while about 6,500 sq. km area on either side of the Assam-Nagaland border received up to 490% more rainfall than normal, contributing to the floods in Sivasagar and Charaideo.
Mining menace
When India’s National Green Tribunal banned Meghalaya’s hazardous rat-hole coal mining in April 2014, green activists in Assam sought attention to similar, potentially “more dangerous” activities along the State’s borders with Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. More than a decade ago, Golaghat-based activist Apurba Ballav Goswami said the water bodies in Assam linked to the Nagaland-origin Dikhow, Disang, Jhanji, and Teyap Rivers were turning acidic due to run-off from unscientifically established mines. This, he said, was foreboding for downstream areas in Assam.
A 2018 PIL (public interest litigation) filed by Congress leader Debabarata Saikia, then a Congress MLA from Nazira, in the Gauhati High Court indicated rampant coal mining was not the only source of disaster for Sivasagar and adjoining districts. It conveyed that illegal sand and stone mining and encroachment of fragile river beds were also inviting trouble. The PIL focussed on the Dikhow, Sivasagar’s lifeline-turned-sorrow, seeking an immediate ban on the potentially catastrophic riverbed mining.
Following the court’s directive, the government sent teams from January to March 2019 to verify the allegations, concentrating on Bihubar and adjoining areas near the Assam-Nagaland border. The inquiry revealed eight stone quarries, 81 stone crushers, and the seizure of about 10,000 cubic metres of minor minerals in the area. The report described Bihubar and the surrounding areas as a hub of mining, distribution, supply, and interstate transportation. It also said that most of the gravel and boulders were transported from Nagaland.
Saikia petitioned the High Court again in 2019, arguing that illegal mining was continuing despite the damning government report, which the court had reproduced in its order. The second petition sought a specialised mining task force, a high-powered committee to study the fragile ecosystem of the Dikhow, measures to prevent changes in the river’s course, and a master plan covering illegal mining, bank erosion, drainage, and associated problems.
In October 2019, the court directed the Assam government to constitute a dedicated Mines and Minerals Task Force Battalion and a high-level committee for river conservation, adding that it expected action within three months.
“The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government virtually ignored the directive. Unchecked stone and sand mining in the Dikhow contributed to the extensive soil erosion along its course from Nagaland. The outcome is the ordeal our district went through in July,” Saikia, from oil town Nazira near Sivasagar, says. Nazira is the Assam Asset’s headquarters of ONGC, whose office-residential complex was submerged, forcing many executives to stay in hotels and homestays on higher ground.
Sivasagar MLA and Raijor Dal president Akhil Gogoi was more vocal about the “indiscriminate” coal and stone mining. “Rainwater accumulated in the hollowed coal pits in Nagaland, eventually burst out and caused widespread devastation in Assam,” he says, also pointing to the “rape of the rivers” by the mining mafia. His Sivasagar-based party leader Manas Konwar went a step further, naming two local BJP legislators, one of them a Minister, as the kingpins of the stone and coal mining operations along the Assam-Nagaland border.
After the floods, local YouTubers and reel-makers filmed the mining activities along the border. Some of them showed several earthen roads built across the Dikhow River to facilitate the movement of trucks carrying coal, stone chips, and sand. “Built during the dry season, these roads are like multiple dams that block the water upstream, within Nagaland. The accumulated water swells during the monsoon and cuts through these dams,” a Brahmaputra Board official says, declining to be quoted. The primary role of this Board, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, is to plan, coordinate, and integrate implementation of measures to control floods, mitigate riverbank erosion, and harness water resources across the northeastern region.
While the Assam Chief Minister, speaking to the media, denied any mining activities in Assam, community-based organisations in Nagaland rejected “theories” that their hill State and their people were responsible for Assam’s floods.
Former Nagaland minister Mmhonlumo Kikon noted reports that Nagaland’s insurgent groups are financially involved in coal mining, and that mining in Nagaland materially caused or intensified the eastern Assam floods. He also said the reports frequently move from allegations, anecdotes, and general environmental risks to an implied conclusion about criminality and flood causation without producing the evidence needed to make that connection. “A clear and thorough report on the investors from Assam or elsewhere, the market where this coal is sold, the number of challans (invoices) issued by the relevant departments in Assam, or even the Assam police record on the trucks transporting the coal would have been helpful,” he says.
Post-flood trauma
Sivasagar was formerly known as Rangpur, the administrative and political capital of the Ahoms, who ruled large swathes of Assam for 600 years until the British took control of the region in the early 1800s. Historians say Sivasagar (Charaideo was carved out of it in August 2015) was strategic for the Ahoms to administer a vast region, and that the region was relatively flood-free compared to the rest of the Brahmaputra Valley. The Ahom royal chronicles refer to flooding in and around the capital at intervals of more than a hundred years, including in 1691 and 1793.
“Sivasagar’s misery indicates that the flood cycle may have reduced (after the last one recorded 60 years ago) and become more catastrophic due to several factors, mostly man-made. The unpredictable climate change scenario is adding to this misery, making old water discharge data on which flood control measures are designed redundant,” says Bibhash Sarma, an engineering teacher and consultant to Assam’s Water Resources Department.
Aaranyak’s Das adds that the ever-changing rainfall pattern is the new normal. “The administrative machinery must understand that no part of Assam or anywhere else in the northeast is safe from floods and associated disasters. Everyone, down to the farmer, needs to be wired to anticipate such calamities during the six rainy months in the region.”
According to disaster watchers, getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management will not be enough to reduce disasters in a State where living with “normal” floods has been a way of life. “Disaster preparedness has to be designed around the realisation that there is not an inch of flood-free land in Assam, and that areas considered zero- or low-risk can become high-risk overnight,” Das says. Others called for surface water management by undoing or minimising the damage done by unscientifically planned roads, flyovers, hydropower, housing, and other infrastructure projects, which have largely claimed wetlands that once acted as water sponges during floods.
The pessimism “unless corrective measures are initiated now” has sunk in among Sivasagar-Charaideo’s flood survivors. Neighbours joked about taking refuge in her house during extreme floods when Lakshmi Devi began constructing her RCC house at Bihubar Nepalikhuti in 2022.
In 2026, more than 60 of them did take refuge on the roof of her house when the “tsunami” struck the village on July 19. “I could not imagine then that the joke would become a reality in less than four years,” she says, mourning the loss of her 10 cows. “I may have to add another floor to our house, but there’s no guarantee that the next flood will not reach the second-floor ceiling,” she adds.
District officials say the challenges in the areas returning to normality include clearing several feet of silt and debris from houses and paddy fields, sanitising the foul-smelling flood-hit areas, and ensuring adequate healthcare for livestock and people vulnerable to water- and vector-borne diseases such as Japanese encephalitis, which claimed 19 lives this year, before the floods.
The biggest challenge could be the trauma of expecting the worst in a State that recorded 160 and 181 human deaths during the 2017 and 2022 floods, respectively. “I don’t think anyone in Jorhat, Sivasagar, or Charaideo can sleep peacefully, at least during the remaining two months of the monsoon this year, if not later,” says Sarmah, whose Tamuli Gaon village is 18 km south of the Brahmaputra. “The Brahmaputra has been a bigger sorrow for Assam than the Dikhow this time, and much closer to us,” he says.

Uttar Pradesh Animal Husbandry department on Sunday (August 9, 2026) said it is strengthening the capacity for early identification and reporting of emerging zoonotic diseases, surveillance systems, laboratory strengthening, outbreak preparedness, pushing the One Health approach framework.
“Recently, the Animal Husbandry Department developed a Compendium for Veterinarians on Zoonotic & Priority Animal Diseases,. The compendium has been designed to strengthen the knowledge of field veterinarians on priority zoonotic diseases, standardized case definitions, surveillance and timely disease reporting. We are strengthening the capacity for early identification and reporting of priority zoonotic and other important animal diseases. The state will also enhance its diagnostic capacity through ELISA-based testing for priority zoonotic diseases. Interventions to strengthen farm-level biosecurity in Pilibhit and Gorakhpur districts, promoting improved disease prevention and infection control practices, is also taking place. The State is committed to strengthen One Health systems through coordinated interdepartmental action,” told Mukesh Kumar Meshram, Additional Chief Secretary, Animal Husbandry, Dairy Development and Fisheries Department, to The Hindu.
Mr. Meshram, a 1995-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer said that under the RISE Global Health Security (RISE GHS) Project, the Animal Husbandry Department, in collaboration with the Forest and Wildlife Department, successfully conducted active surveillance for Avian Influenza among wild migratory birds at 19 Ramsar and other important wetland sites across Uttar Pradesh.
“During the previous migratory season, over 1,100 samples were collected and tested at IVRI, Bareilly. Building on this success, similar surveillance will be undertaken during the upcoming migratory bird season across all Ramsar sites and other important wetlands in the state. A State-Level Training of Trainers (ToT) programme for government veterinarians will be conducted to strengthening One Health systems through coordinated interdepartmental action. headline: In a crackdown on cybercrime network, the Cyber Crime Wing (CCW) of the Tamil Nadu Police launched a 48-hour “State-wide Special Drive against Mule Account Holders” commencing on August 6, and arrested 837 cyber criminals across the State.
full_text:
In a crackdown on cybercrime network, the Cyber Crime Wing (CCW) of the Tamil Nadu Police launched a 48-hour “State-wide Special Drive against Mule Account Holders” commencing on August 6, and arrested 837 cyber criminals across the State.
The operation was focused on identifying persons involved in opening, operating, and facilitating the misuse of bank accounts for receiving and withdrawing proceeds from cyber fraud.
Acting on the instructions of the Director-General of Police and Head of the Police Force Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal, special teams of the CCW conducted the operation in all the districts and cities.
It was based on accused profiling through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (NCRP) and the Pratibimb portal of the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
Financial data analysis done
The profiling was further strengthened through bank fund-trail linkages established by financial data analysis of cybercrime networks.
“Mule accounts are bank accounts used by cybercriminals to receive, transfer, layer, or withdraw money obtained through fraudulent and illegal activities. Individuals who allow their bank accounts to be used for such transactions facilitate the movement of illicit funds,” Dr. Aggarwal said.
Investigators targeted individuals linked to 9,804 complaints involving fraudulent transactions amounting to more than ₹545 crore, and arrested 837 cyber criminals involved in 601 cases. Also, 157 new FIRs were registered across the State to curb the operation of mule bank accounts for facilitating cyber fraud.
The police said 204 mobile phones and other storage devices, some cash, and bank documents were seized from the premises of the accused.
Dr. Aggarwal said the arrests marked a significant achievement in disrupting and dismantling the organised cybercrime network operating in Tamil Nadu.
The operation was directly supervised from the police headquarters by the Additional Director-General of Police, CCW, Bala Naga Devi, to ensure seamless coordination and real-time monitoring throughout the drive.
The police were analysing the digital evidence seized and interrogating the arrested persons to uncover layers of the criminal network and identify their associates operating in other States. Efforts were on to trace and apprehend other members of the network, recover defrauded funds, and establish wider linkages with nationwide cybercrime operations, the police said in a statement.

headline: For 26-year-old Sarita Munda, the struggle to get a government job has stretched across years, exam cycles and disappointments.
full_text:
For 26-year-old Sarita Munda, the struggle to get a government job has stretched across years, exam cycles and disappointments.
She came to Ranchi from a village near Latehar with a familiar plan among young Adivasi youth in many parts of Jharkhand: study, prepare for the State recruitment examinations, find a government job and build a life that guarantees a place in the system that governs them, visibility and ways of income other than agricultural work or daily wage labour.
But preparation costs money. Ms. Sarita has been doing domestic work in Ranchi to support herself while studying. Her brother and sister have also spent years preparing for the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) examinations.
Jharkhand student protests: Follow LIVE updates on August 9, 2026
She appeared for an examination in 2024, only to see it cancelled. The following year brought another round of uncertainty and allegations of irregularities. Now, in 2026, she finds herself once again in the middle of a student movement demanding that the recruitment process be made credible.
For her, the dispute is not simply about an examination. It is about whether the years spent preparing for it will lead anywhere. That is the question that has brought students to the streets of Ranchi, where a protest over recruitment examinations has entered its 16th day.
Secure job, recognition
For many, JPSC and JSSC represent perhaps the clearest route to secure employment in a State where the private sector offers limited opportunities, particularly for young people from rural and Adivasi communities.
The choice, as several aspirants describe it, is stark: continue tilling the land that often provides enough to sustain a family but little surplus or spend years studying for a competitive examination that can potentially change the family’s economic circumstances.
“Either it is agricultural work, not for profit, but to sustain ourselves on our own land or we study somehow and try to get these government jobs,” is how one aspirant described the calculation.
‘Core Adivasi issue’
Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar in 2000 after a long political movement built around questions of identity, land, resources and self-determination. More than two decades later, many young Adivasis say the promise of social and economic inclusion remains unfulfilled.
According to the 2011 Census, Scheduled Tribes account for roughly 26% of Jharkhand’s population. The Census also maintains separate data on the educational levels of Scheduled Tribe communities in the State, reflecting the importance of education in understanding the State’s social and economic inequalities.
For Adivasi youth, government job means being the first person in a family to enter the formal system that makes decisions about the community that remains on the margins.
That is why Akriti Lakra believes the current agitation cannot be separated from the Adivasi question. Ms. Lakra, who is from a village near Namkum, has been attending the protest and joined the Adivasi Bachao Yuva Manch’s programme around International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples on Sunday.
Standing before protesters, she questioned the absence of an Adivasi voice from much of the visible leadership of the agitation.
“How can we just celebrate when the youth of this State has been protesting,” she asked, arguing that education has always been at the heart of the Adivasi struggle after jal, jungle, zameen (water, forests, land.)
She was later confronted by a protester who told her, “This is not platform for Adivasi issues, it won’t work here.”
But students from Adivasi communities, she said, have been part of the protest from its beginning, even while leaving behind agricultural work during monsoon. “This is the season of field work,” she said, making the point that many students who have come to Ranchi have had to choose between participating in the agitation and working at home.
In some villages, she said, government recruitment examinations have become almost a family aspiration. “Someone from every family is preparing for JPSC or JSSC,” she said.
That dependence is visible in the stories of aspirants who have spent years preparing. There is the cost of books, coaching, rent, food, travel and examination fees. There is also the opportunity cost: years that could otherwise have been spent working, earning or pursuing another career.
Every delay, therefore, carries a different meaning for a student who has already spent several years preparing. “By the time another opportunity arrives, private-sector employment may no longer be an easy alternative, and returning to the village may mean returning to agricultural work,” said Nishi Kumar, 39, who has lost all her to unsuccessful conduct of exams.

headline: The Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee will meet shortly to consider the Kerala High Court directive to rename ‘Kodathi Vilakku’, the ceremonial lighting of lamps at Guruvayur Sree Krishna Swami Temple, held as part of the annual temple festival.
full_text:
The Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee will meet shortly to consider the Kerala High Court directive to rename ‘Kodathi Vilakku’, the ceremonial lighting of lamps at Guruvayur Sree Krishna Swami Temple, held as part of the annual temple festival.
The event is considered one of the major offerings at the Guruvayur Temple, where all the lamps in the temple are lit and a procession with three elephants is held. A Nadaswaram concert is also held. The Vilakku is organised by the Sree Guruvayurappan Ekadashi Court Vilakku Celebration Committee, comprising members of the Chavakkad Munsiff Court Bar Association.
The Devaswom Bench of the court, comprising Justices Raja Vijayaraghavan and K.V. Jayakumar, observed that the nomenclature ‘Kodathi Vilakku’ may inadvertently create an impression of an institutional association or endorsement by the judiciary in relation to an event connected with a particular religious tradition. The Bench suggested adopting a name that would serve the interest of maintaining the perception of institutional neutrality.
The court issued the direction on a petition filed by Rajeswari, administrator of Gurubaba Ashram, Guruvayur.
The petitioner argued that the Kodathi Vilakku was continuing at Guruvayur Sree Krishna Swami Temple despite the court banning it in 2022. She had also sought a ban on ‘Police Vilakku’, ‘Postal Vilakku’, ‘SBI Vilakku’, ‘Canara Bank Vilakku’, and ‘Dhanalakshmi Vilakku’ at the temple.
A Single Bench of Justice A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar, in 2022, had advised judicial officers in Thrissur not to “actively involve themselves in the organising of the said event, either by consenting to be a part of the organising committee or in any other manner.” The Bench further said that they should not feel compelled or obliged to attend the event. However, the Bench felt that the use of the name ‘Kodathi Vilakku’ was unacceptable as it gave the impression that the courts were in some way connected with the organisation of the event. As secular democratic institutions under the Constitution, the courts cannot be seen engaging in activities that promote any particular religion, the Bench had held.
Responding to the developments, A. V. Gopinath, chairperson of the Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee, said a decision on the name would be taken in consultation with the festival organising committee and in full compliance with the High Court order.
“The organising committee would decide the name, and accordingly we would proceed with the programme. The only hiccup that might arise would be if the committee says that it can’t decide on a name; even then, we would consult with the High Court and proceed,” he said.

headline: What Brij Bhushan's lawyers said after his acquittal in sexual harassment case
full_text:
What Brij Bhushan's lawyers said after his acquittal in sexual harassment case
A Delhi court acquitted Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh and Vinod Tomar in the case brought by six women wrestlers. The defence said the order turned on contradictions, omissions, hostile testimony and lack of corroboration.
Lawyers representing former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief and former BJP MP Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh on Monday said the Delhi court’s acquittal order found that the prosecution had failed to prove the allegations levelled against him by six women wrestlers and highlighted what they described as serious inconsistencies in the case.
In a statement issued after the verdict, the defence team said the trial court did not acquit Singh merely because of isolated discrepancies in witness testimony. According to the lawyers, the court assessed the evidence in its entirety and took note of material contradictions between successive statements of witnesses, alleged improvements made at later stages, documentary evidence that was inconsistent with the dates and circumstances cited, lack of corroboration, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints.
The defence lawyers said the court also examined issues relating to the identification of alleged places of occurrence, the conduct of purported eyewitnesses, and the fact that no complaints were made at the time despite the incidents allegedly being witnessed by or disclosed to several individuals.
Referring to portions of the judgment, the defence said the court observed that the allegations against the accused were “false and fabricated” and appeared to have been made as part of a “deep conspiracy” that seemed politically motivated. According to the lawyers, the court noted similarities in the allegations, the timing of the complaints and the circumstances in which they were made, which, in its view, indicated prior planning.
The defence further highlighted the court’s observations regarding two witnesses who later turned hostile. According to the lawyers, these witnesses stated during the trial that they had been asked by certain individuals, including wrestlers and coaches associated with Mahadev Academy, to falsely implicate Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh. The witnesses allegedly claimed they were told that Singh’s continuation as WFI president would harm the prospects of wrestlers from Haryana and that removing him from the post was necessary.
The defence also pointed to the court’s findings regarding an allegation linked to the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta. According to the lawyers, the court noted that the allegation was not mentioned in an earlier affidavit submitted before the Oversight Committee and surfaced only later in the complaint. The court reportedly treated the omission as significant because the affidavits contained detailed accounts of other alleged incidents.
Citing the judgment, the defence said the court concluded that the prosecution had “miserably failed” to establish the allegations beyond reasonable doubt after considering witness depositions, documentary evidence and other material on record.
The Delhi court subsequently acquitted Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh of charges under Sections 354, 354A and 506 (Part I) of the Indian Penal Code. Co-accused Vinod Tomar was acquitted of the charge under Section 506 (Part I) of the IPC.

headline: Akali Dal-BJP relationship: A complex love-hate journey since 1952
full_text:
Akali Dal-BJP relationship: A complex love-hate journey since 1952
Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Delhi as the SAD backed key bills. The moves have revived debate over a possible BJP-SAD alliance before the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections.
Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president Sukhbir Singh Badal’s recent meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Delhi, followed by the party’s support for key bills, has reignited speculation about a possible BJP-SAD alliance ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections.
The meeting, the first significant public engagement between the two sides since their split over the farm laws in 2020, has also brought renewed attention to a relationship that has rarely been straightforward. While political exchanges between the two parties had remained strained in Punjab over the past several years, the relationship between the Shiromani Akali Dal and the Jana Sangh, and later the BJP, has historically oscillated between confrontation and cooperation.
Their political journey reflects decades of shifting alliances, ideological disagreements and electoral compulsions. It also offers insight into the roots of mistrust towards the BJP among sections of the Sikh community.
At the core of the relationship was not necessarily ideological convergence, but a shared opposition to the Congress. This common ground, at various points, also brought the Akalis closer to Left parties despite significant ideological differences.
THE RELATIONSHIP DATES BACK TO 1952
The political engagement between the Akalis and the Jana Sangh can be traced to the first general elections of 1952 and the political developments that followed in Punjab.
There were periods when the Akali Dal worked with the Congress, while the Jana Sangh opposed such arrangements. The Hindi-Punjabi language divide later emerged as one of the most significant points of contention between the two parties.
HINDI AGITATION AND PUNJABI SUBA MORCHA
The demand for a Punjabi Suba became one of the biggest fault lines in the relationship. While the Akali Dal strongly advocated for a Punjabi-speaking state, the Jana Sangh firmly opposed the demand.
The language issue became deeply intertwined with Punjab’s politics and widened the ideological and political divide between the two sides.
The Nehru-Tara Singh agreement also became a source of disagreement. Jana Sangh leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee questioned aspects of the understanding, reflecting the party’s broader opposition to the Akali position on Punjab’s political and linguistic demands.
FROM CONFRONTATION TO COALITION GOVERNMENTS
Despite their differences, political compulsions eventually brought the Akali Dal and the Jana Sangh together.
The two parties formed coalition governments in Punjab at different points, with their partnership largely driven by the objective of challenging Congress dominance.
Former Punjab Chief Minister Justice Gurnam Singh’s observations on the Jana Sangh’s role in coalition politics provide important insight into the nature of this alliance.
However, the partnership remained fragile and often vulnerable to disputes over regional and identity-related issues.
GURU NANAK UNIVERSITY ISSUE EXPOSES FAULT LINES
Differences resurfaced over the jurisdiction of Guru Nanak University.
The Jana Sangh eventually withdrew from the coalition over the issue, highlighting how questions concerning Punjab’s identity, institutions and regional interests could quickly strain the alliance.
THE 1981 CIGARETTE-BEEDI CONTROVERSY
The relationship came under strain again in 1981 when a march supporting the interests of the cigarette and beedi trade was taken out in Amritsar under the leadership of a BJP legislator.
The episode emerged as another flashpoint at a time when political and social tensions in Punjab were already escalating.
ARTICLE 25 AND THE GROWING POLITICAL DIVIDE
The debate over the constitutional status of Sikhs became another major point of contention.
When Parkash Singh Badal burnt a copy of Article 25(b) of the Constitution as a mark of protest, Vajpayee criticised Prime Minister Indira Gandhi over the prevailing situation rather than fully endorsing the Akali position.
The period also saw the BJP and Jana Sangh leadership taking a firm stand on the use of military force, describing Army action as unavoidable and opposing what they viewed as attempts to reach a political compromise with the Akalis.
1996: A NEW PHASE IN THE RELATIONSHIP
By 1996, the Akali Dal and the BJP entered into an alliance without conditions, marking a significant transformation in their relationship.
The partnership went on to become one of Punjab’s most significant political alliances, with both parties working together for nearly two decades.
Yet the history of the relationship suggests that the alliance was built less on complete ideological agreement and more on political necessity, particularly their shared opposition to the Congress.
That complicated legacy—marked by alternating phases of confrontation and cooperation—remains central to understanding the continuing debate over the BJP’s relationship with the Sikh community and the Akali Dal.
According to Akali Dal insiders, any future alliance discussions could revolve around issues such as national security and law and order, given Punjab’s status as a border state. Efforts to create an urban-rural electoral balance, seat-sharing arrangements, the political space occupied by Punar Surjit and Waris Punjab De, and a Punjab-centric agenda are also expected to feature in discussions.
With both sides appearing to soften their stance towards each other, rival political parties have also begun recalibrating their strategies in anticipation of possible political realignments in the state.

headline: Amit Shah likely to table bills to change Kerala's name, expand NCDC financing powers in Lok Sabha today
full_text:
Amit Shah likely to table bills to change Kerala's name, expand NCDC financing powers in Lok Sabha today
Amit Shah is scheduled to present two bills in the Lok Sabha: one to rename Kerala as Keralam and another to enhance NCDC's financing powers.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah is scheduled to introduce two bills — one seeking to rename Kerala as Keralam and another expanding the financing powers of the National Co-operative Development Corporation (NCDC) — in the Lok Sabha on Monday, amid a logjam in both Houses of Parliament. With just four days left in the ongoing monsoon session, the Opposition parties are seeking a statement from the home minister over the use of force against protesting students on July 20.
The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 seeks to amend the First Schedule of the Constitution to change the name of Kerala to “Keralam”. The proposal follows a resolution passed by the Kerala assembly seeking the change. The Union Cabinet has already approved the proposal.
NCDC bill proposes wider funding powers
The second bill, the National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeks to expand the mandate of the NCDC. Instead of largely financing programmes through cooperative societies, according to the draft bill, the corporation will also be able to fund a wider range of organisations involved in “co-operative development”.
Also read | No direction from Rajya Sabha Chair to Amit Shah to attend House: Rijiju amid Oppn uproar
The proposed changes come as the government argues that the cooperative sector has “expanded and diversified considerably” over the years. According to the statement of objects and reasons accompanying the bill, statutory bodies, state government agencies and other specialised organisations now provide infrastructure, technology, processing, marketing and financial services to cooperatives. As many of these organisations are not themselves registered as cooperative societies, the NCDC cannot finance them directly under the existing law, resulting in “procedural delays and limited uptake” as proposals have to be routed through state governments or cooperative societies.
To address this, the bill allows the corporation to extend loans and grants directly not only to cooperative societies but also to “any entity engaged in co-operative development”, and, with the Centre’s approval, invest in the share capital of such entities.
The broader wording has prompted questions over which organisations could qualify for funding. L Viswanathan, senior partner at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, said the provision should not be interpreted as opening the door to all entities.
“Entities must be engaged in co-operative development”
“The key is that these entities must be engaged in co-operative development,” he said, adding that the board would determine eligibility based on the purpose and mandate of the organisation.
Besides widening the funding net, the bill also seeks to expand the definition of foodstuffs to include additional food items notified by the Centre, removes geographical restrictions on financing industrial goods, updates obsolete statutory references, empowers the corporation to collect and share credit information with banks and other financial institutions, and grants it incidental powers to carry out its functions more effectively.
Also read | Shah meets Shinde, Fadnavis over student protests and Sena case
The bill also authorises the NCDC to acquire equity in entities engaged in cooperative development, subject to prior approval of the Centre. On concerns over safeguards, Viswanathan said the law itself places limits on how funds can be used. “The end use of the funds is specified in the law. The law provides for audits and reports to be filed by NCDC. Anything beyond that will be ultra vires,” he said, adding that any equity investment would also be subject to greater checks and balances on the end use and activities.
On Sunday, the Opposition Congress intensified its demand for a statement from Shah on police excesses during the July 20 march to Parliament. Drawing a parallel with the Opposition’s demand for a response from Shah following the December 13, 2023 Parliament security breach incident, Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said: “History should not be repeated.”
“The entire opposition repeatedly demanded that the Union Home Minister make a statement on this (Parliament breach) incident, but no statement came from him. They remained silent even then, just as they are now silent on the brutality inflicted by the Delhi Police on the youth who were protesting last month,” he said on X.

Sourav Ganguly, wife Dona Ganguly receive death threat letters, cops begin probe
The matter came to light after Sourav’s secretary approached Thakurpukur police station to register a complaint.
Former Indian cricket team captain Sourav Ganguly and his wife Dona Ganguly allegedly received letters threatening to kill the couple on Monday, police said.
The former BCCI president had been receiving several letters with objectionable remarks in recent months but the matter was initially not taken seriously, his secretary told the police. On Monday, Sourav’s office received two letters, containing explicit threats to kill him and his wife and harm people close to him.
“Initially we didn’t pay much attention to these letters, assuming that they were merely the work of someone who disliked Ganguly and was sending letters expressing his or her personal resentment,” the secretary said in his complaint with Thakurpukur police station in south Kolkata on Tuesday.
The complaint alleged the sender was identified as Arun and the letters were sent from Belghoria in North 24 Parganas district.
The police said they are examining the contents of the letters and trying to confirm the identity and motive of the sender.
"We are taking the complaint seriously and have begun an investigation. We are examining the letters, their source and the courier trail to identify the person responsible," a police officer said on condition of anonymity.
The police, the officer added, have begun examining the movement of the SIM card allegedly used by the sender and have contacted the courier agency concerned to gather details of the consignments. "We have spoken to the people from the courier service and tracked down one mobile number. We are trying to spot it," the officer said.
The police are also ascertaining whether all the letters were sent by the same person, the officer added.
There was no immediate comment from Sourav and his wife at the time of filing this report.

headline: TN CM's resolution on Tamil Thaai Vazhthu unanimously passed in Assembly

TN CM's resolution on Tamil Thaai Vazhthu unanimously passed in Assembly
Chennai, The Tamil Nadu Assembly on Monday unanimously passed a resolution mandating the rendition of Tamil Thaai Vazhthu at the commencement of government events in the state.
The resolution, piloted by Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, was supported by several legislature parties, including the opposition DMK and AIADMK, who endorsed the government's stance that the state song should be sung first in the sequence of songs to be rendered at government functions.
Moving the resolution, Vijay said his Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam government will not compromise on Tamil Nadu's linguistic and cultural rights.
"Tamil is not only a language but also our life and emotions," Vijay said in an emotive speech and stressed that the "mother tongue is as pure as one's mother."
"Singing the Tamil Thaai Vazhthu is not against the political system or India's unity. On the contrary, it reflects the nation's high principle of unity in diversity. There's no need to make this demand of singing the Tamil Thaai Vazhthu first into a political debate," he said.
As per the resolution, the state song should be sung at the commencement of programmes conducted at educational institutions, universities, government offices and public sector undertakings in Tamil Nadu.
The move comes in the backdrop of the latest advisory from the Union Home Affairs Ministry asking the states and union territories to "strictly comply" with its January 28 directive that the National Song Vande Mataram be played before the National Anthem at official events.
It may be recalled that the Tamil Nadu government issued an order on November 23, 1970, insisting that the Tamil Thaai Vazhthu be sung at the beginning of official events.
The state government officially recognised it as state song on December 12, 2021, making it compulsory to render this first in the sequence of songs to be played at official functions.
"This Assembly proudly records that Tamil is the ancient classical language of the world and Tamil civilisation is one of the oldest cultural traditions in the world. Tamil Thaai Vazhthu taken from the play 'Manonmaniam' written in 1891 by Manonmaniam Sundaranar, must be sung first at government functions from November 23, 1970," the resolution stated.
The government has issued an order which has come into effect, it noted. "It has been officially recognised as the state song from December 12, 2021 and it has been ordered that Tamil Thaai Vazhthu will be sung before the start of the event at all educational institutions, universities, government offices, public sector undertakings and other public organisations located in Tamil Nadu," the resolution further said.
Announcing that the resolution had been passed unanimously, Speaker J C D Prabhakar informed the House that its implementation required no permission from anyone.
"This is an Assembly resolution and the chief minister's voice represents the entire Tamil population," the Speaker emphasised.

headline: ‘Narendra naam ka khauf…’: Sports minister Mandaviya reacts to boxer’s Pakistan anecdote for PM Modi
full_text:
‘Narendra naam ka khauf…’: Sports minister Mandaviya reacts to boxer’s Pakistan anecdote for PM Modi
Mansukh Mandaviya’s post came after boxer Narender Berwal recalled what a Pakistani opponent told him after a 2015 bout, leaving PM Narendra Modi laughing
Union sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya on Monday reacted to Indian boxer Narender Berwal’s anecdote about a Pakistani opponent, who, according to the boxer, told him he had begun to hate the name “Narendra”.
“Narendra naam ka khauf hai Pakistan mein,” Mandaviya posted on X in Hindi, meaning, “The name ‘Narendra’ is feared in Pakistan”. He was referring to the anecdote Berwal narrated during his interaction with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Berwal, who won a silver medal in the men’s 90kg boxing category at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, was among the Indian medal winners who met PM Modi at his residence in New Delhi on Sunday.
During the interaction, a video of which has gone viral, Narender Berwal recalled an incident involving a Pakistani boxer at the 2015 World Military Games. He said that after he defeated the Pakistani opponent, whom he did not name, the two went to hospital for treatment after suffering cuts when their heads collided during the bout.
Berwal said the Pakistani boxer then pointed out that his name was Narender, his coach was also named Narender and India’s prime minister was Narendra.
“Bhai jaan… Mujhe Narendra naam se nafrat ho gayi hai,” Berwal quoted the Pakistani boxer as saying, “Brother dear, I have come to hate the name ‘Narendra’!”
The remark prompted Modi to laugh. The video was shared also on the Prime Minister’s YouTube channel and other social media outlets.
Narendra and Narender are the same name with regional variations in spellings depending on phonetics — the boxer is from Haryana, and Modi from Gujarat.
Narender Berwal was among 10 Indian boxers who returned from Glasgow with medals. India won seven gold and three silver medals in boxing, its best-ever haul in the sport at a Commonwealth Games.
India finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze — and finished fourth in the overall standings.
India is set to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, the home state of PM Modi and minister Mandaviya.

headline: Is TMC rebel camp cracking? 3 MLAs share stage with Mamata loyalists
full_text:
Is TMC rebel camp cracking? 3 MLAs share stage with Mamata loyalists
Their appearance alongside senior leaders Sovandeb Chattopadhyay and Kunal Ghosh at a press conference has fuelled speculation over whether some MLAs are moving back towards Mamata Banerjee's direct political fold.
Is the Ritabrata Banerjee-aligned Trinamool faction beginning to fray just three months after it emerged as a separate power centre within the party?
The question has gained traction after three sitting MLAs who had earlier aligned with the Ritabrata camp were seen sharing the stage with senior leaders from the Kalighat camp on Thursday while protesting the alleged attack on Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee.
The development came days after the former West Bengal CM visited Halisahar to protest the death of a Trinamool worker and faced demonstrations there, with allegations that stones and mud were thrown at her vehicle.
As Kalighat-aligned Trinamool workers staged protests across the state condemning the incident, three MLAs previously associated with the Ritabrata camp appeared alongside senior Kalighat leaders outside the Assembly.
They were Abdul Khaleque Molla from Metiabruz, Mohammad Tausif Rahman from Basirhat North and Bibhas Sardar from Baruipur East.
Later, their appearance alongside senior leaders Sovandeb Chattopadhyay and Kunal Ghosh at a press conference has fuelled speculation over whether some MLAs are moving back towards the former CM’s direct political fold.
‘WHEREVER DIDI IS, TAUSIF IS THERE’
Basirhat North MLA Tausif-ur-Rahman left little ambiguity about his loyalty to Mamata Banerjee.
“Wherever Didi is, Tausif is there too. I wouldn't secure even ten votes from Basirhat without Didi's picture; that is the reality of the Trinamool Congress in West Bengal,” he said.
He added that despite his security cover being withdrawn, his political identity and support in Basirhat remained firmly tied to Mamata Banerjee and the Trinamool Congress.
Baruipur East MLA Bibhas Sardar, meanwhile, stressed party unity rather than factional allegiance.
“We won under the ‘Jora Ful’ symbol. We won under the symbol given by Mamata Banerjee. When she was attacked, we protested,” he said.
Sardar added that all 80 Trinamool MLAs should protest the alleged attack on Banerjee and maintained that, despite internal groupings, all factions ultimately remained part of the Trinamool Congress.
Metiabruz MLA Abdul Khaleque Molla took a more nuanced position.
“An attack was carried out against Mamata Banerjee. I participated in the protest programme against it. I do not wish to specify which faction I belong to. Currently, I align with the Ritabrata faction, yet I am protesting the attack on Mamata Didi,” he said.
RITABRATA PLAYS DOWN SPECULATION
Leader of Opposition Ritabrata Banerjee sought to play down suggestions that his camp was losing support.
“It is not my responsibility to speak for Bibhas Sardar or Tausif Rahman. I can state that Abdul Khaleque Molla is with us,” he said.
“And the count is 65. I can assure you the number will not be lower than that. If the Kalighat faction of Trinamool is so confident, let them submit a letter and claim that their numbers are higher,” Ritabrata added.
The remarks indicate that while the three MLAs joined the Kalighat camp in protesting the alleged attack on Mamata Banerjee, there is still no clear evidence that all of them have formally abandoned the Ritabrata group.
FACTION DEBATE RETURNS
The timing has nevertheless renewed attention on the internal equations within the Trinamool Congress.
The Ritabrata-aligned group had emerged after the Assembly polls in May as a parallel power centre within the party. The sight of MLAs associated with that camp now appearing alongside Kalighat leaders has therefore revived speculation about its cohesion.
Leaders from the Kalighat camp argue that the attack on the Chief Minister has brought party MLAs together irrespective of internal groupings.
For now, the public line remains that “all factions are one”. But the changing optics, with MLAs appearing on different political stages within three months, have ensured that the debate over competing camps inside the Trinamool Congress is unlikely to disappear soon.

headline: Indian student sent girlfriend's mother series of texts after murder, was in US on F-1 visa: What we know so far
full_text:
Indian student sent girlfriend's mother series of texts after murder, was in US on F-1 visa: What we know so far
Victim's mother said messages were “inconsistent” with the way she communicated, which is why she called the cops to go and check on her at her Tucson flat
Indian national Varun Batchigari, 20, accused of murdering his 19-year-old girlfriend in Tucson, Arizona, allegedly used her phone to send a series of messages to her mother after the killing, before fleeing the United States and being arrested in Germany, according to police.
Batchigari, 20, has been charged with first-degree murder in the death of Julissa Rubi Salazar, a US national who was found dead at her apartment near the University of Arizona on August 6.
According to the Tucson Police Department, firefighters responding to a welfare check requested by Salazar's family after they grew suspicious .
The felony warrant said she had strangulation marks and scratches on her neck, “obvious signs of trauma”, as per local broadcaster 13 News.
What happened after the killing
Investigators allege Batchigari took Salazar's cellphone and bank cards after killing her. He then allegedly used her phone to send messages to her mother,.
Salazar's mother, who lives elsewhere, told investigators that the messages were “not consistent with the way her daughter usually communicated”, according to 13 News. These messages raised concerns among the family, prompting the welfare check that led to the discovery of Salazar's body at her Tucson flat.
Police later found that Batchigari had travelled to the Tucson International Airport and used Salazar's bank card to book the taxi to it.
Headed to India, caught in Germany
He flew from Tucson to Houston and then boarded a flight to Germany. He intended to continue to India but was arrested after arriving in Germany, police said
The arrest was made with assistance from the FBI's Tucson office and its legal attaché office in Berlin, police said. Batchigari is currently in German custody and is awaiting extradition to Arizona.
Entered US on student visa
Batchigari had entered the United States through Los Angeles International Airport on January 8, 2024, on an F-1 student visa, Fox News reported citing unnamed federal law enforcement sources.
Batchigari had been studying business analytics at the University of Arizona, according to a video posted by him on his YouTube channel, as per local broadcaster KOLD. It further reported that he was expelled from the university following a fight.
Reports also said Batchigari had recently lost his job, creating difficulties in paying rent and potentially affecting his immigration status.
Authorities are now working to extradite him to Arizona to face the first-degree murder charge.
What's known about the relationship
According to the felony warrant, one of Salazar's roommates told investigators that Salazar had planned to break up with Batchigari.
The roommate also alleged that Salazar had previously been assaulted by Batchigari and was afraid of him because of his alleged history of violent behaviour.
Another roommate told investigators that loud screaming and yelling came from Salazar's room on August 5, the day before she was found dead. The roommate said the disturbance lasted several minutes, followed by a period of silence and another brief outburst.
The roommate later texted Salazar asking if she was okay.
According to the warrant, Salazar replied that she was fine and that she and Batchigari had only been arguing — a message that may have been sent by the killer from her phone.
The warrant also records an allegation from another person who told investigators that Batchigari sexually assaulted her at a Halloween party. She did not report the alleged incident to police at the time.
Batchigari had also previously been involved in an assault case handled by the University of Arizona Police Department, as per a report in The New York Post. That case was filed in Pima County Court on May 26.

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday moved a government resolution in the assembly making the rendition of Tamil Thai Vazhthu, the state song, mandatory at the beginning of official programmes across the state.Moving the resolution in the state assembly, Vijay said his Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam government would not compromise on Tamil Nadu's linguistic and cultural rights and urged legislators to set aside political differences in supporting the measure."Our mother tongue is as pure as our mother," Vijay said in an emotive speech, adding that, "Tamil is not only a language but also our life and emotions.""Tamil means pride, Tamil means power. The moment you say 'Tamil', the entire Tamil Nadu will come together and stand as one," he said."Tamil Thai Vazhthu must hold the first place in Tamil Nadu. Giving first place to Tamil Thaai Vaazhthu is our state right," he noted."Saying that Tamil Thai Vazhthu should be sung first does not need to become a political debate," the Tamil nadu CM said, appealing to members across party lines to support the resolution.Under the resolution, Tamil Thai Vazhthu will be sung first at programmes held by educational institutions, universities, government offices, public sector undertakings and other public institutions in Tamil Nadu.

"Therefore, this House ( Tamil Nadu Assembly ) emphasises that "Tamil Thai Vazhthu" is an expression of respect for the Tamil language and Tamil culture. In accordance with the linguistic and cultural rights guaranteed by the Constitution of India, and with a view to preserving the Cultural identity of Tamil Nadu, the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly unanimously resolves that "Tamil Thai Vazhthu" shall be mandatorily sung first, before the commencement of programmes held by all Educational Institutions, Universities, Government Offices, Public Sector Undertakings and other Public Institutions in Tamil Nadu," the resolution said.The resolution also notes that Tamil is one of the world's oldest classical languages and describes Tamil civilisation as one of the world's oldest cultural traditions.Tamil Nadu had first directed that Tamil Thai Vazhthu be sung at the beginning of official functions through a government order issued on November 23, 1970.The state government formally accorded the song the status of the state song on December 12, 2021, making its rendition mandatory at official programmes and institutions across the state.

headline: Total number of airports, seaports and land ports allowing entry of e-visa holders rises to 88
full_text:
Total number of airports, seaports and land ports allowing entry of e-visa holders rises to 88
NEW DELHI: The government has notified 11 more international ports in the country, including 9 land ports and 2 airports, for the entry of eligible foreigners arriving on electronic visas (e-visas). They can now land with e-visa at Bhopal and Tirupati airports and clear immigration.The additional landports via which e-visa holding foreign nationals can enter India include Attari in Punjab; Gede, Ghojanga and Jaigaon in West Bengal; Darranga in Assam; Agartala in Tripura; Moreh in Manipur; and Haridaspur in Odisha.E-visas currently make up 78% of the total visas issued in the country. India provides approximately 95% e-visas applications in less than 72 hours.The home ministry, in a statement on Monday, said the addition of 11 international ports further enhances attractiveness and utility of electronic visa.The Narendra Modi govt has taken a number of significant initiatives over the last few years to liberalize, streamline and simplify visa regime with a view to facilitating the legitimate foreign travelers while simultaneously ramping up the technological infrastructure to enhance internal security.
With the latest addition of 11 international airports to the e-visa scheme, the total number of international ports enabling entry of e-visa holder foreigners has risen to 88, including 37 airports, 38 seaports and 13 land ports.E-visa facility, with electronic travel authorisation (ETA), was introduced in 2014 to liberalize and simplify the Indian visa regime, especially the tourist visa regime. Having taken off with 43 eligible countries, the facility is now available to nationals of 172 countries.
E-visa is presently issued under 17 sub-categories; namely tourist visa, mountaineering visa, business visa (six types), medical visa (four types), student visa (two types), transit visa, miscellaneous visa and group visitor visa (cruise).
