Send CVs: Prashant Kishor vows jobs for 10,000 Bankipur youths days after poll win
Prashant Kishor asked Bankipur families to send CVs of educated unemployed youths to his office. He said he would use his network to help 10,000 families find private-sector jobs over the next two years.
Days after ending the BJP’s three-decade hold over Bankipur, Jan Suraaj Party leader Prashant Kishor has announced an employment push for the constituency, promising to help at least 10,000 youths find jobs over the next one to two years. He has asked families to send the CVs and biodata of their educated but unemployed children to his office.
Kishor made the announcement on Tuesday during his first visit to Bankipur after his August 3 bypoll victory. He was touring the constituency as part of a thanksgiving exercise and thanked voters for reposing their trust in him. “I am not travelling anywhere. I am working for you,” Kishor said in response to criticism that he had been away from the constituency for five or six days after his election victory.
He said he would use his network of contacts with companies and individuals across the country to help eligible youths secure private-sector jobs. Kishor, however, made it clear that he could not promise government employment and said some young people may initially have to move outside Bihar for work.
He appealed to families with educated but unemployed children to prepare their CVs and submit them to his office. His aim, he said, was to help at least 10,000 families in Bankipur get employment for their children within the next one to two years.
Kishor said the situation could change if the Jan Suraaj Party comes to power in Bihar. In that case, he said, the focus would be on creating enough employment opportunities within the state so that young people do not have to leave Bihar in search of jobs.
The employment promise comes soon after Kishor scripted the Jan Suraaj Party’s first electoral victory on August 3, defeating BJP candidate Neeraj Kumar Sinha by 19,324 votes in the high-stakes Bankipur Assembly bypoll. Kishor polled 64,151 votes against Sinha’s 44,827, while RJD’s Rekha Gupta finished a distant third with 14,273 votes.
The victory ended the BJP’s uninterrupted 30-year hold over Bankipur, considered one of its strongest bastions in Bihar. Kishor had surged ahead in the early counting trends and steadily increased his lead, with the result becoming virtually certain by the 15th round of counting out of 32.
After his victory became clear, Kishor had said his immediate priority would be to honour the trust placed in him by Bankipur voters. He had promised to work towards improving the constituency, saying residents would start seeing changes within two to three months.
At the time, Kishor had also tempered expectations, saying his election as an MLA would not turn Bankipur “into Bengaluru overnight”, but assured residents that visible improvements would begin taking shape within the next few months.
Besides jobs, Kishor has listed education, a monthly pension of Rs 1,100 and food grains among his four key priorities for the constituency.

headline: RSS chief Mohan Bahgwat to interact with Gen Z in Nagpur on Independence Day
full_text:
RSS chief Mohan Bahgwat to interact with Gen Z in Nagpur on Independence Day
The RSS chief’s outreach to Gen-Z comes against the backdrop of growing political engagement among young people
After reaching out to Gen-Z in Mumbai, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat is set to engage with students and young people in Nagpur on Independence Day, seen as an effort to strengthen the saffron organisation’s connect with the younger generation.
Bhagwat will interact with youth at a programme organised by a local media house at Kasturchand Park in Civil Lines on August 15. He is also scheduled to hoist the national flag at 9.30am at the venue, where chief minister Devendra Fadnavis inaugurated a 200-foot-high national flag installed by the Lokmat Media Group in March this year.
The RSS chief’s outreach to Gen-Z comes against the backdrop of growing political engagement among young people and recent student-led protests on issues concerning the government.
These developments have prompted political and social organisations, including the RSS, to step up efforts to engage with the younger generation.
People familiar with the matter said Bhagwat’s interaction with young people will be part of a wider effort to understand their aspirations, concerns and expectations. Other senior RSS leaders are also expected to hold similar interactions with students and the younger generation from time to time.
Bhagwat’s Nagpur engagement comes shortly before his scheduled appearance at a major Hindu-American gathering in New York City on August 29, coinciding with Raksha Bandhan. Bhagwat, who has headed the RSS since 2009, is expected to deliver the principal address.

The organisers said the programme will highlight the growing role of Hindu Americans in public life and their contributions to education, healthcare, business, public service, philanthropy and civic engagement. The theme of the gathering is Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam—“The World Is One Family.”
Bhagwat’s appearance in New York is expected to attract considerable attention.

headline: SC asks Centre to treat PIL for supervisory mechanism against digital harms as representation
full_text:
SC asks Centre to treat PIL for supervisory mechanism against digital harms as representation
New Delhi, The Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Centre to consider a representation seeking remedial measures to deal with serious forms of cybercrime, including threats of physical violence, disclosure of private information such as children's school locations and non-consensual intimate content.
A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a PIL filed by Narendra Kumar Goswami, appearing in person, seeking the creation of an effective supervisory mechanism to address grave unlawful digital harms.
During the hearing, Goswami posed a hypothetical situation to underline the urgency of the issue, asking whether a woman's home address, accompanied by a rape threat, posted online at 9 pm could be allowed to remain accessible.
The CJI said that the petitioner "highlighted very well" the various modes, kinds and facets of cybercrime.
"How to detect them and what preventive measures are to be taken are matters for domain experts," the CJI said.
The petitioner told the court that the issues had already been raised before the authorities concerned through a representation.
When the CJI asked whom the representation had been addressed to, Goswami said it had been submitted to the Centre through the secretaries of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministries of Home Affairs and the Law and Justice.
The bench, in its order, said that the PIL sought directions for an effective supervisory mechanism to deal with "grave unlawful digital harms", including acts or threats of physical violence, dangerous toxins, disclosure of private particulars, including children's school locations, non-consensual intimate content and harmful digital impersonation.
The plea said that such cyber crimes seriously impinge upon fundamental rights, including the rights to equality, freedom of speech, privacy, dignity and life.
The petitioner had also drawn a comparison with international regulatory frameworks and the different measures adopted by other jurisdictions to tackle unlawful digital activities.
The bench noted that the petitioner had already raised the issues in a representation dated June 22 addressed to the ministries concerned.
At this stage, the remedial action required was for the authorities concerned to consider the issues raised in the representation, the bench said.
It asked the three ministries along with all other stakeholders to examine the issues raised in the representation and take such remedial measures as may be required.

headline: Minute-by-minute of August 15: What exactly happens at Red Fort on Independence Day
full_text:
Minute-by-minute of August 15: What exactly happens at Red Fort on Independence Day
The Independence Day ceremony at Red Fort blends the precision and discipline of the armed forces with national symbolism.
As India marks its Independence Day every year on August 15, the historic Red Fort in New Delhi serves as the centre stage for the official ceremony, which is also shown live across platforms. This year, India is celebrating its 80th Independence Day, completing 79 years since the country gained freedom from British rule in 1947.
The event is tightly scheduled and choreographed, keeping in mind the magnitude of the situation and the importance of the day.
Also Read | 1948 Independence Day Speech: What Nehru Said On Religious Hate On 1st I-Day After 1947 Liberation
What exactly happens during the Independence Day ceremony?
The ceremony blends the precision and discipline of the armed forces with national symbolism. Here is a step-by-step guide on what happens every year during India’s Independence Day ceremony:
Phase 1: Morning arrivals and assembly
Long before the official ceremony begins, multi-layered security cordons secure the Red Fort area in the national capital, while on the morning of the ceremony special guests take their seats across designated enclosures.
Phase 2: Arrival of the Prime Minister
Early in the morning, the Prime Minister reaches the Red Fort, where the Union ministers and senior officials are present. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, the ceremony at Red Fort consists of the presentation of a Guard of Honour by the Armed Forces and the Delhi Police to the Prime Minister.
Phase 3: Flag unfurling, national anthem, and 21-Gun Salute
Now the core moment of the ceremony takes place:
Unfurling the Tricolour: The Prime Minister pulls the ceremonial cord to unfurl the Indian national flag at the top of the ramparts.
Salute and national anthem: As the flag rises, the military band plays ‘Jana Gana Mana’, and the assembled contingents present a salute.
21-Gun salute: Artillery guns fire a 21-gun salute to mark the occasion.
There will be a special place for the National Song, Vande Mataram, too this time in this sequence.
Phase 4: Address to the nation
With the Tricolour fluttering above, the Prime Minister steps up to deliver the Independence Day address. The speech usually outlines the following points:
Tributes: Remembering the sacrifices of freedom fighters and honouring them.
Review of past year: The speech also highlights economic, social, and other achievements of the past year.
Future: The PM also announces policy initiatives, national schemes, and goals for the years ahead.
Phase 5: Nationwide celebrations
The ceremony serves as the apex event of the day, followed by flag-hoisting rituals by Chief Ministers at their respective state capitals, schools, colleges, district headquarters, and civic institutions across the country.
Also Read | Full Vande Mataram to ring out from Red Fort for 1st time on Independence Day
Special place for Vande Mataram this year
As for this year, defence secretary RK Singh said that as part of the Independence Day celebrations, for the first time, the National Song, Vande Mataram, would be sung from the ramparts of the Red Fort.
"The sequence is that he (Prime Minister Modi) arrives on the rampart, then the national song is played, and everybody keeps standing. Thereafter, he unfurls the flag and the national anthem is played," he said.
An official statement noted that an Mi-17 helicopter of the Indian Air Force (IAF) will carry a banner commemorating 150 years of Vande Mataram, and shower flower petals over the people at Red Fort.
According to details shared by the defence ministry, the Independence Day celebrations this year will commemorate Yuva Shakti (youth power), acknowledging the contribution of young India in building a Viksit Bharat (developed India) by 2047.

headline: Theatre artists repaint Kolkata’s Academy of Fine Arts white from saffron
full_text:
Theatre artists repaint Kolkata’s Academy of Fine Arts white from saffron
The Academy of Fine Arts was established in 1933 by Lady Ranu Mukherjee and Maharaja Prodyot Kumar Tagore to promote Indian art
Theatre artists of Kolkata painted the old ticket counter at the heritage Academy of Fine Arts white on Tuesday, a month after some Hindutva group members painted the structure saffron and erected a portrait of Bharat Mata -a lion-riding goddess holding a saffron flag - beside it.
The Academy of Fine Arts was established in 1933 by Lady Ranu Mukherjee and Maharaja Prodyot Kumar Tagore to promote Indian art. The old ticket counter is beside the main gate.
“We raised our voice and met Samik Bhattacharya (the state president of the Bharatiya Janata Party) after some people painted the room saffron around July 6. He did not support the act and said he would get the room repainted,” prominent theatre personality Chandan Sen said.
“The ticket counter was originally painted terracotta. Now it is white. Let there be no colour. We did not wait for Bhattacharya any longer and decided to do the job on our own,” Sen added.
Several thespians and playwrights including Sen, Meghnad Bhattacharya, Bibhash Chakraborty, Arun Mukhopadhyay, and Debasis Majumdar wrote to Samik Bhattacharya last month condemning the act.
The letter said that those who painted the old ticket counter saffron claimed to be BJP workers. Samik Bhattacharya at that time said that the BJP did not believe in the politics of changing colours.
Commonly referred to as just the Academy, the institution started in a small room at the Indian Museum on Chowringhee Road and shifted to its current location beside St Paul’s Cathedral in the 1950s with help from the then chief minister Bidhan Chandra Roy and then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
Apart from a special gallery featuring some personal artifacts and manuscripts of Rabindranath Tagore, the works of masters such as Gaganendranath Tagore, Jamini Roy, Ramkinkar Baij, Benode Behari Mukherjee and Nandalal Bose are preserved at the galleries.
The auditorium, where the state’s annual theatre festival has been held since 1984, once witnessed stalwarts such as Sambhu Mitra and Utpal Dutt staging some of their masterpieces. Sambhu Mitra and Bijon Bhattacharya created the iconic theatre group Bohurupee in 1948.
“The ticket counter was opened only for Bohurupee,” Chandan Sen said.

headline: Communist Party of India (Marxist) State secretary M.V. Govindan on Tuesday sought to highlight the arrest of four Youth Congress leaders on synthetic drug peddling charges as emblematic of the “rot” in Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s office.
full_text:
Communist Party of India (Marxist) State secretary M.V. Govindan on Tuesday sought to highlight the arrest of four Youth Congress leaders on synthetic drug peddling charges as emblematic of the “rot” in Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s office.
Mr. Govindan told a press conference that the police had “inadvertently” arrested Youth Congress leaders Muhammad Hussien, P.A. Abdul Salam, and P. Abbas based on anonymous information without realising their political heft. He alleged that the accused managed Mr. Satheesan’s social media handles, including the dissemination of social media reels lionising the Chief Minister.
He said the videos of Mr. Satheesan fraternising with them in the Chief Minister’s Office and also visiting their houses had gone viral on social media. “There is official footage of one of them accompanying Indian Union Muslim League leader and Industries Minister P.K. Kunhalikutty to the Assembly,” he added.
Mr. Govindan accused Mr. Satheesan of using the government’s heft to persuade corporate owners of social media platforms, including META, to erase posts critical of the “Chief Minister’s proximity and obvious familiarity with narcotic peddlers” from the digital domain.“ “Mr. Satheesan has borrowed a page from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s playbook for stifling domestic criticism,” he added.
Ceding power
He said the UDF government had set a constitutionally ill-advised precedent by seeking the mediation of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) State president Rajeev Chandrasekhar to commandeer Central forces, including the Navy, Coast Guard and Air Force, to search for fishers who went missing off the coast of Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam recently.
“The government has ceded its self-determining executive power to the ruling party at the Centre, using the disaster that struck Kerala’s coast as a pretext to build bridges with the BJP,” he added.
False claim
Mr. Govindan accused Mr. Satheesan of making a false claim that the UDF would do away with the “legal constraint” that prevents administrations from disbursing relief to the families of persons missing in the aftermath of natural calamities.
The Left Democratic Front government had waived the restriction to disburse ₹22 lakh each to 142 fisher families who had lost their breadwinners to the sea, including to the 33 fishers whose bodies could not be recovered, during the 2016-17 Okhi cyclone. “The LDF gave the victims’ families jobs, built them houses and underwrote their children’s education,” he added.
Mr. Govindan accused the UDF of dismantling the search-and-rescue infrastructure, including a voluntary rescue force of 200 fishers and boats, to respond immediately to calamities at sea. He said despairing families had to knock on officials’ doors to mount rescue operations in vain for nearly a week. “Ministers and ruling front MLAs avoided fisher families for days and attempted to offer cold comfort by belatedly knocking at their doors,” he said.

headline: ‘Are you a staunch Hindu, do you eat non-veg food?’ Ram Temple CEO candidates asked to fill Google form
full_text:
‘Are you a staunch Hindu, do you eat non-veg food?’ Ram Temple CEO candidates asked to fill Google form
The 18 candidates who were shortlisted from a pool of 5,200 applicants were also asked about their work experience and their families.
“Do you keep shikha (sport a braid)? Do you wear a janeu (sacred thread)? Do you eat non-vegetarian food?”
Candidates who were interviewed for the post of first full-time chief executive officer (CEO) of Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Tuesday were asked a wide range of questions – from their religious practices and eating and drinking habits to their vision for the Ram Temple, people familiar with the matter said.
The 18 candidates who were shortlisted from a pool of 5,200 applicants were also asked about their work experience and their families, and practices of the Hindu religion, in an exhaustive 34-point Google form that was required to be filled before the interview held in Ayodhya. Besides, the interviewees were asked about their leadership abilities and religious-social engagements, the people cited above said.
Also Read | Ram temple donation ‘theft’ probe: Payments to construction contractors under scanner
The decision to appoint a full-time CEO was taken after the allegations of embezzlement of donations came to light. The allegations have led to scrutiny of the Trust's financial management even as eight accused have been arrested in the case while three officials, including the Trust's former general secretary Champat Rai, stepped down from their posts.
All the 18 candidates earlier faced an online interview. On Tuesday, a face-to-face interview was held for only eight candidates, including four former IAS officers.
Also Read | UP govt reconstitutes SIT in Ram temple donation ‘theft’ case after Supreme Court order
“Questions such as do you keep shikha (tuft), do you wear a janeu (sacred thread), are you pure vegetarian or do you eat non-vegetarian food, do you consume alcohol or are you a teetotaller, are you a staunch Hindu, will you be comfortable wearing attire according to the Hindu religion were asked in the Google forms,” one of the persons said, seeking anonymity.
“The other questions were where have you worked, what big crowds have you managed and what is your faith in Lord Ram. They asked the candidates about their families,” the person added.
Also Read | Trust, distrust converge in Ayodhya amid Ram Mandir donation theft case
A second person said the interview of each candidate lasted for around one or two hours. “It sought to test not just the candidate’s administrative skills but also devotion, temperament and vision for the world’s most high-profile temple project,” this person said, also seeking anonymity.
Who are the probable candidates?
The identities of the shortlisted candidates are yet to be made public but according to a third person aware of the details, former IPS officer Rajesh Pandey is among those on the list. He is scheduled to appear for the in-person interview on Wednesday.
Pandey is a former inspector general of Uttar Pradesh Police. Earlier, he served as Lucknow senior superintendent of police and was also the founder-member of the UP Special Task Force. He last served as inspector general of police, Bareilly range. He is also the secretary of Lucknow’s historic Hanuman Mandir in Aliganj, which records massive turnouts of devotees on festive occasions.
Also Read | Ram Temple donation probe expands to 12 districts as SIT hunts for ‘benami’ assets
Retired IAS officer Yogeshwar Mishra, who served as Faizabad district magistrate from January 7 to March 26, 2016, neither confirmed nor denied reports that he has been shortlisted for the interview. He last served as the divisional commissioner of Gonda division.
Selection panel, process
The selection panel comprises former Supreme Court judge Justice Pramod Kohli, Lt Gen Vishnukant Chaturvedi (retd), and Suresh Haware.
The committee is tasked with shortlisting three names and submitting them to the Trust before September 2. A meeting of the Trust’s executive committee is scheduled to be held on that day.
The Trust will then interview and pick the CEO from among the final three candidates.
Also Read | BJP ‘running away’ from debate on Ram temple donation theft: Akhilesh
The CEO will be the highest executive authority of the Trust. The role mainly centres around managing statutory, financial and administrative functions, building various systems for a temple that sees crores of pilgrims, coordinating security with central and state agencies, and ensuring smooth functioning of rituals and festivals.
A senior Trust member told HT that given the sensitivity of the post, the final selection is likely to be done under the direct supervision of the Centre and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. “The person who sits on the CEO’s chair will be someone both the government and the Sangh are comfortable with,” the member said, requesting anonymity.
Even future appointments in the CEO’s office will likely require approval from the Centre and the RSS, the member added.

full_text:
Heavy to very heavy rain likely in parts of Delhi over next 3 hours; waterlogging, traffic snarls expected
Another spell of very light to light rain is expected towards the evening or night. Only 0.5 mm of rain was recorded in Janakpuri on Tuesday morning.
Heavy to very heavy rain is likely in parts of Delhi-NCR on Tuesday as widespread thunderstorms from Uttar Pradesh are expected to move into the region over the next couple of hours. The IMD has issued a yellow alert for the capital and surrounding areas as multiple spells of rain continue across Delhi-NCR.
The IMD said one or two spells of very light to light rain were expected at most places from the forenoon to afternoon, while moderate rain was likely at a few places. Another spell of very light to light rain is expected towards the evening or night. Only 0.5 mm of rain was recorded in Janakpuri on Tuesday morning.
“Intermittent spells of light to moderate rain are very likely at most places in Delhi, with heavy rain expected at isolated places,” the IMD said in a bulletin on Tuesday. The warning is until 3pm today.
Meanwhile, weatherman Navdeep Dhaiya said heavy to very heavy rain would begin in Ghaziabad by 11 am. Moderate to heavy rain is likely in Noida, Delhi and Faridabad after 11:30 am, while Gurgaon is expected to receive moderate to heavy rain after 12 pm, mostly.
According to IndiaMetSky Weather, rainfall is likely to be heavy, which may lead to waterlogging in low-lying areas. The rain is expected to continue for around two hours before easing by the afternoon. Scattered showers are likely to persist through the rest of the day.
The city received 4 mm of rainfall in the 24-hour period ending at 8.30 am on Tuesday. Lodi Road recorded 4.8 mm of rainfall, while the Ridge received 6.9 mm. Palam recorded trace rainfall and Ayanagar recorded no rainfall during the period, news agency PTI reported.
Delhi has experienced an above-normal monsoon between June 1 and August 10, recording 534.3mm of rainfall during the period.
Weather update for the week
Very light to light rain is expected on Wednesday, Thursday, and Sunday. Multiple spells of rain will follow on Friday and Saturday.
The IMD categorises rainfall up to 15.5mm as light, between 15.6mm and 64.4 mm as moderate, 64.5mm to 115.5mm as heavy, and 115.6 to 204.4 as very heavy.
Heavy rain lash Mumbai
Meanwhile, several parts of Mumbai experienced heavy rainfall in the early hours of Tuesday, prompting SpiceJet to issue an advisory to passengers. The airline cautioned travellers scheduled to fly today that adverse weather could affect flight schedules and advised them to plan their journeys accordingly.
According to IMD latest nowcast, areas including Santacruz, Colaba, Worli, Chembur, Mulund, Borivali, Powai and Navi Mumbai are likely to receive light to moderate rainfall today.

NEW DELHI: Isha Foundation founder Sadhguru on Monday launched a new photography book called "Disappearing Faces", featuring photographs of people he encountered during his journeys through the remote Himalayas of Nepal and Tibet.Published by Penguin India, the book was launched by Union minister Mansukh Mandaviya at the India International Centre in New Delhi.The launch was followed by a conversation between Sadhguru and commentator Anand Ranganathan, exploring the stories and experiences behind the photographs featured in the book.âThese faces represent an era that will soon disappear: faces etched only by sensory perception of light and darkness, heat and cold, of springs and winters - above all, uncontaminated by information that is disconnected from our senses. Our senses lead to a certain sense of life where there is no Non-sense," Sadhguru said during the conversation."These are the visages that represent life that seems rudimentary but is rich with strong experiences of the land, the winds, the waters and the people. Over the last five decades, year after year, beyond the beauty and wondrous nature of the mountains, these faces have drawn me into the deep crevices of the Himalayas," he added.
Carrying a camera along the way, Sadhguru began documenting faces shaped by a life lived close to nature and increasingly distant from the cities.The book offers an intimate visual record of the people Sadhguru encountered during his journeys.Sadhguru first journeyed to Manasarovar and Mount Kailash in 2006 and has since returned repeatedly, leading seekers on the Himalayan pilgrimage. After undertaking his first motorcycle journey to Kailash in 2025, Sadhguru is set to return once again this year on a motorcycle, continuing his unique engagement with the sacred landscape of the Himalayas.The Himalayas have remained a significant part of Sadhguruâs life over the years, alongside his efforts towards human wellbeing, raising human consciousness and his commitment to ecological regeneration.

headline: The road not taken, every day: Why do potholes keep coming back
full_text:
The road not taken, every day: Why do potholes keep coming back
Aastha Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 11, 2026, 21:38 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Pothole-related deaths in India rose by over 53% in five years, from 1,555 in 2020 to 2,385 in 2024.
Do you also have a âwork in progressâ sign permanently living outside your house?One day, someone digs up the road to lay a water pipe. A few days later, another team arrives to fix a cable. Then comes the patchwork. And just when you think the road is finally back to normal, congratulations, it is dug up again.The road outside your house may technically be the same road, but it has seen so many rounds of digging, filling, breaking and repairing that it almost has a career history.And then, inevitably, the potholes arrive.We often blame potholes on bad roads, heavy rain or poor construction. But a pothole is rarely born overnight. In fact, that annoying crater that makes your car suspension groan or sends a two-wheeler rider swerving usually has a long backstory.A crack appears. Water gets in. The road weakens. Traffic keeps pounding it. The surface finally gives way.And if the underlying problem isn't fixed, filling the hole may only be a temporary solution.The road gets dug up. Again. And again.Before we get to the pothole itself, there is another character in this story: road digging.
Roads don't just carry vehicles. They carry water pipelines, sewage lines, electricity cables, telecom networks and other utilities underneath them. Whenever something needs to be repaired, replaced or newly installed, the road may have to be opened.The problem begins when the road is not restored to the same standard after the work is completed.
From a tiny crack to a full-blown pothole, here's how road damage turns into a recurring cycle of patch and repair.
A poorly compacted patch can become weaker than the surrounding pavement. Water can seep into the edges. Traffic repeatedly hits the repaired section. Eventually, cracks appear.And suddenly, the âtemporaryâ patch becomes the next pothole.This is one reason why road maintenance cannot simply mean filling visible holes. What happens underneath the road matters just as much as what you see on top.
Every pothole starts small
The first warning sign is usually something you wouldn't give a second glance: a tiny crack.Road surfaces are constantly under pressure. India's roads have to handle enormous traffic volumes, heavy vehicles and, in many parts of the country, intense heat followed by heavy monsoon rain.Temperature changes cause pavement materials to expand and contract. Repeated traffic loads create fatigue. Overloaded vehicles put additional stress on the surface.Then the monsoon arrives.
A police officer fills a pothole with stones on a road, at Edappally, in Kochi. (Image credit: PTI)
That tiny crack suddenly becomes a doorway.Water is the real troublemakerRain itself isn't necessarily the villain. Water getting beneath the road is.Once water enters through a crack, it can reach the layers beneath the asphalt. If drainage is poor, clogged or badly designed, the water may remain there instead of being carried away.The result is gradual weakening of the road's foundation.The surface may still look fine from above. Underneath, however, the supporting layers can lose strength and material can be washed or displaced, creating weak spots and voids.And then traffic does what traffic does best: keeps coming.Then the tyres take overImagine standing on a floor that has suddenly become slightly hollow underneath. Now imagine thousands of vehicles repeatedly pressing down on that same spot.That is essentially what happens to a road whose underlying layers have weakened.With every passing vehicle, the damaged surface experiences another load. Bits of asphalt loosen, the depression grows and eventually the surface collapses.That is your pothole.And once it forms, it can become a vicious cycle.Rainwater collects in the depression. More water finds its way into the surrounding pavement. The edges weaken. Vehicles hit the damaged section. More material breaks away.A small pothole can therefore become a much bigger one surprisingly quickly, especially during the rainy season.
Why does the pothole come back after it is fixed
Now comes the question every commuter has asked at least once:âDidn't they just repair this?âYes. But repairing the hole and repairing the road are not always the same thing.If workers simply fill the visible depression while the layers underneath remain damaged, the surface may fail again.It is a bit like filling a dent in a wall without fixing the leak behind it.The road may look perfect for a while. Then water gets in again, traffic starts pounding the weak section and â hello, pothole.
Potholes on Bengaluru roads (Image credit: PTI)
This is why preventive maintenance matters. A small crack can often be dealt with before it becomes structural damage. Once the road base itself has deteriorated, the repair becomes more complicated, expensive and disruptive.And not all potholes are equally dangerousA pothole's danger isn't determined by its size alone.A small hole on a busy, high-speed road can be far more dangerous than a giant one on an empty lane.For two-wheelers, an unexpected depression can destabilise the vehicle. On a crowded road, a driver trying to avoid a pothole may suddenly brake or swerve. At night, poor lighting can make the defect difficult to spot. During rain, water can completely hide its depth.So the real danger is a combination of the pothole, speed, traffic, visibility and road conditions.
What data shows
Potholes claimed 9,438 lives across India between 2020 and 2024, with annual fatalities rising from 1,555 in 2020 to 2,385 in 2024 â a jump of more than 53% in five years.Uttar Pradesh accounted for more than half of the national toll, reporting 5,127 deaths. Madhya Pradesh followed with 969 fatalities, while Tamil Nadu recorded 612, Odisha 425, Punjab 414 and Assam 395. Among Union Territories, Delhi reported the highest toll at 50.But the numbers also raise questions about how pothole-related crashes are recorded. States such as Andhra Pradesh and Bihar reported zero crashes, injuries or deaths under this category, even as states such as Manipur, Nagaland and Tripura reported fatalities. Experts say gaps in objective crash-cause reporting could mean the data does not fully capture the scale of the problem.The toll, however, remains below the 2017 peak of 3,597 pothole-related deaths. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance of the issue in 2018, observing that authorities responsible for maintaining roads were failing in their duties.
Can we stop pothole before it becomes a pothole?
Fortunately, the answer isn't simply âkeep filling holesâ.A 2021 IIT Madras study found that nearly 78% of urban potholes reported by citizens remained unfixed for more than two weeks, with delays particularly serious in high-traffic areas.Technology can help road agencies identify damage earlier through road-condition monitoring, GIS mapping and scanning systems. Quick repair methods can deal with certain defects before they expand.Citizen reporting can also help â provided complaints actually lead to inspection and action.Because the person who encounters a dangerous pothole may not be a road engineer inspecting the highway once a month. It may be a delivery rider passing through it ten times a day.But technology alone won't solve the problem.Road agencies need better coordination too. If one department digs up a road to lay a cable and another has to repair it later, someone needs to ensure the road is restored properly. Otherwise, the same stretch can enter an endless loop of dig â patch â crack â pothole â repair â dig again.
How speed, rain, poor visibility and heavy traffic can turn a road defect into a serious hazard.
The pothole is only the final chapterSo, the next time you see a pothole outside your home, remember: that hole probably didn't just âappearâ.
It may have started as a tiny crack.Then came rainwater. Maybe a badly repaired utility cut. Maybe years of heavy traffic. Maybe poor drainage. Maybe all of them.By the time you notice the crater, the real damage may already be underneath.Which is why the real solution isn't simply asking, âWho will fill this pothole?âIt is asking a much more important question:âWhy did this road fail in the first place â and why wasn't it fixed before it got this bad?âBecause if the answer remains unclear, that freshly filled pothole may just be waiting for its next monsoon comeback.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

The incident came to light after Bengaluru hotel's security manager contacted the police about the suspected deaths of two children.

headline: Chennai: Christian faith is in the eye of a political storm in Tamil Nadu after Assembly Speaker J. C. D. Prabhakar’s anti-abortion remark Monday, followed by finance minister N. Marie Wilson’s separate assertion Tuesday that Tamil couldn’t teach him...
full_text:
Chennai: Christian faith is in the eye of a political storm in Tamil Nadu after Assembly Speaker J. C. D. Prabhakar’s anti-abortion remark Monday, followed by finance minister N. Marie Wilson’s separate assertion Tuesday that Tamil couldn’t teach him the language of love, the Bible did that.
The two remarks have put the ruling TVK government on the defensive, with the Opposition accusing it of allowing religion to enter public policy and constitutional offices. The government, however, has sought to distance its health policy from the Speaker’s personal views, while defending the finance minister’s comments as a response to criticism of his Tamil skills while reading the budget.
Attacking the TVK government and questioning its secularism. state BJP chief Nainar Nagenthran said the Speaker’s participation in a procession chanting “abortion is murder” challenged Supreme Court judgments affirming abortion as a fundamental right linked to bodily autonomy under Article 21, and ran counter to Tamil Nadu’s progressive and social justice traditions.
BJP leader Tamilisai Soundararajan questioned, “How can a Speaker participate in a religious procession? They are claiming to be a secular party. And the finance minister is saying, I am a Christian, so I cannot talk Tamil! And the Speaker is advocating abortion because he is a Christian. I strongly condemn because the Speaker should be neutral. Speaker should be secular.”
“In the morning, they pass resolutions to elevate Tamil for the sake of language pride, but in the evening, a minister from the ruling party speaks as if Tamil and love have no connection, and as if his religion alone teaches love, this is strongly condemnable. This shows that Tamil exists only on their lips, not in their lives,” she wrote on X.
Speaker Prabhakar was the chief guest at the fifth National March for Life, a pro-life rally organised by Catholic groups in Chennai on 8-9 August. The rally criticised the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, with slogans such as ‘Let’s stop abortion’ and ‘Abortion is murder’.
He said, “Every unborn child has dignity, all children are God’s blessings since they are God-given and we have no right to abortion.”
Coming after such comments, the finance minister’s remark added to the debate on faith and secularism under TVK, which is led by Chief Minister Joseph Vijay whose father is a Christian and mother a Hindu.
The TVK finance minister’s statement came in response to MDMK MLA T.M. Rajendran’s criticism that the former’s speech contained grammatical errors in Tamil before he switched to English. Wilson said that Christianity had taught him “the language of love, the language of peace, the language of compassion. No matter how much Tamil is studied, some people will not understand these values. I have read it in the Bible. I am a born Christian,” Wilson said in the Assembly.
The finance minister said his priority was governance and the progress of Tamil Nadu rather than linguistic formalities. He further said that members were mocking his communication style and background instead of focusing on his work.
Rattled by the backlash over the Speaker’s anti-abortion remarks, Tamil Nadu Health Minister K. G. Arunraj sought to clarify the TVK government’s position, saying that abortion is regulated by the MTP Act, under which women can legally terminate a pregnancy up to 20 weeks (and in certain cases beyond).
Speaking at a press meet on the sidelines of an event in the city, he emphasised that abortion is often a medical necessity. Distancing the state’s health policy from the Speaker’s remarks, Arunraj said he did not know the context in which Prabhakar had spoken and urged the public not to misinterpret the comments.
Opposition parties and women’s rights activists strongly criticised Speaker Prabhakar’s participation in the pro-life rally, arguing that a constitutional office-holder should not endorse a campaign that challenges women’s reproductive autonomy. DMK leader T. K. S. Elangovan criticised the Speaker and said decisions on abortion are medical, not political, and must be left to doctors based on the patient’s condition.
“How can it be decided by anyone else? For some conditions, if medication is not sufficient, doctors may recommend surgery. What is wrong with that? Why should the government comment on such matters? …This government has nothing else to talk about. They are not talking about the Cauvery issue; instead, they are talking about all these things,” he told PTI.
Author-activist Shalin Maria Lawrence said that abortion rights are constitutional in India. “At a time when we are asking for bodily autonomy and women rights, it is not men who are bearing the burden of pregnancy so how can such messages be preached? Contraception for men is not practised in India and the whole burden falls on the woman to give birth; and raising a child is a bigger responsibility. We cannot replicate western playbook on issues such as abortion in India,” she told ThePrint.
Shalin also emphasised that we need to take the shame away from abortion which is a taboo subject in the state. “Religion cannot be used as a controlling tool for any individual. It sends a very wrong message to society, even if it was Prabhakar’s own belief. Even the availability of morning-after pills has been a problem in the state for many years and we cannot be imposing such beliefs on women,” she added.
BJP leader and spokesperson Narayanan Thirupathy, in a statement on X, said that there is nothing wrong with the Speaker being a believer in the Christian faith, but showing eagerness to impose that religion and its beliefs on the public is not appropriate.
“If anyone in Tamil Nadu had acted similarly based on Hindu beliefs, political parties such as the Congress, DMK, Communists, and VCK would have sharply criticised Hindu beliefs and gods by now. However, because minorities vote along religious lines, none of these political parties dare to call these incidents ‘communalism’. Therefore, these political parties and politicians themselves are the real communal parties and the people of Tamil Nadu will understand that what they preach is pseudo-secularism,” he said.
Speaker Prabhakar was formerly with the AIADMK and joined the TVK in January 2026. He had quoted verses from the Bible during his maiden address as Speaker from the Tamil Nadu Assembly chair.
He has frequently addressed Christian gatherings, including events organised by the Tamil Nadu Christian Churches Federation, where he spoke of the government’s outreach to minorities and assured that community’s demands would be taken to Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

headline: ‘Trump, Modi have good working relations; will work it out’: US official amid 100% tariff threat
full_text:
‘Trump, Modi have good working relations; will work it out’: US official amid 100% tariff threat
The Lindsey Graham Bill passed by the US Senate can levy tariffs on top five countries that purchase Russian crude, which includes India and China.
Responding to a question on potential US tariffs against India under the Lindsey Graham Bill, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro on Tuesday said Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump would “work it out.”
“…The President and your Prime Minister have a very good working relationship. They are going to work that out amongst themselves, and it's not for me to get between that...,” Navarro told ANI news agency, in response to a question on the Russia Sanctions Bill supported by Trump, which could levy upto 100 per cent tariffs on India.
The Bill, which carries the name of late Senator Lindsey Graham, can impose tariffs on the top five countries that purchase Russian crude oil and natural gas, which includes India and China.
Navarro reiterated his stance on the matter, saying, “With respect to your question, the president and your Prime Minister have a very good working relationship. They are going to work that out amongst themselves, and it's not for me or any gaggle to get between that.”
Also Read | India, China ‘main culprits’, key targets of Russia sanctions bill: US senator
‘Got firebombed by Indians on Russian oil remarks’: Navarro
Navarro, while answering the question, recalled an op-ed that he wrote which was published in the Financial Times, saying he was “firebombed” on the internet.
“During the Ukraine-Russia war, 6-8 months ago, I think I wrote wrote an op-ed in the Financial Times, which absolutely factually correctly pointed out that prior to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, India was not involved in the oil trade with Russia, but afterwards it got heavily involved and was selling a lot of refined products on behalf of Russia, which helped feed the war machine,” Navarro said.
He said that the “issue” had been resolved, adding, “Maybe I had a little bit to do with that with that op-ed, but I can tell you, I got actually firebombed by the Indian continent on the internet.” The White House trade adviser said that was “not how we resolve problems in America", while adding, “Don't do that.”
What is the Lindsey Graham Bill?
The Bill, also known as the Russia Sanctions Bill, was passed last week through the Senate on bipartisan vote, 86 to 11. However, it needs a vote in the US House of Representatives before it can become a law.
Apart from countries purchasing Russia's crude and natural gas, it can also place mandatory sanctions on top figures in the Russian government, including President Vladimir Putin, and foreign companies supporting Russia's defence industrial base, according to a CNN report.
The final tariff level on the top five countries purchasing from Russia would be determined by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. However, the Bill allows an exemption for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s total natural gas exports and are working to significantly lower their use of Russian natural gas.
The passage of the Bill came days after late Senator Graham passed away. He had announced, the day before he died, that the administration and the bill’s key Senate backers had finally reached a deal on the package. The Senate took its first procedural vote on the package in the hours after Graham’s DC funeral, CNN reported

headline: ‘Sunil Tatkare’s election illegal’: Complaint challenges Maha NCP chief's reappointment
full_text:
‘Sunil Tatkare’s election illegal’: Complaint challenges Maha NCP chief's reappointment
A complaint filed with the ECI challenges Sunil Tatkare’s re-election as Maharashtra NCP chief, alleging violations of the party’s constitution.
Days after poll strategist Prashant Kishor allegedly advised the removal of Maharashtra NCP president Sunil Tatkare, a complaint has been filed with the Election Commission of India (ECI) challenging Tatkare’s reappointment to the post on the grounds that it was illegal.
The complainant is Bhausaheb Gore, an NCP office-bearer from Jalna. “His election was illegal as it violated the provisions of the party’s constitution, which is not acceptable to party workers who are loyal to Ajit Pawar,” Gore told a Marathi news channel.
“The election programme was not announced and no dates were declared for filing or withdrawing nominations. Nor was a returning officer appointed. Without following any of these prescribed procedures, Tatkare got himself elected when his three-year term was due to end in July 2026.”
Also Read | Prashant Kishor’s meeting with Sunetra Pawar sparks churn in NCP, unease in BJP
Gore has urged the ECI to declare Tatkare’s re-election invalid. His complaint comes weeks after another NCP office-bearer, Sachchidanand Singh, approached the ECI challenging the election of Sunetra Pawar as the party’s national president on similar grounds. The development is being seen as a sign of intensifying infighting within the NCP, which is an ally of the BJP in Maharashtra as well as at the Centre.
NCP infighting intensifies over leadership polls
Tatkare was re-elected as Maharashtra NCP president on February 26 alongside Sunetra Pawar, who was elected as the party’s national president, and Praful Patel, who was elected national working president.
A leader close to Tatkare, however, denied any violation of the party’s constitutional provisions.
“Sunil Tatkare was elected at the national convention, which was convened under unusual circumstances following the death of NCP president Ajit Pawar,” he said.
Also Read | Khopoli murder takes political turn, Tatkare’s close aide in spotlight
Questions over Tatkare’s role resurface
This is not the first time party office-bearers have openly voiced their opposition to Tatkare.
Leaders such as Rupali Thombre-Patil had demanded his resignation as state president soon after reports emerged that poll strategist Prashant Kishor had suggested that the NCP leadership replace Tatkare with a new face.
After taking charge as NCP national president, Sunetra Pawar introduced a series of organisational and constitutional changes.
One of the more contentious changes involved the omission of Praful Patel’s designation as national working president and Sunil Tatkare’s designation as Maharashtra state president from the national Working Committee.
She later clarified that the omissions were inadvertent, but the changes were not subsequently rectified.

headline: House panel criticises continuing delays in construction of Eklavya schools
full_text:
House panel criticises continuing delays in construction of Eklavya schools
The standing committee said construction was underway at 249 locations, and 51 schools were at the pre-construction stage
A parliamentary standing committee has criticised the continuing delays in the construction and operationalisation of Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS), saying measures taken have failed to resolve recurring problems. It recommended an independent agency to oversee the work for the boarding education scheme for Scheduled Tribe (ST) students in remote areas.
In its report on the Union tribal affairs ministry’s action on recommendations in the Report on the Demands for Grants, the Standing Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment noted that 723 EMRSs have been sanctioned against a target of 728. It added that only 428 school buildings were completed as of April 30. Construction was underway at 249 locations, and 51 schools remained at the pre-construction stage.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party lawmaker PC Mohan-led 31-member committee said it was dissatisfied with the ministry’s response. It added the National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS) had reported utilisation of ₹4,896.40 crore in 2025-26.
The panel said that the ministry’s measures to accelerate the construction and operationalisation of EMRSs are repetitive. It added that the ministry had largely taken these measures earlier also, but the same problems persist.
The panel noted that delays could increase construction costs and unnecessarily increase the budget of NESTS. It urged the ministry to consider setting up an independent agency capable of resolving bottlenecks and ensuring that schools become operational in their own buildings within a fixed time frame.
The panel expressed concern about functional schools as well. Of 499 functional EMRSs, 377 operated from permanent buildings, 111 from other government buildings and 11 from rented premises. The committee said rented premises may not provide facilities needed for modern education, including AI and technology labs, smart classrooms and sporting arenas.
The committee flagged a decline in beneficiaries of the Scheme for Residential Education for Students in High Schools in Targeted Areas, which provides support for Scheduled Caste (SC) students to study in residential and non-residential schools NGOs and voluntary organisations run. The number of schools selected under the scheme fell from 142 in 2022-23 to 137 in 2024-25 and 130 in 2025-26. The number of selected students declined from 16,479 in 2022-23 to 14,281 in 2024-25.
The committee said it expects the number of schools and students to increase every year to achieve the objective of the scheme. It urged the Union and state governments to popularise the programme to attract more eligible students.
The government attributed the decline to the closure or discontinuation of projects because of factors such as non-renewal of school recognition certificates, non-availability of valid SC certificates, non-compliance with scheme guidelines and closure of NGOs and voluntary organisations. It said that the number of beneficiaries rose to 13,051 in 2025-26 and that it was monitoring empanelled institutions while examining measures to strengthen implementation and outreach.
The report flagged implementation gaps under Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) for socio-economic development of 75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. It added that work in health, education, roads, sanitation and other areas lagged behind targets.
The panel asked the ministry to develop a mechanism for timely execution during the extended implementation period for PM-JANMAN, which was launched in November 2023.

headline: Nasa invites Isro for Moon base programme, seeks wider space cooperation with India

NEW DELHI: Nasa on Tuesday invited Isro to join its Moon Base programme under the Artemis Accords, as India and the United States discussed expanding cooperation in civil and commercial space activities.The two countries also agreed to advance discussions on sharing open scientific data under the Artemis Accords, according to a US Embassy press release.The developments came during the ninth meeting of the India-US Civil Space Joint Working Group (CSJWG), hosted by India on August 5-6 at the Indian Space Research Organisation's headquarters in Bengaluru.The meeting focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation in civil and commercial space, while exploring future partnerships in space science and human spaceflight technologies.ISRO chairman and department of space secretary Dr V Narayanan and US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor addressed the opening session and highlighted the importance of further strengthening bilateral space cooperation.The meeting was co-chaired by M Sankaran, Director of ISRO's UR Rao Satellite Centre, on the Indian side, and Dr Wesley Brooks, assistant secretary of state for oceans and international environmental and scientific affairs, and Kathleen Karika, Nasa associate administrator for international and interagency relations, on the US side.
The discussions were held under the India-US Transforming the Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology (TRUST) Initiative and followed the February 2025 Joint Leaders' Statement issued by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump.
Both sides discussed expanding cooperation following the successful launch of the joint Nasa-Isro Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission last year, besides exploring future collaborations in space science and human spaceflight technology.They also reaffirmed their commitment to advancing United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) guidelines on the long-term sustainability of outer space activities and reviewed ongoing multilateral efforts to strengthen the committee's effectiveness.

Nasa invites Isro to join Moon Base program under Artemis Accords
The two sides have also agreed to advance discussions for cooperation on open scientific data sharing under the Artemis Accords.
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Nasa) has invited the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) to join its Moon Base program in a bid to deepen the India-US partnership under the Artemis Accords, the US Embassy said on Tuesday.
The two sides have also agreed to advance discussions for cooperation on open scientific data sharing under the Accords that seek to to enhance the governance of the civil exploration and use of outer space.
Nasa is building a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole to strengthen US' leadership in space, unlock scientific discovery, drive innovation with industry and international collaborators, and prepare humanity for missions to Mars.
On June 21, 2023, India became the 27th signatory of the Artemis Accord, to guide space exploration cooperation among nations.
The release said India and the US advanced their discussions on civil and commercial space cooperation and also focused on pursuing future science and human space flight technology partnerships.
These discussions, the release added, took place during the 9th meeting of the India-US Civil Space Joint Working Group (CSJWG), hosted by India on August 5 and 6 at the ISRO headquarters in Bengaluru.

At least eight people were killed and several others injured, including two who were placed on ventilator support, after two separate multi-vehicle collisions occurred within 15 minutes of each other in Zaheerabad on Tuesday (August 11), causing severe traffic disruption on the Hyderabad-Bidar road.
In the first accident, six people were killed and several others injured when a speeding tanker hit an overloaded autorickshaw near the Mahindra & Mahindra facility on the Zaheerabad-Bidar road around 7.45 p.m. The victims were reportedly in the autorickshaw that was taking a U-turn when the tanker crashed into it.
According to Zaheerabad town CI Ravi, the deceased were workers from Bidar returning home from work. They were identified as Rekha, Sridevi, Devadas, Kavitha, Reshma and Nikitha. Radhika, Shilpa and Shoba were among the injured and were shifted to a hospital for treatment.
Nirmalamma, Thuljamma and Chandrakala were among those receiving treatment, with their condition described as critical. Two of the injured are on ventilator support, the officer said.
In the second accident, which occurred about 15 minutes after the first within the limits of Kohir police station, two people were killed and two others injured after an Ertiga allegedly crossed the road divider while travelling towards Hyderabad and collided with vehicles coming from the opposite direction.
CI Ravi explained that the Ertiga, while apparently attempting to overtake another car, crossed the divider and first collided with another Ertiga before crashing into an Innova travelling in the opposite direction.
The two occupants of the Ertiga died in the collision. They were identified as Mallikarjun, an employee of MRF, and Shankar. Two others sustained injuries and were shifted to a hospital for treatment.
The two accidents brought traffic on the Zaheerabad-Bidar road to a standstill, with vehicles backed up for nearly 5 km as police and emergency personnel cleared the wreckage and managed traffic.

headline: ‘Uncle sends his regards’: Mumbai thieves use innovative WhatsApp codes to run pickpocket gang
full_text:
‘Uncle sends his regards’: Mumbai thieves use innovative WhatsApp codes to run pickpocket gang
The WhatsApp codes were allegedly used to know if every gang member was safe, if anyone was caught by the cops or if the day’s planning could be executed.
Some perfectly normal phrases that may sound like casual greetings, like "uncle sends his regards" or "how is the weather today?", carried a very different meaning for the ‘Dhakka gang’ of pickpockets in Mumbai.
According to a Times of India report, the MIDC Police Station team cracked the WhatsApp codes of the pickpocket gang, which ran a carefully orchestrated operation.
The WhatsApp codes were allegedly used to know if every gang member was safe, if anyone was caught by the cops or if the day’s planning could be executed.
The case revealed how Mumbai's pickpockets have now gone high-tech, running their syndicate through smartphones and daily-changing WhatsApp codes.
The daily changing code
The investigation, led by DCP (West Zone 3) Datta Nalawade, revealed that the gang's main kingpin contacted members every morning via WhatsApp. A new code was sent on WhatsApp every single day, like a one-time password.
DCP Nalawade said the communication was less about planning the theft than checking whether it was safe to proceed.
“The purpose wasn’t to discuss the theft. It was to find out whether anyone had been picked up by police,” he was quoted by TOI as saying.
Only after receiving an "all-clear" would they decide which BEST bus route to target and where to meet up. Immediately after two gang members were arrested in Andheri, the remaining members changed their hideout and shifted to Juinagar in Navi Mumbai.
No to stealing iPhones
The MIDC police team recovered 135 expensive smartphones from the gang. The market value of these phones ranges from ₹90,000 to ₹1.5 lakh. According to the police, this gang actively avoided stealing iPhones because they are extremely difficult to unlock.
Furthermore, iPhones yield a very low resale value in their primary black markets, which are located in Bangladesh and Nepal.
Officers explained that the 4- to 5-member gang would board BEST buses and, without speaking a word to each other, 2 or 3 members would distract the victim by jostling them or creating a commotion. Meanwhile, the main member of the gang—referred to as the "Machine"—would pick up the phone or wallet from the victim's pocket. Following the heist, all members would disperse and escape by getting off at different bus stops.

‘We were just giving an update’: Outgoing Air India CEO on meeting with MoCA, DGCA over flight altitude drop
Campbell Wilson stated that the briefing was focused on sharing preliminary findings and progress on the ongoing probe into the incident.
Air India's outgoing Chief Executive Officer, Campbell Wilson, on Tuesday met with senior officials from the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) in New Delhi to provide an update regarding the recent mid-air incident involving a Phuket-Delhi flight.
Addressing reporters following the meeting, Wilson stated that the briefing was focused on sharing preliminary findings and progress on the ongoing probe into the incident.
"We were just giving an update on the status of the investigation... It is up to him (MoCA Minister) to give an update."
The meeting comes in the backdrop of a serious safety incident on August 4, 2026, involving Air India flight AI2379, operated by an Airbus A320neo carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members. Cruising en route from Phuket to New Delhi, the aircraft experienced a sudden 300-foot altitude drop over Odisha, resulting in injuries to passengers and crew members.
Meanwhile, Air India on Monday said it cannot comment on any findings or observations related to the investigation into the Phuket-Delhi flight incident that took place earlier this month, as the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) continues its probe under the provisions of the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) Annex 13.
According to a statement by a spokesperson from the airline, the carrier said that it would continue to provide all necessary cooperation to the concerned authorities as required for the probe.
"The investigation into the incident is being conducted by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) under the provisions of ICAO Annex 13. As the investigative process is ongoing, Air India cannot comment on any findings or observations related to the investigation. We will continue to extend our full cooperation to relevant authorities as required," the spokesperson said.
Airbus also issued a statement amid the probe, stating that it is providing technical assistance to the relevant investigating authorities in accordance with ICAO Annex 13.
"In accordance with ICAO Annex 13, Airbus is providing technical assistance to the relevant investigating authorities. We are actively supporting the airline and will provide further information as it becomes available. A team of specialists is being dispatched to assist with the investigation," Airbus said in a statement.
This comes as AAIB is investigating an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi after the aircraft experienced a sudden loss of altitude of approximately 300 feet during cruise on August 4. The aircraft subsequently stabilised and landed safely in Delhi.
"The occurrence has been classified as a Serious Incident and is under investigation by the AAIB," the Ministry of Civil Aviation said in a statement on Sunday.
As part of the standard operating procedures following such an occurrence, both flight crew members underwent the prescribed psychoactive substance screening test. (ANI)

headline: Tech Tonic: Mark Zuckerberg, an AI manifesto, and curating a tech guru aura
full_text:
Tech Tonic: Mark Zuckerberg, an AI manifesto, and curating a tech guru aura
From downplaying environment concerns to claiming we’ll all become entrepreneurs, Mark Zuckerberg wants to be the adult in an AI room. Should we let him?
We’ve had a stream of this. Just this year, apart from all the incessant noise, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Sir Demis Hassabis, who is now Chief Scientist of Alphabet, Chair of Google DeepMind, and the Co-founder and CEO of Isomorphic Labs, have given us long-drawn explanations of their vision for AI. In parallel, Sam Altman, Satya Nadella and Jensen Huang also leave no chance to tell us how great artificial intelligence (AI) is. And now Mark Zuckerberg, Founder, Chairman, and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Meta, wants to be the adult in the room, telling us all will be okay. Will it? I’m not so sure.
I write this column on this theme, because a few hours ago, Mark Zuckerberg posted what can only really be classified as a manifesto. And typical to all AI companies and AI bosses, it must tick the boxes of being self serving and in a way telling the world’s citizens they’ve understood the impacts of AI all wrong. Either Mark hasn’t been tuning in to social media, or was too busy interviewing the next million dollar pay check hire—but we’ve been told by almost all AI bosses I’ve name-checked above have regularly told us there will be unusually painful (the exact words of Amodei, if I’m not mistaken), the world must plough in trillions of dollars for AI development, and we’ll run short of electricity and clean water (but that’s supposed to be okay). Altman, earlier this year in India, compared the food humans eat in a lifetime versus the energy AI models need.
Also Read: Tech Tonic | Big AI keeps making the same mistake about Chinese AI companies
“Humanity has witnessed many transformative advances. Each time there is fear that people will be left behind. But each time humanity has come out with more people sharing greater prosperity, health, and freedom. We believe this will be true with AI as well, and the abundance of the future can be shared by everyone,” beautiful words penned down by Mark, but they would probably have been believable 24 months ago. Not now.
I’ve decoded four key takeaways from Mark’s manifesto attempt, and let you judge whether it’s self serving, or reality for the greater good.
Assuage fears about data centers: There is a concerted attempt to counter the counter the reality of AI infrastructure. “Sustainable infrastructure development means that communities must benefit significantly from each project,” he writes. The realities of staggering local energy and water demands, as well as the cost of setting up AI data centres, isn’t lost on anyone—and that scale is true, irrespective of geography, but underlying conditions may further worsen impact.
And of course, if I was to collect a ₹ for every time I’ve heard the railroad, highways and electrification argument given by AI bosses and their megaphones lower down the ecosystem hierarchy, I’d probably have a million much needed bucks in my bank account. Mark repeats the same too, and since he’s the wise adult in the room apparently, he also mentions broadband for some reason. I don’t want to get into that.
A Gartner analyst recently told HT that “India’s data-centre capacity is already around 1.5 GW and could reach about 6.5 GW by 2030, with water use around 150 billion litres annually in 2025 and expected to more than double by 2030.” When Mark says that water-efficient data centres will restore more water than they use by 2030 and “with high water stress, our goal is to restore 200% of the water we use,” it is scarcely believable. As scarce, as clean water will be in data centre regions by that timeframe.
AI will fight for good against evil: Of course, and we’ve heard this before particularly from Amodei. “With AI, the defenders will also have more compute to generate significantly more intelligence from the same models — and in some cases they’ll have more advanced models as well,” writes Mark.
Zuckerberg’s manifesto argues that if everyone has a cybersecurity AI, all systems become hardened and safer. This relies on the flawed assumption that offence and defence scale equally. In cybersecurity and biotechnology, they often do not. It only takes one malicious actor with “invention superpowers” to engineer a novel bioweapon or a catastrophic computer virus. A million benevolent AI tutors and personal assistants cannot retroactively stop a pandemic or a collapsed power grid. By democratising capabilities, Meta and Mark downplay the fact that destructive power is inherently easier to unleash than to contain.
To that point, Zuckerberg also writes that “While there are risks to releasing capable models, the most dangerous scenario from this perspective would be leading AI labs training powerful models and keeping them for themselves.” I’m sure he has Altman’s phone number.
OpenAI this week said it must slow down development of its upcoming Astra model, because it showed “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity,” which means OpenAI cannot exactly “rule out critical cyber capabilities.”
Everyone is an entrepreneur, apparently: To address the fear of AI taking jobs, the manifesto claims that because everyone will have the tools to build businesses, there will be more employment. “If people can use AI to invent incredibly valuable new things, then it will make more sense to allocate it towards that rather than automating existing jobs. The more superintelligence serves as a tool of invention, the more likely that individual capability outpaces automation and the future is better for people,” he writes, gently mentioning Superintelligence too.
This is a remarkably Silicon Valley-centric view of human nature and the economy. Not everyone can be an entrepreneur (there are often societal and financial conditions that define a human’s professional trajectory), nor is a society made up entirely of solo founders truly sustainable. None of the AI companies seem to acknowledge the existence of millions of people who rely on stable, routine work and therefore income. Handwaving away a massive societal transition of mass unemployment by simply saying everyone can start a business now, simply ignores the shockwaves that are headed our way.
Importance of open source AI: This is one aspect where Zuckerberg is saying all the right things, and Meta for the most part, has been walking the talk. “Open source is a positive and important force for empowering people and preventing centralisation that is detrimental for both safety and the economy. Meta continues to be strongly supportive of open source, including open source AI models. The current open source ecosystem is strong, and we think it would be a mistake to restrict it,” he clearly pens his thoughts.
Meta has been countering a push to closed ecosystems from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, with open-source architecture. Meta’s latest open models include the Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark 1.2 and the previous flagship Llama series. The Muse Glimmer is a 30-billion parameter dense model featuring a 120K+ context window, and released under an Apache 2.0 license. It is trained using distillation from larger proprietary systems, optimised for a single consumer GPU, and tailored for always-on local AI agent workflows. The Muse Spark 1.2 is Meta’s high-performance multimodal reasoning and agentic model, whose weights Meta plans to make publicly available to developer.
Vishal Mathur is the Technology Editor at HT. Tech Tonic is a column that looks at the impact of personal technology on the way we live, and vice versa. The views expressed are personal.

headline: Maharashtra orders ban on illegal highway dhabas, sets 60-day demolition deadline
full_text:
Maharashtra orders ban on illegal highway dhabas, sets 60-day demolition deadline
The order is aimed at keeping land reserved for national highways free of roadside commercial structures that may obstruct traffic, create safety risks or interfere with highway operations.
The Maharashtra government has issued road safety directions to all local authorities, ordering an immediate ban on dhabas, eateries and other commercial structures built illegally within the Right of Way along all national highways in the state.
As part of the order, district magistrates have been asked to ensure that new and existing illegal roadside structures within highway safety zones are demolished within 60 days.
They have also been told to set up task forces for regular checks, while no department, authority or local body can grant or renew any licence, no-objection certificate or trade approval for such sites without prior clearance from the National Highways Authority of India or the Public Works Department.
The order, issued by the rural development department, is aimed at keeping land reserved for national highways free of roadside commercial structures that may obstruct traffic, create safety risks or interfere with highway operations.
It also referred to the Supreme Court’s April 13 directive asking district councils, panchayat samitis and gram panchayats in Maharashtra to implement its directions strictly.
The government has said that existing licences for such sites must be reviewed within 30 days. It has also directed collectors in every district with a national highway to form a highway safety task force comprising officials from the district administration, police, the NHAI or the concerned land-owning agency, the PWD and local bodies.
According to the order, district collectors and police commissioners or superintendents will share responsibility for the timely removal of encroachments.
The task force will have to hold review meetings every fortnight and maintain minutes of those meetings. For roads under district councils and other district roads, the government referred to its February 21, 2024 circular on accident-prone stretches and asked the concerned authorities to implement those measures and send periodic action-taken reports to the Rural Development Department.
In effect, the order lays down a statewide mechanism to remove illegal roadside structures along national highways, tighten approvals within highway safety zones and monitor compliance through district-level task forces and regular reviews.

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor held discussions with National Security Advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday to deliberate on US-India strategic cooperation, describing the meeting as "fruitful".
In a post on X, Ambassador Gor underscored the significance of the robust bilateral partnership in tackling global security challenges, emphasising that both nations share several common objectives. He further noted that diplomatic engagement between Washington and New Delhi continues to strengthen.
"Had a fruitful meeting with National Security Advisor Ajit Doval to discuss deepening US-India strategic cooperation. Our close partnership with India is vital to addressing global security challenges. The United States and India share many of the same goals, and our engagement continues to grow!" the US Envoy posted.
The interaction follows Ambassador Gor's meeting with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri in New Delhi on Monday evening, where both diplomats discussed key facets of India-US bilateral relations amid ongoing diplomatic exchanges over various bilateral matters.
"Always good to meet with Foreign Secretary @VikramMisri," Ambassador Gor wrote on X, sharing a glimpse of the interaction without elaborating further on the deliberations.
These back-to-back diplomatic interactions unfolded against the backdrop of sustained momentum at the highest levels of leadership, coming just days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi received a phone call from US Vice-President JD Vance on Saturday evening.
During their telephonic conversation, PM Modi and Vance evaluated avenues to further deepen the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, while also exchanging views on regional and global developments.
PM Modi also extended congratulations to JD Vance and his wife, Usha Vance, following the birth of their son, conveying best wishes to the family.
"Received a phone call from US Vice-President JD Vance. We discussed ways to further deepen India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership across key areas. Warmly congratulated him and the Second Lady on the birth of their son and conveyed best wishes to the entire family," PM Modi stated on X.
According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), both leaders noted the sustained momentum in high-level engagements and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening cooperation in various sectors.
"They noted the sustained momentum in the high-level engagements and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening cooperation in trade, defence, critical and emerging technologies, energy security and critical minerals. They also exchanged views on regional and global developments of mutual interest," the PMO stated.
This flurry of high-level engagement builds on groundwork laid earlier in July, when US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar conferred in Manila on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' meetings.
During that meeting, the two foreign ministers agreed to accelerate work on key defence agreements and conclude an interim bilateral trade deal that Washington described as "almost complete", signalling fresh momentum in the strategic partnership between the two nations while reviewing developments in the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.
