headline: Nitin Thakker: ‘Political leaders were far more approachable, had clean image’
full_text:
Nitin Thakker: ‘Political leaders were far more approachable, had clean image’
India@79: Donning the black gown since 1968, Thakker has been on the electric tram that ceased operations in '64 and the underground Metro Line 3 opened in 2025
A packed room at the Bombay Bar Association (BBA)’s meeting called to protest against the Emergency, tales of renowned criminal lawyer Ram Jethmalani’s ‘ghoda-gaadi (horse carriage)’ in pre-independence Karachi, carving out the state of Maharashtra from the larger Bombay state in 1960, and the spontaneous reaction of the judges of the Bombay high court who rose early from proceedings after receiving the news of Jayprakash Narayan’s death in 1979 – senior advocate Nitin Thakker, 79, is the keeper of the storied history of one of the oldest high courts in the country and the events that shaped the young nation’s “city of dreams”.
An archetypal SoBo (South Bombay) boy, the two-time president of BBA, Thakker’s first fee as a young lawyer in 1969 was three gold mohurs or ₹45.
Donning the black gown since 1968, Thakker has been both on the electric tram that ceased operations in 1964, and also the underground Metro Line 3 inaugurated in 2025.
Deep Dive
Also Read | Indra Mohan Pandey: ‘Panditji just passed by us... I could see him clearly’
With humble beginnings in Kalbadevi, once a hotspot for cloth trade and home to a large Gujarati community, Thakker is now a resident of the upscale Altamount Road. His father, Gordhanbhai Thakker, a lawyer and later a judge, worked closely with freedom fighter Bhulabhai Desai. His mother Sarlaben Thakker too distributed information pamphlets about the movement.
Thakker was born on a day ahead of the June 3 declaration of 1947 that announced the end of British rule in India and the partition of the country into India and Pakistan. Patriotism was perhaps his first inheritance.
His first courtroom visit was at age 11 when his father, then a sessions court judge, presided over a criminal trial. It did not leave a lasting impression. “I visited the court during my school holidays. I was perhaps too young to decide anything,” said Thakker. He studied in the St. Xavier’s Boys Academy’s Gujarati-medium school.
Also read | Pushpa Singh: Only a few of us champions are left, the rest are out
He treasured a memory of his principal, a Spanish priest who spoke Gujarati and had the novel idea to raise funds for a new school building in the early 1960s. “They had a screening of (the film) Mughal-e-Azam and we, the children from Gujarati-medium, were asked to sell tickets,” Thakker reminisced.
One of his early childhood memories was watching the funeral procession of then deputy prime minister Vallabhbhai Patel in 1950 as it passed his balcony. He remembered making a dash as a school boy to the SNDT university after hearing of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru’s arrival. “We just got a glimpse of him when he came out of the gate. In those days, the PM didn’t have the kind of security they have now. Political leaders were far more approachable and they had a clean image,” said Thakker.
During those days, even if decisions were made in Delhi, their effects were immediately felt in the Bombay HC and BBA that counted Dr. B R Ambedkar, M K Gandhi, Nani Palkhivala, and Fali Nariman among its erstwhile members.
During the 1964 food shortage when PM Lal Bahadur Shastri gave a call to avoid cooking grains for one meal to reduce India’s foodgrain dependency, Thakker’s home followed it to a tee. “My mother stopped cooking grains on Mondays. We decided we would only eat vegetables,” said Thakker.
In 1966, he graduated from the Sydenham College of Commerce and then studied law at the Government Law College, the alma mater of some of the finest legal minds in the country. “My father was firm that he will not mentor me. I did a nine-month internship at Kanga and Company, and then joined the chambers of senior advocate Anil Divan.”
Also Read | Lt Gen Arvind Mahajan (Retd): ‘We were hailed as the generation of New India’
In 1975, during the Emergency that Thakker describes as a “blot on our democracy”, BBA passed a resolution to abstain from court as a mark of protest. Thakker was present in Room No. 57 of the HC. “Hardly any lawyers participated in the general body meeting or debates we held before that. But that day was chock-a-block. There weren’t enough chairs. We were all standing with all the doors open because there was no AC…The resolution was passed with an overwhelming majority,” said Thakker.
Then in 1990, BBA passed a resolution showing “complete lack of confidence” against four sitting judges of the HC amid allegations of corruption. “I was part of that resolution. I remember the debate going on in the bar association in the general body meeting. We were urging the then chief justice not to allot any work to these four judges.”
Over the years, the relationship between the bar and bench has evolved but social media is the game-changer, he said. “Social media has not just changed courts or the judiciary but it has brought every person under scrutiny,” said Thakker. He also added that it may have made judges more guarded because sometimes video clips of observations are taken out of context.
AI too raises concerns of client privacy but Thakker said that the age of AI has certainly arrived. “AI is here to stay. BBA was the first bar association in the country to come up with AI guidelines for advocates in July 2025.”
While a new HC building is taking shape in Bandra, the old early English-Gothic building in Fort holds the sentiments of far too many, Thakker agreed. “Everybody loves this building. But in the interest of litigants and the administration of justice, I must say, this building has outlived its utility.”
Thakker said that neither of his two children picked law as a career but 11 years after their wedding in 1969, his wife Nalinee too studied law. A grandfather of three college students, he said, his entire family’s affection is mostly concentrated on Atom, their seven-year-old goldendoodle.

headline: ‘Beginning of another’: How Hindustan Times reported freedom on August 15, 1947
full_text:
‘Beginning of another’: How Hindustan Times reported freedom on August 15, 1947
By the time people picked up their newspapers on August 15, the headline was no longer about a country waiting for freedom. India was independent.
India woke up free on August 15, 1947, but its first Independence Day looked very different from the ceremony the country knows today.
The transition began on the night of August 14 inside Constitution Hall in New Delhi. Members opened the session with the singing of Vande Mataram -- the song is set to return to the Red Fort this August 15, for the first time since Independence. Assembly President Dr Rajendra Prasad spoke first, paying tribute to those who had sacrificed their lives for the country’s freedom.
Take a look at a glimpse of the Hindustan Times newspaper from that historic morning 80 years ago:
As midnight approached, Jawaharlal Nehru rose to speak. “At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.” In his now-famous ‘Tryst with Destiny’ speech, Nehru celebrated the moment but also reminded the Assembly that freedom came with responsibilities. The new country still had to confront poverty, ignorance, disease and inequality.
By the time people picked up their newspapers on August 15, the headline was no longer about a country waiting for freedom. India was independent. The front page of Hindustan Times that morning read: “Journey's end - Beginning of another.” The paper carried photographs of Lord Mountbatten, Nehru, Rajendra Prasad and others, along with reports on the historic events unfolding in Delhi.
Independence activist Hansa Mehta then presented the national flag on behalf of the women of India. The flag had been adopted by the Constituent Assembly only weeks earlier.
India had entered a new chapter.
ALSO READ | Independence Day 2026: Is it 79th or 80th Independence Day? Theme, significance and history explained
Delhi woke up to huge crowds
That morning, Delhi was full of people. A contemporary account published in Fauji Akhbar, India's first army newspaper, described crowds breaking through police cordons around the Constituent Assembly. People gathered around Jawaharlal Nehru and Lord Mountbatten, cheering and waving flags.
The planned arrangements could not contain the crowds. For people on the streets, British rule had finally ended.
India takes charge
With the transfer of power, British rule in India ended. India became an independent Dominion, with Nehru as its first prime minister and Lord Louis Mountbatten as its first Governor-General.
August 15 was filled with official ceremonies as the new government took charge. But the Independence Day that Indians know today had not yet taken shape.
ALSO READ | Independence Day flag-hoisting guide: Dos and don’ts every Indian should know ahead of August 15
The Red Fort tradition came later
The Independence Day ceremony Indians know today did not exist in 1947. Nehru did not hoist the national flag at the Red Fort on August 15 that year.
He raised it there for the first time on August 16 and addressed the gathering. The ceremony later became the template for the annual Red Fort tradition. On August 15 itself, Nehru was occupied with the swearing-in of the new government and other official events.
Freedom came with Partition
India's freedom came as British India was divided into India and Pakistan. Communal violence had already spread across parts of Punjab and Bengal, forcing millions to leave their homes.
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs crossed the new borders as families were separated and communities were torn apart. Data says around 2-20 lakh people died due to violence during the Partition.
ALSO READ | Freedom the same night, but different dates: Why Pakistan marks its Independence Day on August 14
Gandhi chose peace over celebration
While Delhi celebrated independence, Mahatma Gandhi spent the day in Calcutta, working towards peace.
He stayed at Hyderi Manzil in Beliaghata, where he fasted, prayed and met people who came to see him, as per Gandhi Heritage Portal. He had arrived there to help bring Hindus and Muslims together and worked with former Bengal premier Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy to restore peace.
Calcutta remained largely peaceful on August 15, with Hindus and Muslims joining the celebrations. The episode later became known as the “Miracle of Calcutta.”
PM Modi’s Red Fort address
Over the decades, the Red Fort has become the centre of India's Independence Day. Prime Ministers of the country have used the annual address to look back at India's journey while setting out their priorities for the future.
In recent years, PM Modi's speeches have focused heavily on Viksit Bharat 2047, self-reliance, reforms, technology, youth and national security. His 2025 address lasted 103 minutes, his longest Independence Day speech so far.
This year, India will celebrate its 80th Independence Day. PM Modi will unfurl the national flag and address the nation from the Red Fort. Security has been tightened ahead of Independence Day with a multi-layered anti-terror plan, multiple screening points, mock drills and advance coordination among security agencies.

headline: TV channels can now run more than 12 minutes of ads under new rules
full_text:
TV channels can now run more than 12 minutes of ads under new rules
The advertisement limit was introduced in 2006, when India's television market was much smaller and largely dependent on analogue cable networks.
Television broadcasters will no longer be bound by the 12-minute limit on advertisements after the government moved to change the rules governing ad duration. This will promote fair competition and ease of doing business in the broadcasting sector, the ministry of information and broadcasting said on Friday.
The new rule will start only after the government officially publishes the amended rules in the Gazette, the government’s official record.
TV industry has expanded in the last 20 years
The advertisement limit was introduced in 2006, when India's television market was much smaller and largely dependent on analogue cable networks. There were only 62 TV channels at the time.
ALSO READ | 10 iconic Doordarshan ads from '80s and '90s
The landscape has since expanded sharply, with more than 900 television channels now operating in the country. The complete digitisation of cable television and the expansion of DTH, HITS and IPTV services have also given viewers access to hundreds of channels.
The government said the increased number of platforms and channels has created greater competition and expanded consumer choice.
Digital media changes advertising landscape
This also takes into account the growing importance of digital media, which is not subject to a similar restriction on advertisement duration. According to the ministry, the existing rule put traditional broadcasters at a disadvantage in an increasingly competitive media market.
ALSO READ | 6 funny advertisements of all times that you must watch
The government has therefore decided that the restriction is no longer necessary and has lifted the cap to promote competition and make it easier for television broadcasters to do business.
The government's decision comes months after the Delhi High Court upheld the 12-minute advertising limit. In May, the court dismissed challenges by broadcasters and held that the restrictions were a valid regulatory measure aimed in part at protecting the television viewing experience.
The old rule was actually '10+2'
The earlier framework, commonly referred to as the “10+2” rule, allowed television channels to carry up to 12 minutes of advertising in a clock hour, including 10 minutes of commercial ads and two minutes of self-promotional content.
Why the cap existed
TRAI says the advertising restrictions were introduced partly because excessive advertising was seen as affecting the quality of viewers' experience. The regulator received complaints about long ad breaks, repeated advertisements and interruptions during programmes.
Industry groups had proposed different alternatives before the government opted for complete removal of the ceiling. The Indian Society of Advertisers had suggested a 25% advertising limit, while the Advertising Agencies Association of India favoured a market-led approach. Broadcasters pushed for removal of the statutory ceiling altogether.

headline: Union Ministers on Friday (August 13, 2026) condemned Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s remarks against Prime Minister Narendra Modi and India’s foreign policy, describing them as undignified, undemocratic, and an insult to the country’s international r...
full_text:
Union Ministers on Friday (August 13, 2026) condemned Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s remarks against Prime Minister Narendra Modi and India’s foreign policy, describing them as undignified, undemocratic, and an insult to the country’s international reputation.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said Mr. Gandhi’s comments, made at a Congress event on Thursday (August 13, 2026), were “extremely low-level and condemnable”. He said in his long political life, he had “never seen any Leader of the Opposition” — whether it was Sushma Swaraj, Arun Jaitley, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, L.K. Advani, Manmohan Singh or Sonia Gandhi — “engage in such unseemly conduct”.
Stating that such conduct was a serious warning sign for a healthy democracy in India, he said, “Whatever resentment Rahul Gandhi ji may harbour in his heart toward the Prime Minister, such indecent remarks are utterly unacceptable.”
Mr. Singh further asked if the Congress can claim the legacy of towering personalities such as Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Subhas Chandra Bose, Rajendra Prasad, Lal Bahadur Shastri, Narasimha Rao and Pranab Mukherjee.
The Minister accused Mr. Gandhi of not only insulting the Prime Minister but also disrespecting India’s international reputation, undermining the dignity of democracy, and undermining the position of the Leader of the Opposition. “I cannot even imagine that someone with the word Gandhi attached to their name could give such a shameful statement,” he said.
Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan also expressed anguish. “...while democracy grants everyone the freedom of expression, the violation of decorum is truly distressing. The conduct of the Leader of the Opposition was un-Indian, undignified, and undemocratic — a blatant disregard for all norms of propriety,” he said.
“Does it befit the Congress party to speak in such a manner about the female Prime Minister of an independent and sovereign nation? Do these reflect the true spirit of India? I condemn this in the strongest terms; they must apologise,” said Mr. Chouhan, referring to the remarks of Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit at the same event.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda said it was a “misfortune” for the country to have such a Leader of the Opposition. “What could be more distressing for the Congress itself than having to accept Rahul Gandhi as its leader?” he added.

headline: After Justice Varma’s resignation, LS Speaker asked panel to complete probe, submit report
full_text:
After Justice Varma’s resignation, LS Speaker asked panel to complete probe, submit report
The 126-page report of the committee, headed by SC judge Justice Aravind Kumar, records that on April 29, the joint secretary of the Lok Sabha secretariat wrote to the committee’s secretary
The parliamentary inquiry into allegations against Justice Yashwant Varma did not end with his resignation from the judiciary on April 9. In fact, 20 days after the resignation, the Lok Sabha secretariat conveyed to the three-member inquiry committee that Speaker Om Birla wanted the panel to complete its investigation and submit its report under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
The 126-page report of the committee, headed by Supreme Court judge Justice Aravind Kumar, records that on April 29, the joint secretary of the Lok Sabha secretariat wrote to the committee’s secretary stating that the “Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, had desired” that the Judges (Inquiry) Committee complete its investigation and submit its report in terms of Section 4(2) of the 1968 Act.
The committee then proceeded to finalise its report despite Justice Varma having not only resigned but also withdrawn from the proceedings.
Deep Dive
“The committee accordingly proceeded to prepare the present Report on the basis of available material. It is clarified that the findings recorded herein are founded only upon the material already taken on record in the course of the inquiry, including the statement of defence, additional statement of defence, oral evidence, cross-examination, exhibits, documents and electronic evidence marked during the proceedings,” stated the report.
It also clarified clear that the committee itself had already concluded on April 21 that Justice Varma’s withdrawal could not bring the statutory inquiry to an end. It recorded that by the time he withdrew, the charges had been framed and served, his statements of defence had been received, relied-upon material had been supplied and inspected, interlocutory applications had been heard, nine witnesses had been examined and cross-examined, and documentary and electronic evidence had been marked.
“A statutory inquiry of this nature cannot be made to depend upon unilateral withdrawal after the evidentiary record has substantially come on record,” said the committee, holding that Justice Varma had been afforded the opportunity to cross-examine witnesses, adduce evidence and be heard in defence.
The panel noted that this was not simply a case of a judge staying away from proceedings. Justice Varma had participated through lawyers, challenged the procedure, filed interlocutory applications, inspected records and cross-examined witnesses before withdrawing at the stage when he was required to lead his defence. “At such a stage, withdrawal from participation could not disband the inquiry or efface the evidence already available,” the committee said.
The report also records that Justice Varma had on April 9 communicated his decision to withdraw from further participation after failing to furnish the list of defence witnesses and affidavits within the extended deadline. The committee subsequently discharged the lawyers appearing for him and concluded the proceedings, stating that its report would follow.
It was against this backdrop that the Lok Sabha Secretariat’s communication of April 29 assumed significance. The Speaker’s direction, as recorded by the committee, effectively made clear that the resignation did not bring the statutory inquiry to a close.
The committee thereafter proceeded to prepare its report “on the basis of available material”. It specifically clarified that its findings were based only on material already brought on record during the inquiry, including Justice Varma’s statement of defence and additional statement of defence, oral evidence, cross-examination, exhibits, documents and electronic evidence.
To be sure, Justice Varma had also challenged the initiation of the parliamentary removal process before the Supreme Court. In January 2026, a bench led by Justice Dipankar Datta dismissed his challenge, holding that “constitutional safeguards for judges cannot come at the cost of paralysing the removal process itself”.
The Supreme Court had rejected Justice Varma’s contention that the Lok Sabha Speaker’s decision to constitute the inquiry committee could be stalled because the Rajya Sabha had declined to admit the parallel removal motion or because of the vacancy in the office of the Rajya Sabha chairman. The court held that there was no present or inevitable infraction of any fundamental right warranting interference.
The parliamentary proceedings had their genesis in the controversy over the alleged discovery of burnt currency at Justice Varma’s official residence in Delhi following a fire on the night of March 14, 2025. An in-house committee subsequently found his explanation unsatisfactory, following which then CJI Sanjiv Khanna asked him to resign or face the constitutional process for removal.
Notices seeking his removal were subsequently moved in both Houses on July 21, 2025. While the Lok Sabha Speaker admitted the motion on August 12 and constituted the inquiry committee under the 1968 Act, the Rajya Sabha Deputy chairman declined to admit the parallel motion, holding it defective.
The committee was originally constituted with Justice Aravind Kumar, Justice Maninder Mohan Shrivastava -- then chief justice of the Madras High Court, and senior advocate BV Acharya. Following Justice Shrivastava’s retirement, the panel was reconstituted with Justice Shree Chandrashekhar, then Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court and now a Supreme Court judge.
The committee ultimately went on to record findings that all three articles of charge against Justice Varma were proved, while clarifying that those findings were based on the evidentiary record already created before his withdrawal.
The episode now raises a larger constitutional question: whether Justice Varma’s resignation has brought the removal process to an end, or whether Parliament can still act on the committee’s findings despite his having resigned.

headline: ‘Beijjati hui wo alag’: CJP mocks Bar Council chairman over NALSAR U-turn within hours
full_text:
‘Beijjati hui wo alag’: CJP mocks Bar Council chairman over NALSAR U-turn within hours
The Bar Council of India, in a dramatic U-turn within hours on Thursday, withdrew its order freezing the enrolment of the entire 2026 NALSAR batch.
The Bar Council of India (BCI) on Thursday night withdrew, within hours, its order freezing the enrolment of the entire 2026 graduating batch of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, hours after its initial action triggered a protest threat from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently led a mega youth protest from Delhi's Jantar Mantar against exam irregularities, resulting in the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan
The BCI had on Thursday itself directed all state bar councils not to enroll any student from the batch while it sought details of those allegedly involved in a campaign opposing Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's participation in the university's convocation.
The retreat by BCI came roughly two hours after the order was issued.
Reacting to the issuance of the order, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke hinted at a Jantar Mantar-like agitation again with a post on X, at around 7:25 pm, saying, “What if all legal cockroaches come together?”
BCI chairman Manan Kumar Mishra then, announcing the withdrawal of the order, said in a post on X at around 8:45 on Thursday, “After detailed deliberation, the @barcouncilindia has modified its earlier directions concerning @NALSAR_Official. All 2026 passed-out students of NALSAR will now be entitled to seek enrolment with the State Bar Council of their choice. The factual inquiry will continue, and further action will follow on the basis of the report. No student shall be made to suffer without any fault on his or her part.”
The sequence of events indicates that the BCI's initial order and its withdrawal unfolded within a span of just two hours.
'Beijjati hui wo alag'
Manan Kumar Mishra, in a fresh post after midnight, said the Council had considered representations and reactions from senior advocates, members of the Bar, law students and citizens before concluding that the NALSAR batch "had no role in any disturbance or movement".
"After considering the representations and reactions of Senior Advocates, learned members of the Bar, law students and public spirited citizens, and being satisfied that the 2026 batch of NALSAR, Hyderabad, had no role in any disturbance or movement, the Bar Council of India has decided to close the proceedings altogether. No further action is required," Mishra said.
Mishra wished the students well, while adding that students should voice their opinions "with respect and institutional decorum". He also said that "Dissent is welcome in a democracy; public ridicule of constitutional institutions is often counterproductive."
The CJP, however, mocked BCI and its chairman over the U-turn, suggesting that it made the authorities pull an all-nighter. CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka reacted to Mishra's post, saying, “CJP ne night out padwa diya. Beijjati hui wo alag. [CJP made them pull an all-nighter, on top of it the humiliation]”
Another CJP spokesperson, Saurav Das, argued that the BCI's earlier communication had not been completely withdrawn, pointing to the portion relating to an inquiry and identification of students.
"Mr. Mishra, the order has NOT been fully withdrawn. The part which seeks names of the students and orders for an 'inquiry' against them for their peaceful dissent still stands, as per your own new letter," Das said.
He demanded that the BCI withdraw the communication in full and guarantee that no action would be taken against NALSAR students for their dissent. "No student at NALSAR should face any inquiry or witch hunt for their democratic dissent against the Chief Justice of India," Das said.
Das also said the CJP's call for protests outside the BCI and Mishra's official residence would continue until the demand was met.
In a message to CJP's Dipke and Das on Friday, Manan Kumar Mishra told them the interests of the BCI are the same as theirs, "to protect the rights of the students."
"The Bar Council of India aims to protect the interests of the youth of India. I want to communicate to Abhijeet Dipke and Das (Sourav Das) that our interests are the same as theirs, to protect the rights of the students," Mishra said, speaking to ANI news agency.
What BCI's initial order was about
HT reported earlier that the BCI's initial order had sought an authenticated report identifying those who had initiated, organised, coordinated or mobilised the campaign against the CJI's proposed participation in the convocation. It had also sought details of representations, signatories, meetings, social-media groups and the involvement of faculty members, alumni, student organisations or outsiders.
The initial BCI communication had directed state bar councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 graduates "till further orders". It was subsequently modified, with Mishra saying, "No student shall be made to suffer without any fault on his part."
The controversy began after 70 members of NALSAR's outgoing LLB batch submitted a representation on July 23 opposing CJI Kant's proposed participation as chief guest at the university's convocation. Students from other batches later expressed solidarity with the representation.
The students' objections followed remarks made by the CJI while hearing a plea concerning alleged police excesses during student protests in Delhi. The campaign subsequently drew wider attention, including from the CJP, whose founder Abhijeet Dipke responded to the BCI's initial action by writing on X: "What if all legal cockroaches come together?"
The phrase echoed the language behind the CJP's protest identity, which emerged after the CJI compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches. The movement later gained attention after protests over unemployment and other issues.

headline: A parliamentary panel has flagged the slow rate of digitisation of manuscripts under the flagship Gyan Bharatam Mission launched last year. It has said that the targets set by the mission are attainable only if “force multipliers” such as citizen par...
full_text:
A parliamentary panel has flagged the slow rate of digitisation of manuscripts under the flagship Gyan Bharatam Mission launched last year. It has said that the targets set by the mission are attainable only if “force multipliers” such as citizen participation at national scale and machine assistance are utilised.
Gyan Bharatam is a flagship initiative of the Ministry of Culture aimed at the identification, documentation, conservation, digitisation, preservation, and promotion of India’s vast manuscript heritage. It was formally launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on September 11, 2025, but had been announced earlier that year during the Union Budget 2025-26. The mission mandate is to preserve and establish a dedicated digital platform to share India’s manuscript heritage across the globe, named the National Digital Repository (NDR).
The mission had set a target of digitisation of one crore manuscripts by 2030. However, according to the report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture, tabled in the Rajya Sabha earlier this week, only 7.5 lakh texts have been digitised so far.
“The government has stated the ambition of digitising one crore manuscripts within five years, and the evidence before the Committee recorded a target of 20 lakh by 31 March 2027,” the report titled "From Manuscript to Mission: Preserving, Mapping and Sustaining India’s Cultural Heritage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence” said.
The report further said that while the current pace, computed from the Ministry’s successive official statements, has been around 33,000 manuscripts each month, the target stood at one and a half lakh manuscripts.
“The targets are attainable precisely if, and only if, force multipliers are brought to bear... Citizen participation at national scale, capture standards that avoid rework, and machine assistance directed at the narrowest bottlenecks are those multipliers,” it said.
The committee has also noted the 17-fold increase in the cost of the process. The financial commitment to the Mission has risen from the ₹3.50 crore sanctioned in 2024-25 to ₹15 crore in 2025-26 and ₹60 crore in 2026-27, within a sanctioned outlay of ₹491.66 crore for 2025-2031, it said.
The committee has recommended that the Mission spend the expenditure already provided instead of seeking fresh funding.

headline: Torrential rain floods Bijnor in Uttar Pradesh, roads submerged, bikes stranded
full_text:
Torrential rain floods Bijnor in Uttar Pradesh, roads submerged, bikes stranded
A much-needed spell of rain quickly turned into trouble for villagers, with flooded roads making everyday travel difficult across Bijnor's rural areas.
Torrential rain in Uttar Pradesh's Bijnor district on Friday submerged several rural roads, leaving vehicles stranded and disrupting daily life in many villages. The downpour brought relief from the intense heat and humidity that had gripped the area for the past two days, but widespread waterlogging quickly became a major concern for residents.
A video from Faridpur Maan village in the Pamdawali area shows roads submerged under water after hours of continuous rainfall.
Muddy water covered the roads, with water levels reaching nearly knee-deep in several places.
Motorists could be seen struggling to push stalled two-wheelers through the submerged roads, while villagers drove cautiously through flooded lanes. Rainwater also surrounded nearby houses and pathways.
According to local residents, the situation worsened as rainwater continued to accumulate because of inadequate drainage in the area.
Movement became difficult for commuters, schoolchildren and villagers trying to carry out routine activities. Several bikers reportedly found their vehicles breaking down while attempting to cross the flooded stretches and had to seek help from others to pull their motorcycles out.
Residents said such flooding occurs repeatedly during heavy rain. They said the lack of proper drains allows water to remain stagnant for long periods, affecting transportation and increasing the risk of damage to homes and roads.
While the rainfall brought a noticeable drop in temperature and offered temporary relief from the heat, the respite was offset by the disruption caused by waterlogging.
Villagers said the accumulation of water around homes and access roads had severely affected normal movement and raised concerns about sanitation and public health if the water remains stagnant.
Residents are demanding immediate measures to improve drainage and prevent prolonged waterlogging. Local authorities are expected to assess the affected areas and consider remedial steps if heavy rainfall continues.

headline: Jaisalmer man abducted, brutally assaulted, nose cut off: Police
full_text:
Jaisalmer man abducted, brutally assaulted, nose cut off: Police
The attackers allegedly broke his hands and legs and cut off his nose with a sharp-edged weapon before fleeing after villagers chased them
A 27-year-old man was allegedly abducted at gunpoint and brutally assaulted by a group of men while he was returning home with three children in his camper vehicle in Jaisalmer district on Thursday evening, police said.
The attackers allegedly broke his hands and legs and cut off his nose with a sharp-edged weapon before fleeing after villagers chased them.
Sankra SHO Ran Singh Sodha while confirming the development said that the incident took place around 7pm near the Rajgarh-Khelana border area.
“Rajgarh resident Jamal Khan, son of Farid Khan, was returning home from Bhainsda with three children when two vehicles followed him and forced him to stop.
The accused allegedly took him into their vehicle at gunpoint and abducted him,” the SHO said.
Also Read: Zirakpur: 16-year-old girl on way to school abducted, gangraped
According to SHO Sodha, the accused took Jamal to an isolated location towards the Rajgarh-Khelana border and allegedly attacked him with sticks and sharp-edged weapons. “The assault was severe. His hands and legs were broken and his nose was cut with a sharp-edged weapon,” he said.
The incident came to light when some villagers passing through the area heard cries for help. Suspecting something was wrong, they followed the attackers’ vehicles. Police said the accused, fearing that they were being surrounded, allegedly dumped Jamal in an injured condition by the roadside and fled.
Villagers informed the police and took the injured man to Sankra hospital. After receiving preliminary treatment, Jamal was referred to Pokaran due to the seriousness of his injuries. Doctors at Pokaran subsequently referred him to Jodhpur for further treatment.
SHO Sodha said a case has been registered against six to seven people from Jamal’s own village, Rajgarh, based on his statement.
“The preliminary investigation suggests that the incident may be linked to an old rivalry. Police teams are conducting raids at possible locations to arrest the accused. Further investigation is underway,” he said.

headline: Bullet hits SUV parked outside ex-Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Raghbir Singh's Amritsar home, probe on
full_text:
Bullet hits SUV parked outside ex-Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Raghbir Singh's Amritsar home, probe on
Giani Raghbir Singh said the incident appeared to have occurred late at night on August 12.
A bullet hit the bonnet of a Punjab Police SUV parked outside the residence of former Akal Takht jathedar Giani Raghbir Singh in Amritsar's Pratap Nagar, though the initial probe has ruled out any attack, said police officials on Friday.
The incident came to light on the day when Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president and former Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked at Takht Hazur Sahib in Nanded, Maharashtra, on Thursday.
Giani Raghbir Singh said the incident appeared to have occurred late at night on August 12. However, the family came to know about it only around 5 pm on August 13 when the driver was cleaning the vehicle and noticed the bullet mark. During the examination, police recovered a .32-bore bullet from the vehicle.
Deep Dive
Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP-East) Rainder Singh said, “As far initial investigation of the bullet mark, a portion of the bullet hit the bonnet at 90 degrees. This reflects that nobody hit it horizontally.
The former Jathedar said the sound of the bullet hitting the vehicle was also captured on CCTV cameras installed near the house. The footage purportedly shows a youth arriving near the house on a scooter and later speaking on the phone at a nearby chowk. His identity and motive are yet to be ascertained.
“Some bike riders were also spotted in the CCTV footage, who are seen roaming at that time. We are questioning them, but so far we have got no vital clue”, said the police official.
Police also seized an empty cartridge from the spot. Investigators are examining whether the firing was targeted or the result of an aerial shot.
The former Jathedar said he had not received any direct threat or threatening phone call. However, he recalled that there had been instances in the past when attempts were allegedly made to hit his vehicle from the side or push it into a ditch. He said such incidents had not been taken seriously at the time.
He urged police to treat the latest incident seriously, pointing out that a stray bullet could have hit a passerby or caused a fatality.
An FIR was registered in this connection against unknown persons, and an investigation is going on.
After retirement, Giani Raghbir Singh is staying at his personal residence. The Punjab Police have not withdrawn his security cover after his retirement.
In December 2, 2024 decree, Giani Raghbir Singh-led Sikh clergy pronounced 'tankhah' (religious punishment) on Sukhbir Singh Badal, directing the working committee of the Shiromani Akali Dal to accept his resignation as party chief in three days, besides forming a panel to hold elections for the post of SAD president and office-bearers within six months, in a decision that can potentially have far-reaching ramifications for the Sikh religio-politics. Pronouncing the religious punishment for the "mistakes" committed by the SAD and its government in Punjab from 2007 to 2017, the Sikh clergy announced to withdraw the title of ‘Panth Rattan Fakhr-e-Qaum’ bestowed upon former chief minister late Parkash Singh Badal.
On February 26, the SGPC also removed Giani Raghbir Singh from the post of head granthi of Sachkhand Harmandar Sahib (Golden Temple), a day after he made the allegations during a press conference in Jalandhar on February 18, accusing the Badal family of “grievously hurting” Sikh religious sentiments for political gains and calling for a Sarbat Khalsa to “liberate” the SGPC from “clutches of Badals”.
Giani Raghbir Singh's move came at a time when he was seen as on good terms with the AAP government. Despite Akal Takht taking a tough stand against the recently enacted anti-sacrilege law, Giani Raghbir Singh supported it. He was also seen sharing bonhomie with the AAP leaders.

headline: Parl clears bill to curb states’ tax on minerals; Soren warns of stir
full_text:
Parl clears bill to curb states’ tax on minerals; Soren warns of stir
Parliament passed the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill, limiting state mineral taxes, sparking warnings of agitation from Jharkhand’s chief minister.
New Delhi/Ranchi/Thiruvananthapuram: Parliament on Thursday passed the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, that seeks to curb taxation of minerals by state governments, prompting a warning of a “massive agitation” by the chief minister of mineral-rich Jharkhand.
The bill, which amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, cleared Rajya Sabha after a truncated debate on the last day of the Monsoon session on Thursday, with Opposition MPs saying it infringes on states’ rights and curbs their fiscal autonomy. It was passed by the Lok Sabha, where it saw little debate , a day earlier. It will become law after receiving the President’s assent.
Responding to the debate in the Rajya Sabha, Union Mines Minister G Kishan Reddy said that the legislation standardizes national mineral rates without infringing on state autonomy or revenues. Under the bill, the Centre will regulate major minerals (coal, limestone, iron ore, copper, manganese), while states will retain control over 49 minor minerals, he said.
“Unbalanced imposition of steep taxes and levies will prompt the industry to completely bypass local supply lines, leading to sub-optimal development of markets, increased transportation costs and the resultant pollution load,” says the statement of objects and reasons of the bill.
The bill was passed via voice vote after the House rejected an amendment by DMK’s Tiruchi Siva to refer it to a select committee. Chairman C P Radhakrishnan declined requests for a division of votes, saying it could not be taken up due the din caused by Opposition MPs protesting police action against students at Jantar Mantar and alleged Ram Temple donation thefts.
The amendment bill introduces a new section that says that “no tax, cess or such other levy (by whatever name called) shall be imposed by the state Government on mineral rights; or mineral bearing lands, either based on mineral quantity or mineral value or royalty payable…except in accordance with such conditions or restrictions as may be prescribed by the Central Government..”
The bill also proposes to expand the central government’s powers to regulate mines to mineral bearing lands having ore content in accordance with the parameters prescribed under the MMDR Act.
The proposed amendments are the fallout of a July 2024 ruling by the Supreme Court that upheld the power of states to levy taxes on mineral rights and and mineral-bearing lands. The verdict was hailed as a major fiscal victory for mineral-rich states such as Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan, potentially yielding a revenue windfall, but it deeply unsettled mining companies facing retrospective taxation.
The new section in the bill invalidates state levies that are uncollected or undeposited as of the amendment Act coming into force. Levies already deposited or collected would be not liable for refunds.
Hemant Soren, the chief minister of Jharkhand, which holds nearly 40% of India’s mineral reserves, said the amendment bill undermines the state’s rights over its mineral resources and entitlements. “The Centre passed it in haste, tying Jharkhand’s hands and feet. Jharkhand will launch such a massive agitation to oppose it that the entire nation would see,” Soren said in a post on X. Soren pointed out that the amendment bill will curb fiscal space for social welfare schemes, saying Jharkhand will have to stop all its programmes providing social security to millions.Soren said he has written to the President against the bill.
A week after the Supreme Court ruling, the Jharkhand assembly passed a bill which provided for varying degrees of tax on different minerals mined in the state on a per-metric-tonne basis. The Act was further amended in the 2025 budget session to increase the cess on mined minerals in the state by up to four times. Officials said the state government projected revenue of ₹14,656 crore from the Mineral Bearing Land Cess in the 2026-27 budget and had earmarked these funds for welfare schemes.
Kerala chief minister V.D. Satheesan said the amendment bill effectively transfers states’ rights and authority over land under Schedule 18 of the State List of the Constitution to the jurisdiction of the Union government, which was against federal principles.The legislation, by defining land as mineral-bearing, does not even exclude forests and coastal areas, he said.
In the debate in the Rajya Sabha, the mines minister cited Entry 54 of the Union List, which empowers Parliament to regulate mines and mineral development in public interest, and said taxation was an important tool for regulating and developing the sector. He said the Centre receives only about 11 per cent of mineral revenue, with 88 per cent going to states, and asserted that no state would suffer any revenue loss because of the amendments.
Biju Janata Dal (BJD) MP Manas Mangaraj while opposing the bill during the debate, said it raises concerns over states’ rights, fiscal autonomy and the interests of mining-affected communities. He said for a state like Odisha – which accounts for the largest share of India’s mineral output--revenue from mineral resources was crucial for funding healthcare, education, roads, rehabilitation and environmental restoration.
Congress MP Sasikanth Senthil, representing Tiruvallur in Tamil Nadu, who had on Monday written to the Lok Sabha speaker calling for the bill to be referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Coal, Mines and Steel for a detailed scrutiny, slammed the way the bill was passed.
“I had written to the Hon’ble Speaker at the time of introduction of the Mines & Minerals Amendment Bill, 2026, urging its referral to the DRSC for detailed scrutiny. Instead, the Bill was rushed through Parliament with barely any meaningful debate. If Standing Committees, parliamentary scrutiny and debate can simply be bypassed, what exactly is Parliament being reduced to a rubber stamp?,” Senthil said on X.

TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 14, 2026, 16:00 IST

CM Yogi Adityanath said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power.
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath has accused the Congress of being responsible for India's Partition and the violence that followed, arguing that the country's history could have been different under leaders such as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel or Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Speaking at an event in Lucknow marking Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, CM Yogi said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power and alleged that the consequences of Partition continue to affect India.âHad Narendra Modi been the Prime Minister of India at the time of Independence, nobody would have been able to damage India in the slightest,â he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.He also invoked Patel, saying that a leader of his stature would not have allowed India to be divided.âIf a person like Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were the Prime Minister at that time, nobody would have been able to disintegrate India ... The country had to pay a heavy price for the cowardice of these Congress members -- a character you all witnessed during the CAA protests,â he added.Adityanath alleged that areas including Sindh, Punjab and Bengal were handed over to Pakistan despite what he described as their Hindu and regional demographic character.
âBengal was Bengali-dominated. All Hindu villages were forcibly given to Bangladesh. This shameful act was committed by the Congress, which was extra-restless for power, and on whom the country had reposed its trust. It repaid that trust with betrayal,â he said.The chief minister also criticised the Congress over its response to attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh. He alleged that the party remained silent because it was concerned about losing electoral support.âThey feared that reacting to the events in Bangladesh might cause their vote bank here to drift away. To them, the murder of Dalit Hindus holds no significance; what matters is their own vote bank,â he said.Adityanath further argued that internal divisions based on caste, region and language had historically weakened India and created opportunities for outside forces.âWhen such infighting exists, then conspiracy easily creeps in,â he said.He said the consequences of Partition could still be seen in the form of terrorism, Naxalism, Maoism and extremism. He also questioned the Congress's claims about its role in India's freedom struggle and accused the party of presenting itself as indispensable to the creation of modern India.âThis also draws our attention to the silence we have all maintained regarding that pre-1947 conspiracy. Yet, even today, these people move before society, acting as if they were the ones who created India, and that without them, India would not have come into existence. It is a truly strange situation,â he said, describing Partition as the âdarkest chapter of humanity.âTurning to what he described as the Congress's political legacy, Adityanath said institutions across the country had been named after one political family.âEvery institution in the country came to bear the name of that very clan. Every single institution was named after that clan, and we all stood by silently, merely watching. What are they doing even today? What are their actions like now?â he said.The UP chief minister also defended the Citizenship Amendment Act and attacked the Congress's opposition to it.âThere was no justification for opposing the act. The act contained a provision regarding Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Bangladesh -- territories that were once part of undivided India and share a heritage spanning thousands of years. It stipulated that if a Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist, Parsi, or Christian from these countries had been forced to leave and had sought refuge in India for five years, they would be granted Indian citizenship,â he said.He argued that the legislation did not provide for taking away land or property from Muslims or political parties, and accused opponents of using the issue to provoke protests.âNowhere did it say that we would seize land belonging to Muslims, the Congress, or the Samajwadi Party. There was no such provision in the Act. Yet, attempts were made to incite agitation across the country,â he said.
Adityanath also targeted the Samajwadi Party, claiming that Uttar Pradesh would have witnessed widespread unrest had it been in power during the CAA protests.âWhat kind of unbridled mayhem would have taken place? The rioters knew the price they would have to pay, which is why they could not act as they pleased; yet, their audacity was evident,â he said.âIf you wish to see their true character, you would have witnessed it during the CAA protests, and their silence regarding the recent events in Bangladesh once again puts them in the dock,â Adityanath said.The event also featured a silent march led by Adityanath and other party leaders from the statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel to Lok Bhavan, according to the Uttar Pradesh government.

headline: Bhutanese king expresses solidarity with Assam flood victims; Himanta thanks him for support
full_text:
Bhutanese king expresses solidarity with Assam flood victims; Himanta thanks him for support
Guwahati, The king of Bhutan, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuk, expressed solidarity with the people of adjoining Assam, which faced a devastating flood that claimed the lives of 103 people so far.
The monarch of the Himalayan kingdom also highlighted the shared vulnerability of the region to the consequences of global climate change and the need to confront it in the times to come.
Thanking the neighbouring nation for its support, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma affirmed the historical ties of Assam and Bhutan.
"The people of Bhutan join me in conveying our heartfelt condolences to Your Excellency and the people of Assam, in particular those who have lost their families and homes in the recent floods. We offer our prayers in memory of the deceased," he said in a letter addressed to Sarma, which was shared with the media on Friday.
The king noted that the "increasing frequency and severity of such disasters across our region is a stark reminder of our shared vulnerability to the consequences of a changing global climate challenges that we face together, and must continue to confront in the times ahead".
"Despite the great loss and damage, Your Excellency's strength and resolve in leading the state's response in this time of crisis is admirable," he added, in the letter dated August 3.
The king said Bhutan stands in full solidarity with the people of Assam and extended its wholehearted support and friendship as the state works to rebuild and recover.
Sarma, expressing his gratitude for the solidarity, said in a social media post, "Deeply touched by the warm words and message of support from His Majesty, The King of Bhutan, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, as Assam recovers from the recent floods."
He highlighted the "relationship of exceptional warmth" shared by Assam and Bhutan, "connected by history, nurtured by geography and strengthened by generations of friendship between our people".
"On behalf of the people of Assam, I convey my heartfelt gratitude to His Majesty and the people of Bhutan for standing with us in solidarity and friendship in this difficult hour," the chief minister added.

headline: Union minister JP Nadda undergoes angiography at AIIMS after uneasiness
full_text:
Union minister JP Nadda undergoes angiography at AIIMS after uneasiness
JP Nadda underwent several tests, including a coronary angiography, and is currently stable, the hospital said.
Union minister JP Nadda underwent a coronary angiography at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Delhi, after experiencing uneasiness on Thursday evening, the hospital said in a statement.
Nadda, who is also the Union health and family welfare minister, was evaluated and underwent several tests, including a coronary angiography, on August 13, a statement from AIIMS said, reported news agency ANI.
“Shri JP Nadda, Hon’ble Minister of Health and Family Welfare was evaluated for uneasiness with tests including a coronary angiography on the evening of 13th August 2026. He is currently stable and admitted for observation in the Dept of Cardiology,” the AIIMS statement said.
The minister is currently stable and has been admitted to the Department of Cardiology at AIIMS for observation, the hospital added.
Nadda's hospitalisation came hours after the Monsoon Session of Parliament concluded on Thursday. The final day of the session saw a heated exchange between the Opposition and Nadda, who is the Leader of the House in the Rajya Sabha.
Nadda's response on ‘purification row’
During the proceedings, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge raised the alleged “purification” of a stage at Haldwani’s Ram Lila Maidan, where he had addressed a gathering. Kharge alleged that some BJP workers conducted a havan and “shuddikaran” at the venue after his event.

Three tourists were killed and 19 others, including a 10-month-old infant, were injured after a tempo traveller carrying 22 people plunged into a deep gorge on the Bhowali-Mukteshwar road in Uttarakhand’s Nainital district on Friday afternoon, officials said.

Personnel from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), local police, revenue department and district administration, along with local residents, reached the spot and began evacuating the victims.
Emergency ambulances were deployed to transport the injured to Sushila Tiwari Government Hospital in Haldwani, where medical teams were placed on alert to provide trauma care.
The deceased have been identified as Pradeep (26) and Sumit (25), both residents of Faridabad, and Abhishek, whose details were not immediately available.

headline: ‘Genuine efforts’: Supreme Court drops criminal cases against Samay Raina, 4 comedians
full_text:
‘Genuine efforts’: Supreme Court drops criminal cases against Samay Raina, 4 comedians
The court kept the broader issue arising from the case alive, saying it would issue directions on ensuring greater sensitivity and safeguards in online content
The Supreme Court on Friday quashed criminal proceedings against comedian Samay Raina and four other comedians over insensitive remarks concerning persons with disabilities on the show “India’s Got Latent”, appreciating their subsequent efforts to organise events and raise awareness and funds for people suffering from spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
“Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there. They are very bright youngsters. If they have started working in positive direction, there will be positive output,” a bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, closing the proceedings against Samay Raina, Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar alias Sonali Aditya Desai and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar.
The court, however, kept the broader issue arising from the case alive, saying it would consider suggestions from persons with disabilities and issue appropriate directions on ensuring greater sensitivity and safeguards in online content.
The court recorded that the five respondents organised a chess tournament for persons with disabilities from March 14 to 16 this year, which received widespread media coverage and generated awareness about organisations working for persons with disabilities, including SMA. The event also involved donations to organisations working for the cause.
Four further shows had been planned for fundraising, but could not be organised with the participation of persons with disabilities because of logistical difficulties. The respondents have now expressed their willingness to invite persons suffering from SMA and provide financial support, the court noted.
The bench also appreciated the “constructive conversation” that had taken place between the comedians and the Cure SMA Foundation, which had approached the court over the content concerning persons with disabilities.
The respondents and the NGO had discussed the structure and material for programmes aimed at celebrating the lives of SMA warriors. The respondents had expressed gratitude for the foundation’s guidance and were in the process of obtaining consent from SMA warriors for their participation, the court noted.
“We have no doubt that respondents 6 to 10 will work hard in their endeavour to organise events for celebrating the lives and increasing dignity of SMA warriors,” the bench said.
The court accordingly ordered: “Matter qua respondents 6-10 is closed. Criminal proceedings against respondents 6-10 are hereby quashed. All other related proceedings are set aside.”
The development marks a significant development from the court’s criticism of Raina and the other comedians last month, when it had imposed a cost of ₹3 lakh each for failing to comply with an undertaking given to the court.
On July 13, the bench noted that Raina had taken the court “for a ride” after he failed to comply with an undertaking to make amends for the depiction of persons suffering from SMA on online shows.
“If this is not arrogance, then we may have to change the definition of this term in the Oxford Dictionary,” the bench had said.
The court had earlier directed the five comedians to show remorse and engage with members of the SMA Cure Foundation, including by featuring them on their shows to raise funds and awareness about the condition.
They initially told the court that they had been unable to contact members of the foundation and had instead organised programmes involving other specially abled persons. The explanation had not satisfied the court at the time, prompting it to impose the costs and warn of coercive action if the amount was not deposited.
On Friday, however, senior advocate Aparajita Singh, appearing for the foundation, told the bench that there had since been genuine efforts to engage with the respondents and that discussions were underway on the proposed programmes. “Our main prayer was for the guidelines,” said Singh, adding that the foundation remained receptive to further suggestions and the process was “a work in progress”.
The bench then said that the court was confident that genuine efforts would produce positive results. The court also explained why it was keeping the larger issue open despite closing the criminal proceedings against the five comedians.
The CJI said that he had interacted with several persons with disabilities on Thursday and that the interaction had been “quite a learning and eye opener”.
“Sometimes we feel that we have a fair bit of information but that is not the truth. There are many things that we learn when we meet them and the challenges which they face,” he added.
The court asked persons with disabilities and the NGO to submit their suggestions on measures that could address the broader concerns arising from online content. “You are also going to give us a lot of recommendations. We will wait for that also and then some comprehensive directions can be issued,” it said.
The proceedings had arisen in the larger controversy surrounding the online show “India’s Got Latent”, which had earlier led the Supreme Court to examine the need for safeguards governing online content, and the balance between freedom of speech and the right of individuals and sections of society to live with dignity.
The court had previously asked Attorney General R Venkataramani to assist it on the broader question of framing guidelines to ensure that freedom of speech and expression does not infringe the right of others to live with dignity.

headline: Madhya Pradesh schoolgirls protest higher bus fares, operators restore old rates
full_text:
Madhya Pradesh schoolgirls protest higher bus fares, operators restore old rates
Schoolgirls in Madhya Pradesh's Vidisha district have forced private bus operators to roll back a fare hike after protesting that the increased cost was putting an additional financial burden on their families.
Private bus operators in Madhya Pradesh's Vidisha district have rolled back a fare hike for schoolgirls after students from nearby rural areas protested against the increased fares for travelling to Sironj for school.
The decision followed a meeting involving Sironj Sub-Divisional Magistrate Om Narayan Badkul, the SDOP, tehsildar, police station in-charge and private bus operators.
The rollback came two days after students of Kanya Higher Secondary School in Sironj staged a protest at the local bus stand against the fare increase. The students said the hike was putting an additional financial burden on their families and could affect their regular attendance at school.
On August 12, the students gathered at the bus stand and raised slogans for about 30 minutes, demanding that the earlier fares be restored. They said fares on their routes had earlier ranged between Rs 10 and Rs 15 before being increased. Some reports said the fare for school students had been proposed to increase from Rs 10 to Rs 25.
 
During the protest, the students appealed to local representatives, including Sironj MLA Umakant Sharma, to intervene. They said affordable transport was essential for students travelling from rural areas to attend school in Sironj.
SDM Badkul reached the spot along with the SDOP and the local police station in-charge and spoke to the students. He assured them that the administration would discuss the issue with private bus operators and try to restore the earlier fare. The students then called off their protest.
The administration later held discussions with the bus operators. After the meeting, it was decided that schoolgirls travelling to and from school would be charged the old fare instead of the increased amount.
Students and their families welcomed the rollback, saying it would ease the financial burden on those travelling from villages to Sironj for school.

headline: ‘India can hit hard’: Doval recalls Op Sindoor, says our generosity, tolerance should not be seen as weakness

‘India can hit hard’: Doval recalls Op Sindoor, says our generosity, tolerance should not be seen as weakness
Speaking in the upcoming Discovery docuseries "Declassified: Operation Sindoor", Doval said the objective of the military operation was to destroy enemy camps.
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval has said India's generosity and tolerance should not be mistaken for weakness, asserting that the country is capable of taking risks and "hit[ting] hard" irrespective of the consequences.
Speaking in the upcoming Discovery docuseries "Declassified: Operation Sindoor", Doval said the objective of the 88-hour military operation was to destroy enemy camps, particularly those linked to the Pahalgam terror attack, according to a PTI report.
"We had decided the objective of the operation as destruction of the enemy camps particularly those who had been responsible for the Pahalgam attack," Doval said in his first interview since Operation Sindoor.

'India can hit hard': Doval
"Message to the world is very clear - India's generosity or India being tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness. India can take risks, India can hit hard, irrespective of the consequences," he added.
The two-part docuseries brings together India's military and national security leadership to recount the decisions and events surrounding Operation Sindoor, Discovery said in a statement. It features first-hand accounts from those who oversaw India's response to the conflict.
In the show, Doval offers an account of the decision-making process and the resolve behind India's military response, the broadcaster said.

What was Operation Sindoor?
Operation Sindoor was launched early on May 7 last year in response to the deadly April 22 Pahalgam terror attack. Indian forces conducted precision strikes on multiple terror infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).
Pakistan subsequently launched offensives against India, following which India carried out a series of counter-offensives, with the military actions taking place under Operation Sindoor.
The military conflict between the two nuclear-armed neighbours lasted nearly 88 hours before India and Pakistan reached an understanding on the evening of May 10, bringing the hostilities to a halt.

headline: Relief for Rahul Gandhi, SC quashes criminal defamation complaint in Savarkar remarks row
full_text:
Relief for Rahul Gandhi, SC quashes criminal defamation complaint in Savarkar remarks row
Prior sanction from the Centre or the state is mandatory to prosecute a person under Section 153A of the IPC, which penalises promoting enmity between groups.
The Supreme Court on Friday quashed the criminal proceedings against Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi over his remarks describing Hindutva ideologue Vinayak Damodar Savarkar as a collaborator of the British, noting that the prosecution lacked the sanction required under law.
A bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu allowed Gandhi’s plea challenging the summons issued by a Lucknow magistrate, after noting that the Uttar Pradesh government’s affidavit did not disclose that the requisite sanction had been granted for prosecuting him.
“Sanction is required. But there is no sanction. If there is no sanction, there is no case. You have to follow the law,” the bench said.
“We have heard learned counsel for parties. In affidavit filed by respondent State of UP, there is no disclosure of sanction having been granted. In such view of matter, orders passed by Magistrate shall be quashed,” held the bench.
The row over Gandhi's remarks
The decision brings to an end the criminal proceedings arising from remarks made by Gandhi during his Bharat Jodo Yatra in November 2022, in which he had referred to Savarkar as a “servant” or collaborator of the British and said that he had received a pension from the colonial government.
Gandhi was facing proceedings under Sections 153A (promoting enmity) and 505 (public mischief) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) on a complaint filed by advocate Nripendra Pandey.
Prior sanction from the central government or the state is mandatory to prosecute a person under Section 153A of the IPC, which penalises promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, or language.
The proceedings had reached the Supreme Court after a prolonged legal battle in Uttar Pradesh. Pandey had initially approached the additional chief judicial magistrate (ACJM) seeking registration of an FIR against Gandhi over his remarks. The ACJM dismissed the complaint in June 2023, but the complainant challenged the decision before the sessions court, which remanded the matter to the magistrate.
The Lucknow magistrate subsequently summoned Gandhi in December 2024, holding that his remarks had prima facie spread hatred and ill-will in society. Gandhi then approached the Allahabad High Court seeking quashing of the proceedings.
On April 4, 2025, the high court declined to entertain his plea, holding that Gandhi had an alternative statutory remedy of approaching the sessions court in revision against the summoning order. This prompted Gandhi to move the Supreme Court.
The top court had initially stayed the trial proceedings in April 2025. During the proceedings, however, the bench had taken strong exception to Gandhi’s remarks against Savarkar and cautioned him against making further statements concerning freedom fighters.
“You have a good point on law and you will get a stay. But any further statement by him will be taken up suo motu. No words on our freedom fighters. They gave us freedom and we treat them like this?” the court had said.
A mention of former PM Indira Gandhi's letter
The bench had also referred to a letter written by Gandhi’s grandmother and former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi praising Savarkar and reminded Gandhi of the historical context surrounding the freedom fighter.
The Supreme Court subsequently continued the interim protection while seeking responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and the complainant.
In July 2025, the bench had extended the stay after the Uttar Pradesh government opposed Gandhi’s plea, alleging that he had deliberately spread hatred by describing Savarkar as a British “servant”. The State had argued that the allegations, supported by investigation, brought Gandhi’s conduct within the ambit of Sections 153A and 505 IPC.
Gandhi’s counsel, however, continued to challenge the very maintainability of the criminal proceedings and the ingredients of the offences alleged against him.
