headline: Not backing down: Mahua Moitra defies eviction call amid 'Jai Shree Ram' chants
full_text:
Not backing down: Mahua Moitra defies eviction call amid 'Jai Shree Ram' chants
Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra alleged she was ordered to vacate Krishnanagar Circuit House late Friday night, claiming a crowd outside shouted "Jai Shree Ram". She said the administration repeatedly asked her to leave despite being a sitting MP.
Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra has alleged that the local administration ordered her to vacate her room at the Krishnanagar Circuit House late Friday night, as she claimed a large crowd outside was shouting “Jai Shree Ram”.
Moitra said she received a call from the Additional District Magistrate at around 9:47 pm asking her to vacate the room. She said she had entered the Circuit House at around 6:30 pm and was allotted the same room she usually stays in.
According to Moitra, dinner was served to her in the room at around 9:20 pm, shortly before the administration contacted her. She later said she received a message containing what she described as an “order” to vacate the room at around 10:52 pm.
“I am elected MP till 2029. Lok Sabha ended yesterday & I am staying night in Circuit House Krishnanagar, official accommodation for all MPs,” Moitra posted on X.
In another post, she said the administration had asked her to leave despite her being a sitting MP staying in her own constituency.
“I, as sitting woman MP, staying night in circuit house in my own constituency received call at 9:47 pm from Additional District Magistrate asking me to vacate my room! Imagine the audacity!” she wrote.
Moitra also alleged that the administration was “desperate to keep us out of area” and said she had refused to leave.
“Just received call from local administration asking me to vacate & leave! Told them NO WAY!” she said.
The TMC MP later claimed that a large crowd had gathered outside the Circuit House gates and was shouting “Jai Shree Ram”.
“Outside the gates are huge crowd shouting Jai Shree Ram!” she wrote.
In a subsequent post, Moitra said the crowd was shouting the slogan while the district administration continued to call and message her repeatedly to vacate the room.
“Supreme Court asked me to face bullets so here I am not backing down,” she wrote.
The allegations came a day after Parliament's Monsoon Session ended. Moitra linked the late-night order to her presence in her constituency and suggested that the administration was seeking to prevent Opposition MPs and leaders from staying in the area.

headline: Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Ya...
full_text:
Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Yale's Vice Provost for International Affairs.He has received the 2016 Infosys Prize in Humanities, a 2017 MacArthur Fellowship, and the 2025 Toynbee Prize in Global History, among others. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'.Excerpts from the interview.Q: Why did you feel this book needed to be written?A: It was a coming together of my academic life and the rest of my life. For close to 20 years, I had been researching some of the themes that do make it into 'The Burning Earth'. I've particularly been interested in the relationship between migration, the movement of people and environmental change. So I wrote a book more than 10 years ago called 'Crossing the Bay of Bengal', which I think was my first foray into environmental history, in which I was really thinking about the enormous movement of people, particularly from Tamil Nadu, to southeast Asia in the 19th and 20th century, many of them to work on rubber plantations, but also to work in port cities, places like Singapore and Penang and Rangoon, and understanding that that was actually a moment of fundamental transformation in the environment.
.. At the same time, as a teacher, but also as a parent, as a citizen, the climate crisis became quite unavoidable in my own consciousness. And so for me, that prompted me to scale things up beyond my areas of specialisation towards perhaps the biggest question, which is how did we get to this point of planetary crisis? And that's really what's at the heart of 'The Burning Earth'.Q: You also bring in a kind of storytelling which positions itself in different geographies as if to say, the inherited narratives of Eurocentric histories are not what we're going to look at. A: If the question is what is it about my own perspective that may make this book a little bit different from some of the other books out there on this big theme of the environment, it is the fact that my own training is not in European and North American history. And I think most of what is called global history continues to take as its starting point and as its default, a kind of familiar North Atlantic history. And so by starting the book in China and ending it in Indonesia, I was really trying to write it anchored in Asia... Asia has always been home to the majority of humanity. It still is today. And so it seemed to me completely fitting to really think about the history of this planet with a firm anchor in the part of the world, the part of the planet which has been the most inhabited by most people throughout the longest period of time.Q: How do you bring in a methodology which ensures that what you're positioning and presenting can be as accurate as possible? A: That's the biggest challenge of a book like this. There's no possibility that I can have the primary expertise in all of these areas that I write about in the book. And so in some ways that was a leap that I took. Academia is a collective enterprise. And this is very much a book that builds on my own work in some areas. And in other areas, it's really sort of bringing together my reading in multiple fields of scholarship and different disciplines as well. So I'm a historian, but some of the most exciting new scholarship which I draw on and interpret is actually coming from the physical sciences.There's some phenomenally interesting work in paleoclimatology, for example, which is trying to reconstruct past climates using ice cores, using lake bed sediment, using tree rings. And of course, these disciplines traditionally and even still within the walls of the university barely meet. But what's been very interesting about recent work on climate and environment in particular, is you have this forcing together of completely different ideas of what the archive is.Q: You use the word 'elite' a few times when you're talking about social stratification for a very specific economic growth touted as well-being of a community, but usually you see it as exploitative. A: I don't use the word that many times, but when I do, I think it's doing a lot of work for me. 'The Burning Earth' is not an activist book, which is to say that it is just that bit muddier and less clear about the villains of the piece than activist writing necessarily has to be. And yet there is such a strong core in my own thinking of awareness of just how stark environmental inequalities are and just how much the scale of planetary destruction that has been achieved over the last two centuries has been disproportionately, not exclusively, but disproportionately driven by the elite pursuit of luxuries and of accumulation... There is a story of human need in this book and there's also a story of human greed... I think we need to think about desire, we need to think about states, we need to think about liberation, we need to think about the genuinely liberatory promises that led to some of this environmental destruction which can't be reduced to a question of greed or even of capitalism...There's no question that the social and economic system that has been a driving force in the climate crisis is the capitalist system. But the socialist system in some sense was even more environmentally profligate and wasteful. It was just less successful. And so in terms of its longevity, in terms of the scale on which it was operating, it kind of doesn't compare with what a particular capitalist mode of production does to our ability to treat all of nature as commodity and to lead to this kind of constantly expanding frontier of production.
But my question is really a different one, which is, where were the alternatives? Who was thinking differently?Q: You point out that there are these rather horrific incidents which are almost genocidal. A: I think that's one of the key narratives in the book to show that the moments of the most intensive and accelerated environmental destruction over the last several hundred years have almost always gone together with moments of intense violence. And violence is at the core of 'The Burning Earth'. Not just violence against the earth or against nature, but against other people... Wars that are going on all around us in the world today are part of a very long pattern where armed violence and militarism and military destruction have been inextricably bound with massive environmental destruction.

headline: Manipur: Two farmers killed, two injured in armed attack in Kangpokpi district
full_text:
Manipur: Two farmers killed, two injured in armed attack in Kangpokpi district
The incident occurred at around 8am when the farmers were reportedly attacked by suspected cadres of Kuki Revolutionary Army (KRA) and Kuki National Front (KNF)
Two farmers were killed and two others injured after an armed group allegedly ambushed a group of farmers while they were working in a paddy field in Lanka village in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Friday, officials said.
The incident took place around 7.30-8am at Langka Naga village, where more than 40 armed men carrying sophisticated weapons allegedly attacked the farmers, according to officials quoting local villagers.
The two deceased, W Chawang, 34, and Kawidinang Abonmai, 55, suffered gunshot wounds and died at the spot. Two others, Maliangjinang Abonmai, 52, and Namthiulungbou Prinmai, 50, were seriously injured and later airlifted to RIMS Hospital in Imphal for treatment.
According to locals, the incident occurred at around 8am when the farmers were reportedly attacked by suspected cadres of Kuki Revolutionary Army (KRA) and Kuki National Front (KNF), both militant groups under the Suspension of Operation (SoO) pact.
However, the official reason for the attack is yet to be ascertained, officials said.
The attack has triggered fresh tension in the area, with the Liangmai Naga Council, Manipur (LNC-M) announcing an immediate emergency total shutdown across Liangmai Naga-inhabited areas of the state.
In a statement, the LNC-M condemned the killings and alleged that the attack was carried out by suspected Kuki National Front-President (KNF-P) faction Kuki militants. The council called for immediate steps to ensure the safety and security of civilians.
Under the shutdown, all shops, offices, educational institutions and other non-essential activities will remain closed until further notice. Medical services, fire services and other essential and emergency response operations have been exempted.
The council appealed to members of the community to observe the shutdown peacefully and in a disciplined manner, while urging people to remain calm and united.
Security forces have been deployed in the area following the attack, while further details regarding the circumstances of the firing and the identities of those responsible are awaited.

headline: From Pakistan to US: 36-nation survey reveals how world views India
full_text:
From Pakistan to US: 36-nation survey reveals how world views India
The Pew survey, which was conducted between February and May this year, revealed that people in 36 countries view India more positively than negatively. While Pakistan's view is a foregone conclusion, opinion about India is split in the US.
How does the world see India? Ahead of Independence Day, a new survey by the Pew Research Centre of 36 countries offers a sharply contrasting picture. While India is loved by Sri Lanka the most, there are no surprises in guessing who is at the other extreme - Pakistan. In the United States, meanwhile, opinion about India is almost evenly split.
Overall, the survey, which was conducted between February and May this year and included over 42,000 people, revealed that people in 36 countries view India more positively than negatively. Across these countries, a median of 45% had a favourable view of India, as against 41% who view it unfavourably.
WHAT SURVEY REVEALS ON INDIA'S GLOBAL IMAGE?
The survey revealed that Sri Lanka, at 79%, had the most favourable perception of India among all the countries surveyed. Around 63% of the Sri Lankan respondents also identified India as the country's key ally. Only 11% view India unfavourably.
It is a significant leg-up from 2024, when 65% of the Sri Lankans surveyed had a positive view.
The favourable view of India comes against the backdrop of a reset in Delhi-Colombo ties. Following the 2022 unrest in Sri Lanka due to an economic crisis, India has helped rebuild the island nation through credit lines and financial aid exceeding USD 7.5 billion.
India also commands a favourable perception in Kenya (71%), the UK (71%), Israel (60%), Germany (63%), Italy (56%) and Sweden (55%).
INDIA'S NEIGHBOURHOOD STORY
The picture is more mixed in India's neighbourhood, where several countries like Nepal and Bangladesh have been through turbulent periods and uprisings.
In Bangladesh, 42% have a favourable view of India, as against 51% who have an unfavourable perception. Ties between the neighbours have been turbulent of late over India giving shelter to deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina. Hasina was forced to flee Bangladesh in 2024 amid a violent student-led uprising that left over 500 dead.
In Malaysia, which saw an 'India Out' campaign in 2024, around 58% have an unfavourable view of India.
However, India gets a relatively positive assessment in several other Asian countries. Around 55% of Japanese, 51% of Singaporeans, and 50% of Indonesians view India favourably. India also enjoys strong ratings in the Philippines (49%) and in Thailand (55%).
Expectedly, Pakistan stands out as an overwhelming outlier. According to the Pew survey, 91% of those surveyed in Pakistan have an unfavourable view of India. Interestingly, 7% have a favourable opinion. I said interesting because Pakistan has long been known for suppressing dissent in its hybrid civilian-military setup.
The result, however, is hardly surprising given the long-running tensions between the two nuclear-armed neighbours. Ties reached their lowest ebb following the May 2025 hostilities and the diplomatic spat over India's suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty.
India launched Operation Sindoor last year, destroying terror camps and striking Pakistani air bases in response to the Pahalgam terror attack.
After Pakistan, ratings are the lowest in Turkey (15% favourable) and in the West Bank and East Jerusalem (18%). In Australia, which recently saw anti-immigrant protests, around 55% have an unfavourable view of India.
HOW DOES THE US VIEW INDIA?
The survey reveals that the Americans are divided on India.
Half of those surveyed in the US said they have an unfavourable view of India, while 45% made a positive assessment. In its report, Pew noted that the ratings are some of the lowest since 2008.
In fact, data show that the share of Americans with a favourable view has fallen from 51% in 2023 to 45% in 2026.
However, there is also a partisan divide on how Americans view India. Around 50% of Democrats have a favourable view of India, compared with 42% of Republicans - Donald Trump's party.
Pew also asked Americans about India's influence in the world. While 30% said it was getting stronger, over half of the respondents (54%) said its influence in recent years has remained the same. Another 13% said India's influence was on the wane.
Under Trump, ties between India and the US have been chequered over tariffs and an impending trade deal. Trump's warming up to Pakistan, which has left no stone unturned in massaging his ego, has also led to uneasiness in ties.
Overall, the survey reflects a clear regional divide. India enjoys particularly strong ratings in parts of Asia and Africa, while opinions are more mixed in Europe and Latin America. In the US, the opinion is split.

headline: Tejashwi doing part-time politics in Bihar: JD(U) leader Sanjay Jha
full_text:
Tejashwi doing part-time politics in Bihar: JD(U) leader Sanjay Jha
Patna, JD national working president Sanjay Jha on Friday criticised RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav over his party's proposed August 19 march to the Lok Bhavan against the alleged use of an AK-47 by a policeman during a student protest in Siwan last month, saying Yadav was doing "part-time politics" in Bihar.
Talking to reporters here, Jha said Yadav was touring foreign countries when students were protesting at Jantar Mantar in Delhi and returned only after their demands were accepted.
"Now, Yadav's party will organise a march to Lok Bhavan on August 19… He is doing part-time politics in Bihar, not full-time," he said.
Yadav had recently announced that the RJD would organise the march to the Lok Bhavan over the alleged use of an AK-47 by police during a student protest in Siwan on July 25.
He has questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and sought accountability from the Bihar government and the Centre.
Jha said action had already been taken against the policeman who allegedly used an AK-47 during the protest, and questioned the need to hold a procession over the incident now.
On July 25, members of Left-wing student organisations staged demonstrations and clashed with police in several districts in support of the Bihar Bandh called against the NEET paper leak and police action against protesting students.
The bandh turned violent in Patna, Saran, Siwan, Aurangabad, Bhagalpur, Sitamarhi, Purnia and Bhojpur, while mild protests were reported in Samastipur, Nawada, Nalanda, Madhubani and Sheikhpura.
Protesters pelted police personnel with stones and bricks at Dak Bungalow crossing in Patna, following which several students were detained.
A police constable was suspended after he was purportedly seen using an AK-47 rifle during the protest in Siwan.
A video purportedly showing the constable using the rifle during the student protest had gone viral on social media.
However, PTI could not independently verify the video's authenticity.
Jha said Yadav should instead visit Ranchi, where students have been protesting over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations.
"Since the Mahagathbandhan government is in power there and the RJD is a constituent, Yadav should go to Ranchi and press the state government to accept all demands of the protesting students," he said.

headline: The organisation has asked all its units across the country to hold demonstrations, rallies and dharnas

The organisation has asked all its units across the country to hold demonstrations, rallies and dharnas
NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) has called for nationwide protests on August 17 over a range of pending labour issues, including higher minimum pension, revision of EPF and ESI wage ceilings, restoration of the Old Pension Scheme and changes to provisions of the new labour codes.The organisation has asked all its units across the country to hold demonstrations, rallies and dharnas at district headquarters and submit memorandums to the Prime Minister, finance minister and labour minister. A major protest is planned at Jantar Mantar in Delhi from 10am, with workers and representatives of BMS-affiliated unions and federations expected to participate.Among its key demands, BMS has sought an increase in the minimum pension under EPS-95 to Rs 7,500 a month and its linkage with variable dearness allowance and Ayushman Bharat. It has also demanded that the ESI wage ceiling be doubled from Rs 21,000 to Rs 42,000 and the EPF ceiling raised from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000.The union has sought bonus on full wages in line with the new labour codes, an increase in the wage ceiling used for bonus calculation and gratuity based on 30 days' wages instead of 15 days, without any upper limit. It has also demanded inflation-linked minimum wages, higher honorarium for anganwadi, ASHA, mid-day meal and other scheme workers, and equal pay for contract and outsourced workers doing the same work.
Other demands include a five-day work week in banks, filling vacancies in government services and public establishments, convening the Indian Labour Conference and restoring OPS.BMS has also reiterated its opposition to several provisions of the Industrial Relations Code and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, arguing that they could weaken workers' rights, job security and social security. It has sought formal consultations between the Centre and central trade unions before amendments are made.The organisation also wants the Centre and states to reconsider the status of more than one crore âscheme workersâ, saying many work 10-12 hours a day but remain outside effective labour-law and social-security protection.

headline: Independence Day flag-hoisting guide: Dos and don’ts every Indian should know ahead of August 15
full_text:
Independence Day flag-hoisting guide: Dos and don’ts every Indian should know ahead of August 15
People celebrate the Independence Day through various traditions, most notably by hoisting the national flag, and unfurling the Tricolour.
India celebrates its Independence Day annually on August 15, marking the historic day in 1947 when the nation gained freedom after roughly 200 years of British rule. The occasion is commemorated with immense fervor and joy across the country, in government offices, educational institutions, private organisations, residential societies, and homes alike.
People celebrate the day through various traditions, most notably by hoisting the national flag, unfurling the Tricolour, and singing the national anthem and national song.
The hoisting and handling of the flag are strictly guided by the Flag Code of India to preserve its honour.
Deep Dive
The Flag Code of India governs the display of the national flag by all institutions.
Also Read | Independence Day 2026: How to properly display, handle the Indian flag - Your six-point tricolour guide
Dos and don'ts for hoisting the national flag
Check out the rules for hoisting the national flag on August 15:
1- What material should be used for the national flag?
According to the information available on PIB, the national flag shall be made of handspun and handwoven or machine-made cotton, polyester, wool, silk, khadi bunting.
2- Timings
When the national flag is displayed in the open or on the house of a member of the public, it may be flown day and night.
3- Can the national flag be displayed at home?
Members of the public, private organisations and educational institutions may hoist and display the national flag on all days and occasions, provided its dignity and honour are maintained, according to the PIB.
4- Position of honour
Whenever the flag is on display, it should occupy the position of honor and should be distinctly placed.
Also Read | Minute-by-minute of August 15: What exactly happens at Red Fort on Independence Day
5- Other things to always remember while hoisting or displaying the national flag:
- The national flag should not be flown from a single masthead simultaneously with any other flag.
- Never hoist the national flag upside down. The saffron band should not be the bottom band.
- It shall not be dipped in salute to any person or thing.
- Never let it touch the ground, floor, or trail in the water.
- Never hoist a damaged or disheveled flag.
- Never write on the national flag.
- It shall not be used to cover a speaker's desk, nor shall it be draped over a speaker's platform.
- It shall never be used as a portion of costume, uniform, or accessory of any description which is worn below the waist of any person, nor shall it be embroidered or printed on handkerchiefs, napkins, cushions, undergarments, or any dress material.
India's Independence Day
The path to independence for India was long. Countless freedom fighters made extraordinary sacrifices to break the colonial rule and secure the nation's future.
Every year on August 15, India comes together not only to celebrate its independence, but to pay tribute to the heroes who brought freedom to life.
The national ceremony takes place at the historic Red Fort in Delhi. The Prime Minister hoists the national tricolour. Following the ceremony, the PM delivers an address to the nation.
Similarly, the ceremonial flag hoisting and parades take place in all state capitals, presided over by the chief ministers.
Independence Day serves as a moment of celebration and reflection for all the citizens.

headline: GOBARdhan scheme: How India plans to turn cattle dung, crop waste and garbage into fuel
full_text:
GOBARdhan scheme: How India plans to turn cattle dung, crop waste and garbage into fuel
Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 14, 2026, 19:35 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
The government has now positioned GOBARdhan as a national framework for the Compressed Biogas industry (AI image)
For years, India has spoken about the enormous amount of energy locked inside its agricultural residue, cattle dung and organic waste. The challenge has been turning that potential into a commercially viable industry.Now, the government is making one of its most serious attempts yet.
The Union Cabinet on August 6 approved GOBARdhan, the National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with a total outlay of Rs 23,731 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36. The scheme has set a target of ten-fold increase in domestic production of Compressed Biogas (CBG) and brings together everything from assured demand and pricing to capital assistance, pipelines and credit under a single framework.The idea sounds simple: take waste that would otherwise be burnt, dumped or left to decompose, and process it in a biogas plant and turn it into fuel that can be used much like natural gas.
The initiative aims to increase nation's CBG production
But the government's ambition goes much further.It wants villages to become centres of energy production, farmers to become suppliers to the energy industry and organic waste to become an economic resource rather than a disposal problem.
The question is whether the new scheme can solve the problems that have held back India's CBG industry for years.
What exactly is GOBARdhan?
GOBARdhan is not an entirely new idea.The initiative was originally launched in 2018 under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen as a waste-management programme. Its focus was on converting cattle dung, kitchen waste, crop residue and other organic material into biogas and bio-slurry, helping villages manage waste while generating useful products.The 2026 version is much broader.The government has now positioned GOBARdhan as a national framework for the Compressed Biogas industry, bringing several existing measures under one umbrella and placing the scheme under the ministry of petroleum and natural gas.These include the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) initiative, the Market Development Assistance scheme for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery scheme, pipeline infrastructure support and central financial assistance for CBG plants.In simple terms, the government is moving from âhow do we manage organic waste?â to âhow do we build an industry around it?â
How does waste become fuel?
The process begins with organic material such as cattle dung, agricultural residue, press mud from sugar mills and municipal organic waste.This material is fed into an anaerobic digester, where microorganisms break it down in the absence of oxygen and produce biogas. The raw biogas contains methane along with carbon dioxide and other impurities.The gas is then purified to remove these impurities and compressed.
Production process of CBG
The resulting Compressed Biogas, or CBG, has properties comparable to natural gas and can be used within the existing gas ecosystem. This is one of its biggest advantages: India does not necessarily need to create an entirely separate fuel infrastructure for it.The process also produces organic material that can be processed into fertiliser.That means one plant can potentially create several economic outputs:Waste â CBG + organic manure + rural jobs + additional income opportunitiesThis is the circular economy the government is trying to build.
Why does India need CBG?
The biggest reason is energy security.India currently imports nearly 50% of its natural gas requirement, according to the government's latest GOBARdhan backgrounder. That leaves the country exposed to international gas prices, shipping disruptions and geopolitical shocks.Domestic CBG offers a way to produce a portion of that gas from resources that India already has in abundance.
Importance of CBG for India
The government estimates that lower dependence on imported fossil fuels under GOBARdhan could eventually save more than Rs 40,000 crore in foreign exchange. That is a government projection rather than a guaranteed saving, but it illustrates the scale of the ambition.There is also an environmental argument.Agricultural residue that is not economically used can become a waste-disposal problem, while organic waste dumped in landfills can generate methane and other emissions. Converting such material into fuel gives it an economic value while potentially reducing waste-related emissions.For farmers, the attraction is an additional market for residue and dung.For energy companies, it is another source of domestic gas.For the government, it is a way of connecting waste management, rural development and energy security.
India has tried CBG before. So what went wrong?
This is where the GOBARdhan story becomes more complicated.India's push for CBG production predates the new scheme by several years.The government launched SATAT in October 2018, with an ambitious target of establishing 5,000 CBG plants producing 15 million tonnes a year.But the industry struggled to scale at the pace initially envisaged.A 2022 review by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas found that against the target of 5,000 plants by 2023-24, only 40 had been set up at that point. The committee also highlighted problems with financing, multiple approvals, pricing and feedstock availability.One of the biggest problems was that a CBG plant needs much more than a piece of land and a digester.It needs a reliable supply of biomass, equipment to collect and transport that biomass, storage facilities, technology, financing and, crucially, a buyer for the gas.One big complication with agricultural residue is that it is seasonal.Crop waste may be available in large quantities for only a few months of the year, forcing plants to invest in storage and logistics if they want to operate throughout the year. The parliamentary committee specifically flagged this issue.Bansal estimates that India generates around 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue annually, suggesting that the problem is not a shortage of biomass but the difficulty of turning dispersed and seasonal supplies into a reliable, year-round feedstock chain.GOBARdhan's focus on biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure and district-level planning is therefore critical to making plants operate at high utilisation.There was also a financing problem.Banks and investors were wary of projects whose revenues depended on uncertain feedstock supplies and evolving CBG prices. The committee noted concerns over the low internal rate of return of plants and called for more remunerative pricing.This is the gap GOBARdhan is now attempting to close.Kapil Bansal, partner, energy transition and decarbonization at EY-Parthenon India, told TOI that the biggest change is that GOBARdhan tackles the entire CBG value chain rather than individual bottlenecks.Earlier measures addressed issues such as biomass aggregation, organic manure, pipelines and financial assistance separately, but developers continued to face uncertainty around demand, pricing and financing.âThe sector is moving from a project-led approach to a market-led approach, where demand, pricing and financing visibility are available before developers invest,â Bansal said.The combination of assured offtake, a ten-year pricing framework, capital assistance, pipeline connectivity and credit guarantees, he said, should improve project bankability and give investors greater confidence.
What changes under the Rs 23,731-crore scheme?
The government has structured GOBARdhan around six major components, each designed to address a different weakness in the existing CBG ecosystem.
New changes introduced in the upgraded scheme
1. Assured demand for CBGPerhaps the biggest change is that producers will have greater certainty that someone will buy their gas.City Gas Distribution companies will procure CBG in line with a notified obligation that rises from 3% in FY 2026-27 to 4% in FY 2027-28 and 5% from FY 2028-29 onwards for the CNG transport and PNG domestic segments.This creates a predictable demand signal.For investors, that matters because a plant is much easier to finance when there is greater clarity about who will buy its output.
2. A stable price
GOBARdhan introduces a government-backed CBG price of Rs 2,110 per MMBTU, with a minimum ten-year framework.The objective is to give producers greater revenue visibility and make projects more attractive to investors and lenders.This directly addresses one of the problems identified in the earlier CBG ecosystem: uncertainty over whether the economics of a plant would work after it was built.
3. Capital assistance
Eligible greenfield CBG projects will receive capital assistance of up to Rs 2 crore for every tonne per day (TPD) of installed capacity.Importantly, the support is not restricted to the core plant.It can also cover critical assets linked to feedstock aggregation, organic manure processing and value addition. Brownfield projects expanding existing capacity will also be eligible.That matters because the economics of CBG depend on the entire supply chain, not just the digester.
4. Pipelines to connect plants with buyers
A CBG plant cannot be commercially successful if its gas cannot reach the market.GOBARdhan therefore provides for cluster-based and standalone pipeline infrastructure connecting plants with trunk pipelines and City Gas Distribution networks.The aim is to reduce evacuation costs, improve reliability and expand the market available to producers.
5. Credit guarantees
The scheme also attempts to solve the financing problem through a dedicated credit guarantee mechanism.By sharing part of the lending risk, the government hopes banks will be more willing to finance MSME-based CBG projects.This could bring smaller companies, cooperatives, women entrepreneurs and first-time developers into an industry that has so far been dominated by larger players and institutional initiatives.
6. A district-level ecosystem fund
The final component focuses on the problem that often receives the least attention: where will the feedstock come from?The CBG Ecosystem Challenge Fund will support biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure, district-level development plans, technology adoption, process improvements and organic manure value addition.The objective is to build the local ecosystem around each plant rather than treating the plant as an isolated piece of infrastructure.
What does this mean for farmers?
The government's larger pitch is that farmers should become participants in India's energy economy.Crop residue and cattle dung can become feedstock for CBG plants, creating potential additional income for farmers and local aggregators.The benefit does not stop with the gas.
Scheme to empower the farmers
The material left after the biogas production process can be processed into organic fertilisers such as Fermented Organic Manure and Liquid Fermented Organic Manure.This creates a second revenue stream while returning nutrients to agriculture.The government has already been supporting this side of the industry through the Market Development Assistance scheme. Together, these measures are intended to create a cycle in which agricultural and livestock waste becomes an input for both energy and agriculture.That is why GOBARdhan is being presented as more than an energy scheme.It is also a rural infrastructure and waste-management programme.
How big is India's CBG industry today?
This is perhaps the most revealing part of the government's latest numbers.As of August 6, the GOBARdhan Unified Registration Portal had recorded 1,908 registered CBG/Bio-CNG plants. Of these, 217 had been commissioned, while another 339 were under construction, according to the government.The numbers show both the opportunity and the problem.
Current capacity of CBG in the country
There is considerable interest in building CBG capacity, but the number of plants actually operating remains far below the number registered.The government says the various initiatives introduced over recent years have helped commission more than 200 CBG plants and establish the initial production and offtake ecosystem. GOBARdhan is now intended to take that foundation to a national scale.In other words, the new scheme is not starting from zero.It is an attempt to make the existing pipeline of projects commercially viable and scalable.
Can GOBARdhan finally make CBG commercially viable?
That remains the biggest question.Government support can reduce the initial cost of a plant and create a market for its gas. But it cannot eliminate the fundamental logistical challenge of collecting biomass.Bansal cautioned that commercial viability will still vary from project to project because feedstock costs, transportation distances, plant utilisation and financing costs will continue to determine returns.
âA project with reliable access to high-quality feedstock can achieve significantly better plant efficiency and returns than a project relying on dispersed or lower-yield biomass resources,â he said.A plant located far from its feedstock source may face high transportation costs. Agricultural residue is seasonal. Competing uses for biomass can raise prices. Plants also need to maintain reliable operations and consistent gas quality.These problems were highlighted by the Parliamentary Standing Committee even before the latest scheme was announced. It pointed to the uneven availability of feedstock, the need for storage and the importance of synchronising CBG production with the national gas grid.This is why the six components of GOBARdhan matter together.A subsidy without a buyer does not solve the problem.A buyer without a pipeline does not solve the problem.A pipeline without reliable feedstock does not solve the problem.And a plant with all three still needs affordable financing and efficient operations.GOBARdhan is effectively trying to solve all of these problems at the same time.
What could India get by 2035-36?
The government has set an ambitious ten-year vision.It expects GOBARdhan to deliver nearly ten-fold growth in domestic CBG production, attract large private investment, create rural employment and expand the organic fertiliser economy. It also projects lower fossil-fuel use and significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.These are targets and government projections, not guaranteed outcomes.The more important test will be whether the number of operating plants grows alongside registrations, whether plants remain viable after initial assistance and whether farmers and local businesses actually benefit from the new demand for biomass.If that happens, GOBARdhan could change the economics of waste in India.Instead of paying to collect, transport and dispose of organic waste, communities could potentially build local industries around it.
The bigger picture
India's CBG journey has already shown that having abundant biomass is not enough.The country had an ambitious 5,000-plant target under SATAT, but financing constraints, feedstock logistics, approvals, pricing uncertainty and weak project economics slowed the industry's development.GOBARdhan is the government's attempt to address those weaknesses through one national framework.At Rs 23,731 crore over ten years, the bet is substantial.But the real significance of the scheme is not the size of the allocation. It is the attempt to connect India's farms, villages, waste streams and gas networks into one economic system.
If the model works, cattle dung and crop residue will no longer be treated merely as waste. They could become feedstock for a domestic fuel industry, while the by-products return to farms as organic fertiliser.That would turn the government's âwaste-to-wealthâ slogan into a functioning business model.The challenge is making sure the economics work beyond the subsidy period.For GOBARdhan, success will therefore not be measured simply by how much money is spent or how many plants are registered. It will be measured by how many plants actually operate, how much CBG they produce, whether farmers earn from supplying biomass and whether India's dependence on imported gas falls.India has plenty of waste. GOBARdhan now has to prove that it can turn that waste into a dependable source of energy, income and economic value.

The Supreme Court on Friday quashed all FIRs against comedian Samay Raina and four others over alleged insensitive jokes about persons with disabilities during his 'India's Got Latent' show.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the order, noting Raina and others' compliance with the top court's direction to conduct awareness programmes and raise funds for persons with disabilities.
Apart from Raina, the others who have received relief in the case are Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar alias Sonali Aditya Desai, and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar.

Deep Dive
The court praised the efforts of Raina, Goyal, Ghai, Thakkar and Tanwar in organising shows for persons with disabilities.
"Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there. They are very bright youngsters. If they have started working in a positive direction, there will be positive output," the court said.
However, the top court will continue hearing the matter to consider suggestions from persons with disabilities on ways to ensure better checks on such content and issue appropriate directions on the broader issues involved.'
"Matter qua respondents 6-10 (the accused comedians) is closed. Criminal proceedings against respondents 6-10 are hereby quashed. All other related proceedings are set aside. List to issue directions on the larger issue," the Court said.
What was the controversy?
The controversial episode of 'India's Got Latent', now being examined by the top court, was recorded on November 14, 2024, but was broadcast later.
Several people who featured on the comedy show faced multiple criminal cases over allegations of making obscene and insensitive remarks.

headline: Eminent Marxist historian and scholar of modern Indian history, Sumit Sarkar, died at a private hospital in New Delhi on Thursday (August 13, 2026). He was 87.
full_text:
Eminent Marxist historian and scholar of modern Indian history, Sumit Sarkar, died at a private hospital in New Delhi on Thursday (August 13, 2026). He was 87.
He spent several years teaching History at the University of Delhi, and was a Fellow of Wolfson College, Oxford. He had also been a visiting professor at several prestigious universities in the United States and Europe.
His works include Swadeshi Movement in Bengal, 1903-1908 (1973), Modern India (1989), and Writing Social History (1998), among others. He also co-edited Women and Social Reform in Modern India (2007) and Caste in Modern India (2013) with his wife, Tanika Sarkar.
He completed his BA (Honours) in History at Presidency College in Kolkata before going on to do his Master’s and Ph.D. at the University of Calcutta.
His former students and colleagues remembered him not only as a “doyen of historians”, but also as the “kindest of human beings”.
Ravikant, a professor at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, and Mr. Sarkar’s student from 1988 to 1991, recalled his “scintillating” lectures, saying, “He would look at one word and speak a full paragraph at one go. That was how succinct his summaries were,” he said.
Anirban Bandyopadhyay, a professor of History at the Kalinga Institute of Social Sciences, described Mr. Sarkar as “one of the rare Marxist historians to delve deeply into culture and emotions as opposed to the economy”.
“With regard to 19th and 20th-century Bengal, there was nothing that he did not write about,” said Mr. Bandyopadhyay, who was closely acquainted with Mr. Sarkar and his wife and described the death as a “personal loss”, in addition to being a loss to all history students. “From 2005, I met him on numerous occasions, went to their place in Delhi, and read to him. He always listened to younger people, and always had a smile,” Mr. Bandyopadhyay said.

Atleast 25 local people were employed under MGNREGA during different durations to develop each of these ponds. They have also taken up slope pitching, to stabilize the inner side slopes of the pond to prevent soil slipping. They have also taken up local tree plantation and planted local tree species like Neem, Peepal, and Banyan trees around the ponds to improve local ecology and shade, he said.

headline: Ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly election, political parties in the State are getting their houses in order.
full_text:
Ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly election, political parties in the State are getting their houses in order.
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a party traditionally associated with Hindu voters, is working to project itself as pro-Sikh, even as the Congress, the principal Opposition, continues to grapple with infighting. The ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) is focused on consolidating the Hindu vote, a voter base it shares with the BJP and the Congress, as it seeks to retain power.
The BJP recently appointed Kewal Singh Dhillon, a Jat Sikh face, as its Punjab president. Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini, often seen donning a dastar (turban), has been making frequent visits to Punjab for social and religious functions. The party has been trying to strengthen its pro-Sikh image by drawing attention to steps taken by the Union government for the community, setting up of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the 1984 anti-Sikh riots cases, the initiative to start the Kartarpur Corridor, which connects the Dera Baba Nanak in India to the Darbar Sahib Gurdwara in Pakistan, and the waiving of GST from ‘langar’ (community kitchens).
These moves are widely seen as part of the BJP’s broader effort to strengthen its ‘pro-Sikh’ credentials and in its efforts it appears to be competing with other ‘Panthic’ (Sikh) parties to position itself as a Sikh party. Many believe the BJP risks alienating its core Hindu vote base and sensing this opening, the AAP has found an opportunity to mobilise Hindu voters in Punjab.
Hindus account for nearly 38% of the State’s electorate and traditionally have been inclined towards the Congress. The BJP’s core support base is also concentrated among Hindus, especially among the urban voters. Now, as the BJP is seen busy promoting its ‘pro-Sikh’ image and the Congress is currently caught up in internal fighting, the AAP is trying to capture that space.
In 2026, the AAP government unveiled a set of initiatives indicating its outreach for the Hindu electorate. In June, at an event in Amritsar, AAP supremo Arvind Kejriwal announced the construction of a temple dedicated to ‘Mata Janaki’ (Sita) and her sons Luv and Kush, connected to the belief that they were born on Amritsar’s soil. The AAP has orgaised devotional events (bhajan sandhyas) — ‘Ek Shaam Bhagwan Shivji Ke Naam’ — in the State. It is also holding a theatrical production, ‘Humare Ram’, to depict the timeless ideals of Lord Ram and disseminate the message of ‘Sanatan’ through the historical epics of Ramayan.
On August 12, the State government announced an expansion of its free-of-cost pilgrimage scheme — ‘Mukh Mantri Teerath Yatra Yojna ‘ — which has expanded to include a much larger set of Hindu pilgrimage destinations across Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, and Uttar Pradesh.
There is a view among political observers that if the BJP shifts focus from its Hindu vote bank toward the Sikhs, Hindu voters may drift away from the party. It is natural that when a party leaves a space vacant, another party tends to step in.
The AAP is offering that space and is positioned to capture it, partly because Congress, which has also drawn Hindu votes in the past, is dealing with infighting and the BJP is busy building an image with Sikh voters. The AAP, which is battling anti-incumbency after four-and-a-half years of its rule, could gain ground with the Hindu support base of both parties — the BJP and the Congress.

headline: BRS did black magic to defame Congress govt, alleges Revanth Reddy
full_text:
BRS did black magic to defame Congress govt, alleges Revanth Reddy
Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy accused BRS leaders of performing occult rituals to malign his government. He paired the charge with claims of secure Hyderabad water supply and a fresh housing push.
Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy on Thursday alleged that BRS leaders had performed occult rituals, including black magic, to defame the Congress government. Speaking at a public meeting after laying the foundation stone for Indiramma Housing Towers for the urban poor, he also said recent rains had improved the water situation and ensured there would be no supply problem for Hyderabad.
Reddy used the event to highlight the state government's housing and welfare measures, while also attacking the previous BRS government over its record on housing, land issues and debt. He said the Congress government was going ahead with its schemes despite financial strain left behind by the earlier administration.
Referring to the recent rains, Reddy said the Yellampally project on the Godavari had filled up even though deficit rainfall had been forecast because of the impact of the El Nino weather pattern. He said this had ensured that there was no problem for water supply in Hyderabad.
Alleging that some BRS leaders had carried out rituals to wish ill on the government, he said, "Some went to Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and performed aghora pujas wishing that there should be drought, people should die and government should be defamed. Such evil people are also there. Though they performed aghora pujas, God is not with them. God is with us. Because, our resolve is good."
Reddy said he did not claim to be very intelligent or highly qualified, but said his intentions were good and that this would make the gods help him. He also said that though BRS president K Chandrasekhar Rao had "everything", he was under attack from his own people.
"Is it right for a party which was in power for 10 years and which has been in existence since the last 25 years to perform such occult practices," he asked. He added that practices such as black magic would have a reverse impact if intentions were not good, and would make things difficult for BRS leaders. There was no immediate response from the BRS.
On housing, Reddy said the government had decided to provide one lakh houses in the first phase through the Indiramma Housing Towers project for the urban poor in Hyderabad. He also criticised the previous BRS government for not fulfilling its promise of a double-bedroom house for every poor family.
On land concerns, he referred to worries over the inclusion of lands in the Section 22 prohibited list and assured people that no one would lose ownership of their land. He said there was no need to worry and appealed to people not to believe false propaganda on social media about prohibited lands.
Highlighting welfare measures aimed at women, Reddy said the distribution of Indiramma Sarees, free bus travel for women in state-run RTC buses, bank linkage loans worth Rs 65,000 crore for self-help groups, and the setting up of petrol bunks and solar plants by women SHG members had brought major change in their lives.
He added that the government was implementing all its schemes despite a huge debt burden incurred by the previous BRS government.
On August 4, Telangana Congress president B Mahesh Kumar Goud had alleged that BRS MLA T Harish Rao performed "kshudra puja" to prevent rainfall in the state in the hope of gaining political mileage from a drought. Harish Rao later issued a legal notice to Goud over the remarks.

headline: When officials inspected four irrigation tanks in Gudipala mandal in May 2025, farmers and residents raised concerns about a problem that has become increasingly visible across Chittoor’s traditional water-storage network: shrinking storage capacity ...
full_text:
When officials inspected four irrigation tanks in Gudipala mandal in May 2025, farmers and residents raised concerns about a problem that has become increasingly visible across Chittoor’s traditional water-storage network: shrinking storage capacity due to silt accumulation and alleged encroachments.
Chittoor District Collector Sumit Kumar inspected Bangarappa Cheruvu, Reddamma Cheruvu, Ramireddy Cheruvu, and Narayanareddy Cheruvu after farmers and residents raised concerns.
“The tank used to hold water for much longer. With silt accumulating and parts of the tank area being occupied, the storage capacity has been reduced. Sir, you know very well that we farmers are increasingly vulnerable to poor rains in Chittoor, and we have no other option but to depend on borewells when the tanks don’t fill,” P. Rangaiah, 48, tells the Collector when the latter interacted with the residents.
The Collector immediately directed officials to survey encroachments, prepare estimates for desilting, and examine the supply channels connecting the tanks. The Irrigation officials were given a free hand to use MGNREGS funds. The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) officials were asked to remove soil reportedly deposited near Bangarappa Cheruvu during expressway construction, as farmers complained that the dumped soil had affected the water-spread area.
The Gudipala inspection is a testimony to a persisting problem that extends across Chittoor district.
The 2023 District Survey Report lists 4,121 minor irrigation tanks in Chittoor district. Their combined designed storage capacity was recorded at 15,133.73 million cubic feet (mcft), against a current storage capacity of 8,924.23 mcft, leaving a difference of 6,209.50 mcft.
A revenue official in Nagari said that the figure should not be described as the quantity lost to encroachment. “Storage capacity can decline because of siltation, damaged structures, reduced inflows, changes in catchment areas, and other factors. The survey records a substantial gap between the capacity for which the tank network was designed and the capacity recorded at the time of assessment,” he said.
Chittoor Municipal Corporation, the district headquarters, was once surrounded by 14 tanks that quenched its thirst for drinking water. Eleven of them had been fully encroached upon, while Gangineni Cheruvu and Kattamanchi Cheruvu had been contaminated by drain water and rendered unusable. Kajuru Cheruvu on the Chittoor-Palamaner road, within the city limits, was subjected to gross neglect, with its feeder channels completely shut for the last four decades, according to an official of Irrigation Department. The NTR Jalasayam on the outskirts is a saving grace, as it continues to serve the civic population.
Despite the vagaries of time, the condition of Gangineni Cheruvu continues to attract public attention. “Gangineni Cheruvu has changed considerably over the years. Wastewater, weeds, and garbage have affected the water body, while the surrounding area has become increasingly built up,” Ulaganathan, a resident of Chittoor, said.
Stating that the issue is not limited to the tank bed, a municipal official says that feeder channels, surplus channels, and drainage routes determine whether rainwater reaches and leaves a tank. Blocking any of these can alter the size of a water body even when its recorded land area remains unchanged, he explains.
Meanwhile, an Anantapur-based NGO, the International Human Rights Protection Commission (IHRPC), had approached the Chittoor district court, seeking protection of the buffer zone of the Gangineni Cheruvu from encroachment.
“Towards the Deer Park side and along the Vellore Road, the Gangineni Cheruvu had been subjected to ruthless encroachments. While its area was over 80 acres, it’s now not even half. We are also approaching the Andhra Pradesh High Court in this regard, as there has been no response from the district-level officials. This case clearly illustrates the continuing interface between urban land use and protected water bodies,” IHRPC general secretary R.K. Shobha Rani says.
Agarampalli Ayacut Cheruvu near Kanipakam provides another documented example. In a 2025 Andhra Pradesh High Court proceeding, petitioners identified themselves as ayacut farmers and alleged encroachment of the tank. The revenue records showed the tank’s total extent at 47.84 acres. The petitioners alleged that 16 acres had been encroached upon and that garbage was being dumped in the tank. They also referred to representations made to the authorities in 2007, 2020, and 2024.
“We have been approaching the authorities for years because the tank is our irrigation source. If a sizeable portion of the tank area is occupied, both storage and the ayacut are affected,” an ayacut farmer alleges.
Responding to the allegations, a revenue official states that tank encroachment could not be assessed based on local allegations. “Survey numbers, revenue classification, Full Tank Level, and the legally protected extent of the water body all become relevant,” he said.
The narrowing and encroachment of the Neeva River within Chittoor city continues to be a major public-safety concern. The issue is widely viewed as not merely an encroachment or revenue matter.
“It has become a flood-management and public-safety concern. When the natural river corridor is narrowed or obstructed by construction, dumping, or other activities, the river has less space to safely carry flood flows. During rains, the municipal and revenue authorities rush to the riverbed zone, alert the residents in encroached areas, and everything will be silent later,” Somasekhar, a resident of Chittoor, says.
During the October 2017 floods, 13 of 15 colonies in the Thena Banda and Veerabhadra areas were submerged, while residents of nine colonies were advised to evacuate, and these colonies were developed following encroachments on the Neeva riverbed, he says.
In 2022, more than 300 families were reported to be living along the banks of the river Neeva. Even today, the residents approach the district administration to show them a housing site, but the issue has remained vexed for years without a solution.
In 2024, the Andhra Pradesh High Court directed the Chittoor District administration to ensure that no sand mining was permitted in the Neeva riverbed without authorisation.
Residents observe that the top priority should be a scientific, transparent survey of the Neeva through Chittoor Corporation, comparing its original and present alignment and width. Every encroachment and obstruction should be mapped, legally examined, and removed wherever required.
“The river must not be allowed to become narrower at the cost of Chittoor’s flood safety,” Siva Kumar of Jendaman Street, close to the Neeva riverbed, says. Incidentally, in the Indira Nagar area, the Neeva River’s width remains truncated to a mere 20 feet.
Not only in Chittoor, but encroachments of irrigation tanks and their feeder channels in the Kuppam and Palamaner revenue divisions are raising concerns over the effective utilisation of water resources in the drought-prone region. Though a comprehensive, tank-wise official figure on the extent of encroachments is not publicly available, the issue assumes significance with the expansion of irrigation infrastructure.
“Encroachments can reduce storage capacity, obstruct inflows, and weaken the functioning of these traditional water bodies. The Kuppam branch canal, though launched with much fanfare when the TDP came to power, is yet to fulfil its promise. A majority of the tanks are on the verge of getting dry with no rains, coupled with tampering of the feeder channels, particularly due to encroachments,” says Manikyam, a farmer in Gudipala mandal.
Municipal authorities observed that the government has begun funding water-body rejuvenation through urban infrastructure programmes across Chittoor district.
The AMRUT 2.0 project lists a ₹7.70-crore water-body rejuvenation project in Chittoor. The other listed works included ₹1.23 crore in Punganur, ₹1.60 crore in Kuppam, ₹2.20 crore for Suragunta Tank at Kakavedu in Nagari, and ₹2.20 crore for Gobillakoturu Cheruvu near Agarabathi Colony in Palamaner.
Chittoor also has AMRUT 2.0 projects relating to sewerage infrastructure, including a sewage treatment plant and sewerage-network works.
“The sewage component is relevant to water-body protection because rejuvenation of a polluted tank can be undermined if wastewater continues to enter it,” an official said.
Reacting to the scenario of encroachments along water bodies, Chittoor Collector Sumit Kumar says the people of undivided Chittoor district should be proud of their terrain, with an extraordinary and unique network of micro-irrigation tanks, the other being the Uttarandhra region.
He said that the encroachment of water bodies in Chittoor district, particularly in urban areas, is “negligible and not visible”. The recent “Jaladhara Jalaharathi” water conservation programme of the State government had proved a boon for the drought-prone district.
“We did clear the feeder channels for over 1,250 tanks, and spent close to ₹200 crore for the works, along with deploying the NREGA force,” he said.
“When allegations of encroachment of water bodies emerge, they are mostly imaginative and unfounded, though the authorities would definitely verify all. Historically, the catchment areas and feeder channels remained disturbed. When we allow private players to dig gravel within permissible limits, the vehicle movement from tank beds would make one imagine that the water body is getting encroached upon,” he said.
“But there are certain isolated incidents. The Kajur Cheruvu in Chittoor city remained neglected for 40 years. The feeder channels were deliberately disturbed by vested interests so that the tank would not receive any rainwater. I did inspect the tank and initiated steps on a war footing to rectify the malady,” the Collector says.
Regarding the Neeva riverbed, “several families there have been residing there for decades.” The Collector says that the families that face annual evacuation are economically poorer sections.
“We can’t disturb them. But, there are no recent encroachments. We are also planning to provide families along the riverbed, vulnerable to floods, with alternative arrangements,” Sumit Kumar says.

headline: Ram Temple CEO race narrows; Yogeshwar Mishra, Rajesh Pandey emerge as frontrunners
full_text:
Ram Temple CEO race narrows; Yogeshwar Mishra, Rajesh Pandey emerge as frontrunners
The race for the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust CEO post has narrowed to three names after interviews concluded. Former bureaucrats Yogeshwar Ram Mishra and Rajesh Pandey are among the prominent contenders as the trust prepares to make the final appointment.
The race for the post of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust has narrowed to three names, with former bureaucrats Yogeshwar Ram Mishra and Rajesh Pandey emerging as prominent contenders, according to government sources.
The interview process for the post has been completed and a panel of three names is being prepared for submission to the temple trust, which will take the final decision on the appointment.
Mishra is considered one of the leading contenders because of his administrative experience, particularly his work during the development of the Kashi Corridor. Pandey, a former police officer, is also in contention and is known for his policing career in Uttar Pradesh, including his involvement in high-profile encounters.
Sources said officials who rose to the IAS or IPS through the Provincial Civil Services (PCS) route could have an edge over direct-recruit officers. The CEO of the Kashi Vishwanath Temple Trust is also a PCS officer, while several temple trusts in Uttar Pradesh have government representatives from the PCS cadre.
The trust is looking for an experienced, honest and competent administrator with an understanding of temple management. Both Mishra and Pandey are believed to fit these criteria, sources said.
Several retired armed forces officers were also among the 16 shortlisted candidates. Their presence means a retired military officer could still emerge as the final choice.
No woman has so far emerged as a prominent contender among the 16 shortlisted candidates. However, the eligibility criteria for the CEO post did not specify any gender restriction.
The selection process began with 5,585 applications. Of these, 3,877 candidates submitted detailed CVs, while 1,580 applications and presentations underwent detailed evaluation. The process was subsequently narrowed to 111 online interactions, then to 16 shortlisted candidates, and finally to a three-member panel.
The final appointment will be made by the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust.
