headline: For Bengalureans, food safety inspections over the past few days have challenged an assumption that often goes unquestioned: that a higher-priced meal, a well-known hotel or a familiar brand necessarily comes with better food safety standards.
full_text:
For Bengalureans, food safety inspections over the past few days have challenged an assumption that often goes unquestioned: that a higher-priced meal, a well-known hotel or a familiar brand necessarily comes with better food safety standards.
The Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) conducted raids, casting its net wide to include roadside eateries, smaller food businesses, three- and five-star hotels, international fast-food chains, government canteens, Indira Canteens and warehouses supplying quick-commerce platforms. The inspections have brought to light expired food, rotten meat and vegetables, mislabelling, poor storage and hygiene practices, and concerns over used cooking oil.
The ongoing drive that began on August 7 covered over 60 three-star and five-star hotels in Bengaluru Urban and the Greater Bengaluru area till August 9. Thirty teams collected 77 food samples for laboratory analysis. Officials seized 640 kg of mutton, chicken and fish, 276 kg of rotten or mould-affected vegetables, 45 litres of expired milk and curd, 12 kg of expired bakery products and 67 kg of mislabelled or expired cereals and other food products in three days. Nearly 49 litres of used or non-compliant cooking oil were also seized.
The findings have been unsettling for consumers precisely because the inspections were not confined to establishments where poor hygiene is assumed.
For Prashanti Naidu, who never hesitated to eat at fine-dining restaurants, the findings came as a shock. “When you eat at a five-star hotel or a fine-dining restaurant, you assume that the standards are automatically higher. You are paying a premium and you expect the ingredients, kitchen and storage to meet that standard. You never imagine that something as basic as expired food could be present in a professional kitchen,” the software professional said.
What troubled her was the part of a restaurant that customers never see. “The dining area can be spotless and the food can be beautifully presented. But you cannot see the refrigerator, the storage room or how the raw materials are handled. That is where the real food safety question lies,” she said.
What the inspections found
The hotel inspections revealed expired food products, non-compliant labelling, misbranding, improper storage of meat, fish and poultry, fungal growth in vegetables and inadequate segregation of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food.
Officials also found products carrying shelf-life declarations that exceeded the applicable period. In some cases, products with a declared shelf life of one year were found carrying declarations extending to two years. Some imported products had subsequently been repacked.
The department has issued notices and recommended cases before the respective adjudicating officers. Kitchens at high-end pubs and restaurants in malls were seized or closed for enforcement action. The food articles found unsafe or unfit for consumption were subsequently disposed of in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
The inspections were subsequently extended to fast food outlets and their supplying warehouses. Samples of mayonnaise, chicken and bread were collected for laboratory analysis.
At a popular fast food outlet on Brigade Road, officials found magnesium sulphite being used for the treatment or purification of used frying oil. A notice was issued and the matter is being examined under the applicable provisions.
The used-oil question
Used cooking oil has emerged as an important part of the food safety exercise because the problem is largely invisible to the consumer.
Under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO) initiative, used cooking oil is to be diverted from the food chain and collected through authorised agencies for conversion into biodiesel or other non-food products. FSSAI has fixed a limit of 25% for total polar compounds (TPC), beyond which vegetable oil should not be used for frying.
Karnataka has collected nearly 45.9 lakh litres of used cooking oil between 2024 and 2026 through four FSSAI-recognised agencies. The agencies channel the discarded oil to authorised biodiesel manufacturers.
The State’s enforcement exercise has brought renewed attention to whether used oil is being properly disposed of rather than finding its way back into kitchens. FSSAI also requires food businesses using more than 50 litres of edible oil a day for frying to maintain records of used-oil disposal.
For a diner, however, there is no way of knowing how many times oil has been reused or whether it has crossed permissible limits.
Government kitchens under scrutiny
The inspections have also moved into government premises. On August 12, food businesses at Vidhana Soudha, Legislators’ Home, Vikasa Soudha and the M.S. Buildings were inspected. At a canteen on the government premises, officials seized 500 grams each of expired suji rava and coconut powder. An advisory notice was issued over unhygienic conditions and a case is to be registered before the adjudicating authority. Ironically, even the canteen Arogya Soudha did not entirely meet the standards.
A milk parlour was issued a notice for labelling violations. Several hotels operating within the government complexes were also issued notices. The inspections also covered Indira Canteens. Officials reported violations involving labelling, misbranding and food handling.
Quick-commerce sector too
The food safety net has also reached the rapidly expanding quick-commerce sector.
Quick commerce warehouses in Hoskote taluk of Bengaluru Rural and Sakalawara of Bengaluru Urban were inspected on August 11 and 12. Officials reported non-compliant labelling, misbranding and unhygienic food handling and storage. One of the warehouses was sealed and a notice was issued to the other, with a case recommended before the adjudicating officer.
The move reflects a change in the way food safety has to be monitored. Food no longer moves simply from a market to a restaurant and then to a customer. Packaged food and fresh produce can pass through warehouses, cold storage facilities and quick-commerce fulfilment centres before reaching a household.
A lapse at any one of these points can compromise the product.
‘Public health must come before revenue’
Health Minister U.T. Khader said the decision to intensify inspections of premium establishments was not prompted by a specific complaint. He also said the government was not targeting hotels and acknowledged the contribution of the hospitality industry.
“We are not against anyone. We respect all the hoteliers for the contribution they have made to society. But they should not cheat the people,” he said.
Hotel managements might not always be aware of every lapse committed by employees, he said, but that could not be an excuse for inadequate systems. “They should not see only the revenue. They should also see the health of the public,” he said.
Mr. Khader indicated that the government was examining additional ways of monitoring food establishments, including the possibility of surveillance teams at the taluk level.
The health consequences
Concerns raised by the inspections are finally about how they impact people’s health.
Senior Hepatobiliary and Transplant Surgeon Sonal Asthana said the monsoon was a period when doctors typically see an increase in food- and water-borne infections. “Every monsoon, we see an upsurge in infections such as typhoid and hepatitis A, which are predominantly linked to contaminated food and water,” he said.
Certain infections can have complications affecting other organs. Bacterial infections can, in some cases, be followed by neurological complications such as Guillain-Barré syndrome. “The infection itself may not directly cause it, but some of the secondary sequelae of the infection can cause substantial damage,” Dr. Asthana said.
Hepatitis A and E can also, in severe cases, progress to acute liver failure. He said he had seen patients with these infections acquired through contaminated food or water, including cases where improperly washed raw vegetables had been a source of infection.
His message to consumers was not to stop eating out, but not to equate reputation with safety. “Just because you are eating in a posh place, do not assume that all the precautions have been taken,” he said.
“You cannot rely on just the outside facade. There has to be a high degree of compliance, not just at the personal level but also through enforcement of the law,” he said.
The kidney risk
Senior nephrologist and transplant surgeon Sankaran Sundar said food safety lapses could, in some infections, have longer-term consequences.
He pointed to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, which can be associated with undercooked meat or inadequately washed produce. Such infections can trigger haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition that can affect kidney function.
A proportion of patients recovering from HUS can develop longer-term complications such as proteinuria, hypertension and reduced kidney function.
“Hygiene lapses in kitchens are not just about an episode of food poisoning. They can, in some cases, leave a lasting kidney damage,” Sundar said.
He stressed the importance of proper storage, adequate cooking and careful handling and washing of produce.
Rotten meat never safe
The sight of spoiled meat has also prompted questions about implications of consuming it.
Vaishnavi Joshi, Consultant, Medical Oncology and Haemato-Oncology, said there was no established scientific evidence that eating rotten meat directly causes cancer. “The immediate concern is food poisoning caused by bacteria and their toxins. Spoilage can also produce compounds such as histamine, putrescine and cadaverine,” she said. “It has established dangers through contamination by bacteria or toxins,” Joshi said.
She distinguished this from the established evidence on processed meat, which the WHO classifies as carcinogenic to humans, with colorectal cancer being the strongest association. Her advice is simple: spoiled meat should be discarded, not washed, cooked or reheated in an attempt to make it safe.
What next after the raid?
Food Safety and Drug Administration Commissioner Srinivas K. said enforcement did not end with an inspection.
Reputed hotels and food establishments, he said, had also been found not following procedures prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, including cases involving expired milk and mislabelling of fish and meat.
He explained that a notice is generally issued by the designated officer in such cases. The Commissioner can call the food business operator for a personal hearing, following which fines can be imposed and the establishment required to rectify the deficiencies and submit a compliance report.
Where legal samples are found to be unsafe, the operator is given the prescribed opportunity to appeal. If the adverse finding is upheld after analysis by the Central laboratory, a prosecution case can be filed before the jurisdictional JMFC court.
Mr. Srinivas said regular surveillance was already in place and that food business operators were required to have their premises audited annually and report compliance.
The department had analysed about 45,000 samples annually during the past two years.
Industry seeks regular inspections
The hotel and restaurant industry has welcomed the inspections, but sought a more regular enforcement regime than one done in fits and starts.
G.K. Shetty, president of the Karnataka State Hotels’ Association, said inspections should be conducted at least once every three months. “If there are violations, let them give the hotels and restaurants a warning and a week to address the cleanliness and hygiene issues,” he said, cautioning that sudden closures could create fear among customers.
Mr. Shetty also sought simpler SOPs suited to Indian kitchen practices, saying the industry currently had nearly 100 guidelines to follow.
Ananth Narayan, president of the Bengaluru chapter of the National Restaurants’ Association of India, called for greater consultation with the industry. “FSDA officials and the Health Department must take all the stakeholders into confidence. They need to create awareness and educate everybody, but not through a raid,” he said, suggesting that discussions and warnings should complement enforcement.
Beyond the raids
The recent inspections have exposed gaps at very different points of Bengaluru’s food economy — from luxury hotels and international chains to government canteens and quick-commerce warehouses.
For the regulator, the challenge is to ensure that the exercise produces lasting changes rather than temporary compliance when an inspection team arrives. “The enforcement drive ultimately seeks to reinforce that food safety must begin with procurement and storage, continue through preparation and handling, and remain an everyday practice long after an inspection team has left,” the Health Minister said.
For the consumer, the lesson is basic. A sparkling dining area, a five-star rating or a familiar brand name cannot by itself establish what happens behind the kitchen door. The requirement is simple: When you pay for a meal, you expect good food and service — but, above all, you expect it to be safe and not put your health at risk.

headline: Rs 65-crore CBG plant in Ludhiana to tackle Budha Nallah pollution, sewer blocks
full_text:
Rs 65-crore CBG plant in Ludhiana to tackle Budha Nallah pollution, sewer blocks
Bhagwant Mann laid the foundation stone for a compressed biogas plant at Haibowal in Ludhiana. The project aims to stop dung from polluting Budha Nallah while generating fuel, fertiliser and jobs.
Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann on Friday laid the foundation stone of a Rs 65-crore compressed biogas plant at Haibowal in Ludhiana. The project is aimed at tackling sewer blockages and pollution in Budha Nallah by scientifically processing cattle dung generated at the dairy complex.
Officials said the plant, being developed on 2.5 acres, is expected to become operational by September 2027. It will process 300 tonnes of cattle dung every day, benefit 435 dairy owners under the 'Waste-to-Wealth' mission, and produce around five tonnes of compressed biogas and organic bio-fertiliser daily.
In a post on X, Mann said, "Today, laid the foundation stone of the Rs 65-crore Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) Plant at Haibowal, Ludhiana, which will be ready by September 2027. Under the 'Waste-to-Wealth' mission, the plant will scientifically process 300 tonnes of cattle dung every day. This will prevent waste from entering the Budha Nallah, help resolve the problem of sewer blockages and directly benefit 435 dairy owners."
Addressing a gathering after laying the foundation stone, the chief minister said, "Around 435 dairy owners in the area will directly benefit from this project, which is a major step towards the concept of 'Waste-to-Wealth'. Scientific utilisation of cattle dung will create new sources of income for dairy farmers. The plant will produce organic bio-fertiliser, helping reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers, improve soil fertility and promote organic farming. The plant will generate approximately five tonnes of CBG every day and create new opportunities for direct and indirect employment for the youth."
On green energy, Mann said, "More such plants will be installed across Punjab to promote green energy on one hand and curb the menace of pollution on the other. I also appeal to the people to ensure that untreated water is not put into the water sources of the state so that their purity can be maintained for the well-being of every human being." He also spoke about the expansion of canal irrigation infrastructure, saying, "Our government has laid 14,000 kilometres of pipes to provide canal water to farmers. In addition to this, another 7,000 kilometres of pipes will be laid by the end of this year. We have laid pipes and watercourses across Punjab to facilitate farmers in every nook and corner of the state, and this is benefiting them greatly by catering to their irrigation needs."
Mann also said the AAP would again form the government in 2027 and claimed opposition leaders would forfeit their security deposits in the polls. The Haibowal plant is being presented by the state government as a project that will address waste management and pollution, generate green energy, and create income opportunities for dairy owners.

headline: Despite the ₹5 lakh financial assistance provided by the Telangana government for the construction of houses under the Indiramma Indlu scheme, several beneficiaries have dipped into their savings or taken loans, as rising construction material and la...
full_text:
Despite the ₹5 lakh financial assistance provided by the Telangana government for the construction of houses under the Indiramma Indlu scheme, several beneficiaries have dipped into their savings or taken loans, as rising construction material and labour costs have pushed expenses beyond the sanctioned amount. Officials say shear wall technology could help keep construction costs within ₹5 lakh. However, the technology has not yet gained widespread acceptance.
G. Suraj (name changed), a youngster from Sangareddy district, was among the beneficiaries who saw his dream of owning a house take shape with the Indiramma Indlu scheme. But completing the house cost him an additional ₹5 lakh over and above the government subsidy.
While construction stretched over nine months as the prices of cement, steel, sand and other materials steadily increased, the delay was compounded by a shortage of labour, with masons and workers taking up other projects. He finally held his housewarming ceremony this year.
His experience is not an isolated one. Several beneficiaries across the State have had to dip into their hard-earned savings or take hand loans to complete their houses.
Rising costs
Meanwhile, beneficiaries cited two main reasons for spending beyond the ₹5 lakh subsidy: rising construction material costs, particularly those of bricks and sand, and increasing charges for masons and labourers. Some also pointed to delays in receiving subsidy instalments and masons taking up multiple projects.
This apart, the Telangana Housing Corporation Limited (TGHCL) officials point to another factor — the size of the house. The scheme envisages houses of 400 sq. ft., but beneficiaries sometimes extend slab projections beyond the permissible limits. Such additions, along with spending on tiles, tapware, woodwork and other costlier materials, can substantially increase the overall expenditure. The concern is particularly significant as the scheme expands. Unless costs are contained, more beneficiaries from economically weaker backgrounds could be forced to exhaust their savings, take on debt or face prolonged delays in completing their houses.
₹1 lakh hurdle
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy launched the Indiramma Indlu scheme in Bhadradri Kothagudem in March 2024, providing ₹5 lakh in 100% subsidy to poor, houseless families for constructing houses. The first phase envisaged 4.5 lakh houses, with 3,500 houses in each Assembly constituency. Only those who owned land but did not have a house were considered under Phase I.
The subsidy was to be released in four instalments. But beneficiaries had to spend ₹1 lakh on laying the foundation before becoming eligible for the first instalment. For many beneficiaries, arranging this initial amount itself has been a challenge.
Speaking about the progress of the scheme last month, Housing and Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivasa Reddy said that housewarming ceremonies were held for 1.35 lakh houses constructed under Phase I, while slabs had been laid for another 1.25 lakh houses.
The State government launched Phase II on June 1 this year, with plans to allot 2.5 lakh houses. Housing Minister said people living in huts would be given first priority.
Housing Department Secretary and TGHCL Managing Director V.P. Gautham said applications were received and the selection of beneficiaries was underway with officials conducting on field verification.
However, the ₹1 lakh requirement for laying the foundation remains a concern, particularly with Phase II targeting some of the State’s poorest families. According to sources, some applicants living in huts expressed their inability to arrange the money. “Some of them are already in debt. We are looking at options to help them generate the money. They definitely cannot afford to spend any amount over the ₹5 lakh subsidy,” sources said.
Slab extensions
The Housing Corporation has been aware of the problem of beneficiaries borrowing money to complete their houses. In a government order (G.O.) issued on June 27, Gautham noted that a majority of beneficiaries were extending slab projections from the permitted three feet to as much as eight feet beyond the building plan.
“This increase in slab area is resulting in substantial additional construction costs, compelling beneficiaries to borrow from private lenders or halt construction midway due to financial constraints. The above situation defeats the core objective of the government to provide subsidy housing to shelter-less poor families,” the G.O. stated. It said there was a need to restrict the maximum slab area to prevent cost escalation, avoid putting beneficiaries into a debt trap and facilitate completion of houses within the sanctioned financial assistance.
Housing Project Directors in various districts said planning and construction decisions play a crucial role in either containing or increasing costs. They suggested restricting slab extensions to three feet on the front side and one foot on the other three sides. Suggestions were also made on materials and designs that can prevent rainwater from entering through door and window openings without adding significantly to the construction cost.
Mr. Gautham said tokens for sand — a material whose cost can steadily increase — would be provided when a house is sanctioned, reducing beneficiaries’ dependence on private sellers. Talks have also been held with construction material manufacturers to reduce the number of intermediaries in the supply chain and provide materials directly to beneficiaries.
Shear wall solution
Another solution being explored by the Housing Corporation is shear wall technology, which officials say could help keep construction costs within the ₹5 lakh subsidy. Under this method, formworks or moulds made of plastic, aluminium or other materials are placed according to the required house design. Steel rods or mesh are embedded inside the moulds, which are then filled with cement. The roof can also be cast at the same time. Apart from reducing construction costs, the technology can significantly shorten the construction period. and this method is widely used in high-rise construction.
Saddi Mahender Reddy, Managing Director of A.S.A. Consultants, said aluminium formwork systems were commonly used for repetitive, mass-housing reinforced concrete construction, particularly residential towers with repetitive floor plans. However, the system requires a high initial investment. Formwork design, fabrication and procurement are project-specific and costly, making the technology economical when the cost is spread over a large number of repetitive pours — commonly 200-plus repetitions or 500-plus identical units or floors.
The technology can help complete a floor in three to five days, including walls, slab and staircase in a single pour, compared with seven to more than 10 days using conventional methods. But it requires careful planning since modifications to walls constructed using shear wall technology are difficult, electrical and plumbing sleeves have to be planned and embedded before casting. “Constructions using shear wall technology require early, finalised structural and architectural coordination — all wall positions must be locked before formwork fabrication, leaving little tolerance for late design iteration,” Mr. Mahender said.
Housing Project Director, Sangareddy, Ch. Chalapathi Rao said the technology was particularly viable in areas such as Patancheru, where land was scarce. It could also benefit beneficiaries who cannot afford to take time off to supervise construction for several months. Houses can be built in 15 to 30 days using shear wall technology, he said.
The technology has already been tested in some parts of the State. Houses were constructed in 12 days in Asifabad. In Aroor village of Sadashivpet mandal in Sangareddy district, nearly 10 Indiramma houses have been built using the shear wall technology.
One of the beneficiaries, Padma Anthaiah, had earlier lived in a house that suffered from seepage. He said he did not spend anything over the ₹5 lakh subsidy on constructing his new 400-sq.-ft. house, apart from the cost of a metal staircase outside the house.
The new houses in the village are interspersed with the new structures built using shear wall technology. Showing the exterior walls of one of the houses, Reshma Katakam, Assistant Engineer (Housing), Sadashivpet mandal, said that they do not need another layer of cement for a smooth finish, unlike conventional brick walls.
Aroor Panchayat Secretary Malkapuram Mallesham said the technology was particularly useful for people who could not afford additional expenditure on house construction. However, there is a hiccup. Private contractors who build the houses using shear wall technology are demanding ₹5 lakh upfront payment and not in instalments.
Upfront payment hurdle
In Aroor, Sarpanch Naikoti Lavanya Madhu said discussions were held with contractors to find a solution. Construction materials were provided in coordination with store owners, while beneficiaries and village leaders signed bond papers to facilitate the transfer of instalments after construction. But beneficiaries in some other parts of the State said they did not have ₹5 lakh to pay contractors upfront and, therefore, could not opt for the shear wall technology. Unless the upfront-payment issue and delays in the release of instalments are addressed, widespread adoption of shear wall technology could face roadblocks. Officials also believe that greater awareness of the technology among Gram Panchayat members is necessary.
Housing Corporation officials said there was no mandatory time gap between different stages of construction for releasing instalments. If a house is completed within a few weeks, the instalments can be released at one go.
The officials also said that one of the ways to address the issues with need for capital upfront is to help women Self Help Groups (SHG) own these formworks (molds) and give them on lease to local masons. “If the lease amount is collected later, the burden on beneficiaries will come down. The SHGs may have sufficient business since the second phase of the housing scheme too is rolled out,” said an official from the corporation.
SHGs could provide the answer
Officials are also exploring a model that could reduce the need for beneficiaries to arrange large sums upfront. One proposal is to help women’s Self-Help Groups (SHGs) own the formworks and lease them to local masons. The lease amount could be collected later, reducing the immediate financial burden on beneficiaries. “If the lease amount is collected later, the burden on beneficiaries will come down. The SHGs may have sufficient business since the second phase of the housing scheme too has been rolled out,” a Housing Corporation official said.

headline: Bengaluru: The Karnataka government has proposed a Bill to regulate the usage of public spaces by ‘unregistered organisations’, which would bar such entities from using public property and spaces without requisite permissions.
full_text:
Bengaluru: The Karnataka government has proposed a Bill to regulate the usage of public spaces by ‘unregistered organisations’, which would bar such entities from using public property and spaces without requisite permissions.
The latest move by the Congress-led government further intensifies the growing conflict between the ruling party and its objections to organisations like the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), which has a significant presence in the southern state.
Priyank Kharge, Karnataka’s minister for home affairs said that the Cabinet has approved The Karnataka Regulation of Use of Government Premises and Public Property Bill, 2026 which seeks to regulate and govern the use of Government premises and public property by private individuals, organisations, associations and societies.
“It provides a legal framework to safeguard, preserve, and ensure the responsible utilisation of Government lands, buildings, playgrounds, parks, roads, and other public assets, preventing misuse while protecting them for public benefit and good,” he wrote in a post on X.
He added that the government is not using this Bill to target any institution or organisation. “Why is everyone thinking this is to curtail or curb any particular institution, association, organisation, society, club, union, syndicate or NGO? Beats me.”
The Cabinet has approved The Karnataka Regulation of Use of Government Premises and Public Property Bill, 2026.
The Bill seeks to regulate and govern the use of Government premises and public property by private individuals, organizations, associations and societies. It provides…

Though details of the proposed Bill are yet to be made available, it follows a previous dispute 10 months ago regarding a proposed RSS march on 19 October 2025, in Kharge’s constituency of Chitapur (Kalaburagi), which was halted over law and order concerns.
At the time, a petition filed on behalf of the RSS saw the courts direct the authorities to review the application and submit a report by 2 October. This led to heated exchanges between the ruling Congress and RSS, the ideological parent of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the principal Opposition in Karnataka.
The RSS is legally recognised by courts and tax authorities as a “body of individuals”. “We have nothing to hide. There are many institutions and traditional organisations that are not registered. We function publicly, invite people to understand our work and are transparent about our activities. Such political gimmicks are not new to us,” RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat had said at the time.
Kharge has used several platforms to question the historical record and legal status of the RSS, warning that the Karnataka government will introduce legislation requiring the organisation to register under the law.

“That was the RSS. That died. It’s gone. Today the RSS is the instrument of Mr (Gautam) Adani. That’s all it is. And they stand there with their lathis and all, making a fool of themselves,” Gandhi said on Thursday.
The Karnataka home department, under Kharge, has spared no opportunity to pull up the RSS, including over its ‘Har Ghar Tiranga’ campaign.
“For over five decades after Independence, the RSS did not hoist the National Flag at its Nagpur headquarters. The tricolour was officially hoisted only in 2002. Before lecturing every Indian on patriotism, perhaps the BJP should first explain why its ideological parent choose the Bhagwa Dhwaj over the Tricolour and why the national flag was absent from its own headquarters for so long,” Kharge posted on X.

headline: TMC national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee had met Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Wednesday
full_text:
TMC national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee had met Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Wednesday
NEW DELHI: The Trinamool Congress is preparing to move the Supreme Court against the 20 rebel Lok Sabha MPs who merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India. A disqualification petition will be filed within 10 days, TMC sources said.TMC national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee had met Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Wednesday to reiterate his demand for a speedy decision on the disqualification petitions submitted by TMC in June. Later addressing the media, Banerjee had expressed concern over the lack of any action on the matter so far and said that he did not receive any satisfactory response.âIf the Speaker does not decide on these petitions within the period required by law and applicable judicial directions, I will be compelled to approach the Supreme Court and seek its intervention,â Banerjee said.Banerjee had earlier met Birla on July 27 in Parliament urging him to expedite his decision on pending petitions seeking disqualification of the 20 MPs, elected on TMC symbol, who have aligned with NCPI.Banerjee, a Lok Sabha MP, had also sought revocation of changes made to the seating arrangements of his partyâs MPs to allow the rebel members to sit separately. He had submitted separate letters to the speaker on each of his concerns.
In one of the two letters, Banerjee stated, âMore than five weeks have elapsed since filing of the petitions. To date, no notices have been issued, no hearings have been scheduled, and no procedural directions appear to have been passed. Such continued action is a matter of grave concern.â On June 19, a TMC delegation led by Banerjee had submitted the 20 disqualification petitions to Birla.He had said the urgency of the matter has been further accentuated by the decision of parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju to invite the members against whom the disqualification petitions are pending, as a separate group, to the all-party meeting held on July 19. âSuch developments underscore the imperative for an expeditious determination of the petitions,â he stated to emphasise his point.

headline: Referring to the news item, SC said these issues have highlighted the poor disposal rate of consumer commissions including the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).
full_text:
Referring to the news item, SC said these issues have highlighted the poor disposal rate of consumer commissions including the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).
NEW DELHI: Flagging slow disposal in consumer forums, Supreme Court on Thursday said the consumer dispute redressal commissions cannot be the place for rehabilitation of retired judges and bureaucrats and said a detailed pan-India performance evaluation exercise of these quasi-judicial bodies is urgently needed.In a case relating to pay and allowances of members of consumer forums across the country of which the court had taken suo motu cognisance five years ago, a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it came across a disturbing news report narrating the plight of consumers who are denied a hearing for four years. âIf this is the way the consumer forums function, what benefit is it for the consumers who are mandated to approach the specialized quasi-judicial body? The members of consumer forums are asking for more and more facilities and perks. Vacancies and infrastructure in these forums remain a cause for concern. But are the forums justifying their salaries, perks and facilities? The purpose of constituting these commissions appears to have been frustrated,â the CJI said.Referring to the news item, SC said these issues have highlighted the poor disposal rate of consumer commissions including the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).
Advocate Priyadarshi told SC that vacancy position, infrastructure and pay and allowances of members of consumer forums should be heard together. âWe request the president of NCDRC to send a report with respect to â total pendency of cases, total composition of the commission (vacancies), average rate of disposal, estimated time to decide pending matters and the need for increasing the strength of the commission,â it said and sought report within two weeks.
It also sought details from the states about the pendency and disposal rate of state and district commissions. More than 5.7 lakh cases are pending in the three-tier consumer dispute redressal commissions, of which the district forums account for more than 4 lakh cases and state forums another 1.2 lakh cases.SC also asked additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati to inquire from Union govt the feasibility of creating benches of NCDRC in four regions to prevent poor consumers from travelling to Delhi for grievance redressal.

headline: Vipul Goyal to Samay's friend Balraj: Who are the other 4 who got Supreme Court relief over disabled persons remarks?
full_text:
Vipul Goyal to Samay's friend Balraj: Who are the other 4 who got Supreme Court relief over disabled persons remarks?
The court noted their efforts and said they had taken steps in a positive direction following the controversy surrounding the show.
The Supreme Court on Friday quashed all FIRs against comedian Samay Raina and others over alleged insensitive remarks about persons with disabilities made during the comedy show 'India's Got Latent'.
The court passed the order after noting the accused's compliance with its directions to conduct awareness programmes and raise funds for persons with disabilities.
The other comedians who received relief are Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar alias Sonali Aditya Desai, and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar.
Deep Dive
The order came after Raina and the other accused complied with the Supreme Court's earlier directions to conduct awareness programmes and raise funds for persons with disabilities.
The court noted their efforts and said they had taken steps in a positive direction following the controversy surrounding the show.
Also Read | ‘Very bright youngsters’: SC relief to Samay Raina, others over disabled persons remarks on Latent show
What did SC say?
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the order on Friday.
The court specifically took note of the efforts made by Raina, Goyal, Ghai, Thakkar and Tanwar to organise shows for persons with disabilities as part of the directions issued in the case.
"Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there. They are very bright youngsters. If they have started working in a positive direction, there will be positive output," the court said.
Also Read | ‘Genuine efforts’: Supreme Court drops criminal cases against Samay Raina, 4 comedians
Criminal proceedings against Raina and others come to an end
The Supreme Court's order brings the criminal proceedings against the five comedians to an end. The court said that proceedings against respondents 6-10, who are the accused comedians in the matter, stood closed and that the criminal proceedings against them were being quashed.
"Matter qua respondents 6-10 (the accused comedians) is closed. Criminal proceedings against respondents 6-10 are hereby quashed. All other related proceedings are set aside. List to issue directions on the larger issue," the Court said.
However, the broader issue surrounding the regulation and scrutiny of content that may be insensitive towards persons with disabilities remains before the Supreme Court.
The top court will continue hearing the matter to consider suggestions from persons with disabilities on ways to ensure better checks on such content. It is also expected to issue appropriate directions on the larger issues involved in the case.
What was the controversy?
The controversy stems from an episode of 'India's Got Latent' that was recorded on November 14, 2024, and broadcast later. The episode subsequently came under scrutiny over allegations that some of the remarks made on the show were obscene and insensitive towards persons with disabilities.
The controversy led to multiple criminal cases being filed against several people associated with the show and those who appeared on it. The matter eventually reached the Supreme Court, which considered the cases and issued directions to the accused comedians as part of the proceedings.
As part of the relief process, the comedians were directed to undertake awareness initiatives and contribute towards efforts for persons with disabilities. The Supreme Court on Friday noted their compliance with these directions before quashing the FIRs and related criminal proceedings against them.

headline: The State-wide demonstrations called by AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami on Friday saw scores of his camp followers taking part in the agitation and the ranks of rebels suffering a split. Mr. Palaniswami addressed a rally in Thanjavur...
full_text:
The State-wide demonstrations called by AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami on Friday saw scores of his camp followers taking part in the agitation and the ranks of rebels suffering a split. Mr. Palaniswami addressed a rally in Thanjavur, along with his party colleagues deputy leader of the party in the Assembly O.S. Manian and former Food Minister R. Kamaraj, who was a member of the dissidents’ camp three months ago. The agitation was called to criticise the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led regime for not effecting a full waiver of cooperative crop loans taken by farmers; being “lax” on the Mekedatu dam issue; and on not securing the State’s share of Cauvery water, besides demanding the supply of 24-hour power supply to farmers. Among the prominent rebels who broke ranks on the day was former Electricity Minister P. Thangamani, who participated in the protest in Salem and expressed hope that Mr. Palaniswami would soon become the Chief Minister again. Former Ministers P. Balakrishna Reddy and K.C. Veeramani were present at the protests in their designated places of Namakkal and Tirupattur respectively. After 25 rebel MLAs of the AIADMK voted in favour of the TVK-led regime, which eventually won a vote of confidence in the Assembly on May 13, Mr. Palaniswami removed Mr. Thangamani, Mr. Reddy, Mr. Kamaraj, and Mr. Veeramani from their party position as district secretaries for Namakkal, Krishnagiri, Tiruvarur, and Tirupattur respectively. Those who did not take part in the day’s agitation, despite being named to lead the programme, were deputy general secretary Natham R. Viswanathan, who was assigned Ramanathapuram; another deputy general secretary S.P. Velumani (Theni) and K.P. Anbalagan (Ranipet). Till the middle of May, the three also held the posts of district secretaries for Dindigul (east), Coimbatore (suburban-south), and Dharmapuri respectively. Mr. Palaniswami urged the State government to ensure the supply of adequate water to farmers in the delta during the samba cultivation season. He explained how farmers had “suffered” for want of water during the current kuruvai season. Accusing the TVK-led government of failing to fulfil its electoral promises, he called upon the government to at least honour its commitment with regard to the full waiver of crop loans, as stated in its manifesto.

headline: The Ministry of Defence on Friday (August 14, 2026) signed contracts worth ₹1,577 crore with Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL) and NIBE Ltd for the Indian Army.
full_text:
The Ministry of Defence on Friday (August 14, 2026) signed contracts worth ₹1,577 crore with Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL) and NIBE Ltd for the Indian Army.
The procurement of 84 loiter munition systems, 840 loiter munitions and accessories will enhance the Army’s precision-strike capability at ranges of up to 100 km.
The contracts, signed in the presence of Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh in New Delhi, have been processed under the ‘Buy Indian’ category through the Fast Track Procedure. The procurement provides for 60% overall indigenous content, including a minimum of 50% indigenous content in materials, components and software.
TASL, the L-1 vendor, will supply 54 loiter munition systems and 540 munitions at a cost of ₹1,013.77 crore, while NIBE, the L-2 vendor, will provide 30 systems and 300 munitions for ₹563.36 crore.
The systems, with a range of up to 100 km, are intended to bridge a gap in the Army’s precision-strike capability. At present, the Army’s precision-strike capability beyond the 40-50 km range is largely dependent on BrahMos missiles.
A limited number of artillery regiments and batteries have already been operationalised with loiter munition systems under Phase-I, and more units are proposed to be equipped under the latest procurement.
The Ministry said the acquisition would enhance the operational effectiveness of Artillery Regiments and provide a major boost to indigenous defence manufacturing and the government’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
The equipment is scheduled to be delivered within 12 months from the date of advance payment.

headline: Karnataka minister seeks to skip I-Day flag-hoisting duty, BJP demands his removal
full_text:
Karnataka minister seeks to skip I-Day flag-hoisting duty, BJP demands his removal
A political row erupted in the Karnataka Assembly on Friday over Housing Minister Zameer Ahmed Khan's letter seeking relief from his Independence Day flag-hoisting assignment, with BJP MLA Sunil Kumar questioning his decision and Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara defending him.
Karnataka Minister Zameer Ahmed Khan's request to be exempted from Independence Day flag-hoisting duty in Vijayanagara triggered a heated political row on Friday, with the BJP accusing him of disrespecting the national festival and demanding his removal from the state Cabinet.
Khan, who represents Chamarajpet in Bengaluru and holds the Housing portfolio, had written to Chief Minister D K Shivakumar on Thursday seeking exemption from both the flag-hoisting duty and the responsibility of Vijayanagara district in-charge minister. Following his request, the state government assigned the August 15 flag-hoisting duty in Vijayanagara to Minister K S Basavanthappa.
WHY ZAMEER SOUGHT EXEMPTION
In his letter, Khan cited upcoming local body elections, including those to the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), Assembly bypolls and party organisational activities as reasons for seeking exemption from the district in-charge responsibility.
He said he would not have sufficient time to discharge the duties of a district in-charge minister and requested that he not be assigned the responsibility of any district.
Khan also said he had been assigned to hoist the national flag in Vijayanagara on August 15 but would not be able to attend, seeking exemption from the duty.
He noted that he had earlier been tasked with assessing the drought situation in Vijayanagara and had already submitted his report.
Khan had served as the in-charge minister of Vijayanagara during the previous Siddaramaiah-led government. Both Khan and Basavanthappa were inducted into the Cabinet on August 3.
BJP ATTACKS ZAMEER OVER I-DAY DUTY
The issue was raised in the Assembly by senior BJP MLA Sunil Kumar, who questioned why a minister would seek exemption from hoisting the national flag on Independence Day.
"If a minister cannot attend a national festival, then why have such a minister? Is he so big and busy that he cannot hoist the national flag?" Kumar asked.
Displaying Khan's letter, Kumar questioned whether accepting such a request reflected a lack of respect for the national flag and the Independence Day celebrations.
He demanded action against Khan, saying Karnataka did not need a minister who did not have time to participate in the national celebration.
BJP MLA and former Deputy Chief Minister C N Ashwath Narayan also criticised Khan's decision. "This act cannot be defended or supported. No Indian would conduct themselves in such a manner, but it is unfortunate such a person is the Minister in Karnataka. This is an insult to the state, country and the national flag," he said.
PARAMESHWARA DEFENDS MINISTER
Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara defended Khan, saying the minister's request appeared to be aimed at being assigned another district and that health concerns were involved.
"He is unwell to go to Vijayanagara, as it is far away. He has made a request," Parameshwara said.
However, BJP members pointed out that health reasons were not mentioned in Khan's letter, which cited his political and organisational responsibilities and said he would not be able to attend the August 15 programme.
Sunil Kumar rejected the Deputy Chief Minister's explanation and accused the government of defending the minister. "What health? People can't tolerate such things... Don't defend such things. Suspend such a minister. Why keep him?" Kumar said.
Parameshwara reiterated that Khan appeared to be indicating that he would be unable to travel to Vijayanagara due to ill health and that the Chief Minister had accordingly made alternative arrangements.
BJP WALKS OUT OF ASSEMBLY
The exchange escalated as Sunil Kumar questioned the government's handling of the issue and said the BJP did not need lessons on respecting the national flag.
BJP MLAs subsequently staged a walkout from the Assembly, describing the government's handling of the matter as "disgraceful".
Speaking to reporters outside the Assembly, Leader of Opposition R Ashoka termed Khan's decision "an insult to the country" and demanded action from the Chief Minister.
Ashoka warned that failure to act against the minister could encourage others in the government to behave similarly.
"No stringent action has yet been taken against those who had raised pro-Pakistan slogans at Vidhana Soudha. Now, a minister has also shown disrespect towards the country. If action is not taken against the minister, the people themselves will teach him a lesson," he said.

headline: A 45-year-old autorickshaw driver was arrested by Gudiyatham town police in Vellore on Friday for murdering his wife, a head constable who was on duty, over a family dispute.
full_text:
A 45-year-old autorickshaw driver was arrested by Gudiyatham town police in Vellore on Friday for murdering his wife, a head constable who was on duty, over a family dispute.
The police identified the arrested person as K. Aravindan, 45, a resident of Erthangal village near Gudiyatham town.
The couple Aravindan and Thamarai Selvi, 41, had two sons and lived in Erthangal village.
The police said the couple had been quarreling over a share in Aravindan’s ancestral property. As a result, Thamarai Selvi was living with her children at her mother’s house in the same village for the past two months. She refused to return to Aravindan’s house before the property issue was settled.
The police said that in July this year, Aravindan’s brother and family had given a petition at the Office of Superintendent of Police about threats from Thamarai Selvi over property share. An inquiry into the allegations is also under way.
Thamarai Selvi was on duty in Erthangal village near town when Aravindan told her that he wanted to discuss the family dispute. The police said that she went with him near a lake where a heated argument broke out. In a fit of rage, Aravindan allegedly stabbed her on the neck with a pair of scissors. She collapsed in a pool of blood on the spot. He also inflicted injuries upon himself, police said.
Passersby saw the injured couple and alerted the ambulance. They also informed Gudiyatham police. Thamarai Selvi was declared dead by doctors at Government Taluk Hospital in Gudiyatham town. Aravindan was shifted to Government Medical College Hospital in Vellore town for treatment. A case was registered. A probe is under way.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Friday (August 14, 2026) said the government has accorded the highest priority to modernising the armed forces and building a self-reliant, future-ready defence sector, with India emerging as a major defence manufacturing hub and net exporter.
Addressing soldiers through Akashvani on the eve of the 80th Independence Day, Mr. Singh highlighted the transformation of the defence sector over the past 12 years under initiatives such as ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ and ‘Make in India’.

He said domestic defence production had risen from ₹46,000 crore in 2014 to a record ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, nearly a four-fold increase. Public sector entities accounted for around 76% of production, while the private sector’s share rose to 24%.
Defence exports, he said, had increased from ₹686 crore in 2013-14 to an all-time high of ₹38,424 crore in 2025-26, a rise of more than 5,500%. India now has 145 defence exporters supplying products to more than 80 countries. Mr. Singh said the government was confident of achieving the ₹50,000-crore defence export target by 2029.
The Defence Minister said the defence budget had increased from ₹2.53 lakh crore in 2013-14 to ₹7.85 lakh crore in 2026-27, while capital expenditure rose to ₹2.19 lakh crore. The R&D allocation has also increased by 90% to ₹29,100 crore.

Procurement reforms
Over the past year, the Defence Acquisition Council has accorded Acceptance of Necessity to projects worth more than ₹8.75 lakh crore. Mr. Singh also highlighted procurement reforms, including doubling the financial powers of field commanders and facilitating more than ₹1.25 lakh crore of procurement through the revenue route to promote indigenisation.
Listing recent technological achievements, he referred to trials of the Tactical Advanced Range Augmentation system, MIRV-equipped Advanced Agni missile, Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile, RudraM-II, Naval Anti-Ship Missile-SR and Pinaka Long-Range Guided Rocket.
He said the successful test of an active-cooled full-scale scramjet combustor for over 1,200 seconds had placed India among select nations pursuing hypersonic missile technology. He also cited the first successful test of the indigenous Kusha long-range surface-to-air missile.
Mr. Singh also underlined the government’s focus on border infrastructure, welfare of serving and retired personnel, and greater participation of women in the armed forces. He cited the commissioning of the first batch of women cadets trained at the National Defence Academy and the tri-service all-women circumnavigation expedition, ‘Samudra Pradakshina’.
Noting that 2026 marks 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’, Mr. Singh urged citizens to celebrate Independence Day with patriotism and dedicate themselves to nation-building and the goal of Viksit Bharat.

headline: The government on Friday (August 14, 2026) said it has decided to remove the 12-minute advertisement duration cap for television channels to enable fair competition and ensure ease of doing business.
full_text:
The government on Friday (August 14, 2026) said it has decided to remove the 12-minute advertisement duration cap for television channels to enable fair competition and ensure ease of doing business.
“In India, the sector is heavily dependent on advertising, irrespective of whether a channel is ‘pay’ or ‘free-to-air’. Furthermore, there was a non-level playing field for traditional TV channels vis-à-vis digital media, where no such stipulation on advertisement cap regulation exists,” said the Information & Broadcasting Ministry.
The Ministry said there is adequate competition within the TV industry and between TV and digital media, and the government has therefore decided to remove the duration cap.
“The decision shall come into effect from the date of notification of the amendment in the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994 in the Gazette,” it said.
The cap was introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, when there were only 62 TV channels, compared with more than 900 currently.
At that time, Cable TV, the main platform for delivering TV channels, was analog and had limited carriage capacity, offering consumers very limited choice.
“Following the complete digitisation of the Cable TV sector, all TV distribution platforms, including DTH, Cable TV, HITS and IPTV, are now digital. These platforms currently carry 300 and 500 channels or more, meeting diverse consumer needs and enabling greater variety,” said the Ministry.
“Consequently, there is now adequate competition in market dynamics. In view of the changes that have occurred in the TV broadcasting sector, a need was felt to revisit the stipulations relating to advertisement duration,” it added.

headline: Weather Bee: Dry second week of August erased monsoon gains from the first week
full_text:
Weather Bee: Dry second week of August erased monsoon gains from the first week
India monsoon: Dry second week of August erased gains from the first week, pushing the cumulative rainfall deficit back to 10.5%, IMD data shows.
The correlation between El Niño and India’s monsoon rainfall is best assessed at the seasonal scale, meaning a week or two of heavy or deficient rain does not necessarily reflect its impact. August so far is a case in point: after a rainy first week, a dry second week pushed the monsoon’s cumulative deficit back to the July 31 level, even as the area under deficient rainfall remains marginally lower.
The biggest impact of the rain in the first week of August was seen in a decline in the cumulative deficit. India’s cumulative deficit compared to the 1971-2020 average, which the India Meteorological Department (IMD) considers as the Long Period Average (LPA) for tracking rain’s performance, reached 9%, the lowest it has been since June 5. This happened despite the August surplus at the time being a modest 1.6%. This is because August is one of the two rainiest months of the monsoon in the LPA, which leads to even small surpluses in the month mattering more for the cumulative deficit.
The second week has had the opposite effect. With big deficits, August rain has developed a 10.5% deficit. This has also returned the monsoon’s cumulative deficit to 10.5%, the same level it was on July 31.
To be sure, the cumulative deficit going back to July 31 does not mean that the area under “deficient” or “large deficient” categories has increased in any meaningful way. These categories are reserved for a local deficit of 20%-59% and 60% or more, respectively.
Surpluses of similar degrees are called “excess” or “larger excess”, while rain within 20% of the LPA is called normal. The area under the deficient categories was 46.2% on July 31. This decreased to 45.3% on August 7 and has increased only marginally to 45.4% by August 14.
In fact, compared to August 7, the area under the excess categories has also increased from 16.6% to 16.7%.
To be sure, the geographical pattern of the area under deficient categories has changed significantly compared to July 31. For example, states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand, Assam, and Haryana have seen deficient area decrease by almost 10% of their total area. Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka have also seen such area decrease by over 5%. On the other hand, deficient area has increased by over 5% of the state’s total area in Telangana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Chhattisgarh, and Maharashtra since July 31.
These trends highlight that assessing the overall monsoon situation after a couple of weeks of good or bad rain is not wise. This is especially true of the geographical distribution of rain. For example, as HT has reported earlier, even the correlation between El Niño and rainfall is not uniform for all regions of the country. It has become weaker over time for central India while remaining relatively stable for northern and southern India. The final impact of El Niño will only be seen in the final print of the monsoon on September 30, with the current status not very far from the forecast for the season by the IMD.

Vijayendra said: “Though the name of the RSS has not been directly mentioned in the Bill, it is clear that the Chief Minister and the Home Minister are trying to indirectly target the RSS.”

I have the protection from the Constitution to come out of my house and I have the moral courage given by Babasaheb Ambedkar to talk freely.”

headline: West Bengal started serving an unmarked proforma across the madrasas, mosques, and idgahs across the State seeking details of foreign funding source, foreign visitors, and also the distance of the premises from the international border.
full_text:
West Bengal started serving an unmarked proforma across the madrasas, mosques, and idgahs across the State seeking details of foreign funding source, foreign visitors, and also the distance of the premises from the international border.
The incident sparked an outrage by the madrasa and mosque authorities while a group of human rights activists also submitted a memorandum to the Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari and Director General of Police Siddh Nath Gupta seeking an immediate inquiry into the matter and clarification for such survey.
The said proforma distributed by police in multiple madrasas across districts such as Barrackpore, Birbhum, Malda, Murshidabad, Haroa, North and South 24 Parganas, the authorities of these religious organisations have been asked at least 26 questions under a title ‘Proforma for survey of Madrasah’ or ‘Proforma for survey of mosque/ idgah/ mazar’.
Apart from their name, address with GPS coordination, categorical affiliation, ownership, registration number, photograph of the premises, number of staff and students, these questions include the source of foreign funding, the details of the foreign visitors in the last three years, any foreign exchange programme of students being run currently, and the distance of the prmeises from border areas.
The information regarding any legal dispute over the premises, FIR or chargesheet filed against any staff, and political affiliation of any staff, faculty, or alumni have also been sought in the questionnaires.
The survey is being run by the police and the Department of Minority Affairs of West Bengal. However, what rose concerns among the people and the activists that the proforma does not bear any reference to any related government notification, name of the issuing authority, official stamp, seal, memo or order number, date, or any specific legal provision under which the survey is being conducted.
The staff from several madrasas and mosques also reported that the police served it late at night and also often engaged in heated exchange with the locals. At around 12 a.m. on August 12, a team of police personnel including the inspector of Nimta Police Station in Barrackpore visited the Masjid Baitul Muazzam and a nearby madrasa to serve the form and asked to submit all the details at the police station by next morning, said a staff Jahangir Ali.
In Birbhum’s Lohapir Jama Masjid, three civic volunteers from Nalhati Police Station served the proforma on August 6 for all the mosques and madrasas to one mosque head, Azizur Rahman. “When we objected, they said it is part of a regular survey. We also asked for the government notification, seals, and issuing authority names. They didn’t respond anything but said we must submit all the details within a day. However, we all have decided not to submit it now until they serve a professional proforma with a government notification attached to it,” said Mr. Rahaman.
The Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR), West Bengal Chapter, has expressed concern over survey forms being handed over to the committees of mosques, madrasas, Idgahs and mazars in different parts of the State.
“Such an exercise, particularly when it involves sensitive information concerning religious institutions, should be carried out only on the basis of a clear and identifiable government order and under a defined legal framework. At present, the copies of the forms available with APCR do not clearly mention any Government Notification, Memo Number, date, issuing authority or specific legal provision under which the information is being sought. The question is therefore simple and legitimate: If these forms have been issued under an official government or police order, why has that order not been made available to the concerned institutions and the public?” said the secretary of APCR, Umar Awais.
The acitivists also expressed their concerns over the purpose of the government to conduct this survey. It stated that hat the statewide survey of madrasas initiated by the Department of Minority Affairs and Madrasah Education is a separate matter. The existence of a government-approved madrasa survey cannot, by itself, establish the authority for every separate police form or for the collection of additional sensitive information.
In their letter to the CM and DG, they also urged to maintain the transparency of such survey in which the government asked a slew of sensitive information. “However, such exercises must be transparent, lawful and non-discriminatory and must not result in profiling or selective targeting of any particular religious community. If this is an official government survey, let the government order be made public. If it is a police initiative, the authorities must clearly state under which law and for what purpose such sensitive information is being collected from religious institutions,” it said.
DG Siddh Nath Gupta did not respond to the calls. However, Birbhum SP Vidit Raj Bhundesh said that he has no knowledge about the survey. The inspector of Nimta Police Station in Barrackpore, Rahul Deb Mondal admitted that he served the proforma to some local madrasas but refused to comment further on the development.

headline: India@79: Age, wage and rage | Number Theory
full_text:
India@79: Age, wage and rage | Number Theory
India enters its 80th year of independence today.
India enters its 80th year of independence today. The journey so far has been tumultuous in many ways but also one of significant achievements. Today, as the world’s largest democracy and its most populous country – India only overtook China on this count in 2023 – India’s challenges are best described by talking about the country’s demographic, its employment prospects and the anxieties around these two factors. Here is what data can tell us about it.
- India has the largest number of people and young people in the worldIndia’s expected population, according to UN estimates, is around 1.48 billion in 2026. It is the most populous country in the world for a and is expected to remain so until 2100, the last year for which UN projections are available. Even if one were to look at the share of the young population at multiple thresholds – under fifteen, under twenty, or under thirty – India continues to be the most populous by a distance.
- But India is not the youngest country in terms of median ageIf one were to compare the median age of the population for all 237 countries for which UN data is available, India’s 2026 median age of 29.2 years is ranked 95th youngest. Even if one were to restrict the comparison to top ten countries by population, India is ranked only fifth youngest behind Nigeria, Ethiopia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
- And the average Indian has been getting older for a long time nowIndia’s long-term median age trend, according to UN data, bottomed out in the 1970s at just about 18. Since then it has been increasing steadily, crossing 20 and 25 in 1993 and 2015. India’s median age will cross 30 in 2029 and 40 in 2056, if UN projections are to be believed. India’s workers, if one uses government reports on labour market – Employment Unemployment Surveys till 2011-12 and periodic Labour Force Surveys subsequently – are about to hit a median age of 40. The numbers were 33, 35, 36, 38 and 39 in 1993-94, 2004-05, 2011-12, 2017-18 and 2025.
- Younger Indians are increasingly moving out of farmingThis is the most important demographic factor when it comes to Indian workers. Between 1993-94 and 2025, the median age gap between workers in agriculture and outside agriculture increased from zero to six years.
- This is what makes it generating well paying jobs the most important challenge facing IndiaYoung workers giving up on farming, getting educated and aspiring for better jobs in India. But a large number of salaried jobs in India, especially outside the government, do not even give basic safeguards to workers. This shows in India’s official labour market statistics, which show that almost half of them do not offer either a written contract, paid leave or social security. Unless India fixes the decent wage problem , the rage of the young Indian will keep increasing.

headline: Data will remain confidential, canât be used for legal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosure
full_text:
Data will remain confidential, canât be used for legal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosure
NEW DELHI: The second phase of Census 2027 â involving population enumeration â will, for the first time, capture caste âas declared by the respondentâ among its 40 fields, which include new ones such as number of bank accounts, place of Covid vaccination and voter card number.Enumeration by caste will not delve into whether it falls under the other backward classes (OBC) category. However, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes will be enumerated as earlier.The questionnaire notified Friday shall also seek name of spouse, parentsâ particulars and nationality â elements captured by the National Population Register (NPR) exercise undertaken alongside Census 2011. NPR updation was, however, delinked from Census 2027.The new fields in the list of 40 questions â up from 29 asked during Census 2011 â also include respondentâs nationality as declared, permanent address, mobile-phone number, Aadhaar number, passport number and availability of driving licence. While mobile-phone number, Aadhaar number and voter ID may be shared if available, passport number is required only from an Indian passport holder.Sources told TOI that mother and fatherâs particulars are likely to capture their names, date of birth and place of birth.
While these are key factors that determine citizenship/nationality, their capture will have no impact on individuals since individual census data must remain confidential and cannot be used for âlegal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosureâ, as per the govt.Sources also said giving a drop-down menu for recording OBC status was not found feasible because states have different castes categorised as OBCs and a mismatch between communities recognised as such by Centre and those at state level. They also pointed to states expanding their respective OBC lists by adding more castes â something that could have created logistical problems once census was under way.Officials told TOI that unlike the socio-economic caste census conducted in 2011 â which had returned around 46 lakh castes, making it unusable â the digital mode of Census 2027 and availability of modern, AI-based tools can surmount compilation and segregation challenges.
Also, full confidentiality of an individualâs caste declaration is guaranteed by Census Act.TOI was the first to report on Aug 4 that the Phase 2 questionnaire shall capture caste âas declared by respondentâ, and, in a first, also capture parentsâ date and place of birth.Phase 2 is due to start in UT of Ladakh and snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of J&K, Uttarakhand and Himachal on Aug 17. For the rest of India, it will resume in Feb 2027, culminating in the population headcount with March 1, 2027, as the reference date.

Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the âprimeâ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in Indiaâs neighbourhood.

An electricity department employee was allegedly assaulted by a homeowner and injured by his three dogs when the former went to take the power meter reading in Madhya Pradesh’s Gwalior district, police said on Friday (August 14, 2026). The homeowner has been arrested by the police.
According to the police, the incident took place on Thursday (August 13, 2026) in Indira Nagar area under Hazira police station limits when two contractual staffers of the power department had gone to take the record the power consumption units and generate a bill.
Gwalior Superintendent of Police (SP) Dharm Vir Singh told The Hindu that there was an argument over the bill after which the accused — Beeru Tomar — unleashed his pet dogs on them, and that one of the employees suffered dog bite injuries.
Mr. Singh said that Mr. Tomar, who has a criminal record, has been booked under various sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including provisions related to negligent conduct with respect to animal.
“He is a man of goon like conduct and has previous criminal cases against him. The complaint is that he assaulted them and left dogs on them. We have arrested him,” Mr. Singh said, adding that one of power department employees has suffered about five wounds but there is no serious injury.

headline: India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack
full_text:
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack
SRINAGAR: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned at an event in Islamabad on Friday that Pakistan would take any step to protect its water rights under the Indus Waters Treaty, saying âevery single dropâ of Pakistanâs water is a âred lineâ and âIndia must come to the right pathâ or it would âbe given a direct responseâ. His comments drew a reaction from Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah who said the treaty has been kept in abeyance and should remain so.âYes, our blood. We have been saying this only, that our blood has been sucked. Thankfully Shehbaz Sharif came to his senses. This (IWT) has sucked the blood out of us. These are our rivers. We have the first right on them,â Omar told reporters here. âFor the sake of saying, Pakistanis say that they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was his sympathy when our permission to use our rivers was taken away from us,â the CM said.âOut of the six rivers, three which belonged to Punjab were kept by India and our three rivers were handed over to Pakistan. From then till today we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,â Omar said, adding that under the treaty J&K could neither extract drinking water from the Chenab nor use the Jhelum for irrigation or building a barrage at Tulbul. âOur blood has been sucked and now the IWT has been cancelled.
This should remain cancelled so that we can use this water properly,â Omar added.The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. In May last year, after the treaty was placed in abeyance, Omar called for restarting the Tulbul Navigation Project on Wular Lake in north Kashmir. The project is located on Wular Lake in the Sopore area of Baramulla district. Pakistan has opposed construction of a 439-foot-long, 40-foot-wide barrage, also known as the Wular barrage or Tulbul Navigation Project, with a navigation lock on the lake.The Union govt began work on the project in 1984 to regulate water levels and facilitate navigation. However, work was halted a year later after Pakistan objected. Pakistan raised the issue with the Indus Waters Commission in 1986 and work was stopped in 1987.The governing National Conference in J&K has opposed the IWT all along, calling it detrimental to the interests of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.

headline: Defence Attachés posted at Indian embassies and High Commissions abroad will be required to learn the local language and undergo periodic evaluation of their language proficiency, as the Ministry of Defence moves to streamline their role with a great...

A senior Ministry of Defence official said Defence Attachés (DAs) would be assessed on their language skills and other parameters before their appointment and upon completion of their assignments. “There will be an evaluation of language skills and other parameters of DAs before their appointment and when they return from their assignment. The Ministry is actively evaluating the role of DAs appointed at various locations,” the official said.
The move comes amid an expansion of India’s defence diplomatic footprint and a renewed push to leverage military missions abroad to promote defence cooperation, exports and indigenous defence products.
India’s defence exports have risen sharply, from ₹686 crore in 2013-14 to a record ₹38,424 crore in 2025-26, an increase of over 5,500% in 12 years. Defence equipment is now exported to more than 80 countries, with the exporter base expanding to 145 companies. The Government has set a target of ₹50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029.
Expanding India’s Defence representation
The Ministry has also expanded India’s defence representation abroad. India had around 50 defence wings in its missions for several years, which has been increased to more than 70, while more than 120 Defence Attachés from over 70 countries are currently posted in India. The Government has recently approved several new Defence Attaché billets for the Army, Navy and Air Force across key regions.
The new deployments include first-time postings in several African countries, besides strategically important locations in Asia and Europe, including the Philippines and Armenia. The expansion is aimed at strengthening military partnerships and responding to a rapidly evolving geopolitical environment.
The Defence Attaché system is an established instrument of military diplomacy, enabling countries to build institutional relationships, facilitate defence cooperation and support strategic objectives.
In March, Rashtriya Raksha University hosted the Defence Attaché Roundtable 2026, bringing together Defence Attachés, policymakers, academia and industry representatives to discuss defence trade, co-development and emerging technologies.
