headline: Uttar Pradesh traders on Friday (August 14, 2026) demanded regulatory mechanism for the security of foreign trade, amid growing cases of fraud.
full_text:
Uttar Pradesh traders on Friday (August 14, 2026) demanded regulatory mechanism for the security of foreign trade, amid growing cases of fraud.
They demanded a regulatory body for the security of foreign trade which can provide assistance in cases involving fraud, payment defaults, and cross-border commercial disputes.
“I suffered a loss of over ₹25 lakhs by a Bangladesh based client. It is not the first setback faced by me, common issue faced by us with foreign clients are default in payments, container theft at ports and payment stuck in foreign banks and the foreign customer goes into hiding. India’s exports stood at about $860 billion and $979 billion in imports, roughly 50% in value of GDP. Millions of importers are safeguarded only by few tools, most commonly ECGC or Bank Letter of Credit (L.C.). Some customers buy on credit which is backed by Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (ECGC), which provides export credit insurance support to Indian exporters and banks. However, in terms of payment failures, ECGC takes help from foreign lawyers and then tries to recover from the court. However, in some cases, the customer goes into hiding and, in such cases, the entire payment fails. Also, in case of failure of payment, we fail to collect full loss from present ECGC mechanism, hence we demand Regulatory body for the Security of Foreign Trade which can provide assistance in cases involving fraud, payment defaults, and cross-border commercial disputes. A dedicated department should initially be established in all major states,” said Samir Qaiym, a trader from Kanpur.
Shobhit Mehrotra, a brass trader from Moradabad who supports the idea said the proposed idea of Regulatory body for the Security of Foreign Trade should have offices in major exporting states to deal with these types of fraud. “They can connect to the local embassy followed by connecting to law officers and local intelligence to hunt those people down who have been doing frauds,” added Mr. Mehrotra, who faced similar payment defaults by foreign client twice in the last five years. He added an import and export credit score can be used to verify traders involved in import and export.
Vineet Singh, a Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) rank officer with U.P. police supported the idea and said such a framework should consist of professionals from relevant fields, including: Legal experts and officer’s familiar with commercial and international law. “It can also include Police and intelligence officers with experience in fraud investigation and enforcement. Representatives or designated officers from the Ministry of External Affairs or the relevant external-affairs authorities. Other officials with expertise in international trade, banking, insurance and cross-border transactions. The department should maintain direct coordination with the Indian embassy/high commission in the relevant foreign country, as well as local law-enforcement authorities, police officers and legal professionals,” said Mr. Singh.
The U.P. officer pushed for a two-way cooperation. “The idea should operate on a two-way basis. If a foreign company or individual faces fraud or a serious commercial dispute involving an Indian businessperson, the relevant foreign authorities should also be able to approach this department through their embassy or designated diplomatic channels. The department could then coordinate with the appropriate Indian legal, police and regulatory authorities to investigate and resolve the matter. This two-way mechanism would improve trust, accountability and confidence in international trade, while also providing legitimate businesses with a structured system for dealing with cross-border fraud and commercial disputes,” said Mr. Singh.

The younger generation must also be made aware of the efforts and struggles behind the achievements visible today.”
He added, “Society is changing rapidly. With Generation Z and Generation Alpha in mind, there is a need to reconsider how communication and information are presented. The future belongs to the youth, so development and changes taking place across different sectors need to be viewed through the lens of young people.”
Efforts would be made to connect young people more effectively with Uttar Pradesh Sandesh, Mr. Singh said. The magazine will be presented on online platforms while keeping the needs and interests of young readers in mind.
“Uttar Pradesh Sandesh is currently published in Hindi. In the future, efforts will also be made to publish articles in English. Through the magazine, content related to development taking place in Uttar Pradesh and the achievements of the state government will be able to reach a wider readership,” he said.
He said efforts should be made to examine developments in different sectors from the perspective of young people and present subjects in line with the expectations of the new generation.
“Honouring individuals is an integral part of India’s cultural tradition. Recognition for a writer’s work boosts morale and creates enthusiasm to undertake new initiatives. The scholars being honoured have made significant intellectual contributions in journalism, writing and social service. Many of them have dedicated a substantial part of their lives to these fields,” he said.
Mr. Singh added that while the recognition might appear modest in view of the quality of their work, the sentiments behind it are significant. The process of honouring writers for outstanding work will continue in the future.

headline: A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice to Union govt through MeitY and law ministry
full_text:
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice to Union govt through MeitY and law ministry
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Friday agreed to examine a plea seeking prosecution of social media and online platforms under the stringent Pocso Act for showing child sexual abuse content and not reporting it to police, reports AmitAnand Choudhary. A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice to the Union govt, through the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) and the ministry of law and justice. It asked the petitioner NGO, 'Just Rights for Children Alliance (JRCA)', to implead intermediaries in the case to ensure compliance with the court's 2024 judgment.
Sections 19 and 20 of Pocso Act make it mandatory for anyone who knows about a child sexual offence to report it to local police and the petitioner said the provision was also applicable to intermediaries and they too were liable to be prosecuted for non-compliance.JRCA, described as India's largest civil society network with over 250 NGOs working against child sexual exploitation, child trafficking and child marriage, filed the application following a BBC report alleging that Instagram had carried paid advertisements promoting CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material).

headline: Thirukkural with the Times explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text âThirukkuralâ. Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. This text is divided into three boo...
full_text:
Thirukkural with the Times explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text âThirukkuralâ. Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. This text is divided into three books with teachings on virtue, wealth, and love and is considered one of the great works ever on ethics and morality. The Kural has influenced scholars and leaders across social, political, and philosophical spheres.Motivational speaker, author and diversity champion Bharathi Bhaskar explores the masterpiece.
Last week, our college friend group of eleven girls lost one of our own. Through our four years in college, we had become inseparable. Three decades later, we were still together.
And then, Devi was no more.
For two years, she fought cancer bravely. She was the first to wish us on birthdays and anniversaries. We would wake to find her messages, often at 5.30 in the morning. Her love was like dawn. It brightened the lives of all around her. Her smile seemed to rise from the altar of her heart.
We wept. Yet, strangely, there is also a quiet peace in knowing that she may now be in a place without pain. Where that place is, none of us know. But perhaps the more important realisation is that all of us are travelling towards it, each at our own pace.
Losing someone we love shakes up our lives. Guilt arrives uninvited, whispering about words left unsaid and things left undone. Then life, with its extraordinary insistence, pulls us back. There are mails to send, vessels to wash, clothes to fold, work to finish. We think we are moving on, until suddenly, it returns, and we are thrown back into the tide of longing.
Perhaps that is because love does not leave as easily as a person does.
And perhaps the people we have loved have not entirely left us. Are they watching us? Are they closer than before? Sometimes I imagine them as passengers who have quietly got down from the train before us, without the chance to say goodbye. We continue our journey, carrying their memories with us.
Younger colleagues approach the world differently. At home, children no longer listen to us. But with school and college friends, time seems to freeze.
That is our safe haven. When one of us leaves that circle, however, we suddenly become conscious of the passing years.
Valluvar captured this truth with remarkable simplicity in Kural 334:
âNaalena Ondrupol Kaatti, Uyirerum
Vaaladhu Unarvaar Perin.â
âEvery day appears to be merely a day, but to those who understand, it is a sword quietly cutting away a portion of life.â
In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira is asked by the Yaksha, âWhat is the strangest thing in the world?â
He replies, âCountless beings leave the world every day, yet those who remain believe they will remain forever.â What greater wonder could there be?
But perhaps this need not frighten us. It can awaken us, instead.
Every day is a flower that blooms for exactly one day. The July rain, the December chill, the fragrance of neem in summer; all carry a beauty that will never return in precisely the same form.
The lesson is not to fear the passing of days, but to live them fully. To laugh a little. To say what we keep postponing. To savour the morning light and coffee.
Kahlil Gibran asks, âYou want to know the secret of death. But how shall you find it unless you seek it in the heart of life?â
That is where the answer lies.
Not in knowing how the journey ends, but in making every day of the journey luminous.
Devi did that for many of us. I will remember her; not as someone who has left, but as someone who taught us quietly how much radiance one life can leave behind.

headline: Mahatma Gandhi's last fast made India pay Rs 55 crore to Pakistan. What was the trigger?
full_text:
Mahatma Gandhi's last fast made India pay Rs 55 crore to Pakistan. What was the trigger?
Even as India gained independence, the Partition triggered a humanitarian catastrophe because of communal strife. In January 1948, Mahatma Gandhi undertook his last fast, for the minorities in India and Pakistan. India released Rs 55 crore for Pakistan.
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi's last fast, in January 1948, is often remembered for a dramatic consequence. Gandhi's fast made India release Rs 55 crore to Pakistan even as the two newly created nations remained locked in the bitterness of Partition and a looming war in Kashmir.
But the objective of Gandhi's fast, which was also his last, was much wider.
He was fasting to stop communal hatred from tearing the country apart, to secure the rights and safety of Muslims in India, while also seeking peace for minorities — Hindus and Sikhs — in Pakistan.
The payment of Rs 55 crore was linked to a larger moral argument. For Gandhi, India could not demand justice and peace from Pakistan while withholding money that, according to him, was legally owed to it. To him, it was India's obligation to its new neighbour.
The 78-year-old Freedom Fighter's fast began on January 13, 1948, at Birla House (now Gandhi Smriti) in New Delhi. Gandhi, who was already physically weakened by an earlier fast in Calcutta (now Kolkata), announced that he would not eat until he was satisfied that "communal reconciliation" had genuinely taken place.
Historian and author Ramachandra Guha, in Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World 1914-1948, writes that Gandhi told a prayer meeting on January 12 that "the recent riots had been contained by police and military action, but there remained a storm within the breast that may burst forth any day. His fast would end only when he was satisfied that there is a reunion of the hearts of all communities brought about without any outside pressure, but from an awakened sense of duty."
That distinction is crucial to understanding why Gandhi's final fast was linked with the Rs 55 crore payment to Pakistan.
Today, as India celebrates its 80th Independence Day, its journey in terms of communal harmony has been a roller-coaster ride. Yet, even in difficult times, India has continued to stand for peace and harmony. This spirit was reflected not only during Gandhi's 1948 fast and his insistence that Pakistan receive its due payment, but also in the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, under which India paid Pakistan $174 million as part of the settlement, worth about $1.6 billion today after adjusting for inflation.
GANDHI'S LAST FAST WAS BORN OUT OF PARTITION'S HORROR
Partition had left India and Pakistan engulfed in violence and displacement of millions.
Delhi had itself become a city of refugees. Communal tension was everywhere. Gandhi had spent months trying to calm the situation, first in Bengal and later in Delhi. He envisioned an India where a person's religious identity did not determine their rights.
In his newspaper Harijan, Gandhi wrote that "the Indian Union and Pakistan belong equally to all who call themselves and are, sons of the soil, irrespective of their creed or colour". He urged, "Let the past be buried. Do not rake it up. Think of the future".
Gandhi wanted India to assure liberty of religious profession to every single individual. For him, this was not a minor concession to minorities.
The January 1948 fast, therefore, emerged out of this communal crisis. Gandhi believed that military and police measures could suppress violence, but they could not produce genuine reconciliation.
The Hindustan Times, edited by Gandhi's son Devadas in January 1948, reported that "the announcement had come as a complete surprise to his colleagues and the members of the Government". Gandhi's associates were anxious because his health remained fragile after the Calcutta fast.
"Gandhi had been deeply affected by the all-round misery and chaos, thousands of refugees streaming to him with tragic tales," Guha wrote in his book.
Gandhi's son Devadas himself pleaded with his father to stop and not hold fast.
"You and all the others should bear in mind that it is equally unimportant whether God ends my life or allows me to survive," Gandhi wrote in response, according to Dominique Lapierre and Larry Collins' Freedom at Midnight book.
The book also noted that Gandhi added in the letter, "I have only one prayer to offer: O God, keep me firm during the fast lest I should hastily break it in the temptation to live."
HOW RS 55 CRORE BECAME PART OF GANDHI'S LAST FAST DEMANDS
India's decision to withhold Pakistan's share of the financial assets inherited from British India was another issue which was troubling Gandhi.
During Partition, the division of the assets of undivided India included the sterling balances owed by Britain. Pakistan was entitled to Rs 75 crore from India. Of this, Rs 20 crore had already been paid, leaving Rs 55 crore.
But relations between the two newly born countries had deteriorated dramatically. Pakistan-backed forces had invaded Kashmir, and the Indian government delayed the transfer of the remaining amount.
For India's leaders, the decision to withhold the money was rooted in security concerns. But for Gandhi, the principle was different.
Guha writes in his book that although the stated reason for Gandhi's fast was the deteriorating communal situation, "it seems Gandhi was also upset with the Government's decision to withhold from Pakistan its share of the sterling balances owed by Britain to (undivided) India after the War."
His position was rooted in a broader moral principle that a financial obligation did not cease to exist because relations between the parties had turned hostile.
Freedom at Midnight highlights the episode more starkly. "The Cabinet came to Gandhi's bedside because of his demand for the payment of Pakistan's 550 million rupees (Rs 55 crore)."
The demand had angered many in the government, particularly Deputy Prime Minister Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Nehru and Patel attempted to explain why the money had been withheld. Gandhi listened to them. Then came one of the most dramatic moments of Gandhi's fast.
The fast was rapidly deteriorating Gandhi's body.
"Slowly, painfully tears in his eyes, Gandhi raised himself on his elbows and looked at the man who had stood by his side during so many bitter struggles," Lapierre and Collins wrote in their book.
"You are not the Sardar I once knew," Gandhi told Patel, according to Freedom at midnight.
GANDHI'S FAST NOT ONLY ATTRACTED ADMIRATION, BUT ALSO ANGER
The fast held by Gandhi was not welcomed by all. Hindu and Sikh refugees who had suffered during Partition increasingly viewed Gandhi's position with anger. Some believed that he was putting the "interests of Muslims" ahead of those who had fled Pakistan.
"When will that old man stop bothering us?" was the reaction of some in Delhi's markets and refugee neighbourhoods, according to Lapierre and Collins' book.
At one point, refugees demonstrated outside Birla House. Gandhi heard the slogans. "What are they doing?" he asked. "Chanting slogans," Gandhi's aide Pyarelal replied.
When asked about what were they chanting, Pyarelal told Gandhi "They are chanting, 'Let Gandhi die'."
After all, Gandhi was asking people who had experienced immense suffering to show compassion towards members of the community they associated with that suffering.
But Gandhi insisted that his fast was not a political bargain. At his prayer meeting on January 17, he said, "My fast was not a political move in any sense of the term. It is in obedience to the peremptory call of conscience and duty", Guha recorded in his book.
Rs 55 CRORE TO PAK AND GANDHI'S OTHER DEMANDS TO END FAST
The government's decision to release Rs 55 crore to Pakistan became a key outcome of Gandhi's fast. Guha, in his book, records that the payment was made as a contribution "to the non-violent and noble effort made by Gandhiji... for peace and goodwill".
Gandhi opposed withholding it despite the Kashmir conflict because, in his view, a debt had to be honoured regardless of whether the other side was a friend or an enemy.
But the money was only part of Gandhi's demands. On January 17, as his health deteriorated, he laid down seven conditions for ending the fast which also included restoring occupied mosques, ensuring Muslims could move freely and return to their homes, protecting them from economic boycotts and allowing the Mehrauli Urs to proceed peacefully.
The conditions like communal harmony, security for Delhi's Muslims after the horrors of Partition reflected the real purpose of Gandhi's fast.
Two lakh people signed a peace pledge affirming that Muslims should be "as free as the rest of us to live in Delhi in peace and security and with self-respect," according to the book Freedom at Midnight.
The appeal also resonated in Pakistan. "It was in Pakistan that emotions seemed strongest. A telegram from Lahore said: 'Here everyone asks only one thing: how can we help save Gandhi's life? Muslim League leaders called Gandhi 'the archangel of fraternity'," Lapierre and Collins wrote.
On January 18, Hindu, Muslim and Sikh leaders pledged to fulfill Gandhi's conditions. Reassured, Gandhi accepted a glass of lime juice and ended his fast.
The money became one of the most controversial outcomes because it collided with the raw emotions of a country still mourning its dead and housing millions of refugees.
Yet Gandhi's argument was that India's obligations could not be selectively applied. If India wanted to build a just state, it had to protect its minorities. If it wanted peace with Pakistan, it had to honour its financial commitments. And if it wanted to overcome the legacy of Partition, it had to bury the politics of revenge.

headline: Congress alleges 19 child deaths linked to contaminated water in MP's Balaghat
full_text:
Congress alleges 19 child deaths linked to contaminated water in MP's Balaghat
Umang Singhar visited Balaghat's affected tribal villages and alleged 19 children died after a suspected contaminated water outbreak. He accused the state government of concealing the toll and demanded urgent care, clean water and a fair probe.
Madhya Pradesh Congress leader and Leader of Opposition Umang Singhar on Friday claimed that 19 children had died after an outbreak of illness linked to contaminated water in tribal-dominated villages of Balaghat district, and accused the state government of concealing the actual toll.
Calling the situation "extremely worrying", Singhar visited the affected villages of Kundekasa, Bondari and Korka, where he reviewed the situation, met affected families and visited a hospital to enquire about the condition of ailing children and the healthcare facilities available there, according to a statement issued by his office.
Singhar said local villagers told him that the illness had been spreading for several days due to contaminated water and infection, and had led to the deaths of 19 children in nearby villages so far. They also alleged that the administration was trying to hide the figures.
'SITUATION IS EXTREMELY WORRYING'
Demanding immediate intervention, Singhar called for health screening, treatment, adequate nutrition and clean drinking water for residents of the affected Baiga tribal-dominated villages.
"The situation is extremely worrying amid apprehensions of contaminated water and malnutrition in the affected villages. The government should immediately conduct health check-ups of every person, particularly children," he said.
He also sought proper and free treatment for ailing children, adequate nutrition, clean drinking water and financial assistance for affected families. He said the government must ensure that every child received proper treatment and that no family lost a child due to a lack of medical care.
Singhar also demanded an impartial probe into possible administrative lapses and strict action against officials and others found responsible.
The Congress leader alleged that the BJP government's negligence had led to the deaths of 19 children in Baiga tribal-dominated areas. "The government is trying to conceal the actual number of deaths instead of bringing the real figures before the people," he alleged.
Targeting Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, Singhar said he was taking out a Tiranga Yatra but had no time to "wipe the tears" of tribal families and save children's lives.
"CM Mohan Yadav talks about tribal pride. He should answer what he has done for these tribal children," Singhar said. MLAs Sanjay Uikey, Madhu Bhagat, Anubha Munjare and Vivek Vicky Patel accompanied Singhar during the visit, as he reiterated his demand for urgent medical care, clean water and accountability in the matter.

headline: A proposal to establish a new plant at Brahmapuram with a capacity to treat 150 tonnes of biodegradable waste was passed through voting amid stiff protest from the Opposition Left Democratic Front (LDF) at the Kochi Corporation Council meeting on Fri...
full_text:
A proposal to establish a new plant at Brahmapuram with a capacity to treat 150 tonnes of biodegradable waste was passed through voting amid stiff protest from the Opposition Left Democratic Front (LDF) at the Kochi Corporation Council meeting on Friday (August 14).
The proposal, submitted by G3 Renewables Private Limited, which operates a facility on Willingdon Island, to set up the plant at an investment of ₹25–30 crore, provided the Corporation allots three acres on a 25-year lease, was included in the agenda. The plant proposes to employ proprietary mechanical processing technology recognised by the Suchitwa Mission.
The LDF opposed the agenda, following which it was put to vote and approved by 40 votes to 19, with BJP councillors also supporting the proposal. V.A. Sreejith, LDF parliamentary party leader, alleged that the agenda was being passed without the Mayor or the Corporation secretary having visited the Willingdon plant and without inviting expressions of interest (EoI). “The Council has been made to approve an agenda without knowing the finer points. The Mayor had no answer when asked whether Suchitwa Mission had examined the Willingdon facility. The compressed biogas plant already functional at Brahmapuram has failed to achieve its optimum capacity because of mixed waste being fed by the Corporation. Unless segregation is streamlined, the same problem will recur with the new plant,” he said.
Mayor V.K. Minimol countered that proposals must be vetted by the standing committee concerned, and that there was no precedent for the Mayor or the secretary to personally examine them. In this case, she said, the health standing committee had visited the plant. “We cannot afford to delay the proposed facility as nearly 100 tonnes of waste are now being dumped at Brahmapuram daily for want of adequate treatment capacity, with the CBG plant functioning far below its optimum. The company has agreed to transport waste from six primary collection points of the Corporation to the plant for a mere 20 paise per kilogram. This will substantially reduce lorry rent from the exorbitant ₹4.50 crore,” Ms. Minimol said, adding that an EoI would be invited.
Shortly thereafter, LDF councillors stormed the well of the council hall, accusing the Mayor of denying discussion on restricting subsidies for biomedical waste collection to eligible sections alone. Reasoning that the Opposition had already registered its protest when the matter was discussed in the health committee, Ms. Minimol left the dais, announcing that the Council agenda had been passed. Following this, Opposition councillors shifted their protest to the front of the Mayor’s chamber, even as she exited the Corporation office through another route.

Noting that there was no sanction to prosecute leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha Gandhi for his remarks against V D Savarkar,

 Friday quashed proceedings against him initiated by a Lucknow court. headline: In Halmulla in south Kashmir’s Anantnag district, larger-than-life pictures of cricket stars such as Sachin Tendulkar, Virat Kohil, M.S. Dhoni, Shahid Afridi, and Babar Azam line the bat shops on National Highway-44.
full_text:
In Halmulla in south Kashmir’s Anantnag district, larger-than-life pictures of cricket stars such as Sachin Tendulkar, Virat Kohil, M.S. Dhoni, Shahid Afridi, and Babar Azam line the bat shops on National Highway-44.
Fawzul Kabiir, 40, founder of GR8 Sports, is busy inspecting the English willow clefts neatly stacked into a 12-foot-high tower. Clefts, or wedge-shaped blocks of willow wood cut from timber, are turned into bats and customised to meet the evolving demands of cricket.
While displaying different bars, Kabiir says, “A bat used by an opener is different from that which is used by a middle-order batsman and a slogger. Bats used for one-day matches are different from those used in the T20 format. Each player has a preference of his own.”
The craftsmanship of local bat-makers comes into play in producing bats sturdy enough to endure wallops or dents, even after being hit by a leather ball. “Seasons are important in maintaining the uniqueness of the bat. We allow the willow clefts to brave the rain and snow in the open. Sun-dried clefts are the best to compete in international markets,” Kabiir explains.
Inside his well-equipped bat factory, Kabiir tosses a ball into the air and lets it fall onto a bat, listening to the sound to check for the “sweet spot”. “It’s a science I mastered after my bats faced rejection in many countries in 2010, when I showcased some of my samples,” he explains. “Our bats would not meet international standards. And just as we began producing international-quality bats, we have been hit by a shortage of raw material.”
Famous for its mountain slopes, lush meadows and clear streams, Kashmir enjoys another reputation: the craftsmanship of its bat-makers. According to government data, Kashmir has 195 registered bat manufacturers, mainly in south Kashmir, and around 150 cleft dealers. They shape willow planks into sturdy, beautiful bats that find their way to cricket grounds around the world.
This international fame came only in 2021, when a bat-making company from Kashmir was certified by the International Cricket Council (ICC) and bagged a contract to supply bats to the Oman Cricket Board. However, it was during the Cricket World Cup 2022 that the Kashmir willow made it to the spotlight when UAE player Junaid Siddique hit the longest six of 109 meters off a Sri Lankan bowler, Dushmantha Chameera.
The industry is also an important source of livelihood in the region, for at least 50,000 locals. However, it is now grappling with several issues, including shortage of raw material, changes in climate, and smuggling.
A growing industry
The Kashmir willow is a deciduous tree native to Europe and western Asia. It was brought to the Kashmir Valley during British rule in 1895 by British officials Sir Walter R. Lawrence and J.C. MacDonell, the first chief of the Forest Department in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K), to meet fuel needs and provide green fodder for cattle.
According to Yaseer Ahmad Mir, Assistant Professor at the National Institute of Fashion Technology, Salix alba, a species of English willow, was also introduced to make cricket bats, as it was difficult for the British to export bats from England. “They found the climatic conditions of Kashmir suitable for making these bats,” he says.
The willow wood is usually sourced from areas surrounding Anantnag. English willow trees are harvested after 12-15 years of growth, or when they attain a girth of 120 cm at 1.5 metres above the ground and stand about 12 metres tall. They are then cut into blocks or clefts and left to dry under the sun for months.
The wood is hard-wearing, relatively light, and easy to sand and shape. “The quality of willow is improved by drying and pressing it during its production stage,” says Mir.
According to data from the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Agriculture and Science Technology, a mature willow tree with a girth of 100 centimetres produces about 15-20 willow clefts. Accordingly, around 1.2 lakh mature Salix trees are felled to produce 30 lakh cricket bats per year. This is double the number manufactured a decade ago.
Kabiir says 47 international players have used Kashmir willow bats in international tournaments, including the ICC T20 World Cups in 2021 and 2022 and the ODI World Cup in 2023. They include India’s Munaf Patel, Yusuf Pathan, and Wasim Jaffer; Pakistan’s Mohammad Yousuf; Bangladesh’s Saqib Al Hasan, and West Indies’ Kusal Perera and Chris Gayle.
He says: “We have not only made cricket bats lighter, but also ensured that the ping, balance, and stroke is matchless.”
In the 2024 ICC Women’s T20 World Cup, West Indies players Aaliyah Alleyne, Zaida James, and Shamilia Connell wrote a new chapter in Kashmir’s bat-making story by using the bats made in the region for the first time. Kabiir says that achieving this feat in women’s cricket required bat manufacturers to undergo a series of tests. The tests assessed lighter bat weights and sweet spots at multiple points on the blade, based on the preferences of the women cricketers.
Kabiir says the bats are affordable compared to those produced elsewhere. “Compared to English willow bats from the U.K. that cost ₹1.5 lakh-2 lakh, the bats produced here range from ₹300 to ₹20,000. This makes them much more affordable. States such as Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and Delhi queue up with orders for bats every year,” he says.
The plan to tackle the quality crisis
However, just as it was growing towards the ₹700-crore mark and deepening its roots in international cricket, Kashmir’s bat-making industry is struggling to meet both domestic and international orders, Kabiir says. The price of English willow is an indicator of the shortage: per foot, it has gone up from ₹300 in 2021 to ₹1,250. “The Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) government needs to step in to bridge the gap and help the bat industry here expand,” he says.
Javed Ahmed Rana, the Forest Minister of J&K, agrees that the declining availability of quality willow timber is one of the biggest challenges confronting the cricket bat industry in the Union Territory. To tackle the shortage, “a coordinated drive is in place to revive willow cultivation across Kashmir,” he says.
According to the Forest Department, the government plans to plant 1,100 willow trees per hectare across 200 hectares of forest and State land, with a target of 2.2 lakh trees starting this year. The move could help the bat industry increase production to 50 lakh bats per year.
According to Rana, the J&K government is identifying “suitable low-lying and marshy areas across the Valley for expanding willow plantations”. It has roped in the State Forest Research Institute to introduce improved willow species and clones to enhance both productivity and sustainability. He says the government needs to build a self-sustaining willow cultivation ecosystem through scientific management, quality planting material, identifying new plantation areas, and greater farmer participation.
In 1917, the Forest Department under the Dogra rulers, identified alluvial and riparian willow species and planted them along rivers, stream banks, and point bars. Wetland willows were also planted in areas with saturated soils, including around the wetlands of Wular Lake, Harran, Hygam, Hokur-sur, Mirgund, Mamandangi, Gund Jehangir, and Shahgund. An official estimate suggests that about 5 million willow trees existed in and around these areas.
Irfan Ali Shah, Conservator of Forests, North Circle, says the Forest Department at present manages approximately 67 hectares of land under willow plantations. “These plantations are managed scientifically according to approved working plans under the Willow Plantation Working Circle. Sites are selected based on soil moisture, drainage, water availability, productivity, and the ecological needs of the species,” he says.
English willow is particularly suited to mildly waterlogged and moisture-retentive areas, “where adequate soil moisture can support satisfactory growth during its rotation period”. Besides south Kashmir, Baramulla, Kupwara, and Bandipora are also emerging as hubs of willow cultivation.
“The Lidder Forest Division in Bijbehara plans to plant English willow cuttings in available open spaces in the Momandanji and Katriteng plantations, covering about 5 hectares. The initiative aims to expand the existing willow resource and promote scientific regeneration in suitable areas,” says Shah.
Changes in weather patters
Changes in climatic conditions too are adding to the industry’s woes. Nazir Dar, a bat manufacturer from Bijbehara, says many wetlands around local springs have dried up in the past five years. “Springs would feed water bodies and allow willows to grow thick and tall. The construction of houses and the entry of waste, especially polythene, into water bodies have choked scores of springs in Anantnag district,” he says.
Shah too admits that this is a challenge but adds that the situation is under control. “The availability of adequate moisture is an important factor governing the growth and establishment of willow, particularly in areas traditionally associated with wetland or waterlogged conditions. The drying of wetlands or their degradation as well as reduction in water availability can all adversely affect willow regeneration,” he says.
However, he is quick to add that it would be inappropriate to state that wetlands in south Kashmir have completely stopped supporting English willow cultivation solely because of drying of water bodies. “In some locations, declining water levels or changes in hydrology may have reduced the suitability of certain sites for new plantations or natural regeneration,” says Shah.
He says changing climatic patterns could have an impact on English willow particularly because it is closely associated with adequate soil moisture and water availability. The changes in temperature, precipitation patterns, and duration of dry periods events may influence the growth, establishment, and productivity of willow plantations.
“However, it would be prudent not to attribute any observed decline in willow exclusively to climate change without systematic field-based evidence. The observed changes may also be influenced by land use changes, water body degradation, harvesting practices, plantation management, and availability of suitable planting material,” he adds.
Problem of smuggling
Smuggling remains another challenge to the industry in Kashmir.
After the dilution of Article 370 in 2019 by the Bharatiya Janata Party-led Central government, the Jammu and Kashmir Willow (Prohibition on Export and Movement) Act, 2000, was just one of the two local laws retained to “to curb smuggling of willow clefts”.
“Kashmir willow timber is being smuggled to places such as Jalandhar and Meerut, which have their own bat-making units and flourishing export industries,” says Mir.
Until the mid-1970s, Kashmir willow wood was transported to various manufacturing units across India. “But when the J&K government realised the importance of the willow wood and the potential of the industry in Kashmir, it restricted the number of clefts that could be sold outside. After the ban, the smuggling of willow increased. Locals claim that over 25 lakh clefts are smuggled every year,” Mir adds.
English willow timber is harvested twice a year in May and September. Kabiir says he goes to private willow tree fields in Ganderbal and Kupwara every year in the spring and identifies the female species of English willow by monitoring the movement of pollinators. “The willow trees with flowers are the female species. They are light weight, flexible and without knots, and have a good shine. It is this species that allows us to produce Grade A bats of international standard and fetches us the highest profit.”
But access to good-quality timber remains a challenge. With the inconsistent quality of timber denting its reputation in the domestic market, the Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2025 has come as a shot in the arm for the bat industry.
Mir was one of the members of the committee that prepared the dossier report for the GI tag of the Kashmir willow bat. “The GI recognition gives Kashmir willow bats additional value. It is also a strong marketing tool that can help expand their reach and increase their prices,” explains Mir.

headline: Human-elephant conflict logs more deaths in southern India
full_text:
Human-elephant conflict logs more deaths in southern India
Human-elephant conflict in South India rises, with 130 human deaths in 2023-24 due to habitat loss. A new report calls for regional management strategies.
New Delhi: Human deaths caused by elephants and elephant deaths have increased in recent years across Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, with habitat degradation, fragmentation, water scarcity and infrastructure projects affecting elephant movement and pushing the animals closer to human settlements, according to a new technical report by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII).
The report, titled Regional Action Plan for Comprehensive Understanding & Management of Human-Elephant Conflict in South India, was launched by the environment ministry in Visakhapatnam on August 13 as part of World Elephant Day 2026 celebrations. It seeks to provide a regional framework to address human-elephant conflict across the four states.
The report analysed five-year data on human deaths caused by elephants and elephant deaths between 2019-20 and 2023-24. It found that human deaths fluctuated but reached their highest level in 2023-24, while elephant deaths showed an overall rise during the period.
A total of 130 human deaths caused by elephants were reported across the four states in 2023-24, the highest in the five-year period. The number was 110 in 2022-23, 99 in 2021-22, 84 in 2020-21 and 113 in 2019-20.
“On an average, 109 human deaths happen annually in the region with maximum human deaths reported from Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and least from Andhra Pradesh. Also, the conflict cases in terms of reported human deaths appear to be on the rise in the last four years,” the report said.
Elephant deaths increased from 38 in 2019-20 to 50 in 2023-24. There were 39 deaths each in 2020-21 and 2021-22, and 41 in 2022-23.
“The rising incidence of elephants straying into human-use areas is largely driven by severe habitat degradation, the lure of attractive crops grown in forest fringe villages, and the fragmentation and disconnection of habitats that force elephants into areas of human use,” the report said.
State-wise data showed in 2023-24, the number of human deaths caused by elephants was 59 in Tamil Nadu, 48 in Karnataka, 27 in Kerala and only six in Andhra Pradesh.
Prof Raman Sukumar, an elephant expert, who is also the National Science Chair at the Indian Institute of Science, said while the number of human deaths from elephants is the lowest in Andhra, this should be assessed in relation to the elephant population of the state.
“Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have a 45-fold and 20-fold the elephant population of Andhra, yet the number of human deaths in the former is nowhere close to the magnitude seen in the latter state. Andhra thus experiences much higher levels of conflict for its much smaller elephant population which is a legacy of a dispersal into the state which began in 1983 following the El Nino-related drought of 1982. The number of human deaths in the southern states has been increasing over the years as more elephants come out of the forested habitats into agriculture and settlements, a pattern seen widely across the country in recent decades,” he said.
In terms of elephant deaths across the states, Tamil Nadu saw 16 deaths in 2023-24, 14 in Karnataka and 10 each in Andhra Pradesh and Kerala.
The report also examined the impact of infrastructure projects on elephant habitats. In Andhra Pradesh, it flagged highway expansion projects, including NH-716 (Tirupati-Kadapa), NH-71 and the Bengaluru-Chennai Expressway, and railway doubling projects on the Renigunta-Balepalli and Tirupati-Pakala-Katpadi routes. These projects have affected areas where elephants have recently begun using habitats, increasing the risk of road and train collisions. The report recommended wildlife overpasses and underpasses in vulnerable stretches.
In Karnataka, large dams and reservoirs, including Tunga, Bhadra, Hemavati, Linganamakki and Supa, have led to the submergence of elephant habitats, while the upgradation of NH-75 (Bengaluru-Mangaluru) has fragmented elephant corridors. Night-time traffic restrictions have been attempted in some areas.
In Kerala, highways, railway lines, hydropower and irrigation projects, along with tourism infrastructure, resorts and expanding pilgrimage sites, have affected elephant habitats. In Tamil Nadu, highway upgrades, tourism infrastructure, contour canals and flume channels have also been flagged for their impact on elephant habitats and corridors.
The report recommended a landscape-level approach to managing conflict, protection of critical corridors, physical barriers combined with community measures, better compensation mechanisms, stronger monitoring and research, and an inter-departmental task force to coordinate action across agencies.

The apex court bench sought BCIâs explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Friday castigated the Bar Council of India (BCI) for threatening to deny licence to practice to Hyderabad-based NALSAR university students who opposed CJI Surya Kant as their convocation chief guest, shielded them against coercive action, and offered the law graduates a start as legal aid counsel in SC.Taking cognisance of the controversy created late Thursday evening by BCI through an unprecedented letter which had to be hastily retracted, a three-judge bench led by CJI Surya Kant said, âThis is absolutely uncalled for. BCI has nothing to do with it. The students might have written a letter to me. It is a dialogue between me and students. Who are they (BCI) to unnecessarily create an issue? This action is totally uncalled for.âSenior advocate K Parameshwar sought SCâs urgent intervention in quashing the illegal and arbitrary action of the BCI in seeking to coerce VC of NALSAR University, one of the top law schools, to conduct an investigation and identify students who had opposed CJIâs participation in the convocation as chief guest and issuing the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practice by all state bar councils.
SC asks bar council to explain process behind resolutions against studentsTrashing Bar Council of Indiaâs threat to blackball protesting Nalsar students, CJI Surya Kant told senior advocate K Parameshwar to convey to the students, who are completing their graduation in law from Nalsar this year, âto get licences to practice at the earliest and begin their careers in Supreme Courtâ.The apex court bench sought BCIâs explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions prior to issuing a letter to bar licences to protesters, and another shortly after, retracting it.Urging the students to join the SC bar at the earliest, the CJI said, âWe will empanel them and give them legal aid cases. This will be our response to all those who intend to create impediments in their professional career.â
The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression
CJI Surya Kant
He added, âWe should be largehearted. Even if someone makes a wrong statement at a young age, let it rest there. That does not mean they do not have a right to speak.ââDuring my student days, I was actively involved in many student activities. Indulging in activities or protests does not mean the students are wrong. The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. So long as they are lawfully and peacefully raising their voice over an issue, it must be heard, not opposed. Unnecessarily, Bar Council of India meddled in it.
Neither BCI nor any other body has any business to interfere with this,â said the CJI.Earlier, the advocate had raised the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practise by all state bar councils.The CJI-led bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, without even going through the petition by two formerstudents of Nalsar, restrained BCI and all state bar councils from taking any coercive or punitive action against the students and faculty.Accepting the notice on behalf of BCI, advocate Radhika Gautam said the objectionable circular had been withdrawn. headline: The promised three door-to-door visits, which did not happen as part of the Enumeration Phase in the Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls, are set to cost dearly to the electoral officials in Telangana. With a large number of voters not fill...
full_text:
The promised three door-to-door visits, which did not happen as part of the Enumeration Phase in the Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls, are set to cost dearly to the electoral officials in Telangana. With a large number of voters not filling in their details from the final electoral rolls of 2002 SIR as required in the Enumeration Forms, the work for the Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) has increased that much.
Also read | 78.3% voters enrolled in Telangana SIR; draft rolls to be published on August 17
After August 17, the date of publication of draft electoral rolls, the EROs will have to conduct hearings for verification of close to 94 lakh voters within two months’ time, which is next to impossible in practical terms.
Of the 94 lakh, more than 32 lakh are those who did not fill in their details in the first section pertaining to their entries in the rolls of 2002 SIR, or of their parents’ details from 2002 in the second section. They have all been categorised as unmapped voters, officials informed.
Also read | Over a fifth of the electors in Telangana might get deleted in SIR
The forms had three distinct sections: the first one for the electors’ details from 2002 SIR, the second for the relatives’ details for those who were minors in 2002, and the third one for the current details of the electors.
Many voters, not knowing the format, entered the current details as available on the Electoral Photo Identity Cards in the first section, leaving out the Polling Station numbers and Part Numbers blank.
Door-to-door visits by Booth Level Officers, which could have helped them understand the process, did not happen in many instances. BLOs in a large number of localities confined their roles to distributing the forms and collecting them back, sitting at a central location, instead of going from house to house.
Electoral officials, before the start of the Enumeration Phase, repeatedly asserted that the BLOs must visit each household at least thrice during the phase, once for distribution, a second time to explain how to fill in, and one last time to collect the forms back. However, the targets given were impossible for the BLOs, which became evident at the start of the distribution. Eventually, the officials made it the electors’ duty to return the filled in forms, extending the Enumeration phase twice to make that happen.
Of the total forms submitted at the end of the Enumeration Phase, a total of 61.4 lakh logical discrepancies/anomalies were reportedly discovered. When clubbed with the number of unmapped electors, nearly 94 lakh electors will have to be served notices to attend hearings before the EROs concerned, as per the directions from the Election Commission of India.
The notice period would begin on August 17, 2026, and continue up to October 15, 2026, leaving the EROs exactly 60 days to issue notices and conduct hearings. Even if the notices are served within the first fortnight, it would leave 45 days for hearings. With 119 EROs endowed with quasi-judicial powers set to adjudicate over 94 lakh cases in this short window, they would get less than a minute’s time to verify each elector even if they worked 24 hours a day. In a reasonable eight-hour workday with/without weekends and holidays, each elector would get just about 16-28 seconds!
Completion of the process with any reasonable time allocation, say 15 minutes per elector, will need seven to eight years’ time when done with utmost rigour.
EROs will also have to settle claims and objections simultaneously, apart from accepting fresh applications by electors deleted from the rolls.
With the number of anomalies/discrepancies uneven across constituencies, a few EROs will be more burdened than the rest, even with support from the Assistant EROs.

headline: No Partition if Modi had been there in 1947: UP CM Yogi Adityanath
full_text:
No Partition if Modi had been there in 1947: UP CM Yogi Adityanath
CM Yogi Adityanath blamed Congress for the partition and said India ‘paid the price for the Congress’s cowardice’.
Blaming the Congress for India’s Partition in 1947, chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday stated that if a leader like Narendra Modi had been present then, India would have remained undivided.
Addressing a gathering at Lok Bhavan here on the occasion of Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, he alleged that India is paying the price for the Congress’s ‘cowardice’ and described the Partition as one of the darkest chapters in human history.
“Driven by a lust for power, an eternal nation was pushed towards Partition and fragmented,” he said.
“Areas of Punjab and Bengal—home to large populations that were subsequently affected by the division—were handed over to Pakistan. During the Partition, millions were forced to abandon their homes and become refugees. It is essential to bring the agony of the massacres and displacement that occurred at that time to the attention of today’s generation,” he said.
Yogi accuses Cong, SP of spreading confusion on CAA
Referring to the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), the chief minister stated that the Opposition spread confusion across the country regarding the law’s provisions.
“There was no provision in the law to seize anyone’s land or property. Despite this, protests and attempts to incite violence occurred in various parts of the country in opposition to the law,” he said.
Also read: President Murmu on Indus Water Treaty suspension: ‘Decisive step in interest of nation, farmers'
“Political parties like Congress and the Samajwadi Party were responsible for pushing the anti-CAA protests. These are the real culprits responsible for the 1947 Partition and the riots that followed. If India had a PM like Modi at that time, it would have stayed undivided. If India had a PM like Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel at that time, nobody could have challenged India’s unity. The country paid the price for the Congress’s cowardice,” he added.
‘Looting and plundering’
The chief minister stated that in Pilibhit, the documents of thousands of families who had arrived from Bangladesh were rectified, and they were provided with land ownership papers. Similarly, in Lakhimpur Kheri, citizenship was granted to distressed Hindu families who had come from Bangladesh; approximately 16,000 people were granted citizenship.
The chief minister remarked that serious efforts should have been made to rehabilitate those displaced during the Partition and compensate them for their lost property, but previous governments failed to pay adequate attention to this matter.
He stated that it was Congress’s responsibility at the time to first grant citizenship and provide land leases to the displaced people.
“They should have provided land here equivalent to the property lost or confiscated there. Instead, Congress remained preoccupied with protecting and misappropriating ‘enemy property’. They were looting and plundering these assets to amass personal wealth,” he stated.
Also read: ‘Beginning of another’: How Hindustan Times reported freedom on August 15, 1947
He also said that this property should have been distributed among the Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, and Jains arriving from Pakistan. Congress members had gone to great lengths to protect the entire estate of the Nawab of Mahmudabad, he added.
The chief minister also targeted the Samajwadi Party, stating that it championed individuals accused of acting against the country’s independence and playing a role in Partition.
“A Samajwadi Party leader named a university after a person responsible for acting against the country’s independence and responsible for Partition. That same Samajwadi Party is now saying they will make him the home minister. They very well know they are not coming to power, however this also exposes their shameful mindset,” he said.
Recently, senior Samajwadi Party leader Shivpal Yadav commented that “if the SP is voted to power (in the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls), Azam Khan would be made the home minister”
Adityanath further stated that the tragedy of the Partition and other historical events serve as a means to understand the challenges of the present and the future.
“If anti-India forces attempt to create chaos in the society using social media and other platforms, it becomes the responsibility of citizens to present correct facts and raise public awareness,” he added.
He stated that a strong India will emerge only when the society moves forward with a unified identity.
Citing the establishment of the Khalsa Panth by Guru Gobind Singh and the egalitarian tradition of Sant Ramanand, a call was made to rise above caste distinctions and untouchability.
He further said, “A developed India by 2047 will only become a reality if Uttar Pradesh develops, and Uttar Pradesh will develop only when all regions of the state—including Lucknow—become self-reliant.”
CM leads silent march
Chief minister Yogi Adityanath led a silent march in Lucknow on Friday to mark Partition Horrors Remembrance Day. He began by paying floral tributes at the statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in Hazratganj. The silent march conveyed a message of national unity. During the approximately half-kilometer-long procession, Adityanath was seen holding a poster that read, “We will not let the country bow down; we will not let the country be divided again.”

headline: NHRC notice to states, UTs, FSSAI over concerns raised about sale, consumption of 'analogue paneer'
full_text:
NHRC notice to states, UTs, FSSAI over concerns raised about sale, consumption of 'analogue paneer'
New Delhi, The NHRC has issued notices to all states and UTs, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India in the wake of a complaint raising concerns over the manufacturing, sale and consumption of 'analogue paneer'.
The Commission said it considers it necessary for the FSSAI to clarify the nutritional composition and nutritional value of 'analogue paneer', including its protein, fat and other relevant nutritional parameters, and whether such information is adequately disclosed to consumers, reads a case proceedings dated August 13.
'Analogue paneer' refers to an imitation of traditional dairy paneer.
The National Human Rights Commission has also sought clarification as to why the manufacture, regulation and sale of such products are considered necessary, particularly when three states have reportedly already imposed restrictions or prohibitions on 'analogue paneer.'
Further, what nutritional or consumer benefit is being sought by allowing its manufacturing and the sale to continue, the human rights body asked.
The present matter has arisen from a representation and report dated August 11 submitted by the Advanced Study Institute of Asia , Centre for Health Equity, concerning the manufacture, sale, supply, use, labelling, testing and regulatory enforcement relating to dairy analogues, particularly products being sold, supplied or served as "analogue paneer" or as paneer.
The representation raises issues concerning consumer protection, food safety, transparency in nomenclature and labelling, consistency of enforcement across states and Union Territories, and the adequacy of existing mechanisms to enable consumers to "distinguish between milk-derived paneer and dairy analogues," reads the proceedings.
The Commission has also taken note of the accompanying report titled 'Analogue Paneer in India: A Food-Systems Threat to Health Equity', published by the Centre for Health Equity, Advanced Study Institute of Asia.
The briefing note records that FSSAI allegedly "recognises" dairy analogues as products in which non-milk constituents replace some or all milk constituents and states that such products are "not milk, milk products or composite milk products".
It further raises questions concerning the continued use of the term 'paneer' in the nomenclature of such products and the adequacy of existing disclosure requirements, the proceedings add.
The report further records that 'analogue paneer' may involve ingredients including vegetable oils or fats, starches, milk solids, plant proteins, stabilisers, emulsifiers and artificial flavours, and that the resulting product may have a nutritional profile different from conventional paneer.
The Commission is further of the view that, where a food product is permitted under the regulatory framework, the regulatory authorities must nevertheless ensure that its identity, composition and nature are adequately disclosed and that consumers are not misled into believing that a non-dairy analogue is conventional milk-derived paneer, reads the proceedings.

headline: The Bombay High Court on Friday (August 14, 2026) granted protection from arrest to Kamakhya Prasad Das, a former student of TISS, who was booked for raising slogans calling for the release of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam.
full_text:
The Bombay High Court on Friday (August 14, 2026) granted protection from arrest to Kamakhya Prasad Das, a former student of TISS, who was booked for raising slogans calling for the release of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam.
Justice Prafulla Khubalkar agreed to hear Mr. Das’s plea seeking anticipatory bail on August 31 and provided him protection from arrest until then. The court’s order came as a reprieve for the student who had been denied anticipatory bail by a lower court last week. Justice Khubalkar noted that the case required consideration and scheduled the matter for further hearing later this month, with the interim protection remaining in effect until the next hearing date.
The Mumbai Police lodged an FIR in October 2025 against Mr. Das and several other students for participating in an event to pay homage to GN Saibaba. During the event, the students read out Saibaba’s poems and raised slogans for the release of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, both of whom are facing trial under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
Additional Sessions Judge V.B. Bohra had denied anticipatory bail to Mr. Das and another student, Abhirup Paul (32), while granting anticipatory bail to five other students — Nikita Dsouza, Uttkarsh Khuntia, Yash Kaundilya, Avantika and Ishpreet Kaur. The judge observed that the Supreme Court had rejected bail applications of Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid, and as students, the accused were expected to respect the law of the land.
The students argued that GN Saibaba had been acquitted in the UAPA case against him and contended that no offence was made out merely by saying “Sharjeel ko rha karo, Umar ko rha karo” (Release Sharjeel, Release Umar).
The lower court judge, however, stated that while paying homage to Saibaba could not be termed illegal since he was acquitted, the accused students appeared to have gone beyond that. The judge observed that the act of the accused appeared to be not limited to paying him homage, as they allegedly raised slogans for releasing Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam from jail, who are facing trial for an offence under UAPA, which involves unlawful activities against the nation. The judge noted that the event was not a platform for raising such slogans, unlike a public agitation or procession, and emphasised that the accused, being students, were expected to respect the law of the land.
The case, titled Kamakhiya Prasad Das v/s State of Maharashtra, will now be heard by the Bombay High Court on August 31, with the interim protection from arrest remaining in force for Das until that date.
The lower court had earlier refused to grant bail to Abhirup Paul and Kamakhiya Prasad Das, who along with several other students were named in the FIR lodged in October 2025 by the Mumbai Police for participating in the event to pay homage to Saibaba and for reading out his poems and sloganeering to free Sharjeel and Umar. The High Court’s decision to grant interim protection marks a significant development in the case, as Mr. Das awaits the full hearing of his anticipatory bail application later this month.

headline: IPS Nupur Prasad, who led Sushant Singh Rajput CBI probe, to get President's Medal
full_text:
IPS Nupur Prasad, who led Sushant Singh Rajput CBI probe, to get President's Medal
Senior IPS officer Nupur Prasad has been selected for the President's Medal for Distinguished Service. The honour highlights her high-profile CBI tenure, including supervision of the Sushant Singh Rajput death probe.
Senior IPS officer Nupur Prasad, who supervised the CBI investigation into the death of actor Sushant Singh Rajput, has been selected for the prestigious President’s Medal for Distinguished Service this year.
Prasad, a 2007-batch AGMUT-cadre IPS officer, recently completed her tenure with the Central Bureau of Investigation and returned to the Delhi Police. She is currently serving as Joint Commissioner of Police in the Economic Offences Wing.
The award citation describes Prasad as an “accomplished officer” and a leader known for “versatility, integrity and institutional vision”. It highlights her work across the Delhi Police, CBI, West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh, including several high-profile investigations and major policing initiatives.
ROLE IN SUSHANT SINGH RAJPUT DEATH PROBE
Prasad’s role in the Sushant Singh Rajput investigation was among the most prominent assignments of her CBI tenure.
Rajput, 34, was found dead at his Bandra residence in Mumbai on June 14, 2020. The Mumbai Police initially registered an accidental death case and investigated the circumstances surrounding his death.
The case took a major turn after Rajput’s father, K K Singh, filed an FIR in Patna against actress Rhea Chakraborty and others, alleging abetment to suicide, financial wrongdoing and harassment.
Following the legal and political controversy surrounding the jurisdiction of the investigation, the CBI took over the case in August 2020.
The investigation continued for nearly five years and involved examination of witnesses, scrutiny of medical and forensic evidence and investigation of allegations of murder, abetment to suicide and other suspected wrongdoing.
The case generated intense public and media scrutiny, with several theories circulating on social media and television, including allegations of poisoning and strangulation.
In March 2025, the CBI filed closure reports before courts in Mumbai and Patna, stating that its investigation had found no evidence of foul play, abetment to suicide or criminal conspiracy in Rajput’s death.
DISTINGUISHED POLICING CAREER
The President’s Medal citation highlights Prasad’s work across several challenging assignments.
As the first DCP of Shahdara, she was tasked with establishing the district’s policing framework from the ground up. During her tenure, she led action against drug networks and gambling operations and worked to make Anand Vihar a “snatching-free zone”.
As DCP, North District, Prasad oversaw security arrangements for major events, including Delhi University elections and Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort.
She also spearheaded community-oriented initiatives, including women’s self-defence training, hygiene camps in collaboration with the Ladli Foundation, youth skill-development programmes and drug de-addiction initiatives with SPYM.
Her career also includes significant assignments outside Delhi. In West Bengal, she handled security arrangements during the 2011 Assembly elections and the Ganga Sagar Mela.
As Superintendent of Police in Arunachal Pradesh, she worked to restore inter-tribal peace and dismantle extortion networks.
CONTRIBUTIONS TO POLICING REFORMS
During her CBI tenure, Prasad supervised some of the agency’s significant cases, including the AgustaWestland investigation and the Sushant Singh Rajput death case.
She also contributed to the CBI Crime Manual 2020 and the agency’s Vision Document. She was associated with preparations for the Interpol General Assembly 2022 and the G20 Cyber Conference.
After returning to the Delhi Police, Prasad introduced the MyKase software for trial monitoring while serving in the Economic Offences Wing.
She also contributed to the Bureau of Police Research and Development’s National Police Mission, Micro Mission.
PRESIDENT’S MEDAL FOR DISTINGUISHED SERVICE
The President’s Medal for Distinguished Service is among the highest service honours conferred on police personnel.
Prasad’s selection recognises a career spanning investigation, law-and-order policing, community outreach, institutional reform and assignments in some of the country’s most challenging security environments.
Her supervision of the Sushant Singh Rajput investigation remains one of the most high-profile assignments of her CBI tenure, with the agency ultimately concluding that there was no evidence of foul play in the actor’s death.

A Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) event meant to commemorate the horrors of Partition turned into an unexpected display of the party’s internal fault lines in Gurugram on Friday, with Union Minister of State for Planning and MP Rao Inderjit Singh publicly objecting to the programme being projected as a “community-specific” event and questioning why local leaders had not been invited.
The State-level Vibhajan Vibhishika Smriti Diwas programme at Sector 29 brought together BJP national president Nitin Nabin, Union Minister Manohar Lal and Haryana BJP president Archana Gupta. But the spotlight soon shifted from Partition remembrance to the politics within the Haryana BJP.
Taking the microphone, Mr. Singh made it clear that he was unhappy with the way the event had been organised. “People from various parts have come to this event. I think local people have not been invited today. I object to this,” he said, before thanking Ms. Gupta for inviting Mr. Nabin and turning the programme into a party event rather than allowing it to remain, in his words, a programme of a “specific community”.
Draws comparisons
Mr. Singh then directly addressed Mr. Nabin, welcoming him, while pointedly questioning whether he himself would have been invited had the national president not attended. The Gurugram MP drew comparisons with other BJP leaders. If such a programme were held in Panipat, he asked, would Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Bhatia not be invited? And if it were held in Karnal, would local MP Manohar Lal not be invited?
He also took a swipe at Mr. Lal, recalling that Haryana had been the first State to have a Punjabi Chief Minister and stressing that Mr. Lal had become the Chief Minister with the support of people from all communities.
Invoking Gurugram’s political history, Mr. Singh recalled that Dharambir Gaba, the city’s first Punjabi MLA, had won four times – not merely on Punjabi votes, but with support across communities.
“Most of those unsettled from Pakistan came to Haryana, and the people of Haryana welcomed them,” Mr. Singh said, underlining that Partition’s legacy belonged to the people of the entire State rather than any one community.
However, Mr. Singh’s address was stopped midway.
Sources in Mr. Singh’s office said the Minister had not received a formal invitation from the organisers, the Vibhajan Vibhishika Smriti Nyas. According to the sources, when the Chief Minister’s Office contacted Mr. Singh on Thursday afternoon to confirm his participation, his staff pointed out that no formal invitation had been received. The issue reportedly prompted administrative intervention. Ms. Gupta subsequently called Mr. Singh, informed him about Mr. Nabin’s presence and invited him to the programme.
An invitation letter issued by the organisers and shared by Mr. Singh’s office did not list the local MP’s name. An invitation issued by the local administration, however, did mention him as a guest of honour.

headline: Observing that “relabelling expired food products and pushing them back into the stream of commerce is not a mere violation of food safety norms but a calculated assault on public health,” the High Court of Karnataka on Friday refused to quash a crim...
full_text:
Observing that “relabelling expired food products and pushing them back into the stream of commerce is not a mere violation of food safety norms but a calculated assault on public health,” the High Court of Karnataka on Friday refused to quash a criminal case against a firm, licensed to collect and recycle expired food products, after allegations that it resold such products by replacing or altering their expiry date labels.
“To erase an expiry date, affix a fresh label, and place such a product back on the shelf is, therefore, to dress decay in the garb of freshness and deception in the attire of trade. The unsuspecting consumer purchases it believing it to be safe, while what is actually sold is an undisclosed and potentially grave risk to health,” the court observed.
Justice M. Nagaprasanna passed the order while dismissing a petition filed by Earth Recycler Pvt. Ltd, and its representatives, Aamir Ahmed Chuna, Mohammed Dawood S., and Abdul Kadhir Kalathoor.
The petitioner had questioned the legality of the criminal case while contending that the authorities had failed to adhere to the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, including failing to collect samples of the food items before initiating the proceedings under the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006. They had claimed that the FSS Act is a complete code, being a special law, and hence invoking provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) against them was not proper.
Refusing to accept their contentions, the court said samples of food items could have been taken had the petitioners been ordinary retailers or distributors storing food products which, during the course of storage, were alleged to have become unsafe or expired.
Sampling cannot become the answer to the question in this case, as the petitioners are entitled to possess only expired food and the allegation against them is not for storing expired food items but for re-labelling and reselling expired food items, for which Sections 316(2) and 318(4) of BNS concerning cheating and public mischief are attracted, the court said.
The allegations against the petitioners cannot be viewed through the narrow prism of a mere regulatory infraction, as it strikes at the very heart of consumer confidence and, more importantly, at public health, the court pointed out.
“Food is not an ordinary article of commerce. What reaches the market ultimately reaches the human body. A deceptive label upon an expired food product, therefore, is not merely ink upon a package; it is, if the allegation be true, a deception capable of carrying consequences to the health and safety of an unsuspecting citizen,” the court said while emphasising the need for a proper investigation, involving competent authorities under the FSS Act too, against the petitioners.
